This cross-sectional study investigates the relationship between SOD1, SOD2, and SOD3 gene polymorphisms and post-COVID-19 symptoms in 12 long COVID patients, measuring SOD enzyme activity and symptom prevalence. The study identifies systemic and cardiovascular symptoms as most common in long COVID and explores genetic variation as a potential biomarker for disease detection.

This study investigates the relationship between cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation and immune dysregulation in post-COVID syndrome patients by measuring neutrophil phagocytic activity and complement system function. The research aims to identify specific immunological impairments associated with CMV reactivation to inform personalized immunomodulatory treatment approaches.

A structured tele-based pulmonary rehabilitation program was administered to 53 post-COVID-19 patients via WhatsApp or Zoom, including breathing exercises, aerobic/strength training, and yoga. The program showed significant improvements in fatigue, functional status, and depression/anxiety/stress measures.

A pre-experimental case series evaluating pursed lip breathing exercise with semi-Fowler positioning as a treatment for dyspnea in 11 post-COVID-19 patients. The intervention significantly reduced dyspnea severity (mean Modified Borg Scale from 4.36 to 2.18, p=0.003).

This cross-sectional study examines risk factors for depression in people who recovered from moderate to severe COVID-19, with a focus on emotional intelligence as a protective factor. The research used questionnaires and depression inventories across different socioeconomic groups but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

In vitro and in vivo study investigating how Elovanoid-N34 and Resolvin D6-isomer counteract astrocyte activation and neuroinflammation induced by Omicron BA.5 secretome. The work is mechanistic research without clinical trial data or patient outcomes, presenting pre-clinical evidence for potential long COVID brain sequelae interventions.

This prospective study evaluated cardiovascular training during post-acute rehabilitation in 84 patients recovering from moderate COVID-19 pneumonia. While it shows improved functional capacity from training, it focuses on acute post-infection recovery rather than long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks-to-months after infection).

This paper investigates pathogenic mechanisms of SARS-CoV-2 on thyroid pathology through animal model experiments and retrospective clinical analysis of surgical thyroid pathology cases from 2019-2023. It demonstrates increased incidence of autoimmune thyroiditis, nodular formations, and papillary cancer post-COVID but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This study evaluates the efficacy of homeopathic medicines in treating post-COVID syndrome, with emphasis on dyspnea, fatigue, and hair loss in 100 patients. Results showed 77% of patients improved with treatment, with statistical significance (p<0.05) demonstrated by paired t-test analysis.

This study evaluates the effectiveness of inspiratory muscle training on exercise tolerance and quality of life in 41 post-COVID-19 COPD patients aged 45-60 years. Results show statistically significant improvements in 6-minute walk test and quality of life (SGRQ-C) after 4 weeks of training (p<0.001).

A probabilistic modeling study characterizing longitudinal antibody and cytokine responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection across demographic groups. The analysis identifies elevated cytokine responses in those with post-acute pulmonary symptoms but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This paper develops and applies a mathematical compartmental model to estimate the incidence and prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) across population subgroups and counties in Washington State from March 2020 through October 2023. The study found that 6.4% of Washington State adults were experiencing PCC as of October 2023, with substantial disparities across age, race/ethnicity, sex, and geography.

This study investigated microRNA expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from women with Long COVID using sequencing. The researchers identified 37 altered miRNAs, with 28 associated with inflammation and three proposed as potential biomarkers (hsa-miR-1307-3p, hsa-miR-26a-5p, miR-186-5p).

This infodemiology study analyzes Google search trends for long-COVID in the US from 2020-2023 to identify which COVID-19 variants are associated with long-COVID. The analysis suggests Delta or original wild variants had the highest tendency to cause long-COVID symptoms, but this is an observational survey study without any intervention or treatment evaluation.

This study uses a humanized mouse model to investigate long-term cardiovascular effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection, focusing on cardiac and vascular tissue remodeling. The abstract describes a planned study without presenting any results, making it a protocol-only paper.

This cross-sectional study examined post-COVID respiratory changes in 175 children who had persistent symptoms 3+ months after acute infection, using X-ray imaging at a children's hospital in Tbilisi. The study found that radiological changes do not always correlate with disease severity and may persist into the post-COVID period, though no specific treatment or intervention was tested.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed 414 hospitalized COVID-19 patients to identify distinct phenotypic clusters based on clinical symptoms and SARS-CoV-2 variants, examining their prognostic value for severity, mortality, and long COVID occurrence. The study found four clusters with different clinical profiles and prognostic outcomes, with cluster 3 patients showing lower prevalence of long COVID but higher mortality and nursing home admission rates.

This paper describes an automated microscopic technique to measure fibrinaloid microclots and demonstrates that recombinant nattokinase can degrade these clots in vitro. The work provides evidence that nattokinase may have therapeutic potential for long COVID patients and related conditions involving fibrinaloid microclots.

This study examined the long-term effects of mild to moderate COVID-19 on spermological parameters in 14 unvaccinated men, comparing sperm quality before and 3 months after infection. The findings showed no clinically significant changes in sperm count, motility, or morphology following COVID-19.

This paper uses combinatorial genetic analysis to identify 22,411 disease signatures associated with ME in the DecodeME cohort and finds substantial overlap (76/180 genes) with long COVID genetic risk factors. It is a genetic/mechanistic study identifying shared biological pathways and drug repurposing opportunities, not a treatment trial or intervention study.

This paper develops a CNN-based method (VGG16 with image enhancement filters) to automatically classify pulmonary fibrosis from CT images in long COVID patients, achieving 97% accuracy. While addressing a long COVID complication, it is a diagnostic/classification study rather than a treatment intervention trial, and is excluded from the intervention trials pipeline.

This study compares fibrinaloid microclot complexes and post-translational modifications in plasma samples from pre-COVID POTS, Long COVID, and Long COVID-POTS patients versus healthy controls using imaging flowcytometry and proteomics. The findings identify disease-specific PTM patterns across coagulation, immune, and metabolic pathways but do not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This paper combines a retrospective TriNetX cohort analysis with mechanistic mouse studies to investigate whether SARS-CoV-2 spike protein-induced lung injury and elevated thymidine phosphorylase (TYMP) promote lung tumorigenesis in COVID-19 survivors. The study demonstrates increased lung cancer risk post-COVID and identifies TYMP as a potential therapeutic target, but does not test or evaluate a specific intervention in long COVID patients.

This study derived and validated a clinical prediction rule to identify emergency department patients at high risk of developing long COVID within three months of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection using data from 6,070 Canadian patients. Although nine risk factors (female sex, respiratory symptoms, comorbidities) and one protective factor (South Asian race) were identified, the resulting prediction rule had insufficient accuracy (AUC 0.626) to be clinically useful for ED decision-making.

This cross-sectional neuroimaging study compares resting-state fMRI brain dynamics between 20 long COVID patients and 20 matched controls using dynamic functional connectivity analysis. While it identifies significant disruptions in brain network organization and associations with cognitive performance and inflammatory markers, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study uses normative brain imaging (cortical thickness, surface area, subcortical volumes) to map structural deviations in 20 post-COVID patients with persistent fatigue compared to 20 healthy controls. While it provides mechanistic insights into neural circuit disruptions and identifies potential therapeutic targets (serotonergic, glutamatergic pathways), it is a purely observational neuroimaging study with no intervention or treatment evaluation.

This study compares IgG subclass and IgE antibody responses to 14 SARS-CoV-2 spike variants between long COVID patients (n=15) and controls (n=15). The findings identify distinct antibody profiles in long COVID, including IgG3 and IgE elevations suggesting chronic antigen exposure, but no treatment intervention is tested or evaluated.

This study investigates the mechanistic basis of long COVID neurological symptoms by examining SARS-CoV-2-induced damage to the hypothalamic orexin system in mouse models. The researchers demonstrate that orexin dysfunction underlies persistent cortical neuronal injury and that augmenting orexin signaling restores neuronal markers both in vitro and in vivo, identifying orexinergic circuit disruption as a potential therapeutic target.

This paper describes usability testing of public-facing knowledge mobilization resources developed to support the Canadian Guidelines for Post COVID-19 Condition. It evaluates the clarity and accessibility of guideline-related materials rather than testing a treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

A quasi-experimental study evaluating Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation techniques for pain management in post-COVID geriatric patients with comorbidities. The intervention group showed significant pain reduction (7.2±1.5 to 4.5±1.2) compared to minimal change in controls (7.0±1.4 to 6.8±1.3), demonstrating efficacy of the non-pharmacological approach (p<0.05).

This preclinical study uses a SARS-CoV-2 mouse model to investigate neuroinflammatory mechanisms underlying post-COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms, demonstrating viral neuroinvasion, microglial activation, and anxiety/depression-like behaviors. While directly relevant to PASC pathophysiology, this is a basic science mechanistic study in animals with no human intervention or treatment evaluation.

This mechanistic study investigates whether anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike protein monoclonal antibodies possess ACE2-like enzymatic activity that could contribute to long COVID pathogenesis. The authors identify 4 human mAbs with ACE2-like catalytic activity and characterize their kinetic properties, but the study does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

This study investigates immune dysregulation mechanisms in Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) through analysis of monocyte dysfunction, persistent viral RNA, and autoantibodies. While the abstract mentions post-COVID syndromes, the focus is on acute MIS-C pathophysiology rather than long COVID treatment or intervention trials.

Describes a process-oriented digiphysical prototype designed to support cognitive rehabilitation in long COVID patients by integrating digital and physical interventions. Reports initial evaluation findings with rehabilitation professionals and presents five reusable solution patterns for implementing digiphysical rehabilitation services.

This cross-sectional study evaluates liver function markers and cardiac isoenzymes in 150 COVID-19 recovered patients to assess long-term organ damage. Elevated liver enzymes (GPT/GOT) and cardiac isoenzymes (LDH1/LDH2) were found in 12-20% of patients, suggesting persistent dysfunction even after symptom resolution.

A Mendelian randomization study using GWAS data to assess causal associations between COVID-19 genetic susceptibility and post-COVID-19 syndrome symptoms. The analysis identifies potential causal links between COVID-19 and specific PCS symptoms like myalgia, erectile dysfunction, and heart arrhythmia, with social factors as mediators.

This is a basic neuroscience dissertation using mouse models to investigate sex differences in neuroimmune modulation of learning and memory, with long COVID mentioned only as a motivation/context. It does not study long COVID patients or test treatments for long COVID—it is a preclinical mechanistic study in animals.

This study examines neuropathophysiological consequences of SARS-CoV-2 infection by comparing transcriptional and cellular signatures in brain regions of SARS-CoV-2-infected subjects, AD patients, and controls. The findings reveal similar neuroinflammation and blood-brain barrier alterations in SARS-CoV-2 and AD, with potential implications for understanding neuro-PASC and therapeutic approaches.

This study assessed immune activation markers (T-cell activation, cytokines) at 3-12 months post-infection in 63 patients with varying COVID-19 severity and investigated associations with long COVID symptoms. While it confirms that severe disease correlates with persistent immune activation and long COVID symptoms, it is an observational study measuring associations, not testing any treatment or intervention.

This study validates the A-B Neuropsychological Assessment Schedule (ABNAS) as a screening tool for long COVID by testing its sensitivity and specificity in 235 participants (LC patients and controls). The ABNAS total score and subscales (fatigue, mental slowing) demonstrated good sensitivity and specificity for identifying long COVID, but this is a diagnostic validation study, not a treatment trial.

This study validates the sit-to-stand test as a remote assessment tool for evaluating functional capacity in post-COVID-19 patients, comparing in-person, synchronous, and asynchronous tele-assessment methods. While it demonstrates good reliability for remote assessment, it is a methodological validation study rather than a treatment intervention trial.

This cross-sectional study compares the prevalence of ME/CFS in long COVID patients versus controls, finding that while LC patients report significantly higher rates of PEM and other ME/CFS-like symptoms, only 18.8% meet formal ME/CFS diagnostic criteria. The study does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This paper evaluates the Breathing Pattern Assessment Tool (BPAT) for diagnosing breathing pattern disorders in post-COVID patients attending a respiratory clinic. BPAT showed high sensitivity (89.5%) and moderate specificity (78.3%) but this is a diagnostic validation study, not a treatment intervention trial.

A prospective cross-sectional study using multidetector CT scanning and 3D volumetric assessment to evaluate post-COVID-19 pulmonary complications in 30 patients >3 months post-infection. The study demonstrates CT's utility in detecting volume loss and fibrosis but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study compares biomarker levels (GIP-10, Gal-3, HIF-1) in vaccinated vs non-vaccinated COVID-19 patients with pulmonary fibrosis to assess vaccine effects on inflammation. While it examines post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis, it focuses on vaccine status as a natural grouping rather than testing a treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

This cross-sectional study compares HDL lipoprotein functions and PON1 activity between post-COVID-19 syndrome patients, asymptomatic post-COVID individuals, and healthy controls. The study found increased PON1 antioxidant activity in asymptomatic patients and correlations between HDL components and inflammatory markers, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

A QC/QI project analyzing hospital readmission patterns in COVID-19 patients, identifying respiratory failure and COVID-19 sequelae as primary readmission diagnoses. The study examines risk factors and outcomes in readmitted patients but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study uses Golden Syrian hamsters as an animal model to characterize cardiovascular complications associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection and post-COVID sequelae. The research documents pathological changes and identifies metabolic markers but does not test any therapeutic intervention in patients.

Prospective observational cohort study of 478 COVID-19 hospitalization survivors assessed at 4 months post-discharge, documenting prevalence of persistent symptoms including fatigue (31%), cognitive impairment (21%), and dyspnea (16%), along with imaging abnormalities and psychological sequelae. This is a descriptive epidemiological study without any treatment intervention or control comparison group.

This is an in vitro experimental study examining how the SARS-CoV-2 spike S1 protein affects hemichannel activity in HeLa cells transfected with connexin-43. The authors propose that persistent hemichannel opening could contribute to long COVID pathology and might represent a therapeutic target, but the work is basic laboratory research without any human subjects or treatment intervention.

This is an editorial commentary on the COMEBAC study that describes long COVID prevalence and symptoms in hospital survivors at 4-month follow-up. It discusses general observations about long COVID sequelae but is not itself a primary research study with original data collection.

This retrospective cohort study examines whether mRNA vaccination (BNT162b2) reduces the risk of long COVID in health care workers who experienced COVID-19 infection. The study compares long COVID incidence between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups but does not constitute a treatment trial, as vaccination is evaluated for its preventive effect rather than as a therapeutic intervention for existing long COVID.

Multicenter longitudinal observational cohort study characterizing prolonged symptoms in 5,367 children and adolescents with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Identified symptom clusters and developed age-specific research indices for PASC but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cohort study compares long-term cardiovascular outcomes over 18 months in patients hospitalized for myocarditis attributed to COVID-19 mRNA vaccination, SARS-CoV-2 infection, or conventional causes. While it studies post-COVID myocarditis, it is not focused on long COVID syndrome but rather on a specific cardiac complication and does not evaluate a treatment intervention.

This prospective observational cohort study from the RECOVER Consortium develops a standardized definition of PASC (postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection) based on self-reported symptoms in 9,764 participants across 85 sites. The study characterizes symptom frequencies and identifies 37 symptoms with significantly higher odds in infected vs uninfected individuals, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study examining the association between pre-infection healthy lifestyle factors and risk of post-COVID-19 condition in 32,249 women from the Nurses' Health Study II. Found that healthy lifestyle (5-6 factors) was associated with 49% lower risk of PCC, with BMI and sleep independently protective.

Case-control study comparing 1-year adverse health outcomes between 13,435 adults with post-COVID-19 condition and 26,870 matched controls without COVID-19 using commercial insurance claims data. Post-COVID cohort showed significantly elevated risks for cardiac arrhythmias (RR 2.35), pulmonary embolism (RR 3.64), stroke, heart failure, COPD, and mortality (2.8% vs 1.2%), indicating substantial long-term cardiovascular and pulmonary complications.

Cohort study examining whether nirmatrelvir treatment during acute COVID-19 reduces the risk of developing post-COVID condition using VA healthcare databases. Nirmatrelvir was associated with a 26% reduction in post-COVID risk and reduced risk across 10 of 13 post-acute sequelae components.

This paper presents an updated 2024 Long COVID research index from the RECOVER-Adult prospective observational cohort study, refining symptom classification criteria for identifying and characterizing long COVID cases. It reports on 13,647 participants and identifies 5 long COVID symptom subtypes, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention and therefore is not eligible for the intervention trials meta-analysis.

This prospective observational cohort study examined cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) findings in 100 patients recently recovered from COVID-19 (median 71 days post-diagnosis), comparing them to healthy and risk factor-matched controls. While the study demonstrates significant cardiac involvement and myocardial inflammation in COVID-19 recovery, it is a descriptive observational study with no treatment intervention or therapeutic evaluation.

This observational cohort study examines whether nirmatrelvir and molnupiravir reduce the risk of post-COVID-19 condition symptoms in Medicare enrollees. The study compares symptom occurrence between older patients who received these antivirals during acute infection and those who did not.

Prospective cohort study of 238 patients hospitalized for severe COVID-19, followed 4 months after discharge to assess long-term sequelae. Found respiratory impairment (51.6% with reduced Dlco), functional impairment (53.8%), and psychological symptoms (17.2%), but no intervention or treatment was evaluated.

This prospective cohort study examines the duration and variation of recovery from COVID-19 by comparing physiological and behavioral changes between COVID-19–positive and COVID-19–negative individuals. The study characterizes the natural course of post-infection recovery without testing any specific intervention.

This cross-sectional study of 3,972 SARS-CoV-2-infected participants from French population cohorts describes the temporal dynamics and resolution of persistent symptoms lasting ≥2 months after acute infection. The study identifies demographic and clinical factors associated with slower symptom resolution but does not test any treatment or intervention.

This cross-sectional study examines self-reported memory problems 8 months after COVID-19 infection in a cohort of infected individuals. While the paper addresses long COVID sequelae, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline.

Retrospective cohort study examining the use of the ICD-10-CM U09.9 post-COVID-19 diagnosis code in US clinical practice from October 2021 to January 2022, analyzing 12,622 patients with concurrent diagnoses. The study documents diagnostic coding patterns and concurrent conditions by age group but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This Swedish cohort study examines incidence rates of post-COVID-19 condition in children across two regions and compares rates by demographic and clinical characteristics. The study uses health data to describe the occurrence and characteristics of long COVID in the pediatric population.

This cross-sectional study investigates microcirculatory disturbances in post-COVID syndrome patients presenting with trophic ulcers of the oral mucosa, using non-invasive capillary blood flow assessment. The research examines one of the potential mechanisms underlying oral mucosal lesions in long COVID patients.

Prospective cohort study comparing patient-reported physical, mental, and social well-being outcomes 3 months post-infection between adults with positive vs negative SARS-CoV-2 test results. While the study examines long COVID sequelae, it is observational without intervention assignment and therefore does not qualify as a treatment trial.

This prospective cohort study of 1,832 US military personnel followed for 6-12 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection to identify risk factors for persistent post-COVID symptoms lasting ≥28 days. Key findings showed that unvaccinated status, moderate/severe acute illness, hospitalization, and higher comorbidity burden were associated with prolonged symptoms, while post-infection vaccination reduced the risk of symptoms at 6 months by 41%.

Multicenter prospective cohort study following 5,147 Canadian children tested for SARS-CoV-2 infection in pediatric emergency departments, with follow-up at 6 and 12 months. Found low prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition (0.67% at 12 months among infected children) with no significant difference in quality of life compared to uninfected controls.

This retrospective cohort study examines rates and factors associated with documented long COVID care in the Veterans Affairs health system among 198,601 SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals. The study identifies documentation patterns and demographic/clinical risk factors but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study examines the association between multidimensional sleep health prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection and the risk of developing post-COVID-19 condition (long COVID) in 1,979 women from the Nurses' Health Study II. The findings indicate that healthy sleep dimensions, particularly no daytime dysfunction and good sleep quality, are protective against PCC development.

This retrospective cohort study examines ICD-10 code U09.9 documentation rates and clinical characteristics among 388,980 VA patients with post-COVID-19 condition. It identifies risk factors for U09.9 documentation and shows that vaccination is protective, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective population-based cohort study examined the incidence and risk of autoimmune and autoinflammatory connective tissue disorders in 354,527 COVID-19 patients versus 6.1 million controls in Korea. The study found significantly elevated risks for several autoimmune conditions (alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, vasculitis, Crohn disease, sarcoidosis) associated with COVID-19, with increased risks linked to COVID-19 severity, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Cross-sectional survey study of 15,308 test-confirmed COVID-19 survivors examining the association between post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) and employment status. Found that PCC was associated with higher unemployment rates and lower full-time employment likelihood, particularly among those with cognitive symptoms, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining perceived cognitive deficits in early SARS-CoV-2 infection (first 4 weeks) and their association with post-COVID-19 condition development. Found that 36% of patients reported cognitive deficits at 30 days, and those with deficits were significantly more likely to develop long COVID symptoms (42.8% vs 21.4%), suggesting an early neuropsychiatric component to long COVID risk.

This retrospective cohort study compares outpatient health care utilization between 202,803 veterans with COVID-19 infection and matched uninfected controls over a 1-year follow-up period. The study found sustained increases in outpatient visits through 12 months post-infection, with the greatest impacts in older and unvaccinated veterans, but does not test any specific treatment intervention.

This cohort study examined the prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) 6 months after acute infection in 382 SARS-CoV-2-positive and 85 negative-control nonhospitalized adolescents and young adults in Norway. The study found no significant difference in PCC prevalence between infected (48.5%) and control groups (47.1%), with symptom severity at baseline and psychosocial factors (low physical activity, loneliness) identified as main risk factors rather than viral infection itself.

This retrospective cohort study examined the 300-day risk of new autoimmune diagnoses in over 1.7 million adults infected with Delta or Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variants compared to uninfected controls in Singapore. The study found no significantly elevated risk of autoimmune sequelae overall, with modest increases only in hospitalized Omicron cases for inflammatory bowel disease and bullous skin disorders, and booster vaccination appeared protective.

Prospective cohort study comparing cognitive, psychiatric, and neurological outcomes in COVID-19 hospitalized patients versus hospitalized controls and healthy individuals over 18 months. Found that post-COVID brain health was impaired compared to healthy controls but not significantly more than other severe illnesses, suggesting hospitalization severity rather than COVID-19 specificity.

This retrospective cohort study compared self-reported everyday functioning 18 months after COVID-19 infection between 186 veterans with documented COVID-19 and 186 matched controls without COVID-19. The study found no significant associations between COVID-19 infection and fatigue, pain, activities of daily living limitations, mobility, employment, or quality of life.

This prospective cohort study tracked 4,708 adults with self-reported SARS-CoV-2 infection across 14 NIH-funded cohorts to determine time to recovery and identify factors associated with recovery by 90 days. The study found that 22.5% did not recover within 90 days, with recovery less likely in women and those with preexisting cardiovascular disease, and more likely in vaccinated individuals or those infected during the Omicron wave.

Retrospective cohort study of 172,136 children and young adults examining the association between BMI status and risk of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC). Found that elevated BMI was associated with significantly increased PASC risk in a dose-dependent manner, but this is an observational study documenting natural disease progression, not testing a treatment intervention.

This cohort study compares self-reported fatigue and postexertional malaise in 50,115 Danish residents (25,249 test-positive, 24,866 test-negative) over 2-18 months post-SARS-CoV-2 testing. While it documents long COVID fatigue outcomes, it is an observational cohort without intervention assignment—participants were not given a treatment, and the study passively followed natural infection exposure rather than testing a therapeutic intervention.

Prospective cohort study from the NIH RECOVER-Adult cohort examining sex differences in long COVID risk among 12,276 participants with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Finds female sex associated with 31-44% higher risk of developing long COVID compared to males, with effects varying by age, pregnancy, and menopausal status.

This retrospective cohort study of 1.6 million pediatric patients compares GI tract symptoms and disorders in those with and without documented SARS-CoV-2 infection during the postacute and chronic phases. The study found increased risk of GI symptoms in COVID-19-positive children but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study used linked Swedish healthcare data to compare kidney function decline after COVID-19 versus pneumonia in 134,565 individuals, finding that COVID-19 was associated with greater accelerated annual eGFR decline (3.4% vs 2.3%), particularly among hospitalized patients (5.4%). The findings suggest that COVID-19 survivors should receive closer monitoring of kidney function to detect and manage chronic kidney disease complications early.

This prospective multisite longitudinal cohort study compared work impairment and financial outcomes among 3,663 adults with current, resolved, or no long COVID up to 3 years post-infection. While participants with current LC experienced significantly worse work impairment, missed work, and financial distress compared to those without LC, the study does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This case-control study compared cardiac function in 37 severe COVID-19 survivors (10 months post-discharge) with 22 healthy controls using advanced cardiac imaging (CMR). Patients with COVID-19 showed reduced stress perfusion indicating coronary microvascular dysfunction and impaired left ventricular function, with no clear distinction by cardiovascular risk factors or cardiac symptoms.

Case-control study examining the association between prior COVID-19 mRNA vaccination and odds of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) in children aged 5-17 years. Found that vaccination was associated with 57-73% reduced likelihood of developing PCC symptoms compared to unvaccinated children.

Prospective multicenter cohort study (INSPIRE) assessing long COVID prevalence using 5 published definitions from literature in 4,575 participants followed for up to 6 months. Finds that published definitions yield widely variable prevalence estimates (30.8-42% at 3 months, 14.2-21.9% at 6 months) with low-to-moderate sensitivity, highlighting need for standardized definition.

This retrospective cohort study of 1.9 million pediatric patients investigated whether SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with long-term kidney complications, including new-onset chronic kidney disease and composite kidney events. The study found that COVID-19 was associated with higher risk of adverse postacute kidney outcomes, particularly among those with preexisting kidney disease or acute kidney injury.

Longitudinal EHR cohort study examining the association between serious mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder) and PASC risk in 1.6M COVID-19 patients. Patients with SMI had increased adjusted odds of developing PASC (OR 1.10), with higher risk associated with older age, non-Hispanic Black/Hispanic race, higher comorbidity burden, and COVID-19 hospitalization.

This cohort study examines whether COVID-19 pandemic exposures are associated with cognitive decline in middle-aged women from the Nurses' Health Study II. While it includes a small subset with post-COVID conditions (n=62), it is an observational study with no intervention tested, making it ineligible for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

This prospective cohort study from the RECOVER-Adult initiative characterizes olfactory dysfunction in 3,525 long COVID patients using formal smell testing (UPSIT) at a mean of 671 days post-infection. While it documents high rates of hyposmia (79.8% among those with self-reported change/loss) and associations with cognitive problems, it is an observational study with no treatment intervention and therefore ineligible for the intervention trials meta-analysis.

This cohort study assesses the parent-reported incidence and resolution of post-COVID-19 symptoms among children aged 8 to 13 years. It describes the natural history and symptom trajectories in pediatric long COVID without testing any intervention.

This paper examines one-year outcomes in children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C) following acute COVID-19 infection. MIS-C is an acute post-infection complication occurring weeks after initial infection, distinct from long COVID's chronic ongoing symptoms; this study focuses on acute critical care outcomes rather than long-term persistent illness management or treatment interventions.

This multisite longitudinal cohort study characterized long COVID symptoms in early childhood (infants/toddlers 0-2 years and preschool-aged children 3-5 years) by comparing infected and uninfected children. The study derived age-specific symptom indices to identify probable LC cases, finding 14% of infected infants/toddlers and 15% of infected preschool-aged children had probable LC based on distinct symptom patterns.

Retrospective cohort study using QResearch and linked health records to quantify neuropsychiatric risks after severe COVID-19 hospitalization compared to other severe acute respiratory infections. Found elevated risks of anxiety, dementia, depression, and neuropsychiatric medication prescriptions in COVID-19 survivors, similar to SARI survivors.

This prospective cohort study examines whether pre-infection psychological distress (depression, anxiety, worry, stress, loneliness) is associated with increased risk of developing long COVID. The study found that participants with high psychological distress prior to infection had 32-46% increased risk of post-COVID conditions, with those experiencing multiple types of distress having nearly 50% increased risk.

This Danish nationwide cohort study examined the risk of new-onset mental disorders following SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to negative test results and non-COVID hospitalizations. While the paper studies psychiatric sequelae post-infection, it does not focus on long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks-months post-infection) and does not test any treatment intervention.

A prospective cross-sectional study characterizing neurologic manifestations in 100 non-hospitalized long COVID patients (50 confirmed SARS-CoV-2+ and 50 negative controls) presenting to a Neuro-COVID clinic. Findings show prevalent brain fog (81%), headache (68%), and cognitive deficits in attention and working memory, with SARS-CoV-2+ patients showing significantly higher rates of anosmia.

This retrospective cohort study examines the association between COVID-19 diagnosis and subsequent mental illness across vaccinated and unvaccinated populations in England. While it documents elevated incidence of depression and other mental illnesses following COVID-19, it is an observational epidemiological study that does not test any intervention or treatment for long COVID.

This study examined diaphragm dysfunction in 21 severe post-COVID-19 survivors using neuromuscular ultrasound, finding sonographic abnormalities in 76% and reduced diaphragm contractility compared to controls. The work is a descriptive cross-sectional study of post-COVID sequelae without any intervention or treatment evaluation, focusing on characterizing a respiratory complication rather than testing a therapeutic approach.

Retrospective cohort study examining clinical features and burden of postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) in children using electronic health records from 9 US children's hospitals. Study found low overall burden of pediatric PASC with myocarditis as the most common diagnosed condition, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This case-control study compares 22 adults with cognitive long COVID symptoms to 10 controls without symptoms following mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, evaluating cognitive risk factors and cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities. The study found that cognitive long COVID associates with higher pre-existing cognitive risk factors and abnormal CSF findings, suggesting immunologic mechanisms may contribute to cognitive long COVID pathogenesis.

Longitudinal study of neurologic long COVID symptoms in 56 participants with follow-up assessments at baseline and 6 months post-acute infection. Found fatigue and headache most common early, with memory impairment and concentration problems predominant at 6 months; one-third achieved complete symptom resolution by 6 months.

This cross-sectional study examined structural brain changes in post-COVID patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction using MRI imaging (T1-weighted, DTI) approximately 10 months after COVID-19 infection. Patients with olfactory dysfunction showed reduced gray matter volume in olfactory-related brain regions and increased white matter diffusivity compared to those with normal olfaction, but this is observational research without treatment intervention.

Follow-up study of 52 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients (~14.8 months post-infection) assessing evolution of neurologic symptoms, recovery perception, and quality of life compared to a negative control group. No intervention was administered; this is a natural history/observational follow-up study with no treatment evaluation.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes 1,009 COVID-19 patients admitted to Japanese hospitals to identify risk factors for brain fog as a long COVID manifestation and assess its impact on labor productivity. The study is a secondary analysis of existing hospitalization data rather than an intervention trial, so it does not meet inclusion criteria for the clinical trials meta-analysis.

Retrospective cross-sectional study characterizing long COVID symptoms and neurocognitive outcomes in 240 patients evaluated at a specialized neuro-COVID clinic. Study found high prevalence of cognitive complaints (94%) but only 30% had abnormal cognitive test scores, with 62% reporting self-reported improvement within 1 year.

Observational cohort study of 89 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 6 months to identify risk factors associated with persistent neurocognitive symptoms (neuro-PASC). Found 60% developed persistent neurocognitive symptoms, with socioeconomic status, pre-COVID anxiety, female sex, and Hispanic ethnicity as significant risk factors.

This longitudinal study follows 187 post-COVID patients over 9 months to track how cognitive and noncognitive symptoms evolve compared to 207 noninfected controls. While some noncognitive symptoms improved, cognitive and neurological symptoms persisted with no significant improvement in objective memory function.

This cross-sectional study examines structural brain changes in 57 hospitalized COVID-19 patients compared to 57 matched healthy controls using high-resolution MRI. While it identifies associations between reduced cortical thickness and post-COVID fatigue, it is a secondary analysis of the NAPKON-HAP cohort with no intervention tested, making it ineligible as a treatment trial.

Retrospective cohort analysis examining post-COVID-19 mortality outcomes in people with autoimmune/inflammatory rheumatic diseases, comparing rural versus urban residents using medical records from the National COVID Cohort Collaborative. Found that rural residence was independently associated with higher two-year all-cause mortality risk after COVID-19 infection.

Retrospective multicenter study of 1,540 CLL patients infected with SARS-CoV-2, examining post-COVID condition development and clinical characteristics across pandemic phases. Study describes epidemiology and natural history of post-COVID in immunocompromised patients but does not evaluate or test any specific treatment intervention.

This paper uses BRFSS data to examine the prevalence of chronic conditions among working-age adults in 2022 stratified by COVID-19/Long COVID history compared to 2019 pre-pandemic baseline. It is a secondary analysis of surveillance data showing increased prevalence of asthma, diabetes, and other conditions in Long COVID patients, but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

This cross-sectional study compared hemostatic, endothelial, and inflammatory profiles in 39 recovered COVID-19 patients (mean 12.7 months post-recovery) versus 124 healthy controls. The study found persistent hypercoagulability, endothelial dysfunction, and elevated inflammatory markers in approximately one-third of convalescent patients, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study tracking olfactory recovery in 126 COVID-19 patients over 6 months using a modified survey tool. This is a passive follow-up study documenting natural recovery patterns, not an intervention trial—no treatment was assigned or tested.

This prospective cohort study followed COVID-19 patients with olfactory dysfunction for 18 months to characterize recovery patterns and identify variables associated with spontaneous early or late recovery. Patients did not receive specific treatment for olfactory dysfunction; the study is purely observational with no intervention tested.

This paper examines risk factors and characteristics associated with persistent smell loss in COVID-19 patients. While smell loss is a documented post-COVID symptom, this is a cross-sectional observational study of symptom prevalence, not a treatment intervention trial, and does not meet the inclusion criteria for the long COVID clinical trials pipeline.

This cross-sectional study from the UK Coronavirus Infection Survey examines the prevalence and characteristics of long COVID in the United Kingdom population. The paper provides epidemiological insights into the burden of long COVID, likely focusing on symptom distribution and affected demographics.

Prospective cohort study evaluating long-term outcomes of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections for COVID-19-induced olfactory loss at 1-year post-intervention. PRP-treated patients showed significantly greater improvements in smell identification test scores and subjective measures compared to untreated controls.

Retrospective chart review comparing demographics and diagnoses of early-onset dementia patients seen at a Barcelona clinic in 2020 versus 2016-2019. While 16% of non-neurodegenerative diagnoses in 2020 were cognitive disturbances in recovered COVID-19 patients, the paper is primarily a descriptive epidemiological study of dementia clinic demographics during the pandemic, not a long COVID treatment trial.

Prospective longitudinal study comparing self-reported olfactory symptoms with objective psychophysical testing (Sniffin' Sticks) in COVID-19 patients at multiple timepoints over 6 months. Found moderate correlation between self-reported and objective olfactory measures, with persistent olfactory threshold impairment at 6 months despite subjective improvement.

Prospective cohort study investigating long-term cognitive dysfunction and brain changes in 80 COVID-19 ICU survivors at 3, 6, and 12 months post-discharge using neuropsychological testing, brain MRI, and blood biomarkers. This is a protocol paper presenting preliminary 3-month results from an ongoing study with no intervention administered.

This paper uses electronic health record data from the National COVID Cohort Collaborative to assess long COVID's causal impact on cognitive decline in patients with mild cognitive impairment, employing a virtual RCT methodology with machine learning. The study finds that COVID-19 infection increases the risk of developing dementia in MCI patients by 54% within 6 months post-infection, with higher risks for severe COVID cases.

This longitudinal study followed 38 severe COVID-19 survivors aged >60 for 1 year post-discharge to assess cognitive impairment and depressive symptoms. Results showed 18.4% had cognitive impairment and 18.4% had depressive symptoms, with a notable association between the two conditions.

Prospective cohort study assessing global cognitive function in 107 Mexican older adults (median age 70) at 6 months post-COVID-19 recovery using the Mini-Mental State Examination via telemedicine. 12% showed cognitive impairment, with episodic memory and constructional praxis most affected; depression history, lower education, and severe illness associated with impairment.

This cross-sectional study assessed cognitive function in 52 COVID-19 patients (mild-moderate disease) at 2 months post-discharge using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and related measures. 56.2% exhibited cognitive decline, which correlated with oxygen saturation during the 6-minute walk test, suggesting a link between cognitive impairment and physical deconditioning in post-COVID patients.

Cross-sectional and longitudinal study examining associations between MRI brain changes and cognitive/neuropsychiatric complaints in 49 long COVID patients. Found visual memory and executive function correlated with gray and white matter volumes, but no global MRI changes at 6-month follow-up.

Prospective cohort study of 766 older adults in Argentina following SARS-CoV-2 infection to assess long-term cognitive and neuropsychiatric sequelae. Found that severity of anosmia (not initial COVID-19 severity) predicts cognitive impairment, with high rates of persistent functional and cognitive deficits at one-year follow-up.

A prospective cohort study using 7T MRI to investigate neuroimaging correlates and neurodegenerative markers in patients following SARS-CoV-2 infection, including long COVID patients compared to matched controls and healthy controls. Pilot data show persistent or emergent neuroimaging abnormalities (white matter hyperintensities, basal ganglia changes) within one year post-infection, suggesting neuroinflammation and vascular injury in long COVID.

This study measures neurofilament light (NfL) and phosphorylated tau 181 (p-tau-181) blood biomarkers in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and long-term PASC patients with/without brain fog, comparing them to healthy controls. While NfL was elevated in acute hospitalization, neither marker was significantly elevated in PASC outpatients, though the findings suggest potential neurobiological mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to long-term neurological sequelae.

Prospective cohort study comparing cognitive function and functional status in elderly patients 3 months post-hospitalization for COVID-19 versus other causes. Found high prevalence of mild cognitive impairment (55.1%) and dementia (31%) in COVID-19 survivors, with fatigue and frailty as common complications.

A prospective observational study evaluating cognitive impairment evolution in severe neuro-COVID patients treated with a multidimensional rehabilitation program (physical, occupational, speech, swallowing therapy, nutritional and psychological support). Results showed significant improvement in MoCA scores (18→23) and motor function, with cognitive status shifting from 74% mild dementia at ICU discharge to 26% normal/58% MCI/16% mild dementia at one-month follow-up.

A multi-site observational study examining long-term neurological effects of COVID-19 in survivors using 7 Tesla MRI neuroimaging and cognitive assessments. Preliminary findings show 73.8% of COVID-19 survivors had at least one cognitive impairment compared to 52.6% of healthy controls, with survivors showing significantly higher rates of moderate to severe impairment.

Retrospective analysis of 440 post-COVID patients examining prevalence of neurological symptoms and associated factors. Study identifies brain fog (38.6%), headaches (31.1%), dizziness (29%), and memory impairment (23.6%) as common manifestations, with associations to fatigue, sleep problems, anxiety, and olfactory/taste dysfunction.

An ex-post facto cross-sectional study assessing cognitive and emotional outcomes in Peruvian COVID-19 survivors 6-18 months post-infection, comparing patients with PCR/antigen-confirmed infection to evaluate long-term neuropsychiatric sequelae. The study found reduced frontal/executive function and increased anxiety but no significant differences in general cognition, without testing any specific treatment intervention.

This paper examines whether pre-pandemic brain MRI signatures associated with COVID-19 predict dementia incidence in UK Biobank participants. While it addresses neurocognitive sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection, it is not a long COVID study as it focuses on dementia outcomes in a general population cohort rather than studying long COVID patients or their treatment.

This cross-sectional study compared cognitive performance between subjects at risk of dementia with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection in Uruguay. No significant differences in cognitive test performance were found between the groups.

A prospective cohort study of 874 older adult Amerindians examining cognitive sequelae of COVID-19, with extensive neuropsychiatric assessments, biomarkers, and brain imaging. Found that cognitive impairment was associated with older age, severe acute illness, and anosmia, but notably not with SARS-CoV-2 variant.

This cross-sectional study compares sensorimotor function (grip strength, gait speed, olfaction) between 77 COVID-19 survivors and 24 healthy controls across five research sites. COVID-19 survivors showed significantly reduced right-hand grip strength and slower gait speed (both normal and fast-paced walking) compared to controls, suggesting persistent sensorimotor impairment in long COVID.

This cross-sectional study evaluates neurological and cognitive manifestations in 93 long COVID patients through neuropsychological testing, biomarker analysis, neuroimaging, and sleep assessment. The study found high prevalence of cognitive complaints (96.7%), sleep disorders (73.1%), and anxiety (63.4%), but does not test or evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

Cross-sectional study assessing cognitive function in 373 post-COVID condition (PCC) participants and 126 healthy controls from the NAUTILUS Project, examining the relationship between sleep quality and cognitive deficits. Found that poor sleep quality is associated with increased risk of verbal memory and processing speed deficits, suggesting sleep disturbances may contribute to cognitive impairment in PCC.

A prospective cross-sectional study comparing blood biomarkers of neurodegeneration and blood-brain barrier dysfunction in COVID-19 patients versus controls, correlating these with MRI brain volumes. The study found that COVID-19 patients, particularly those with cognitive impairment, showed significant negative correlations between neurodegenerative biomarkers (NFL, amyloid-β-40, GFAP, ptau-181) and regional brain volumes two years post-infection.

Prospective cohort study evaluating clinical, cognitive, and functional impairments in 28 older adults (mean age 69.5) at 3 and 12 months following COVID-19 diagnosis. Found significant increases in frailty and cognitive impairment (57.2% MCI at 3 months), with dyspnea improving significantly by 12 months, while fatigue and depression persisted.

This prospective cohort study characterized cognitive impairments in older African American adults with persistent symptoms ≥12 months post-COVID-19. Findings showed widespread cognitive deficits in attention, memory, executive function, and global cognition, particularly in a socioeconomically disadvantaged population with limited healthcare access.

A case series of 41 long COVID patients with cognitive symptoms who received cognitive rehabilitation over 6 months with assessments at 0, 3, and 6 months. Significant improvements were found in attention, episodic memory, verbal fluency, and psychiatric symptoms post-rehabilitation.

Cross-sectional study comparing cognitive and behavioral symptoms between older adults with and without long COVID using the CAN-PROTECT cohort. Found that long COVID patients reported significantly higher scores on cognitive impairment and mild behavioral impairment scales associated with dementia risk.

This cross-sectional study compares neuropsychological outcomes and depressive symptoms between 31 long COVID patients and 18 controls in a Brazilian cohort of adults over 50 years old. Results show that long COVID patients have impaired working memory, episodic memory, and executive function, with depressive symptoms contributing to worse cognitive performance.

This cross-sectional study compared white matter hyperintensities (WMH) on MRI between long COVID patients (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) and controls. The authors found greater age-dependent increases in WMH volumes in hospitalized long COVID patients compared to controls, suggesting hospitalization during acute infection is associated with microvascular injury in the brain.

This observational cohort study followed 1,105 adults hospitalized with severe COVID-19 for 1 year post-discharge to identify cognitive trajectories and predictors of cognitive decline. The study identified three distinct cognitive trajectory groups and found that older age, female sex, prior dementia, frailty, delirium, and post-discharge readmissions were significant predictors of cognitive impairment.

This study compares Alzheimer's disease-related cerebrospinal fluid and plasma biomarkers in COVID-19 patients with neurological symptoms versus controls and AD patients. It is a secondary analysis examining molecular correlates rather than testing a treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study of 45 participants (25 COVID+, 20 COVID-) who completed monthly smartphone-based cognitive testing over 6 months. COVID+ participants showed significantly greater decline in working memory and sensory processing tasks over time compared to COVID-, suggesting post-COVID cognitive effects.

This cross-sectional study compared neuropsychological performance between long COVID patients and controls stratified by educational attainment in Brazil. Long COVID was associated with lower global cognitive scores on the MMSE, but no specific cognitive domain was particularly vulnerable, and education appeared to confer protective effects.

A cross-sectional study comparing brain morphology and mental health symptoms in 58 Brazilian long COVID patients versus 21 healthy controls using MRI and standardized psychiatric questionnaires. Long COVID patients showed significant mental health symptom differences but no detectable structural brain changes on MRI.

This longitudinal cohort study examines cognitive decline in community-dwelling older adults in Shanghai before and after the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown (2009-2024). While it documents pandemic-related cognitive effects, it does not study long COVID specifically or test any treatment interventions.

This retrospective cohort study examines the incidence of poststroke dementia in acute ischemic stroke patients with COVID-19 infection versus other infection types using Medicare claims data. The study finds higher dementia risk in stroke patients with concurrent COVID-19 or bacterial infection, but this is about acute COVID complications in stroke patients, not long COVID syndrome or long COVID treatments.

Cross-sectional study of 46 long COVID patients assessing cognitive impairment using MoCA and ACE-III cognitive tests, along with depression, anxiety, and quality-of-life measures. Study characterizes cognitive deficits and functional impairment patterns in post-COVID patients 2.5+ years post-infection, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This study evaluated immune cellular changes in 3 severely ill COVID-19 patients at 3, 6, and 12 months post-hospitalization using mass cytometry, comparing them with 4 healthy controls. The findings show persistence of cytotoxic lymphocytes, NK cells, and regulatory T cells throughout the recovery year, suggesting ongoing immune dysregulation in post-acute COVID-19.

Prospective descriptive study comparing neurologic manifestations in 100 hospitalized and 500 non-hospitalized long COVID patients at a Neuro-COVID clinic. Found both groups experience persistent neurologic symptoms with significant differences in demographics, comorbidities, and cognitive dysfunction patterns, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Retrospective cohort study examining sex differences in post-COVID fatigue symptoms among 303 non-hospitalized patients at a Polish university hospital. Findings show women had significantly higher prevalence of chronic fatigue symptoms across all timepoints post-infection, with persistent fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and sore throat being more common in females.

Longitudinal study examining how COVID-19 infection impacts Parkinson's disease patients' motor and non-motor symptoms. While it studies long-duration infection effects, the primary focus is on PD exacerbation rather than treating long COVID itself, and the study observes natural symptom changes without administering any intervention.

This cross-sectional study from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging COVID-19 Brain Health Study investigates the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and myelin content in older individuals using MRI brain imaging. The findings show that among SARS-CoV-2 cases, symptom incidence and severity were inversely associated with myelin content across multiple brain regions, suggesting myelin loss may occur in individuals with greater infection symptom burden.

Prospective cohort study (N=59) evaluating whether olfactory and neuropsychological test performance at 1-3 months post-infection predict post-COVID condition at 1-year follow-up. Objective olfactory dysfunction, but not subjective symptoms, predicted PCC with reduced quality of life; no treatment intervention was studied.

This case-control study compared 71 long COVID patients with 50 COVID-recovered controls to examine relationships between self-reported immune status, cognitive functioning, and depression. The study found that immune status significantly predicted subjective cognitive difficulties in long COVID patients independently of depression and fatigue, but did not test or evaluate any intervention.

This retrospective cohort study compared brain microstructure and network organization in 26 children post-COVID-19 versus 26 healthy controls using MRI and structural analysis techniques. The study found persistent cortical volume reductions in regions like the cingulate cortex and hippocampus, along with network connectivity disruptions, indicating potential long-term neurological sequelae of COVID-19 in children.

This prospective cohort study followed 175 post-COVID-19 patients in a neurological clinic for up to 18 months, assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms, cognitive deficits, sleep disorders, and potential biomarkers (EBV antibodies, cortisol, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies). The study found high initial symptom burden with 76.8% improving over time, high rates of somatization (61%) and psychiatric disorders (28%), but no confirmation of previously suggested biomarkers.

This retrospective cohort study examines post-acute COVID-19 complications in cancer patients across UK and Hong Kong cohorts, comparing COVID-19-infected cancer patients with matched non-COVID controls. The study found significantly elevated risks of cardiovascular disease and mortality in cancer patients post-COVID-19, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 182 COVID-19 hospitalized patients with echocardiography and ECG assessments at 3 and 12 months post-discharge. Found no significant changes in cardiac structure or function over time, with results unchanged across severity groups and persistent dyspnea status.

This retrospective observational study compared physical and psychological outcomes in cancer patients versus co-living individuals after acute COVID-19 infection, with 1-year follow-up assessment. While the paper measures persistent symptoms at 1 year post-infection, it focuses on acute COVID-19 complications in a cancer cohort rather than studying long COVID as a specific syndrome or testing interventions for long COVID patients.

This observational cohort study followed 103 COVID-19 patients to identify clinical and immunological signatures associated with post-COVID-19 syndrome development. The study developed a predictive index (FANSY POSTCOV) based on demographic and immune markers but was a passive observational follow-up with no treatment intervention.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study examining recovery of cardiac function in 91 COVID-19 patients followed from hospitalization to 2 months later. Found that right ventricular function improved during recovery but left ventricular impairment persisted; however, this is a study of acute COVID-19 sequelae during the immediate post-hospitalization period, not long COVID (weeks-months after infection in community settings).

This retrospective observational study followed 67 post-COVID-19 patients over 52 weeks to identify factors associated with late-onset pain development. Fatigue at 26 weeks was the primary predictor of pain onset at 52 weeks, though the study did not test any specific intervention or treatment.

This is a preliminary report from the PAIN-COVID trial presenting a cross-sectional descriptive analysis of pain and quality of life outcomes in critically ill COVID-19 survivors at 1 month post-discharge. The study documents the incidence and characteristics of new-onset pain and its impact on HRQoL, but does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

This study assessed hundreds of biomarkers in 458 COVID-19 patients (mild and severe cases) at 6-9 months post-infection to identify differences between those who developed PASC and those who recovered. Patients with PASC showed distinct CD4+ and CD8+ memory T cell alterations with a TEMRA phenotype, and a machine learning model identified these T cell features as top discriminators of PASC with >80% accuracy.

Retrospective cohort study of 2.04 million British Columbia residents examining the long-term risk of incident type 2 diabetes following SARS-CoV-2 infection over 3+ years of follow-up. Found a 1.18-fold increased diabetes risk in infected individuals (HR 1.15-1.22), with higher risk in severely ill and unvaccinated persons, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Multicenter cohort study examining objective chemosensory dysfunction in 345 acute COVID-19 patients. Found high rates of olfactory and gustatory impairment during acute infection, with longer symptom duration correlating with severe disease, but does not follow patients into the post-COVID period.

Observational study assessing post-COVID symptomatology among hospitalized older adults with and without dementia. Characterizes persistent symptoms in this vulnerable population following acute COVID-19 hospitalization.

Retrospective cohort study comparing 38 people with epilepsy who had COVID-19 infection to 92 uninfected matched controls, assessing neurological and psychiatric outcomes at 6 and 12 months. COVID-infected patients showed increased seizure frequency and psychiatric/neurological symptoms at 6 months that persisted at 12 months, but this is an observational follow-up study without any intervention or treatment.

A prospective follow-up study assessing dyspnea prevalence and predictors in 327 COVID-19 patients at 2 months post-infection. While relevant to long COVID, this is an observational study with no treatment intervention—it documents symptom outcomes rather than evaluating any therapeutic approach.

This longitudinal observational study examined 169 COVID-19 patients to assess whether ABO blood group is associated with in-hospital adverse outcomes and long-term persistent symptoms. The study found blood groups AB and B were associated with higher rates of respiratory support/death acutely, and AB with persistent palpitation and dizziness at 6-month follow-up, but it is an observational cohort study without treatment intervention and thus ineligible for the clinical trials pipeline.

A retrospective case-control study examining the association between acute COVID-19 severity and symptoms with the development of long COVID in a non-hospitalized population. The study found that severe acute infection and higher symptom burden during acute phase were strongly associated with long COVID development, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal cohort study examining T-cell immune responses in COVID-19 survivors at 1 and 6-8 months post-infection using flow cytometry analysis. Found sustained T-cell responses and immune recovery patterns at 6-8 months, but this is purely observational characterization with no treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining associations between acute inflammatory biomarkers (IL-6, CRP, ferritin) during COVID-19 hospitalization and long-COVID symptoms at 3-month follow-up in 144 patients. Found counterintuitive inverse associations between admission biomarker levels and subsequent myalgia, low mood, and anxiety, with gender confounding the relationships.

This observational study assessed the prevalence and characteristics of long COVID among people living with HIV in a tertiary clinic in western India, screening 94 PLHIV with confirmed COVID-19 history. Long COVID prevalence was 43.6%, with moderate-severe acute illness as a significant risk factor, and fatigue and cough as the most common persistent symptoms.

Retrospective cross-sectional study assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using EQ-5D-3L questionnaires in 105 COVID-19 ICU survivors at 1 year follow-up. Found that 69% reported pain/discomfort problems and 51% reported anxiety/depression, with diabetes, longer ICU stay, younger age, and male sex associated with impaired HRQoL.

Cohort study comparing obese and non-obese COVID-19 patients discharged from hospital to assess long-term effects of obesity on clinical manifestations and immune function. Found that obese patients had more severe clinical manifestations, abnormal metabolic indicators, and inversely correlated antibody titers with BMI.

This cross-sectional study assessed the prevalence of sarcopenia in 541 COVID-19 survivors and examined its relationship to persistent long COVID symptoms. Sarcopenia was present in 19.5% of patients and was associated with higher numbers of persistent symptoms, particularly fatigue and dyspnea, suggesting it may be a biological mechanism underlying long COVID syndrome.

This nested case-control study of 94 participants examines demographic, clinical, and immunological factors associated with long COVID, finding that HIV infection is an independent predictor of long COVID (OR=2.7) and that inflammatory marker patterns differ between HIV+ and HIV- individuals. The study identifies respiratory and musculoskeletal symptoms as most common in long COVID patients and reveals differential cytokine responses by HIV status (IL-6 in HIV- group, IFN-β in HIV+ group).

Prospective cohort study of 104 renal transplant recipients followed for a median of 64 days after acute COVID-19 to identify post-COVID complications. 88.5% of survivors developed clinical or laboratory complications including shortness of breath, tiredness, and coagulopathy; most improved by 6 months with persistent elevated D-dimers in some patients.

Retrospective chart review of 798 long COVID patients describing symptom prevalence and complicating diseases, with emphasis on differential diagnosis rather than treatment evaluation. Study identifies non-COVID-related conditions mimicking long COVID symptoms but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

This cross-sectional study uses cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging to characterize myocardial findings in patients with suspected myocarditis during acute COVID-19 (AMCovS) and post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (cPACS). The paper reports diagnostic imaging findings rather than testing or evaluating a treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study examined the clinical features of 58 patients with gastrointestinal long-COVID symptoms out of 943 COVID-19 patients in Japan. The study found that patients with GI long-COVID symptoms had significantly lower quality of life measures (SF-8, EQ-5D-5L) at 12 months and experienced more varied long-COVID symptoms than those without GI symptoms.

This study evaluates fetal cardiac morphology and function in pregnant women 4 weeks after recovery from moderate COVID-19 infection using echocardiography. The findings show no significant cardiac effects in the fetus, with only a minor difference in mitral E/A ratio that does not indicate clinical harm.

This retrospective cohort study examined 51 Wilson disease patients before and ~11 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection to assess physical and mental health outcomes using validated scales. 39.2% were classified as having long COVID, with high rates of concentration disorders (60%), fatigue (55%), and reduced exercise capacity (50%), suggesting WD patients may be particularly vulnerable to long COVID complications.

This study compares mitochondrial membrane potential in leukocytes between healthy controls, acute COVID-19 patients, and recovered individuals at 40 and 335 days post-infection. The findings suggest persistent loss of mitochondrial function in long COVID patients, particularly in females, potentially linking mitochondrial dysfunction to post-COVID sequelae.

This prospective cross-sectional study compares brain gray matter morphology in 38 young adults who recovered from mild COVID-19 without long COVID symptoms against 37 healthy controls using MRI-based morphometry. The study found gray matter alterations including reduced cortical thickness and subcortical volume in the COVID group despite subjects having no subjective neurological complaints at examination, suggesting subclinical CNS changes following mild infection.

Propensity-matched observational study comparing cirrhosis patients with COVID-19 vs. non-COVID sepsis, followed for 1 year to assess decompensation and mortality. Long COVID occurred in 33.3% of COVID-19 survivors with cirrhosis, with higher late mortality compared to non-COVID sepsis controls.

This prospective study evaluated whether quantitative respiratory pattern measures from dynamic high-temporal resolution MRI can stratify postacute COVID-19 patients by cardiopulmonary symptom burden. The analysis found that tidal lung area, lung area coefficient of variability, and respiratory incoherence were significantly higher in patients with two or more cardiopulmonary symptoms, suggesting MRI-derived metrics may help characterize symptom severity.

This cross-sectional MRI study compared cerebral blood flow (CBF) in 39 adults weeks to months post-COVID-19 versus 11 controls with flu-like symptoms but negative COVID tests. The COVID-19 group showed significantly reduced CBF in subcortical regions (thalamus, orbitofrontal cortex, basal ganglia), with additional CBF differences in those reporting ongoing fatigue, suggesting brain physiology changes underlie post-COVID symptoms.

This retrospective analysis examines KL-6 as a biomarker for COVID-19 severity and lung injury in 166 acute COVID-19 patients. While it mentions long-term lung injury prognosis, the study focuses on acute COVID-19 disease severity rather than long COVID syndrome, and it is purely observational with no treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study following 172 COVID-19 patients for 8-10 months to characterize persistent symptoms post-recovery, finding 61% reported one or more long COVID symptoms with fatigue, dyspnea, and depression most common, and age as a significant risk factor. The study documents symptom prevalence and re-infection rates but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This cross-sectional study evaluated radiological findings, pulmonary function, and health-related quality of life in 65 severe COVID-19 survivors at 6 months post-discharge. The paper found pulmonary abnormalities (fibrosis, reduced FEV1/FVC) and impaired quality of life but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study of 328 COVID-19 patients from Johns Hopkins Health System evaluated symptom persistence a median of 242 days post-infection. 33.2% reported incomplete recovery with women disproportionately reporting activity-limiting symptoms, though the study does not test any treatment intervention.

Observational cohort study of 76 COVID-19 patients followed 1 year post-admission to examine long-term symptom persistence and quality of life, with comparison between those who did and did not receive systemic corticosteroids during acute infection. Patients receiving corticosteroids showed significantly lower rates of headache, dysphagia, chest pain, and depression, with improved quality of life scores in bodily pain and mental health domains.

This cross-sectional study investigated the frequency and risk factors of brain fog in 2,696 COVID-19 survivors from Iran, finding that 62.3% reported long COVID syndrome and 7.2% experienced chronic brain fog. The study identified female sex, respiratory problems at onset, and ICU admission as significant risk factors for post-COVID brain fog.

This cross-sectional study examined inflammatory biomarkers (ESR, CRP) and serum albumin levels in patients following recovery from severe versus mild-to-moderate COVID-19. The findings show sustained elevation of inflammatory markers and reduced albumin in severe COVID-19 post-recovery patients, but this is an observational characterization study without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 524 COVID-19 patients in Eastern India followed up ~73 days post-infection during the Omicron wave to estimate long COVID incidence and identify predictors. Found 8.2% self-reported long COVID symptoms with fatigue and cough most common; prior infection and ≥5 acute COVID symptoms were significant predictors.

Observational study examining symptom changes and antibody titers in 42 long COVID patients after receiving their first COVID-19 vaccination. Found that vaccination increased antibody titers significantly, with worsening symptoms associated with the highest antibody titer increases.

This multicenter observational study tracked gastrointestinal and other post-COVID symptoms in 1,593 previously hospitalized patients at two timepoints (8.4 and 13.2 months post-infection) to characterize recovery trajectories. The study found an overall decline in symptom burden over time but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

A cross-sectional survey of 286 long COVID patients attending an outpatient clinic characterizing clinical features, symptom recovery periods, and factors affecting recovery. Respiratory symptoms and fatigue were most common, with COVID-19 severity, symptom burden, delayed treatment initiation, and smoking identified as independent factors slowing recovery.

This study evaluates the psychometric properties and clinical usefulness of the COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRS) in 187 patients with post-COVID syndrome attending a rehabilitation clinic. The C19-YRS demonstrated good internal consistency and validity as an outcome measurement tool, but the paper does not test or evaluate a specific intervention or treatment.

This cross-sectional biomarker study profiled plasma from 181 individuals in the DigiHero cohort to characterize immune dysregulation in post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), including monocyte/macrophage dysfunction and circulating SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. The study found pronounced dysregulation in pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines with PASC-specific patterns, and identified circulating spike protein as an independent biomarker in a subset of PASC patients, illustrating biological heterogeneity in the condition.

This retrospective cohort study followed 211 non-ICU COVID-19 survivors at 8-week outpatient follow-up to assess recovery, symptoms, and mental health outcomes. The study found persistent physical symptoms (fatigue 68%, dyspnea 56%) and cognitive problems (memory impairment 33%, concentration problems 28%) in most patients, with 7.8% meeting anxiety criteria and correlations between physical and mental symptom burden.

This retrospective cohort study follows 47 Omicron COVID-19 patients for 6 months post-discharge to assess dynamic changes in renal function and cytokine profiles.
