Found that 53% of COVID-positive patients reported persistent symptoms, with fatigue, smell/taste disorder, dyspnea, and memory impairment independently associated with COVID-19.

This study examines whether COVID-19 vaccination affects the evolution of six cardinal symptoms in patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (long COVID). The authors assess the association between vaccination status and symptom progression over time in a cohort of long COVID patients.

Multicenter observational study tracking recovery trajectories of loss of smell and taste in previously hospitalized COVID-19 survivors over multiple timepoints. Describes natural recovery patterns rather than evaluating any intervention, with most patients recovering by follow-up but some developing symptoms de novo.

A cross-sectional study of 441 adults presenting to a COVID-19 recovery clinic that identifies two distinct symptom clusters in long COVID patients: neuropsychiatric and pulmonary presentations. The study characterizes demographic and clinical differences between clusters but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining racial/ethnic differences in post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection using EHR data from 62,339 COVID-19 patients in New York City. Black and Hispanic patients showed significantly different odds of developing PASC symptoms and conditions (diabetes, headaches, dyspnea, chest pain) compared to white patients.

Retrospective observational cohort study of 530 acute COVID-19 survivors followed ~1 year post-infection to assess persistent symptoms and functional limitations. Found 41.5% reported worse health, 44.2% reported persistent symptoms, and significant limitations in physical effort tolerance, with no intervention tested.

Prospective observational cohort study of 1,038 COVID-19 patients (hospitalized and outpatient) followed for 60-90 days to assess PASC development and associated demographic/clinical factors. Found 29.8% developed PASC with fatigue and dyspnea as most common symptoms; hospitalization, diabetes, and higher BMI were independent risk factors, while certain populations (organ transplant recipients, Medicaid insured) had lower PASC rates.

Retrospective cohort study examining the incidence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) following acute COVID-19 using South Carolina statewide registry data from March 2020 to January 2022. Findings show COVID-19 was not independently associated with CKD after accounting for severity of illness and acute kidney injury.

This paper analyzes data from the RECOVER-Adult observational cohort to determine the incidence and prevalence of post-COVID ME/CFS among adults infected with SARS-CoV-2. The study found that ME/CFS develops at a significantly higher rate in COVID-infected participants (2.66 per 100 person-years) compared to uninfected controls (0.93 per 100 person-years), with 4.5% of infected participants meeting diagnostic criteria.

Retrospective cohort study examining PASC prevalence 1 year post-infection in 863 diverse urban adults, with logistic regression identifying predictors. Reveals 54.1% PASC prevalence with significant racial/ethnic disparities and higher odds in females and those experiencing loneliness.

Observational cohort study of 1,407 PASC patients identifying four distinct health-related quality of life profiles using PROMIS-GH items at baseline and 12-month follow-up. Patients improved modestly over time with improvement varying by symptom profile, but no treatment intervention was delivered or evaluated.

This cross-sectional study examines sleep disturbance severity and its correlates in post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) patients, with focus on racial disparities. Findings emphasize the importance of identifying sleep disturbances in PASC and highlight racial inequities, informing the need for interventions to reduce PASC-related disparities.

A prospective cohort study following 64 patients hospitalized for severe COVID-19 at 6 and 12 months post-discharge to assess long-term symptoms and respiratory outcomes. The study found persistent dyspnea, fatigue, anxiety, depression, and pulmonary deficits in significant proportions of patients, without any intervention being tested.

This cross-sectional study examined 72 ambulatory post-COVID-19 patients to determine relationships between physical fitness, cardiopulmonary function, and patient-reported symptom severity. Greater physical fitness and cardiopulmonary function were associated with lower severity of symptoms including fatigue and dyspnea, suggesting exercise and physical conditioning may help reduce persistent post-COVID symptoms.

Retrospective cohort study examining the risk of new-onset type 2 diabetes after SARS-CoV-2 infection using EHR data from over 247,000 patients across three cohorts (exposed, unexposed, and historical controls). Found that individuals exposed to SARS-CoV-2 had 1.64× higher risk of new-onset diabetes compared to historical controls, with findings consistent across sociodemographic subgroups.

Prospective observational study evaluating lung ultrasound as a tool for detecting fibrotic-like changes 6 months after severe COVID-19 pneumonia compared to CT imaging. Found that LUS score was significantly associated with CT fibrotic patterns, but this is a diagnostic/prognostic study without any treatment intervention—patients were only assessed, not treated.

Population-based cohort study in Ontario comparing health service use within 12 months post-discharge between adults with and without pre-existing disabilities hospitalized for COVID-19. Finds that people with disabilities had significantly higher rates of ambulatory care, ED visits, and hospital admissions even after adjustment for sociodemographic factors and comorbidities.

This retrospective cohort study examines ethnic differences in long COVID symptom burden and impact on daily life among 864 patients attending a Long COVID Clinic in Denmark. The study describes symptom prevalence and disparities rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study followed 294 COVID-19 survivors (89 ICU, 205 non-ICU) for up to 24 months post-discharge to characterize persistent symptoms and medical specialty usage patterns. The study documented high incidence of ongoing symptoms (neuromuscular, respiratory, fatigue, cardiovascular) and associated specialty care needs but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective analysis of administrative claims data from Lombardy examining drug dispensation and diagnostic test usage in 46,574 COVID-19 recovered patients over 18 months post-infection as proxies for post-COVID healthcare impact. Findings show sustained elevated dispensation of drugs for specific conditions (anticoagulants, antidepressants, diabetes, airways disease) indicating ongoing post-COVID morbidity, but this is not a treatment intervention trial.

Observational study of 55 older patients (mean age 82.3) assessing lung CT findings and functional status 3-6 months after COVID-19 pneumonia hospitalization. Most acute CT abnormalities resolved by 6 months; mild fibrotic changes persisted in 40% but were not associated with functional decline, which correlated instead with pre-existing comorbidities.

This retrospective cohort study used administrative claims data from Lombardy, Italy to assess healthcare resource utilization in 315,593 individuals who recovered from the second COVID-19 wave and 269,605 from the third wave. The study found that hospitalizations, emergency room visits, and outpatient visits post-infection were similar to pre-pandemic levels, but drug dispensation and diagnostic testing increased notably for cardiorespiratory and blood system conditions.

This study analyzed blood cell counts and haematological parameters in 83 long COVID patients compared to 70 healthy controls, finding persistent abnormalities in 81% of patients. The findings suggest impaired immune responses including reduced lymphocytes and IgM memory B cells may contribute to long-term symptoms.

This is a prospective follow-up study of 755 long COVID patients from Italy, tracking symptom persistence at two timepoints (mean 223 days and 453 days post-infection). The study documents natural symptom trajectories and risk factors for persistence without testing any intervention, making it a natural history observational study rather than a treatment trial.

This prospective cohort study evaluates the Multidimensional Prognostic Index (MPI) as a predictor of 3.5-year mortality in 183 older adults hospitalized with COVID-19. The study finds that high MPI scores predict higher mortality and that demographic variables modestly improve prognostic prediction, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective observational cohort study followed 90 patients hospitalized for severe COVID-19 at 24 months to characterize cardio-pulmonary sequelae using pulmonary function tests, walking tests, and echocardiography. The study found mild DLCO impairment in 26% of patients and persistent dyspnoea in 34%, with evidence of increased pulmonary vascular resistance in 20% of those who underwent echocardiography, but no overt pulmonary hypertension.

This retrospective cohort study compared hypertensive patients with recent COVID-19 infection (within 6 months) to those without infection to evaluate blood pressure control and vascular stiffness. While the study shows COVID-19 increases arterial stiffness and blood pressure readings, it does not study long COVID (chronic post-COVID syndrome) or test any treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

Longitudinal follow-up study of 5,610 COVID-19 patients tracking symptom presence at 1, 3, and 6 months post-infection. Identifies risk factors associated with persistent post-COVID symptoms (female gender, older age, hospitalization, comorbidities) but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This study followed 222 ICU patients hospitalized for severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia over 24 months, assessing ventilatory function and diffusion capacity at multiple timepoints. The majority (63%) achieved normalization of lung function by 24 months, with male sex, age, and obesity negatively impacting recovery rates; however, this is a prospective follow-up study documenting natural recovery patterns without any intervention or treatment being tested.

A prospective 6-month follow-up study of 250 COVID-19 survivors examining thyroid function, autoimmunity, and long COVID occurrence, with stratification by interferon beta-1b treatment status. Found that most acute thyroid abnormalities resolved, interferon treatment was associated with modest increases in anti-thyroid antibodies, but thyroid markers did not predict long COVID development.

Retrospective study of 511 COVID-19 survivors examining the incidence of newly diagnosed hyperglycemia and diabetes mellitus and their association with obesity and lipid profiles. Found 3.32% developed new-onset T2DM and 16.82% developed hyperglycemia, with obesity and dyslipidemia as risk factors, but no intervention was tested.

This prospective cohort study examines long-term functional outcomes in older adults who received inpatient geriatric rehabilitation following acute COVID-19 infection. While participants were treated with rehabilitation, the study focuses on acute COVID-19 recovery rather than long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks/months post-infection), making it outside the scope of long COVID intervention trials.

Observational follow-up study investigating new-onset diabetes after COVID-19 (NODAC) and its recovery at 6 months in 1,310 patients. Finds NODAC prevalence of 8.5% with persistence driven by insulin resistance rather than beta-cell dysfunction, but does not test any treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study of 21 children with neuro-COVID-19 (with or without MIS-C) admitted to a hospital from January 2021 to January 2022, documenting neurological manifestations and their persistence up to 7 months post-discharge. Study found no significant difference in outcomes between groups except seizure frequency, but is observational with no intervention tested and therefore excluded from treatment trial analysis.

Prospective cohort study of ENT manifestations in mild and asymptomatic COVID-19 patients followed for 4 weeks. Documents high recovery rates of smell and taste disturbances, with 96% of patients fully recovered by week 4, but does not address long COVID sequelae occurring weeks to months after infection.

Retrospective study of 59 post-COVID mucormycosis patients at a tertiary care center, examining incidence, comorbidities, and treatment outcomes with IV amphotericin B and posaconazole, with surgical debridement in 52 patients. Uncontrolled diabetes, steroid overuse, and ICU prolonged stay were identified as aggravating factors, with 7 mortalities reported.

Observational study examining secondary sclerosing cholangitis (SSC) as a long-term hepatobiliary complication in COVID-19 patients, particularly those who were critically ill with mechanical ventilation. The study identifies SSC occurrence in 1 of 43 ventilated COVID-19 patients and establishes risk factors including tissue hypoxia and fibrinogen-related circulatory disturbances, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cohort study measures T cell phenotypes and responses in peripheral blood of long COVID-19 recovered patients (20-26 weeks post-infection) compared to short-term recovered and healthy controls. While the study is about long COVID recovery, it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it is purely a descriptive immunological characterization of natural recovery patterns.

A prospective follow-up study of children hospitalized with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 or MIS-C, evaluated 1-2 years after discharge for functional, pulmonary, and systemic outcomes. Most children showed significant functional improvement over time, with no pulmonary morbidities and normalization of previously abnormal cardiac findings.

Prospective cohort study examining frailty, falls, balance confidence, and depression in older Turkish adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. While the study notes long-term impacts of COVID-19 on older adults, it is not specifically about long COVID and does not evaluate a treatment intervention.

Prospective follow-up study of 106 children diagnosed with COVID-19, assessed at a mean of 83 days post-infection for long COVID sequelae. Most children were asymptomatic at follow-up with mild sequelae (fatigue in 4 patients, anxiety in 1), no organ-specific damage, and normal troponin levels except in MIS-C cases.

This cross-sectional study compares healthcare consumption and work absenteeism in 129 individuals with persistent fatigue/concentration difficulties versus 96 without such symptoms at 3+ months post-COVID infection. Worse neuropsychological functioning and illness perceptions were associated with work absenteeism in those with persistent complaints, though cognitive-behavioural factors did not explain increased healthcare consumption.

This cross-sectional study evaluated cognitive performance in 46 long COVID patients presenting with cognitive symptoms at a post-COVID clinic in Northern Israel using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and neurological examination. The study found impairments in executive function, attention, and phonemic fluency despite normal laboratory tests and imaging, with cognitive decline occurring independent of acute COVID-19 disease severity.

This prospective cohort study tracked 65 SARS-CoV-2-positive elite athletes from a German Olympic Training Center at two timepoints (baseline and 16 weeks post-negative PCR) to examine long-term clinical outcomes and exercise capacity. 37% experienced symptoms lasting >4 weeks, and at 16 weeks, 64% reported ongoing limitations in sports participation due primarily to mental and physical fatigue, shortness of breath, and musculoskeletal pain.

Prospective cohort study of 422 severe COVID-19 ICU survivors followed for 1 year post-discharge, identifying four distinct functional trajectories using latent class growth analysis. Patients with higher disability trajectories had significantly increased risk of adverse outcomes (falls, rehospitalizations, institutionalization, death) and higher prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition (67.5%), though no specific intervention was tested.

Prospective follow-up study of 59 COVID-19 patients at 3-6 months post-discharge examining residual symptoms and organ damage through clinical assessment and imaging. Found 77.8% of patients had persistent symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, insomnia, anxiety) with mild pulmonary changes and reduced diffusion capacity in a subset.

Retrospective study comparing clinical and kinematic tremor data in 36 essential tremor (ET) patients before and after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Among infected patients, 44% reported subjective tremor worsening and all who worsened had long COVID symptoms, but no treatment or intervention was evaluated—this is an observational cohort study documenting natural history rather than a treatment trial.

A prospective cohort study comparing the prevalence of fatigue, depression, and cognitive dysfunction in 355 post-COVID patients versus 272 sepsis survivors at a German outpatient clinic. Post-COVID patients showed significantly higher rates of fatigue (93.2% vs 67.8%) and depression (81.3% vs 10.9%), with cognitive dysfunction associated with hospitalization severity.

Cross-sectional study evaluating cognitive, mental, and sleep patterns in 40 post-COVID patients 2 months post-hospitalization using validated assessment scales and correlating findings with thorax CT severity scores. Found high prevalence of cognitive impairment, depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbance, but no significant correlation with lung involvement on imaging.

This prospective observational study followed 17 post-COVID-19 patients with reduced DLCO at baseline to assess 1-year evolution of lung function and respiratory symptoms. Most patients showed improvement or normalization of DLCO and respiratory symptoms, though about one-third experienced persistent changes.

Retrospective observational study of 649 COVID-19 patients evaluating whether early antiviral drugs (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, molnupiravir) and monoclonal antibodies reduce long COVID symptoms at 3 months. Treatment with antivirals and mAbs showed significant protective associations against persisting symptoms compared to untreated controls.

This population-based prospective cohort study examined symptom persistence and risk factors predicting prolonged time to symptom resolution in 1,175 long COVID patients enrolled ≥6 months post-infection. Over half reported persistent symptoms at 280 days post-infection, with age, female sex, low education, low resilience, and steroid/no medication use associated with prolonged symptom duration.

Case-control study comparing work performance and antibody response between 69 healthcare workers with post-COVID-19 syndrome and 69 matched controls without the syndrome. Finds that COVID-19 negatively impacts work performance but post-COVID-19 syndrome specifically does not significantly worsen performance compared to those without the syndrome.

A prospective observational study evaluating the feasibility and patient satisfaction of a mobile interdisciplinary post-COVID outpatient clinic in rural areas, assessing physical fitness, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and other symptoms in 125 long COVID patients. The mobile clinic model achieved high patient satisfaction, but the study does not test or evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study of 176 long COVID patients examined the relationship between blood immune cell phenotypes and fatigue severity ~10 weeks post-infection. The study found that CD4+ T cell counts were independently correlated with fatigue severity, suggesting a possible biomarker for post-COVID fatigue, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This study applies a newly developed Post-COVID syndrome (PCS) score to a prospective multi-center German cohort to validate its functionality and correlates with quality of life. The study found that 64.3% of patients had mild to severe PCS, with severity associated with poor quality of life, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study compares endothelial-colony forming cells (ECFCs) and angiogenic biomarkers in 72 post-COVID-19 patients and 31 healthy controls at 6 and 12 months post-infection. Results show persistent endothelial dysfunction in long COVID patients, with elevated ECFC production and inflammatory markers remaining abnormal up to 12 months post-infection.

Retrospective observational study assessing the incidence and risk factors for post-COVID-19 conditions (long COVID) in 653 people living with HIV in Northern Italy. Found 34.9% prevalence of persistent symptoms at 3 months post-infection, with fatigue and muscular pain most common; hospitalization during acute infection was associated with increased PCC risk.

Retrospective cohort study using TriNetX database examining the association between COVID-19 infection and new-onset asthma in children aged 5-18, stratified by vaccination status. Found significantly higher asthma incidence in COVID-19 infected children, but focuses on acute infection sequelae rather than long COVID syndrome.

A prospective multicentre cohort study tracking post-acute COVID-19 sequelae (PASC) burden in 1,704 Swiss healthcare workers over 30 months across five timepoints. While documenting symptom evolution and therapeutic self-management, the study is observational without testing a specific intervention, and therefore does not qualify as a treatment trial.

This multicenter prospective cohort study compared post-COVID-19 symptoms and health-related quality of life between patients infected with delta and omicron SARS-CoV-2 variants, following 758 patients for 3 months post-infection. The study found comparable prevalence of post-COVID symptoms between variants, with fatigue being most frequent, and demonstrated that most patients (69%) maintained stable quality of life.

Population-based cohort study examining recovery from post-COVID condition (PCC) across SARS-CoV-2 variants and vaccination status using the DigiHero cohort. Found that Omicron and Delta variants were associated with faster recovery rates than wildtype and Alpha, though substantial symptoms persisted even in Omicron-infected patients one year post-infection.

Retrospective cohort study of 59,339 German children and adolescents with confirmed COVID-19 and matched controls followed through 2021, examining incidence and persistence of post-acute sequelae. Found 6% PASC prevalence at 0-3 months with most symptoms resolving by 12 months, though excess morbidity persisted in adolescents.

Retrospective cohort study using N3C data comparing sotrovimab treatment versus no treatment in high-risk COVID-19 patients, evaluating impact on developing post-acute sequelae (long COVID). Sotrovimab treatment was associated with significantly lower risk of PASC (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.89-0.96).

This multicenter study compared cardiac structure and function in 679 long COVID patients versus 475 matched controls 1.5 years post-infection using echocardiography and cardiopulmonary exercise testing. Results showed subtle but significant reductions in left ventricular function and exercise capacity in long COVID patients, though changes remained within normal ranges.

Prospective observational cohort study of 171 post-COVID-19 patients undergoing comprehensive neurological diagnostic assessment including imaging, electrophysiology, and neuropsychological testing. Found that objective neurological damage is rare (14.2% with pathological findings) despite frequent subjective complaints, with elevated somatization scores suggesting psychosomatic factors in pathogenesis.

This retrospective, population-based cohort study compares long-term outcomes across respiratory sepsis, SARS-CoV-2-associated sepsis, and influenza-associated sepsis survivors in Germany over 12 months post-discharge. While it includes long COVID patients and documents their burden of impairments, it is a passive observational comparison study with no intervention assigned, and appears to be a secondary analysis of administrative/registry data rather than a primary treatment trial.

This retrospective cohort study using U.S. electronic health records examined whether selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) reduce long COVID risk in patients with depression compared to non-SSRI antidepressants. Results showed SSRIs were associated with significantly lower long COVID risk (HR 0.57-0.59 across timepoints), suggesting potential preventive benefit in high-risk populations.

Prospective multimodal evaluation of 30 long COVID patients and 17 convalescent controls assessing clinical, psychological, virologic, and immunologic characteristics at median 152 days post-symptom onset. Study found high prevalence of psychiatric distress and emerging neurological symptoms (paresthesia, burning pain) but unremarkable biomarkers and no immune response differences between long COVID patients and controls.

This cross-sectional study compares the timing of initial COVID-19 infection among 567 patients with self-reported post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) between the first pandemic wave and later periods. The authors found that PASC patients were significantly more likely to report initial COVID-19 during the first wave, suggesting non-viral factors may influence PASC development, but the study does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Population-based cohort study comparing post-discharge healthcare utilization between COVID-19 and other acute respiratory infection patients in Lombardy using administrative data. This is an observational analysis of existing healthcare records without any treatment intervention—patients were not assigned or given a specific therapy to evaluate.

A prospective cohort study of 448 COVID-19 patients assessing long-term patient-centered outcomes including general health, respiratory function, and symptom duration at 6 and 12 weeks post-symptom onset. The study found persistent symptoms in 39% at 6 weeks and 20% at 12 weeks, with fatigue and breathlessness as most common, identifying male gender, age, and comorbidities as predictors of impaired health outcomes.

Prospective cohort study assessing long-term health consequences in 303 healthcare workers 1 year post-COVID-19 discharge, measuring pulmonary, physical, and psychiatric function. Found persistent diffusion capacity impairment (43.5%), reduced exercise capacity (19.4%), abnormal CT patterns (37.5%), and probable PTSD (21.9%), with worse outcomes in female and critically ill HCWs.

Prospective cohort study examining the association between pre-pandemic diabetes and long COVID risk using UK Household Longitudinal Study data (11,669 adults, Waves 10-14). Found that pre-pandemic diabetes was independently associated with a 60% higher risk of long COVID (RR=1.60, 95% CI: 1.27-2.02).

Longitudinal observational study measuring plasma levels of innate immune response markers (PTX3, C3a, C5a, CHI3L1) in 94 COVID-19 patients at baseline, 1 month, and 6 months post-discharge. Found that greater reduction in PTX3 over time was associated with lower depression and anxiety symptoms at 6 months, suggesting inflammation may contribute to post-COVID psychopathology.

Prospective follow-up cohort study of 94 COVID-19 pneumonia patients re-evaluated ~4 months post-discharge to assess short-term consequences including pulmonary fibrosis, symptom persistence (fatigue, dyspnea, dysgeusia, anxiety, insomnia), and quality of life. Baseline severity indices (Brixia score, Charlson Index, 4C mortality score) significantly predicted extent of lung involvement and clinical outcomes.

This cross-sectional study examines the prevalence of steatotic liver disease (SLD) in 560 post-COVID syndrome patients versus 103 healthy controls using transient elastography and cognitive assessments. The authors found SLD is associated with cognitive impairment and severe COVID-19 history in PCS patients, but no treatment intervention was evaluated.

Secondary analysis of the CLoCk cohort study examining mental health trajectories in children with pre-existing eating problems over 24 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found that children with eating problems had higher mental health difficulties throughout follow-up, but trajectories were stable over time compared to slight increases in those without eating problems.

Prospective multicenter cohort study comparing symptom patterns and exercise tolerance in elite and non-elite athletes infected with SARS-CoV-2 at baseline and 6-month follow-up. Observational study documenting symptom prevalence and recovery patterns without any treatment or intervention being tested.

This retrospective cohort study followed 106 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in 2020 and assessed cognitive function at 6 months post-discharge using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. The study found that pre-existing health burden (NHS score) and acute disease severity (BCRSS) were significant predictors of cognitive deficits at follow-up.

Longitudinal study of 177 older adults hospitalized for COVID-19, assessing changes in frailty status over median 6.3 months of follow-up. Found that 34.5% showed worse frailty scores and 12.4% became frail, highlighting long-term functional decline in this population.

This prospective cohort study examined differences in health-related quality of life and well-being at 3 months post-COVID across racial, ethnic, and gender groups using the PROMIS-29 tool. Black participants reported better cognitive function and fatigue outcomes, while females and gender minoritized groups experienced worse well-being across multiple domains.

Cross-sectional study assessing prevalence of malnutrition in 1,230 COVID-19 survivors at 4-5 months post-acute illness using GLIM criteria. Found 22% malnutrition prevalence, with higher rates in older adults and males, associated with loss of appetite and dysgeusia during acute infection.

A prospective observational study of 84 long COVID patients examining hormonal status and endocrine dysfunction. Found 40.5% had at least one endocrine disorder (prediabetes, low DHEA-S, thyroid abnormalities, low testosterone/IGF-1), but no significant associations between hormone levels and long COVID symptoms.

Observational follow-up study of 189 COVID-19 patients examining whether hyponatremia at hospital admission predicts long-term cardiopulmonary complications at 6-month follow-up. Patients with early hyponatremia showed worse cardiac and pulmonary parameters at follow-up, including elevated biomarkers and right ventricular dysfunction.

This retrospective cohort study examines the association between morphometric vertebral fractures (VFs) detected during acute COVID-19 hospitalization and the subsequent development of long COVID syndrome at 6-month follow-up. The authors found that patients with VFs at admission had significantly higher prevalence of long COVID (28.6% vs 9.5% after matching), identifying VFs as an independent risk factor for long COVID occurrence.

This national cohort study examined the prevalence and risk factors for long-lasting clinical symptoms (LLCS) in French dialysis patients 6 months after acute COVID-19 infection during the pre-vaccination period. Among 1217 surveyed patients, 17.7% reported LLCS, with hospitalization, comorbidities, and longer dialysis duration being significant risk factors.

A prospective observational study assessing health-related quality of life in 137 severe COVID-19 survivors 2 years post-hospitalization using EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS questionnaires. Found significantly reduced quality of life compared to pre-COVID baseline, with female gender, unemployment, and comorbidities as key predictive factors for poor outcomes.

This cross-sectional study evaluates male reproductive health and semen parameters in 80 men 3 months post-COVID-19 recovery compared to pre-COVID control groups. While it documents reproductive outcomes in post-COVID patients, it is an observational characterization study without any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the clinical trials pipeline.

This cross-sectional study screened 255 non-vaccinated COVID-19 patients one year after discharge in China to identify undiagnosed long COVID cases and assess health-related quality of life impacts. The study found that 39.61% of patients reported long COVID symptoms and evaluated risk factors for symptom severity and quality of life outcomes, but did not test or provide any treatment intervention.

This study uses two British birth cohorts (NCDS and BCS70) to examine associations between the age of obesity onset across adulthood and COVID-19 outcomes, including long COVID. Earlier age of obesity onset was associated with increased odds of long COVID (OR 2.15 in NCDS, OR 3.01 in BCS70) and worse COVID-19 severity, though associations were partly explained by contemporaneous BMI and comorbidities.

This prospective cohort study with 14-month follow-up from UK Biobank examined the risk of comorbidities and sequelae following COVID-19 infection by comparing 16,776 COVID-positive individuals to 58,281 matched COVID-negative controls. The study identified 47 short-term comorbidities and 6 long-term sequelae, finding higher risks in older, male, overweight/obese, and hospitalized patients, but did not evaluate any specific treatment or intervention.

This prospective study examined ocular microvascular changes in 63 COVID-19 pneumonia patients two months post-discharge, measuring radial peripapillary capillary vessel density and correlations with inflammatory markers. While it found inverse correlations between specific capillary measurements and D-dimer/IL-6 levels, the study focused on acute COVID-19 complications rather than long COVID syndrome and did not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 424 COVID-19 survivors from Leishenshan Hospital followed 10 August–30 September 2020, examining sequela-free survival and associated risk factors. Anaemia treatment was protective against long-term sequelae, while anaemia on admission, delayed admission, and older age increased risk of sequelae; only 30.2% achieved sequela-free status at follow-up.

This study uses Household Pulse Survey data to assess the prevalence and mental health impact of long-COVID in a nationally representative US population sample. It finds that individuals with long-COVID report approximately twice the rates of anxiety and depression compared to those with mild/asymptomatic COVID-19, with disparities by age, sex, income, and race/ethnicity.

Observational study of 104 post-acute COVID-19 patients followed with low-field MRI exams over 6-24 months to assess lung opacity severity and evolution. Initial COVID-19 disease severity was associated with increased MRI opacity scores, and moderate to severe opacities persisted in 37% of exams beyond 6 months with no significant change over time.

A three-year longitudinal observational study of 47 COVID-19 patients using single-cell RNA sequencing and cytokine profiling to characterize immune dysregulation in long COVID. The study identifies persistent immune abnormalities and Th17-driven chronic inflammation as key features of post-COVID convalescence, but does not test or evaluate any therapeutic intervention.

Retrospective observational study of 29 hospital staff with long COVID who underwent physiological assessment (spirometry, 6-minute walk test, exercise testing) followed by an exercise rehabilitation program. The rehabilitation program resulted in significant improvements in 6-minute walk distance and maximum power output, suggesting benefits for physical conditioning and work capacity in long COVID patients.

This cross-sectional study assessed behavioral and emotional problems in 122 children recovered from acute COVID-19 hospitalization in Wuhan, China using parent-reported questionnaires. While the paper follows children post-discharge, it focuses on acute infection recovery and behavioral sequelae rather than persistent long COVID syndrome, and does not test any treatment intervention.

Observational study examining cardiac abnormalities in 2,338 COVID-19 patients with long COVID symptoms, focusing on palpitations and arrhythmias detected via 24-hour Holter monitoring and echocardiography. Found inappropriate sinus tachycardia in 60% of symptomatic patients and significant correlation between arrhythmias and reduced myocardial strain.

Observational study characterizing cardiovascular manifestations in 126 long COVID patients referred to a specialized cardiovascular clinic. Describes symptoms, diagnostic findings, and identifies that 77% had no new cardiac diagnosis but exhibited exercise intolerance and cardiovascular symptoms without identifiable pathology.

A prospective case series of 630 young COVID-19 patients evaluated 2 weeks to 1 month post-infection for left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS) alterations and correlation with long COVID symptoms. The study found LV-GLS alterations in 52.5% of patients, correlated with dyspnea and chest pain, with 87.5% showing spontaneous improvement at one-month follow-up without intervention.

This retrospective case series evaluates Enhanced External Counterpulsation (EECP) as a treatment for long COVID symptoms in 7 outpatient centers. Results show significant improvements in fatigue, cardiovascular markers, activity status, and 6-minute walk distance, with all previously unable-to-work patients returning to work post-therapy.

Prospective multicenter cohort study examining long-term pulmonary sequelae in COVID-19 survivors over 3 years, comparing outcomes between those with and without diabetes. Diabetes was identified as an independent predictor of persistent radiological abnormalities and pulmonary diffusion dysfunction, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

Retrospective descriptive study of healthcare workers at Charles Nicolle Hospital who experienced persistent dyspnea upon return to work after COVID-19 infection between September-December 2020. The study documents prevalence (13.7% of 588 infected staff), demographic characteristics, and clinical features of post-COVID dyspnea but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This study documents the prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection and associated symptoms in 760 healthcare workers during Omicron BA.5/BF.7 and XBB.1.5 waves between December 2022 and July 2023. While it identifies long COVID symptoms (fatigue, memory loss, cough) as secondary observations, the paper does not evaluate or test any treatment or intervention—it is primarily an epidemiological survey of infection patterns and symptom prevalence.

This cross-sectional study assessed pulmonary function in 53 healthcare professionals with persistent post-COVID complaints at ~3 months post-infection. Key findings include decreased DLCO in 39.6% of participants and persistent symptoms in 47.2%, with correlations between delayed return to work and lower DLCO values.

Longitudinal study comparing cognitive performance before and after COVID-19 infection in 276 essential workers with COVID-19 versus 217 controls without infection. Found significant decline in cognitive throughput post-infection, particularly in those with severe COVID-19 and PASC, equivalent to 10.6 years of normal aging.

This prospective multicenter cohort study examines endothelial function in 798 long COVID patients using digital thermal monitoring (E4-Diagnose Polymath). The study found that 77.4% of patients had long COVID symptoms, with fatigue (42.2%) and chest pain being significantly associated with endothelial dysfunction.

A retrospective cohort study examining long COVID presentation and risk factors in an underserved urban population in Chicago using manual extraction from electronic health records. The study found that hospitalization, BMI >30, and female sex were associated with increased odds of long COVID, with certain preexisting conditions predicting analogous long COVID symptoms.

Prospective cohort study examining menstrual cycle changes following SARS-CoV-2 infection in 127 women from the Arizona CoVHORT study. Found that 16% reported menstrual changes (primarily irregular menstruation and increased PMS symptoms) and those with changes reported more COVID-19 symptoms including fatigue, headache, and shortness of breath.

Prospective cohort study of 46,579 women examining whether pre-existing endometriosis is associated with increased risk of long COVID-19. Found that women with laparoscopically-confirmed endometriosis had a 22% higher risk of developing long COVID-19 compared to those without endometriosis history.

This cross-sectional study compared cognitive function and inflammatory markers in 66 COVID-19 survivors versus 79 healthy controls at 15 months post-discharge, finding impaired executive function on the Trails test and elevated TNF-α levels negatively correlated with cognitive performance. The study identifies inflammation as a potential mechanism underlying long-term cognitive impairment but does not test any treatment intervention.

Retrospective analysis of 809 COVID-19 events in 778 kidney transplant recipients characterizing post-COVID-19 cardiovascular disease incidence and risk factors over 1 year. Post-COVID-19 CVD occurred in 8.7% of patients, with COVID-19 hospitalization conferring equivalent cardiovascular risk as previous CVD history.

Prospective observational study of 930 liver transplant recipients infected with Omicron in China, following outcomes and post-COVID-19 symptoms through May 2023. While the study documents common post-COVID symptoms (fatigue 36.9%, memory loss 35.7%, sleep disturbance 23.9%) and finds protective effects of vaccination, it is a passive observational cohort with no active treatment intervention evaluated.

Retrospective population-based cohort study examining long-term sequelae risk following SARS-CoV-2 Delta/Omicron infection in pregnant women compared to test-negative pregnant women and non-pregnant infected women. Found pregnant women had 1.6× higher risk of postacute sequelae vs uninfected pregnant controls and 13.4× higher risk vs non-pregnant infected women, though absolute incidence was <1%.

This retrospective cohort study uses the National COVID Cohort Collaborative to compare PASC prevalence between solid organ transplant recipients and non-immunosuppressed patients using propensity score matching. It identifies transplant status, infection severity, age, and immunosuppressive medications as independent risk factors for PASC but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective population-based cohort study comparing long COVID risk in Singaporean transplant recipients infected with Omicron vs test-negatives during 2022. Found no significantly elevated overall risk of postacute sequelae in the vaccinated/boosted transplant cohort, though autoimmune and neurologic sequelae showed increased risk compared to test-negatives.

Population-based cohort study assessing the prevalence of ongoing long COVID symptoms and related disability ~2 years after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection in Michigan adults. Found that 24% reported ongoing long COVID with substantial increases in cognition, mobility, independent living, and self-care disability compared to pre-infection baseline.

A retrospective cohort study of 1,802 patients evaluated at a comprehensive post-COVID center in Chicago, assessing specialty clinic utilization and clinical testing patterns. While it documents high prevalence of neurologic, pulmonary, and cardiac abnormalities in long COVID patients, it does not test or evaluate a specific intervention or treatment.

This study compared autonomic dysfunction prevalence and severity in 33 long COVID (PASC) patients versus 33 POTS patients and 33 healthy controls using beat-to-beat hemodynamic monitoring and symptom scales. The majority (79%) of PASC patients met criteria for POTS and showed significantly impaired autonomic function and quality of life compared to controls, supporting routine autonomic testing in long COVID management.

A Japanese multicenter cohort study of 26 institutions followed hospitalized COVID-19 patients over 12 months to identify risk factors for prolonged fatigue in long COVID. The study found that asthma was an independent risk factor for persistent general fatigue, which was the most interfering long COVID symptom in daily life.

Retrospective analysis of 2,389 COVID-19 survivors examining the impact of cardiac and cerebrovascular complications during acute hospitalization on long-term mortality outcomes. Study found that myocardial infarction during hospitalization was an independent predictor of increased mortality at 2.4-year follow-up, but does not study long COVID interventions or sequelae.

Retrospective cohort study comparing cardiovascular event risk in 319 COVID-19+ patients versus 1,036 COVID-19- controls from a healthcare system, followed for median 6 months post-infection. Found that SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with increased risk of cardiovascular morbidity/mortality and all-cause mortality in the late post-COVID period.

This US nationwide cohort study characterizes disability burden in 7,926 long COVID patients at baseline, measuring physical mobility, instrumental activities of daily living, and mental fatigue. The study finds 65% of long COVID participants have at least one disability compared to 6% in resolved COVID controls, identifying risk factors and protective factors like vaccination.

This cross-sectional study compared cognitive function in 210 long COVID patients versus 369 normal controls using comprehensive neuropsychological testing. Patients with long COVID had 3.6× higher odds of cognitive impairment, with 44% showing cognitive deficits ~7 months post-infection; higher BMI was the only differentiator among cognitively impaired long COVID patients.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between sedentary lifestyle and risk of acute and post-acute COVID-19 sequelae in 4,850 participants. Finds that prolonged sedentary behavior is independently associated with higher risk of multiple post-COVID symptoms, while physical inactivity showed contradictory protective effects for some outcomes like insomnia.

Retrospective cohort study of 363 long COVID patients referred for cardiovascular evaluation to assess whether persistent cardiovascular symptoms are associated with objective cardiac abnormalities. Found that only 23.4% had cardiac causes, with 14.3% attributed to COVID, suggesting most symptoms lack objective cardiac explanation.

Retrospective cohort study of 364 COVID-19 patients characterizing persistent symptoms, radiological findings, and functional outcomes at follow-up. Identified fatigue as the most common symptom, chest CT alterations in 76% of patients, and pulmonary dysfunction in 44.7%, with higher risk in hospitalized patients and those receiving corticosteroids or hydroxychloroquine.

Prospective cohort study examining the correlation between pulmonary function test (PFT) abnormalities and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures in COVID-19 patients at 3, 6, and ≥12 months post-infection. Found that patients with normal PFTs had worse mobility impairment and anxiety scores, while HRQoL impairment was not explained by PFT abnormalities alone.

Population-based cohort study comparing cardiovascular outcomes in 129,864 SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals versus 519,456 matched uninfected controls over 260 days median follow-up. Found significantly elevated risk of major adverse cardiovascular events and myocardial infarction in infected individuals, particularly those with severe acute COVID-19.

This cross-sectional study recruited long COVID patients from an online survey and compared objective and subjective audiological measurements (hearing thresholds, otoacoustic emissions) across three groups: long COVID, recovered COVID, and non-COVID controls. No clinically significant hearing loss was detected in long COVID patients, though minor frequency-specific differences were observed.

A prospective cohort study following 254 COVID-19 hospitalized patients over 12 months to characterize functional recovery trajectory and identify predictors of recovery. At 12 months, over half demonstrated clinically important deficits in mobility and cognition, with persistent fatigue, dyspnea, and psychological distress.

This case-control study compared recurrence of audio-vestibular disorders in 50 patients following COVID-19 breakthrough infection versus 50 patients following vaccination. While the paper addresses long COVID sequelae, it is excluded as a secondary analysis comparing outcomes between two groups rather than testing a specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 57 COVID-19 patients with laryngeal dysfunction, examining prevalence of dysphonia, dysphagia, and stenosis, and evaluating outcomes of voice therapy and procedural interventions. Voice therapy improved symptoms in 65% of patients, with improvements also seen in quality of life measures for those with laryngotracheal stenosis.

A single-center prospective cohort study characterizing post-COVID-19 syndrome (PASC) in an ethnically diverse population over one year of follow-up. The study aims to identify clinical phenotypes and biomarkers to predict and manage post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Retrospective chart review of tracheostomy and ventilation management in 213 COVID-19 patients admitted to a long-term acute care hospital from April 2020 to November 2021. Study focuses on acute-phase respiratory management and laryngeal findings in hospitalized patients, not long COVID sequelae or post-acute treatment interventions.

A retrospective observational study evaluating specialized outpatient rehabilitation programs for long COVID in Alberta, Canada, examining program utilization, patient-reported outcomes, and healthcare costs over 180-day pre/post-enrollment periods. Results showed small but statistically significant improvements in functional status and quality of life, modest reductions in healthcare costs, and an ICER approaching the Canadian cost-effectiveness threshold, though authors note these represent preliminary associations rather than causal effects.

Prospective case-controlled study examining olfactory bulb morphology changes in 29 COVID-19 patients with anosmia/hyposmia (Group 1) compared to 24 normosmic post-COVID patients (Group 2) and 25 uninfected controls (Group 3), with 12 weeks of olfactory training intervention. Following olfactory training, Group 1 showed significant improvements in olfactory bulb volume and olfactory function scores, providing evidence for the effectiveness of olfactory training in treating long-lasting post-COVID olfactory loss.

Population-based observational study examining the association between pre-infection COVID-19 vaccination status and long COVID prevalence in Michigan adults. Reports that vaccinated individuals had 40-60% lower long COVID prevalence compared to unvaccinated controls, but this is a secondary analysis of existing surveillance data without testing an intervention in long COVID patients.

Retrospective cohort study of 363,825 US Veterans examining the prevalence and risk factors for post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC). Found 45% prevalence and identified diabetes, severe acute infection, age 50-64, and Black race as strongest risk factors, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study of 832 non-diabetic COVID-19 patients in Tunisia examining development of new-onset diabetes during and after acute COVID-19 hospitalization. Found that new-onset diabetes during acute infection did not significantly impact mortality or hospitalization duration, with 39% remission rate at 24.5-month follow-up.

Retrospective observational study of COVID-19 patients with chemosensory loss, investigating concomitant hearing loss and tinnitus symptoms. Study found 26.2% of respondents reported audiological symptoms with poor recovery rates, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study uses UK Biobank data to evaluate whether COVID-19-induced brain MRI changes increase long-term dementia risk via the front-door criterion causal inference approach. The study finds that brain structural changes attributable to COVID-19 are associated with a 9% higher dementia hazard over 4.7 years of follow-up.

Retrospective analysis of 117 patients treated for acute COVID-19 at a long-term acute care hospital, describing rehabilitation outcomes during the acute/post-acute phase. While patients improved significantly in functional status and ventilator weaning, this is not a long COVID study as it addresses acute/post-acute COVID-19 complications rather than the persistent syndrome that develops weeks to months after infection.

A prospective longitudinal study following 52 adults hospitalized for severe COVID-19 through inpatient rehabilitation and post-acute telephone follow-up at 3, 6, and 12 months. The study identified distinct phenotypes of post-acute COVID-19 based on physical, cognitive, and emotional functioning, with 31% experiencing persistent symptoms across all domains at 6 months.

Prospective cohort study evaluating the impact of COVID-19 on frailty, sarcopenia, and functionality after hospital discharge in 68 patients followed for up to 12 months. The study is excluded because it appears to be a protocol with only preliminary results at 1 and 4 months; no full treatment intervention is being tested, only passive monitoring and assessment.

Retrospective analysis of 19,792 COVID-19 patients examining PASC prevalence (42.8%) and factors associated with rehabilitation utilization. Study identifies demographic and clinical predictors of PASC development but does not test any treatment intervention—it is observational and descriptive only.

Longitudinal observational study examining fibrosis levels in patients coinfected with hepatitis and COVID-19 over 12 months (2020-2021). Found that coinfected patients showed progression from low fibrosis (F0) at baseline to high fibrosis (F4) after one year as a post-COVID condition, suggesting SARS-CoV-2 infection exacerbates liver injury in hepatitis patients.

This cross-sectional analysis of Women's Health Initiative postmenopausal women identifies risk factors for long COVID syndrome using machine learning on baseline health data and COVID survey responses. The study reports that 30% of 1,237 COVID-positive respondents (mean age 83) developed long COVID, with key risk factors including weight loss, mobility limitations, and conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and heart valve procedures.

This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effectiveness of a 12-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program (telerehabilitation or face-to-face) in 184 COVID-19 patients referred to rehabilitation medicine across two Malaysian tertiary hospitals. Patients showed significant symptom improvement, with Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale scores improving from 2.7 at baseline to 1.7 at 3-month follow-up, and 32.1% were diagnosed with long COVID syndrome.

Retrospective cohort study of 184 post-COVID-19 patients admitted to long-term acute care hospitals (LTACHs), measuring Six Minute Walk Test (6MWT) distance improvements during standard inpatient rehabilitation. Nearly one-third of patients showed clinically meaningful improvement in walking distance, though many remained far below thresholds for independent community ambulation, highlighting persisting severe mobility dysfunction in the most critically ill COVID-19 survivors.

Retrospective cohort describing baseline characteristics of 94 patients referred to an outpatient post-COVID rehabilitation program. Study focuses on symptom profiles and patient demographics without evaluating treatment outcomes or efficacy.

Observational study of 324 long COVID patients receiving outpatient rehabilitation, examining psychological, cognitive, and quality-of-life outcomes. Finds high rates of anxiety (38%), depression (31.8%), PTSD (43%), and cognitive impairment (17.5%), with significant disparities by race and socioeconomic status.

Retrospective cohort study of 70 long COVID patients with cognitive difficulties treated with speech-language pathology-based cognitive rehabilitation in an outpatient setting. Patients who completed treatment showed significant improvements in self-reported cognitive quality of life (90% met goals), though anxiety at baseline limited treatment effectiveness and objective memory measures showed no significant change.

A cross-sectional study examining psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, depression, PTSD) in 180 COVID-19 patients at 6 weeks post-discharge. The study found high rates of psychiatric morbidity but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective multicenter cohort study of 205 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examining the biopsychosocial factors contributing to persistent post-COVID fatigue and cognitive complaints at 9 months post-discharge. Found that psychological and social factors significantly complement biomedical factors in explaining fatigue and cognitive symptoms, suggesting multidomain treatment including psychosocial care is important.

A prospective cohort study following 46,258 COVID-19 patients for 2 years in primary care to determine the prevalence of mental disorders and long COVID syndrome. While the paper studies long COVID, it is observational without any treatment intervention—it characterizes the natural progression of mental health outcomes and long COVID prevalence rather than testing a therapeutic approach.

Longitudinal prospective observational study following 40 long COVID patients and 40 age/sex-matched controls over 3 years to assess symptom progression and treatment impact. Found that aerobic/anaerobic physical exercise was associated with improved pain severity, while dyspnea also improved overall; most other symptoms remained stable.

This prospective cohort study assessed cognitive functioning in 38 university-educated patients with post-COVID-19 condition using a comprehensive neuropsychological test battery. The study found significant deficits in verbal learning, memory, and selective attention, with approximately 50% of participants scoring below normative standards on memory measures.

This cross-sectional study compares coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) in ANOCA patients with and without a history of severe COVID-19 infection, finding higher rates of CMD in the COVID group. The study is observational and does not test any intervention or treatment, making it ineligible for the clinical trials extraction pipeline.

This prospective cohort study followed 108 survivors of severe COVID-19 ARDS at 6, 12, and 24 months post-ICU discharge to characterize functional disability and physiological changes. The study identified risk factors for persistent long-term functional sequelae but did not evaluate or test any specific intervention or treatment.

This multicenter Italian study uses nailfold videocapillaroscopy (NVC) to detect microvascular abnormalities in long COVID patients compared to recovered COVID-19 patients and healthy controls. The study demonstrates progressive capillary damage in long COVID patients including reduced capillary density, dilations, and microhemorrhages, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This study evaluated psychiatric symptoms (PTSD, depression, anxiety, insomnia, OC symptoms) in 402 COVID-19 survivors at one month post-hospitalization, examining relationships with inflammatory markers. While it documents psychiatric sequelae in acute COVID survivors, it does not study long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks-months post-infection) and does not test any treatment intervention.

A monocentric comparative cohort study evaluating multidisciplinary outpatient rehabilitation outcomes in 227 post-COVID patients versus 370 patients with other chronic conditions (orthopedic, cardiovascular, metabolic, pulmonary). Post-COVID patients achieved the highest physical function gains (6MWT +60.4m) but reported persistently lower quality of life despite improvements, suggesting targeted mental health and fatigue interventions are needed.

This case-control study examined blood pressure responses to orthostatic challenge in 31 PASC patients versus 32 healthy controls using head-up tilt testing. The study found exaggerated orthostatic blood pressure responses in 34.7% of PASC patients compared to 6.4% of controls, suggesting autonomic dysfunction as a PASC phenotype.

Retrospective cohort study of 10,024 vaccinated individuals with breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to unvaccinated controls, examining post-acute COVID-19 sequelae over 6 months. Vaccination was associated with significantly lower risk of several serious complications (respiratory failure, ICU admission, VTE, seizures, psychotic disorder) but not long-COVID features, renal disease, mood, anxiety, or sleep disorders.

Retrospective observational study of 163 critical COVID-19 survivors attending ICU recovery clinics, examining physical and cognitive impairments and community-based rehabilitation utilization. While patients show significant frailty and cognitive impairment, this is a passive observational study without an assigned treatment intervention—it describes rehabilitation use but does not test or evaluate a specific treatment.

Prospective cohort study of 226 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors evaluating psychiatric and cognitive outcomes at 1 and 3 months post-discharge. Found persistent depressive symptoms in 35.8% and cognitive impairment in 78%, with systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) predicting depression and neurocognitive dysfunction.

This prospective cohort study examined whether pre-infection sleep quality, duration, and insomnia severity predicted long-term symptoms in 713 COVID-19 survivors followed from April 2020 to April 2022. Poor baseline sleep metrics significantly increased the risk of post-COVID-19 symptoms and prolonged recovery, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Retrospective cohort study using TriNetX EHR data to compare neurological and psychiatric sequelae risks in 280,173 hospitalized and 46,573 ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients versus matched controls over 2 years. Found elevated risks of neurological and psychiatric outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19 patients with long-standing trajectories, but similar or lower risks in ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients compared to ICU admission for other causes.

Prospective cohort study comparing cognitive impairment across multiple domains in 417 post-COVID-19 patients versus 151 non-infected controls from the Mount Sinai Health System registry. Found significantly greater odds of executive dysfunction in post-COVID patients (OR 2.19), particularly among those requiring inpatient hospital care, but no significant associations in other cognitive domains.

A retrospective cohort study of 33,908 patients using electronic health records to evaluate whether omega-3 PUFA supplementation reduces psychiatric sequelae following COVID-19 infection. The study found that omega-3 supplementation significantly reduced risks of depression, anxiety, and insomnia in the year after COVID-19 diagnosis, with hazard ratios of 0.828, 0.833, and 0.679 respectively.

This prospective study evaluated cognitive, psychiatric, and inflammatory markers in 72 COVID-19 survivors 2-12 months post-hospitalization, comparing them to controls. Survivors showed significant deficits in global cognition, memory, and executive function, with elevated TNF-α and IL-1β correlating with brain microstructural damage and cognitive impairment.

Retrospective cohort study examining associations between COVID-19 vaccination status and incident psychiatric disorders in long COVID patients across different variant periods in Japan. The study analyzes existing medical claims data rather than testing or evaluating a specific treatment intervention for long COVID.

Prospective cohort study examining the relationship between systemic inflammation, neuroaxonal damage biomarkers (NfL), and long-term cognitive impairment in 96 severe COVID-19 ICU survivors. Findings show prolonged inflammation correlates with increased NfL levels and cognitive deficits at 6-month follow-up, but no treatment intervention is tested.

Longitudinal observational study comparing mental health outcomes in 8,348 Chinese children/adolescents with and without COVID-19 infection over 7 months. COVID-infected youth showed significantly worsened depression, anxiety, stress, insomnia, and emotional symptoms compared to non-infected peers, with cognitive dysfunction and respiratory/GI symptoms as key risk factors.

This prospective cohort study examines the prevalence and characteristics of cognitive impairment (brain fog) in children and young people up to 12 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection (Omicron variant). The study finds cognitive impairment is not systematically treated, but rather observed as a long COVID symptom that correlates with poor mental health, fatigue, and sleep problems.

Prospective cohort study examining associations between childhood abuse and risk of post-COVID conditions across three large cohorts (NHS-II, NHS3, Growing Up Today Study). Found a dose-dependent relationship with 42% higher risk in those with severe versus no childhood abuse, with psychological and lifestyle factors mediating 25.5% of the association.

A two-year prospective cohort study examining relationships between serum cytokines, inflammatory markers, and cognitive/psychiatric outcomes in 108 long-COVID patients assessed at ~7 and ~24 months post-discharge. Found associations between acute COVID severity, sleepiness, and anxiety/depression, with proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory indices showing potential roles in neuropsychological outcomes.

Prospective cohort study examining serum antineuronal antibodies in 314 patients with post-COVID-19 condition, comparing to matched controls without PCC symptoms. Found low prevalence of autoantibodies (12.1% in PCC vs 5.7% in controls), with ICU admission during acute COVID-19 as the only significant predictor, suggesting systemic immune activation rather than specific autoantibody-mediated mechanisms.

Cohort study of 52 COVID-19 survivors assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety, insomnia, PTSD) at baseline and 24-60 weeks post-infection. Found worsening of psychiatric symptoms over time, particularly PTSD, but no intervention was tested or evaluated.

This case-control study compared acute-phase immunological markers (white blood cell counts) between long COVID patients who developed anosognosia (lack of awareness of cognitive deficits) 6-9 months post-infection and those who did not. The study found that monocyte percentage in the acute phase predicted chronic anosognosia but did not test any intervention or treatment.

The CONGA study is a prospective cohort following COVID-19 positive patients to characterize neuropsychiatric sequelae over five years, reporting baseline results from 200 participants at ~125 days post-infection. The study documents high rates of fatigue (68.5%), hyposmia/hypogeusia (30%), and cognitive impairment compared to controls, with racial disparities in cognitive testing.

Prospective cohort study of 96 severe COVID-19 survivors assessed 6 months post-ICU discharge for cognitive outcomes and their relationship to anti-inflammatory therapies (dexamethasone and/or tocilizumab). Found 27% had objective cognitive impairment, but anti-inflammatory therapy did not improve overall cognitive performance, though combination therapy was associated with worse executive function.

This cross-sectional study assessed sleep quality and its predictors in 368 post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients and 123 healthy controls from the NAUTILUS Project, examining relationships with emotional, cognitive, and functional variables. The results showed significantly worse sleep quality in PCC patients compared to controls, with depression, anxiety, quality of life, and physical activity identified as key predictors, but no treatment intervention was tested or evaluated.

This prospective cohort study assessed 184 COVID-19 patients (stratified by hospitalization severity) and 53 controls at three and six months post-infection, measuring subjective and objective cognitive symptoms alongside psychological factors. The study found that one-third of patients reported subjective cognitive impairment regardless of acute disease severity, which was associated with depression and PTSD but not objective cognitive test results.

Cross-sectional study assessing subjective cognitive complaints and objective cognitive screening results in 87 African American post-COVID patients at a PASC clinic. Found high concordance between self-reported cognitive concerns and objective impairment, with depression and anxiety associated with subjective complaints.

This study uses diffusion basis spectrum imaging (DBSI) to examine neuroinflammatory markers in COVID-19 cases versus controls using pre- and post-infection UK Biobank neuroimaging data (N=416). It found increased vasogenic edema in specific brain regions but did not assess or deliver any treatment intervention to participants.

This retrospective cohort study followed 223 non-severe COVID-19 patients in Shanghai for 9 months to characterize long COVID sequelae and identify predictors of fatigue symptoms. The study found that 48.4% reported sequelae lasting >4 weeks, with fatigue being the most common (15.7%), and identified hospitalization duration, non-use of antivirals, and immune markers (IL-6, CD16+CD56+ NK cells) as independent risk factors.

Prospective controlled cohort study of 404 SARS-CoV-2-positive and 105 negative youth (ages 12-25) investigating risk factors for fatigue severity at 6 months post-infection. Baseline symptom severity and psychosocial factors (loneliness, neuroticism) were major risk factors for persistent fatigue, rather than biomarkers or infection status.

This study examined acute serum protein biomarkers and the prevalence of persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms in 97 South African SARS-CoV-2 positive patients at least 6 months post-infection. Over half of participants had persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms including cognitive impairment (44%), though acute biomarkers were not significantly associated with these outcomes.

This longitudinal cohort study from the LoTECA project followed 93 young people with long COVID to identify predictors of fatigue progression from 6 to 12 months post-infection. Non-European ethnicity, higher interferon gamma levels, and lower RR-interval (higher resting heart rate) during acute infection were significant predictors of worsening fatigue, explaining 21% of variance.

A prospective cohort study of 63 COVID-19 patients examining the association between post-acute olfactory impairment and long-term physical capacity over 24 months. The study found that olfactory impairment in the early post-acute phase was significantly associated with reduced physical capacity at all follow-ups, with the association strengthening over time.

This study examines dual inflammation (schizophrenia + COVID-19) and its impact on cognitive function in 119 schizophrenia patients with COVID-19 history versus controls. While the paper includes long COVID patients (70 recruited 2 years post-recovery), it is primarily focused on schizophrenia-specific cognitive impairment and inflammation, not on long COVID as the main condition or on evaluating a treatment intervention for long COVID.

Prospective cohort study tracking cognitive function over 42 months in 1,553 long COVID patients from the Mount Sinai registry, assessing attention, working memory, processing speed, executive function, and memory. While most cognitive domains improved over time, processing speed and executive functioning remained significantly below normative values, indicating lasting cognitive burden of long COVID.

Prospective observational study of COVID-19 ICU survivors examining cognitive impairment and subjective cognitive complaints at 6 and 12 months post-discharge. Cognitive impairment declined from 23.1% at 6 months to 11.1% at 12 months, while subjective complaints remained high and were associated with mental health problems and fatigue.

This study analyzes immune markers from acute COVID-19 hospitalization to identify predictors of post-COVID fatigue 6-9 months later. While it studies long COVID outcomes, it is a secondary analysis examining associations in existing patient data rather than testing a treatment intervention.

This observational study measured plasma levels of orexin A, substance P, bradykinin, and DABK in 78 acute COVID-19 ICU patients, 14 severe COVID-19 survivors at 2.5-year follow-up, and 14 healthy controls. Changes in the bradykinin axis and elevated substance P in long-term survivors were associated with post-COVID syndrome and post-ICU complications, suggesting these biomarkers may relate to long-term neuropsychological impairments.

Prospective multicenter study following 211 severe COVID-19 patients (112 ward, 99 ICU) at 45 days and 6 months post-hospital discharge to assess respiratory sequelae and lung function recovery. Lung function measures improved significantly between 45 days and 6 months in both groups, with greater improvements in ICU patients, though dyspnea persisted in ~65% at 6 months.

This study uses PET imaging with [11C]SL25.1188 to measure astrogliosis markers in the brains of long COVID patients with persistent depressive and cognitive symptoms, comparing 21 cases to 21 healthy controls. The research confirms elevated monoamine oxidase B-labeled astrogliosis across multiple brain regions in COVID-DC participants, particularly since the Omicron variant, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study of 45 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients (22 with PCS, 23 with PCS-ME/CFS) examining olfactory function and fatigue over 28 months using standardized testing. Found olfactory improvements in all patients by 20 months, with odor identification correlating with cognitive function and physical performance, suggesting potential prognostic value.

Study evaluates systemic microvascular endothelial function and plasma cytokine levels in 20 patients 12-15 months after acute COVID-19 using laser doppler perfusion monitoring and multiplex immunoassay. Findings show improved microvascular reactivity and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels post-recovery compared to acute phase, with no differences from healthy controls.

A retrospective cohort study following 24 patients with myocardial dysfunction during acute COVID-19 infection over an average of 8 months post-hospitalization using speckle tracking echocardiography. The study found significant improvement in global longitudinal strain at follow-up, though left ventricular ejection fraction remained stable, with prolonged symptom duration and elevated inflammatory markers associated with worse LVEF outcomes.

Prospective cohort study following 31 severe COVID-19 survivors at 30, 90, and 180 days post-discharge to assess pulmonary function, exercise capacity, and symptom persistence. Found persistent dyspnea, reduced exercise capacity, and restrictive spirometry patterns in a substantial proportion at 6 months, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

A prospective cohort study following 139 COVID-19 survivors at discharge, 1 month, 2 months, and 6 months to document functional disability and persistent symptoms. The study found 51% experienced functional limitations at 6 months, with vaccination emerging as a protective factor, and recommends multidisciplinary rehabilitation approaches.

Prospective cohort study (March-October 2021) comparing health outcomes in 482 Kazakhstani participants stratified by COVID-19 severity (118 hospitalized vs 364 outpatient). Patients with severe COVID-19 had significantly higher risk of infectious/parasitic diseases, respiratory complications, eye pathologies, and subsequent hospitalization.

Retrospective cohort study investigating long COVID prevalence and associated risk factors among COVID-19-infected university students and staff in Thailand, finding 51.9% prevalence with fatigue as the most common symptom. Female sex, age 20-29, comorbidities, severe acute COVID-19, and repeat infections were significantly associated with long COVID development.

Descriptive observational cohort study of 92 post-COVID syndrome patients followed at a teaching hospital in Brazil from June 2021 to June 2022, documenting clinical profiles, symptom prevalence, and natural disease progression. Most patients showed gradual improvement over time, with chronic fatigue (68.6%) and brain fog (73.4%) as predominant symptoms.

This observational study characterizes SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses, inflammatory markers, and antibody levels in 70 individuals longitudinally over 9 months, comparing those with and without post-acute sequelae (PASC). The study finds differences in CD8+ T cell degranulation and interferon-γ responses between PASC and non-PASC groups, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective follow-up cohort study examining post-COVID gastrointestinal sequelae in 320 COVID-19 patients and 600 healthy controls over 6 months using Rome IV criteria. Found that COVID-19 led to significantly higher rates of new-onset functional GI disorders at 3 and 6 months compared to controls, with some cases showing underlying malabsorption, but no treatment intervention was provided or tested.

Prospective 1-year follow-up study of 350 COVID-19 patients examining symptom profiles, functional abilities, and quality of life outcomes in India. Study found 57.7% of participants still experiencing symptoms at 1 year with improved but persistent fatigue, dyspnea, and musculoskeletal symptoms, indicating long COVID symptoms are not self-limiting.

This is a nested follow-up survey within a larger observational cohort study of COVID-19 hospitalized patients, assessing persistent gastrointestinal symptoms and disorders of gut-brain interaction 12-18 months post-hospitalization. The study found high prevalence of DGBIs and identified psychological trauma as a key predictor of GI symptom severity, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Observational study following 90 COVID-19 patients from a Brazilian tertiary hospital at 2 and 6 months post-discharge to characterize post-COVID syndrome and its association with acute disease severity. High prevalence of persistent symptoms (dyspnea 47-56%, fatigue 50%, muscle weakness 41-50%) was observed, with fatigue and cough more common in patients with severe/critical acute illness, though differences diminished by 6-month follow-up.

This population-based cohort study compared mental health outcomes in 6,098 adult survivors of COVID-19 critical illness versus 2,568 survivors of non-COVID-19 pneumonia critical illness in Ontario, Canada.
