Findings show 28.9% reported new-onset POTS with significantly worse health outcomes, higher symptom burden, and greater psychosocial distress compared to long COVID patients without POTS.

A prospective cross-sectional assessment of cognitive function, mental health symptoms, and functional decline in 82 COVID-19 survivors (~4 months post-diagnosis) at Johns Hopkins Post-Acute COVID-19 Team clinic. Found 67% had abnormal cognitive scores (primarily processing speed, verbal fluency, learning, memory), with 35% reporting depression, anxiety, or functional decline; ICU patients showed greater severity of cognitive impairment.

Retrospective cohort study comparing emergency visits and hospitalizations for cardiovascular diagnoses between 177,892 SARS-CoV-2 positive adults and matched negative controls in the postacute phase (>3 months). Found significantly elevated risks for diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, and kidney injury in COVID-19 survivors, particularly those hospitalized during acute infection.

Longitudinal observational study of 75 long COVID patients undergoing neuropsychological testing at ~7 months post-infection and 6-month follow-up. Found that 38.7% had low NP performance initially; while some domains improved by follow-up, persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms remained in most participants with minimal clinical improvement.

This retrospective cohort study examined associations between post-traumatic stress disorder symptom trajectories and long COVID risk among 5,361 World Trade Center Health Registry enrollees with COVID-19 infection. All PTSS trajectory groups showed elevated risk of long COVID compared to the resilient group, with RRs ranging from 1.46-1.86, suggesting that pre-existing mental health conditions are a significant risk factor for developing long COVID.

Cross-sectional assessment of cognitive, depressive, and anxiety symptoms in 90 previously independent mild COVID-19 patients during hospitalization (Nov 2020–Mar 2021). Found 66.7% had impaired cognition (MoCA < 23), particularly in executive function and memory, with age-related severity differences, but no elevated depression or anxiety.

This cross-sectional study examines the association between loneliness (overall, emotional, and social subtypes) and cognitive function in long COVID patients versus recovered controls. The findings show that emotional and overall loneliness are independently linked to objective cognitive difficulties like reduced verbal fluency and memory, suggesting loneliness as a potential intervention target for cognitive outcomes in long COVID.

Observational study analyzing Reddit posts to examine the association between COVID-19-induced loss of smell/taste and subsequent depression or suicidal ideation risk. The study found users reporting anosmia/ageusia had 30% higher risk of mental health crises, with peak risk occurring >100 days post-infection.

This nationwide population-based cohort study examines long-term impacts of prior COVID-19 on severe asthma exacerbations and mortality in Korean adults. While it studies post-COVID outcomes, it focuses on asthma complications rather than long COVID syndrome itself, and is an observational cohort study with no treatment intervention tested.

Prospective cohort study examining mental health outcomes (anxiety, depression, PTSD) and health-related quality of life in COVID-19 survivors stratified by disease severity (moderate, severe, critical) at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-infection. Found persistent mental health burden and reduced quality of life across all severity groups at 2 years, with no significant differences between severity groups except lower PTSD in critically ill patients.

This study evaluated the impact of add-on Ayurveda regimen (Dasamoolkadutrayadi Kashayam and Guluchyadi Kwatham) combined with standard care in acute COVID-19 patients, with extended 9-month follow-up to assess for post-COVID sequelae. Results showed that patients receiving the add-on Ayurveda treatment experienced accelerated symptomatic recovery and early hospital discharge, with no additional late effects or complications observed in the post-COVID phase compared to standard care controls.

Retrospective cohort study examining long-term cognitive and frailty outcomes in older COVID-19 survivors, comparing those with and without in-hospital delirium. Delirium was associated with long-term cognitive decline but not frailty or mortality at ~2-year follow-up.

Retrospective cohort study of 31,084 COVID-19 patients comparing post-acute respiratory symptoms (days 28-180) between patients with and without asthma history. Asthma patients had significantly higher risk of shortness of breath, cough, bronchospasm, and wheezing during the post-COVID period.

A prospective cohort study of 228 elderly residents in Chinese long-term care facilities examining longitudinal changes in long COVID symptoms over three assessment waves from January 2023 to August 2024. The study found progressive symptom improvement over time, with women reporting more severe symptoms and advanced age associated with slower recovery, but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study of 186 severe COVID-19 patients admitted to post-acute care facilities, followed for 180 days to identify characteristics associated with functional outcomes. Found substantial functional improvements from admission to discharge and follow-up, with baseline functional status and comorbidities predicting long-term outcomes, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This retrospective cohort study examines pre-existing medical conditions associated with increased risk of developing post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in 1,224 longitudinal study participants. The analysis identifies respiratory, gastrointestinal, and autoimmune conditions as significant risk factors for PASC but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Nationwide Danish cohort study comparing hospitalization rates and post-COVID sequelae in patients with chronic inflammatory diseases (IBD, RA, SpA, PsA) versus others following COVID-19 hospitalization. Patients with inflammatory diseases had significantly increased risk of respiratory disease and infection-related hospitalizations but no increased risk of nervous system disease or death.

Prospective observational study examining the impact of acute muscle mass loss during COVID-19 hospitalization on long-term fatigue, myalgia, and healthcare costs in 80 survivors. Patients with high muscle loss showed greater prevalence of fatigue (76% vs 46%) and myalgia (66% vs 36%), and significantly higher healthcare costs at 6-month follow-up.

Retrospective cohort study examining asthma exacerbation rates in 12,719 pediatric and adult asthma patients with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection versus uninfected controls. Finds significantly elevated exacerbation risk and cumulative incidence in COVID-infected patients, particularly those hospitalized and those with unmet social needs.

A case-crossover phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analyzing diagnosis patterns in 44,198 COVID-19 survivors, comparing pre- and post-infection occurrences of 1,671 diagnosis codes using conditional logistic regression. The study identified enrichment in respiratory, circulatory, and mental health disorders post-infection but is excluded as a secondary analysis methodology study rather than a treatment intervention trial.

Prospective multicentre study assessing the incidence and clinical features of long COVID in 1,102 people with cystic fibrosis following SARS-CoV-2 infection between 2021-2022. Long COVID was documented in 5.8% of participants with extrapulmonary symptoms more frequent in adults, and pulmonary function was not negatively impacted at 6 months follow-up.

This study evaluates retinal vascular changes in COVID-19 patients using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) at early post-discharge and 6-month follow-up timepoints compared to healthy controls. While it documents persistent vascular flow changes at 6 months, it is a non-interventional observational study examining acute COVID-19 sequelae (not long COVID as defined) without any treatment evaluation.

This prospective observational cohort study followed 105 COVID-19 survivors who required invasive mechanical ventilation, assessing their health-related quality of life, physical function, fatigue, and cognitive outcomes 18 months after ICU discharge. The study found moderate reductions in quality of life and severe reductions in physical functioning, with higher fatigue prevalence in younger and female patients, and low-frequency cognitive impairment.

This study screened 54 college athletes with recent COVID-19 using echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess cardiovascular abnormalities. While it found pericardial involvement in 56% of participants, it focuses on acute/early post-infection cardiac imaging findings in young athletes recovering from uncomplicated COVID-19, not long COVID intervention trials.

This prospective longitudinal study examined choroidal thickness and vascularity changes in 16 COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls using optical coherence tomography at early (days 15-40) and late (9-month) post-infection periods. The study found reversible choroidal thickness reduction in the early phase that recovered by 9 months, with no active treatment intervention assessed.

This retrospective cohort study examined 256 patients with mild COVID-19 at 6-month follow-up to investigate de-novo fragmented QRS (fQRS) as a cardiac injury indicator and its association with post-COVID tachycardia syndrome. While the study identifies cardiac complications of long COVID, it is purely observational with no treatment intervention evaluated.

Prospective cohort study from the UK Household Longitudinal Study examining whether pre-pandemic tobacco smoking independently predicts Long COVID development in 11,944 participants followed from 2018-19 to 2022-23. Smoking did not independently predict Long COVID but may increase vulnerability indirectly through pre-existing long-standing illness or disability.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between COVID-19 infection and subsequent depression diagnoses in German adults, using propensity score matching. While the study follows COVID-19 patients longitudinally, it does not focus on long COVID (persistent post-acute symptoms) and does not evaluate any treatment interventions.

Retrospective chart review of 254 patients who had emergency department re-presentations within 6 months of initial COVID-19 hospital discharge in Australia (July-August 2020 and October 2021). Post-COVID syndrome was the most common re-presentation diagnosis (10-12%), with shortness of breath being the most frequent symptom, but this is an observational epidemiological study with no treatment intervention evaluated.

Multi-center observational study of 90 IBD patients with non-severe COVID-19, examining factors associated with exacerbated gastrointestinal symptoms (EGS) and long COVID development. Study found 30% experienced EGS and 38.1% developed long COVID, but no intervention or treatment was tested—only associations with demographic and clinical factors were analyzed.

This case-control study compared behavioral, emotional, and social problems in 84 Taiwanese children post-COVID-19 infection against 84 matched healthy controls and their own pre-COVID baseline. The study found significantly higher rates of inattention, hyperactivity, emotional/behavioral problems, and poor social functioning in post-COVID children compared to controls.

Prospective observational study of 349 long COVID patients examining associations between oral and gut microbiota composition and symptom subphenotypes using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and latent class analysis. Found distinct microbiota patterns across three symptom clusters (high constitutional burden, smell/taste disturbances, minimal symptoms) but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This prospective cohort study assessed health-related quality of life (HR-QOL) using SF-36 scores among Singapore residents in relation to COVID-19 infection status and timing. While it measured outcomes in people with prior COVID-19, it was a population-level observational study without any intervention or treatment arm, so it does not qualify as a treatment trial.

Retrospective comparison of clinical characteristics and long-term outcomes in septic critically ill patients with and without COVID-19. While the study does assess long-term outcomes, it focuses on acute sepsis and critical illness during active COVID-19 infection, not persistent symptoms weeks-to-months after acute infection (long COVID).

Retrospective cohort study comparing ECG changes in COVID-19 positive and negative patients, with follow-up ECGs recorded before, during, and ~40 days after infection. Found QTc prolongation and spatial ventricular gradient changes in the COVID-19 cohort but not controls, characterizing electrophysiologic manifestations of post-acute COVID-19 sequelae.

A prospective observational study examining airway microbiota composition in 57 patients with persistent cough following SARS-CoV-2 infection, with samples collected at 4 and 8 weeks post-infection. The study identifies dynamic alterations in bacterial families (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus) and proposes that nasopharyngeal microbiota signatures may predict cough severity improvement, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study uses Japanese claims database to describe symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) and diseases diagnosed after COVID-19, comparing 263,456 COVID-19 patients with matched controls. The study finds that PCC symptoms persist over time with declining trends across epidemic waves, with pulmonary thromboembolism, smell/taste disorder, and respiratory failure being most common.

Retrospective observational study of 478 long COVID patients examining the relationship between complement pathway activity (CH50 levels) and neurological symptoms like brain fog and poor concentration. High CH50 levels were associated with brain fog and poor concentration, but this is a descriptive/observational study with no treatment intervention being tested.

This retrospective cohort study examines associations between early-life air pollution exposure and COVID-19 infection/sequelae in 20,012 Chinese children aged 3-6 years. While it identifies air pollutants as risk factors for childhood COVID-19 sequelae, it does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This study assessed physical and psychological outcomes in 83 healthcare workers infected with COVID-19 during a hospital outbreak, measuring quality of life, work motivation, and symptom recovery. While some persistent symptoms (anosmia, fatigue) were noted at follow-up, the focus is on acute COVID-19 infection and immediate recovery in HCWs, not long COVID sequelae or treatment interventions.

Multicenter prospective observational study following 157 mechanically ventilated severe COVID-19 patients for one year to assess whether tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) prevents functional impairments and long COVID sequelae. Tocilizumab was associated with lower prevalence of physical impairment (17.1% vs 23.3%) and mental disorders (19.5% vs 39.7%), though long COVID prevalence was higher in the treated group.

topics: ARDS|post-acute sequelae|exercise capacity|mental health|quality of life
summary: Prospective follow-up study of 113 COVID-19 ARDS survivors at 8 months post-discharge, assessing health status, exercise capacity, and quality of life through physical examination, 6-minute walk test, and psychiatric screening. Findings show 81% had persistent symptoms, >50% had reduced exercise capacity, and 93% developed psychiatric disorders, with worse SF-36 scores than general population.

A multi-center prospective cohort study of 1,233 older COVID-19 patients followed one year after hospital discharge to assess the prevalence and characteristics of long COVID sequelae. The study found that 51.1% experienced at least one persistent symptom (primarily fatigue, sweating, and chest tightness), with disease severity and age as independent risk factors, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study following 465 COVID-19 patients for 9 months to identify determinants of symptom persistence and impact on physical/mental wellbeing. Found that 20% remained symptomatic at month 9, with age >50, ICU stay, and multiple symptoms at onset as independent predictors of long-term symptoms and reduced physical/mental health.

This prospective cohort study evaluated 277 COVID-19 survivors 10-14 weeks after disease onset to determine the incidence of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) and associated risk factors. The study found PCS in 50.9% of survivors but did not test any treatment intervention—it is an observational epidemiological study documenting symptom persistence and recovery patterns.

Prospective cohort study examining the evolution of long COVID symptoms in Swiss healthcare workers infected with Wild-type and/or Omicron BA.1 variants, with repeated symptom assessments over 15 months. The study found no increased long COVID risk from Omicron reinfection or pre-Omicron vaccination, but reports a potential protective effect of physical/social activities.

This is a large cross-sectional study from the German National Cohort examining the prevalence of post-COVID condition across 109,707 participants with varying infection and vaccination histories. While it addresses long COVID risk factors and symptom burden, it is an observational study that does not evaluate any treatment or intervention, making it ineligible for the trials pipeline.

Prospective multicentre cohort study investigating whether SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia and other risk factors predict long-COVID development in COVID-19 patients followed for nine months. This appears to be a secondary analysis responding to prior work, examining associations between viral markers and long-COVID outcomes without testing any intervention.

This prospective cohort study from the BRACE trial compares symptom patterns and persistence following COVID-19 versus non-COVID respiratory illness in healthcare workers across four countries over 12 months. It identifies age, chronic respiratory disease, and pre-existing symptoms as risk factors for post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS), finding higher rates of symptom persistence in COVID-19 cases compared to non-COVID controls.

This retrospective cohort study examines long-term effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection on 63 common laboratory biomarkers in 361,061 matched pairs over 12 months. Most biomarker changes resolved within 1-4 months, with some prolonged effects on immune markers (WBC, neutrophils) lasting 7-8 months.

Population-based longitudinal cohort study of 1.5M COVID cases in England examining prevalence and risk factors for long COVID symptoms using electronic health records. Found 7.4% had long COVID symptoms at 12+ weeks, with female sex, non-white ethnicity, obesity, and pre-existing mental health conditions as key risk factors.

Retrospective cohort study of 139,320 children and young adults examining associations between pre-COVID BMI and post-acute cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Severe obesity was associated with higher risks of cardiovascular disorders, diarrhea, and GERD, with variable neuropsychiatric associations.

This prospective observational study from the ZOE COVID Symptom Study app examined whether SARS-CoV-2 or influenza vaccination affects symptom resolution in individuals with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 (OSC) or post-COVID syndrome (PCS). SARS-CoV-2 vaccination was associated with accelerated improvement in multiple symptoms including fatigue and myalgia compared to natural history, whereas influenza vaccination showed no such benefit.

Longitudinal population-based study tracking symptom burden and post-COVID-19 syndrome in 6,635 German participants at ~9 and ~24 months post-infection. Found stable prevalence of PCS (~30%) with symptom resolution and emergence balanced, suggesting chronicity but with improving quality of life in those whose symptoms resolve.

A prospective cohort study following 291 COVID-19 patients (35% hospitalised) for three years post-infection to assess physical capacity and breathlessness recovery. Physical capacity improved significantly up to two years, with hospitalisation and impaired diffusing capacity identified as strong predictors of persistent impairment and breathlessness.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing Hong Kong electronic health records to examine whether SARS-CoV-2 infection increases multimorbidity risk in patients with pre-existing chronic conditions, stratified by vaccination status. Found COVID-19 infection associated with increased multimorbidity incidence (1.26× unvaccinated, 1.08× vaccinated vs. non-infected controls), demonstrating vaccination's protective effect.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing risk of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) in 3.2 million COVID-19 patients versus matched non-COVID controls using electronic health records. Found COVID-19 patients have significantly higher CFS risk (HR 1.59) across age groups and comorbid conditions, but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study of 276 adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection during the Omicron period, tracking symptom persistence and IgG antibody titers over time. Female sex, incomplete vaccination, and comorbidities were risk factors for long COVID persistence (5% at ≥12 months), with lower anti-S1 IgG titers associated with persistent fatigue.

Track PCC is a surveillance network study examining the incidence of post-COVID conditions across five U.S. geographic sites during the Omicron period (2022-2023). The study found PCC incidence highest 31-90 days post-infection, with no increase during the Omicron era compared to earlier variants, providing epidemiological data on disease burden rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

Ambidirectional cohort study of 222 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for a median of 122 days post-discharge to identify predictors of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS) outcomes including dyspnea, exercise intolerance, chronic fatigue, and well-being. Female gender, pre-existing lung disease, ICU admission, and critical illness were significant predictors of worse functional outcomes and mental health.

A prospective cohort study of 470 Swedish COVID-19 patients followed for up to 3 years post-infection, identifying four distinct symptom clusters (Few Symptoms, Respiratory, Neurocognitive, Multisystem) and their trajectories over time. While most participants improved, a subset experienced persistent symptoms at 3 years, with hospitalisation during acute COVID predicting worse outcomes.

This study tracked changes in the oral microbiome of COVID-19 recovered patients at 1, 3, and 5 months post-infection using 16S rRNA sequencing of tongue samples. The results show gradual restoration of oral microbiome diversity over 5 months of rehabilitation, with significant increases by month 5 compared to month 1.

Longitudinal study comparing innate immune cell profiles in COVID-19 recovered patients (mild, moderate, severe) at 1 and 3 months post-recovery against controls. Found persistent immune dysregulation including elevated monocytes, PMN-MDSCs, and inflammatory cytokines associated with long COVID symptoms, but no intervention was tested.

This study examines clinical and immunological characteristics of pediatric post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in 92 children from the DISCOVER cohort, measuring blood biomarkers and immune responses. The researchers identified elevated anti-nucleocapsid IgG as a potential biomarker for stratifying PASC severity in children, with higher antibody levels correlating with greater symptom burden and monocyte counts.

This cross-sectional study assessed the prevalence and severity of neurological and psychiatric long COVID symptoms among 467 vaccinated healthcare workers stratified by COVID-19 status. The study found no statistically significant differences in symptom severity across groups, highlighting potential biases in symptom reporting rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 625 PCR-confirmed COVID-19 patients in Northern Taiwan monitored for 3-6 months to assess long COVID symptoms and quality of life impacts using EQ-5D questionnaire. Found that older age (≥65 years) and hospitalization significantly predicted greater quality of life impairment, but the study passively follows patients without providing any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 82,070 U.S. veterans examining whether non-severe COVID-19 infection increases risk of developing frailty or pre-frailty over 36 months. Found that positive COVID-19 testing was associated with 66% increase in hazard of becoming frail and 68% increase in pre-frailty, with stronger effects in female patients (330% increase).

This prospective follow-up study examined cognitive impairment and inflammatory markers in individuals with mild COVID-19 over six months. The paper found that 26% experienced persistent visuospatial difficulties, but 66% of those with initial impairments showed improvement, with changes in cytokine levels (CCL11, HGF, CXCL10) suggesting a link between cognitive issues and pro-inflammatory markers.

A prospective cohort study following 791 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors for 6 months, comparing 196 with neurological complications to 186 matched controls without complications. Patients with neurological complications had significantly worse functional outcomes, activities of daily living, and work capacity at 6-month follow-up, though cognitive and quality-of-life metrics were similar between groups.

Observational cross-sectional study characterizing cognitive and behavioral features in 49 COVID-19 patients assessed within two months of hospital discharge using neuropsychological testing and brain MRI. Found high prevalence of executive dysfunction (45%), memory problems (25%), and mood disorders (16-18%), particularly in younger patients, with cognitive impairment independent of structural brain changes.

Retrospective study of 213 Neuro-Long-COVID patients (151 female, 62 male) comparing sex-dependent characteristics and symptom prevalence at a specialized neurology outpatient service. Findings show worse acute phase response in males but no significant differences in chronic neurological symptoms between sexes, highlighting sex-based variation in disease presentation.

Prospective cohort study of 428 severe COVID-19 survivors aged ≥50 years evaluating the one-year evolution of physical and cognitive problems post-discharge. Physical and/or cognitive problems occurred in 83% of participants, but the conditions and their trajectories were discordant, suggesting independent recovery patterns that could inform tailored rehabilitation approaches.

Observational cohort study comparing cerebral microvascular properties in 108 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors (ICU vs general ward) at ~9 months post-infection using diffusion MRI. Found significant microvascular dysfunction in ICU survivors associated with acute disease severity and persistent cognitive complaints, but no causal treatment intervention was tested.

Longitudinal neuropsychological study monitoring cognitive, psychological, and quality-of-life outcomes in 22 COVID-19 patients with subjective cognitive disturbances over 22 months. Found that ~50% had cognitive deficits at baseline (primarily verbal memory), with significant improvements over time but persistent borderline scores; depression and PTSD symptoms were present in 30% and decreased over time.

This cross-sectional study examined neurological and cognitive outcomes in 215 COVID-19 patients at 4 months post-infection, comparing 52 ICU-treated patients with 163 non-hospitalized patients. ICU patients showed significantly greater neurological deficits and cognitive impairment than non-ICU patients, but no intervention or treatment was administered—the study is purely observational assessment of sequelae.

Prospective cohort study comparing brain health trajectories 3 years post-hospitalization in COVID-19 patients versus hospitalized controls (pneumonia, MI, critical illness) and healthy controls. COVID-19 patients showed comparable cognitive and mental health impairments to hospitalized controls at 36 months, with gradual improvement over time in both groups.

Retrospective cohort study comparing long-term outcomes (mortality, MACE, fatigue, mental status changes) in 1,664 COVID-19 patients with pre-existing neurological conditions versus 8,985 non-COVID controls followed up to 3.5 years. Patients with neurological disorders who were hospitalized for acute COVID-19 had significantly worse outcomes including higher mortality and cardiovascular events, but this is an observational study with no intervention tested.

This is a two-year prospective follow-up study of 44 long COVID patients from a neurology outpatient cohort, examining the relationship between autonomic dysfunction and quality of life. The study found that 66% met criteria for autonomic dysfunction, with secretomotor and gastrointestinal symptoms significantly associated with anxiety, depression, and fatigue.

Cross-sectional study examining the relationship between gastrointestinal symptoms and neurocognitive dysfunction in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Patients with GI symptoms showed significantly worse performance on neuropsychological tests including memory, executive function, and visuospatial perception compared to those without GI symptoms.

Prospective observational study comparing long COVID prevalence in children with first-time Omicron infection, reinfection, and test-negative controls at 3 and 6 months post-infection. Found 12-16% of infected children met long COVID research criteria with no significant difference between first infection and reinfection groups.

This study uses electronic health record data from the RECOVER program to identify children with COVID-19 based on serologic testing and characterizes their risk profiles for post-acute sequelae. It is an observational epidemiologic study that does not test any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the clinical trials meta-analysis.

Retrospective cohort study examining incident dyslipidemia and abnormal BMI in 384,289 COVID-19-positive children during the 28-179 day post-acute phase using EHR data from 25 US hospitals. Found elevated risks of new-onset dyslipidemia and abnormal BMI in COVID-positive children compared to negative controls, but this is an observational study documenting metabolic complications rather than testing an intervention.

This prospective cohort study followed 402 COVID-19 survivors for one year to investigate long-term psychiatric outcomes, assessing depression, anxiety, fatigue, and post-traumatic distress at 1, 6, and 12 months. High prevalence of psychiatric sequelae was found (45% with clinical-range symptoms at 12 months), with males showing increasing depression and anxiety over time while females improved.

Retrospective cohort study assessing frequency of persistent physical symptoms and Somatic Symptom Disorder (SSD) in COVID-19 patients 8-10 months post-infection at a French hospital. Identifies risk factors (female sex, older age, PTSD) associated with SSD severity but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 495 COVID-19 patients followed at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-infection, measuring fatigue severity via Fatigue Severity Scale and identifying predictors of persistent fatigue. Found that fatigue worsened over time (22-34% in pathological range), with depressive symptomatology at one month being the only significant predictor of long-term fatigue.

Prospective cohort study examining whether trust in different COVID-19 information sources (government, journalists, medical professionals, social media) at pandemic onset associates with incident persistent symptoms months later in 20,985 French adults. Higher trust in government/journalists and medical professionals predicted fewer persistent symptoms and lower psychological burden, independent of SARS-CoV-2 infection status.

A prospective cohort study of 80 post-COVID patients undergoing a 5-week psychosomatic rehabilitation program, measuring changes in depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) and attention/working memory (TAP test battery). The intervention significantly reduced depressive symptoms (d=1.57) but had no comparable effect on persistent cognitive impairments over the 5-week period.

Longitudinal cohort study examining trajectories of physical and mental fatigue in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus non-infected German adults across three time points (2020-2021). Found that physical fatigue but not mental fatigue was elevated in infected individuals at 12 months post-infection, with baseline mental health symptoms being the strongest predictor of fatigue trajectories.

Retrospective chart review of 286 long COVID patients attending a multidisciplinary day-hospital program, assessing their characteristics, medical conclusions, and satisfaction. Most patients received physical activity rehabilitation recommendations and reported high satisfaction (median 8/10), with diagnoses of functional somatic disorder and severe quality-of-life impairment.

Observational cohort study comparing frequencies of post-COVID symptoms in the Dutch general population (N=4,231) against media coverage of post-COVID symptoms in news articles. The study finds that symptom prevalence does not reflect media coverage patterns, arguing against nocebo effects as a primary cause of post-COVID condition.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study following 451 hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 6 and 12 months post-discharge to assess long-term outcomes including disability, cognition, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Life stressors (financial insecurity, food insecurity, death of close contact) were the strongest independent predictors of worse functional, cognitive, and mood outcomes at 12 months.

Prospective cohort study tracking anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sleep quality in 1,266 COVID-19 survivors hospitalized in March-May 2020 at three timepoints (8.4, 13.2, and 18.3 months post-hospitalization). Findings show declining prevalence of anxiety (22.5%→7.9%), depression (14.6%→6.1%), and poor sleep (32.8%→24.8%) over the first 18 months, with no identifiable risk factors in medical records.

An observational cohort study of 61 post-COVID-19 patients examining how baseline treatment and side-effect expectations associate with outcomes following a 4-6 week multidisciplinary rehabilitation program. Higher side-effect expectations predicted worse outcomes (greater disability, reduced fitness, more somatic symptoms) at 3-month follow-up, suggesting a nocebo effect.

A prospective uncontrolled study of 78 long COVID patients who received a concentrated 3-day micro-choice-based intervention with 12-month follow-up. The intervention led to significant improvements in fatigue, functional capacity, sick leave reduction (63% to 23%), and exercise tolerance.

A prospective observational study of 65 post-COVID patients receiving a 3-4 week multimodal psychosomatic treatment program at a German hospital, measuring outcomes via PHQ-15, fatigue scale, and SF-12 questionnaires at admission and discharge. Patients showed significant symptom improvement post-treatment, though the authors note that a control group would be needed to confirm the treatment's causal effect.

Prospective cohort study of 409 post-COVID patients attending a rehabilitation clinic that identified four symptom-based clusters and assessed prognosis over 12 months. While the study observes patients in a clinical setting, it is primarily descriptive/prognostic rather than evaluating a specific treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline.

Prospective observational study examining coping strategies and their relationship to symptoms and health outcomes in 339 post-COVID patients over ~4.5 months. Found that higher coping competence at baseline predicted fewer fatigue and depression symptoms at follow-up, suggesting targeted interventions strengthening coping may improve PASC symptom management.

A longitudinal cohort study examining the association between psychological distress and subsequent PACS symptoms in Japanese participants over one year. While about long COVID, this is a passive observational follow-up study without any intervention—psychological distress is measured as a predictor, not a treatment.

Retrospective analysis of 272 COVID-19 patients examining the relationship between chest CT pneumonia severity and neuroimaging findings in the post-acute period. Found that 20.6% of patients had neuroimaging abnormalities (ischemic stroke, hemorrhage, microhemorrhages), which occurred regardless of pneumonia severity, but this is an observational descriptive study with no treatment intervention.

This study compares health-related quality of life and socioeconomic factors between two cohorts of long COVID patients (n=422) and persistent physical symptom patients (n=599) at baseline using validated instruments (15D and EUROHIS-QOL-8). The findings show reduced quality of life in both groups, with working status, comorbidities, and education emerging as key determinants, but this is an observational comparison study without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing sperm parameters in 25 men before and 3 months after COVID-19 infection. Found significant decreases in semen volume, sperm concentration, and motility in the post-COVID period, but no intervention was tested.

This retrospective cohort study examined the association between COVID-19 infection and subsequent erectile dysfunction risk using propensity score matching on a large EMR database of 462,162 men. The study found a statistically significant increased risk of ED in men with prior COVID-19 infection (OR 1.120, 95% CI 1.004-1.248), suggesting endothelial dysfunction as an underlying mechanism.

This ecological momentary assessment study examined within-person predictors of physical activity and fatigue in 69 long COVID patients using 3-hourly smartphone data and continuous activity monitoring. While it found that expectation of energy demand and anxiety were significant predictors, the absolute effects were small and clinically negligible, suggesting limited day-to-day relationships between psychological factors and outcomes.

This study prospectively followed 67 male COVID-19 recovered patients over ~6 months to assess psychological distress and erectile function using validated questionnaires. It found that psychological symptoms and erectile dysfunction were initially elevated but improved by the second visit, with no significant difference from controls at ~5.7 months post-infection.

Retrospective cohort study comparing pre- and post-COVID sexual health outcomes and hormone levels in 25 men at 3 months post-infection. Found no significant changes in hormone levels, erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, or anxiety, but unexpectedly observed decreased depression scores post-COVID.

This retrospective cohort study compares post-hospitalization recovery outcomes in mechanically ventilated COVID-19 survivors based on whether they received venovenous ECMO during acute infection. While it documents long COVID-like deficits (physical, psychological, cognitive) at 120 days post-discharge, it is a secondary analysis comparing ECMO vs non-ECMO patients rather than evaluating a specific long COVID intervention.

This cross-sectional study examined vitamin D and zinc deficiency rates in 55 long COVID patients using laboratory testing (ICP-MS and chemiluminescence immunoassay). The study found associations between zinc deficiency and elevated fibrinogen and between vitamin D deficiency and delayed recovery, but did not test or evaluate a specific intervention—it only measured micronutrient levels in patients already receiving unspecified long COVID treatment.

This cross-sectional study examined neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and immunothrombosis markers in acute COVID-19, recovered, and long COVID patients across two Israeli centers. While it identifies NETosis induction as a potential biomarker differentiating long COVID from recovery, it is an observational characterization study without testing any intervention or treatment.

A retrospective study examining the impact and burden of long COVID-19 in the US population over a 9-month period using real-world data. The study characterizes the epidemiology and healthcare utilization patterns associated with long COVID without testing a specific intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining whether COVID-19 vaccination reduces persistent symptoms 3 months after mild Omicron infection in 1,067 Brazilian patients. Found no significant overall protection from vaccination against persistent symptoms, though vaccination was associated with lower mental health symptoms.

Subgroup analysis of a longitudinal study examining the effect of COVID-19 vaccination on long COVID symptoms in 111 Japanese patients followed for one year. Found vaccination did not have clinically important effects, with 82.9% reporting no change in symptoms.

This retrospective cohort study examines healthcare utilization patterns among people with post-COVID-19 condition versus matched controls in British Columbia, Canada over 12-18 months post-infection. While it documents elevated healthcare utilization in the PCC group, it is a secondary analysis of administrative health data without testing any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study assessing the prevalence and risk factors of post-COVID-19 symptoms in 181 previously hospitalized patients from Colombia at ≥3 months post-discharge. Found 77.9% had persistent symptoms (fatigue, joint pain, dyspnea most common), with higher prevalence in women and ICU-admitted patients.

A prospective observational cohort study following 899 US Marines to assess post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) an average of 330 days after infection, with 24.7% developing PASC characterized by persistent symptoms including loss of taste/smell, shortness of breath, and cough, along with increased somatic, depressive, and anxiety symptoms. Those with PASC showed significantly worse physical fitness performance on standardized military fitness tests one year after training, indicating long-term functional impairment in young, previously healthy adults.

Ambidirectional cohort study following 237 COVID-19 patients 18-24 months after hospitalization to assess evolution of lung abnormalities. Found persistent and progressive fibrotic-like lesions with worsening architectural distortion and traction bronchiectasis, particularly in patients who required ICU care and mechanical ventilation.

This retrospective cohort study of 2,511 essential workers investigated risk factors for developing post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), finding that multiple SARS-CoV-2 infections, severe initial COVID-19, and lack of vaccination at first infection were significantly associated with PASC incidence. The study is observational without any intervention or treatment evaluation.

Retrospective cohort study characterizing 253,145 long COVID patients from US health insurance claims data, identifying demographics and prevalent symptoms. While about long COVID, this is a descriptive epidemiological study without any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the clinical trials meta-analysis.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes spatiotemporal patterns of long COVID incidence across 1,063 U.S. counties using data from 5.6 million COVID-19 cases. The study examines associations between long COVID incidence and sociodemographic factors like economic vulnerability and healthcare access, finding that high-risk areas shifted inland after Omicron emergence and that sociodemographic disparities consistently drive spatial disparities.

A prospective cohort study of 710 individuals in Rio de Janeiro assessing prevalence and impact of long COVID in a socially vulnerable community 3+ months post-infection. Found 22% with persistent symptoms, 26% with worsened functional status, and identified dyspnea during acute phase as the strongest predictor of poor long-term outcomes.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study following 3,663 participants with SARS-CoV-2 infection for up to 3 years to assess physical and mental health outcomes by Long COVID status. Current Long COVID was associated with significantly worse PROMIS physical and mental health scores, higher stress, loneliness, fatigue, dyspnea, and insufficient activity; COVID-19 vaccination was associated with better outcomes across all measures.

Prospective multicentre cohort study of 327 COVID-19 survivors assessed at least 3 months post-discharge, examining long-term symptoms, disability, and quality of life. Found 93% reported persistent symptoms (fatigue 83%, breathlessness 54%), with worse outcomes in younger females, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Longitudinal prospective cohort study of 958 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 4-7 months to assess the prevalence and predictors of post-COVID syndrome symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, anosmia, ageusia). Found 27.8-34.8% of patients had at least one persistent symptom at 4-7 months post-infection, with lower baseline IgG, anosmia during acute infection, and diarrhea as risk factors for long-term symptoms.

This prospective cohort study analyzed determinants of recovery from dyspnoea in COVID-19 hospitalized patients using the PHOSP-COVID and COVIDENCE UK cohorts with 5-month and 1-year follow-up data. The study identifies demographic and clinical factors associated with dyspnoea improvement but does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

This is a prospective cohort follow-up study of 165 long COVID patients from the LinCoS study, assessing symptom persistence and functional impact at 24 months post-COVID hospitalization. Although it describes outcomes, it is a secondary/follow-up analysis of an existing cohort with no new intervention assignment, making it unsuitable for the trials extraction pipeline.

This cross-sectional study from the Swedish BAMSE cohort investigates associations between ambient air pollution exposure and long COVID prevalence among young adults. While it confirms long COVID affects 15.4% of infected participants, it is an observational epidemiological study examining risk factors rather than evaluating any treatment or intervention.

Prospective follow-up study of 5,086 non-hospitalised children and young people (2,909 SARS-CoV-2 positive, 2,177 negative controls) assessed over 12 months post-infection to characterize the natural course of health and well-being. Most adverse symptoms declined over 12 months, though some participants reported new onset symptoms at later timepoints, suggesting multiple etiological factors beyond COVID-19.

Retrospective cohort study examining long COVID incidence, symptom nature, and duration among 1,886 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in the Netherlands stratified by migration background. Found 26% long COVID prevalence at 12 weeks with significant variation in symptoms and risk by ethnic/migrant groups, but no treatment intervention tested.

Population-based prospective cohort study examining the association between post-COVID condition and work ability in 672 working-age adults in Switzerland. Finds that individuals with PCC have significantly lower work ability scores and are more likely to report occupational changes, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary interventions.

Multinational observational study assessing the prevalence of physical symptoms up to 2+ years after SARS-CoV-2 infection across 64,880 adults in Iceland, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway. Finds elevated prevalence of severe physical symptom burden in COVID-diagnosed individuals, particularly those with severe acute illness, but this is a descriptive epidemiological study without any treatment intervention.

A 2-year prospective cohort study of 548 COVID-19 survivors (341 with post-COVID condition, 207 fully recovered) identifying factors associated with PCC development and recovery using logistic regression and clustering analysis. Found that acute COVID-19 symptoms and preexisting factors predict PCC development, with only 7.6% achieving recovery during follow-up.

OpenPROMPT is a UK population cohort study measuring the impact of long COVID on health-related quality-of-life using Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs). The study found that long COVID patients experienced substantial losses in quality-of-life (0.37 QALM loss) and higher odds of reporting quality-of-life impairment compared to unaffected individuals, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study of 20 post-COVID ME/CFS patients with elevated β2-adrenergic receptor autoantibodies who received five immunoadsorption sessions. Treatment reduced immunoglobulin G by 79% and improved SF36 physical functioning by a mean of 17.75 points, with 70% of patients showing ≥10-point improvements maintained through 6 months.

A 3-year prospective population-based cohort study examining work ability trajectories and sick leave patterns in individuals with post-COVID-19 condition. The study found that those with PCC reported persistently lower work ability scores and higher rates of work-related impairment compared to recovered individuals, with minimal improvement over time.

Prospective cohort study comparing symptom prevalence in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus uninfected Dutch participants over one year post-infection during the autumn 2023 wave. Found low PCC risk with no significant difference in PCC-related symptoms between groups at 90-360 days post-infection, though self-attributed long-term symptoms were elevated at 90-180 days.

Population-based matched cohort study using electronic health records to examine long-term kidney outcomes in COVID-19 survivors compared to uninfected controls. Found significantly increased kidney failure risk, particularly in those hospitalized, but this is an observational cohort study without any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials meta-analysis.

CO-FLOW is a prospective cohort study following 299 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for 3 years to assess health trajectories and post-exertional malaise (PEM) prevalence. The study documents natural recovery patterns and symptom trajectories without testing any intervention, finding that 36% developed PEM by year 3 with persistent fatigue and cognitive problems.

Nationwide register-based cohort study in Denmark examining the association between repeated SARS-CoV-2 infections and risk of hospital-diagnosed long COVID. Reinfection increased long COVID risk, though the absolute increase was smaller than after primary infection, and vaccination offered substantial protection.

This intensive longitudinal cohort study tracked 376 long COVID patients from clinic and community settings using ecological momentary assessments to characterize symptom fluctuations in response to physical, cognitive, and social activities over 24 days. The study found that all symptoms worsened within 30 minutes of any activity type, with fatigue increasing 1.8 points after high physical exertion and 1.5 points after cognitive effort, supporting targeted self-management approaches.

Retrospective analysis of Virus Watch cohort data examining how socioeconomic deprivation, migration status, and ethnicity associate with functional limitations in 776 individuals with post-COVID-19 condition. Found that socioeconomic deprivation (not migration status or ethnicity) primarily drives functional limitations, with most deprived quintile showing 2-3x higher odds of limitations in work, concentration, self-care, and outdoor activities.

Prospective longitudinal study of 362 COVID-19 survivors in Bangladesh followed at months 1, 3, and 5 post-discharge to assess prevalence, incidence, and evolution of post-COVID syndrome symptoms and risk factors. Found high burden of PCS in hospitalized survivors with conditions like peripheral neuropathy, depression, lung disease, and new-onset diabetes, with older age, female sex, comorbidities, and hospitalization as independent risk factors.

This retrospective study analyzed post-pandemic excess mortality patterns in Hong Kong from 2013-2024, comparing observed deaths against pre-pandemic baselines. While acknowledging post-COVID conditions as a contributing factor, the study does not evaluate or test any specific intervention or treatment for long COVID patients.

Observational cohort study using linked primary care data from 17.8 million English adults (2020-2022) to investigate ethnic differences in Long COVID diagnosis incidence. Found significant variation across ethnic subgroups, with hazard ratios ranging from 0.61 to 1.21 compared to White British populations, suggesting underlying mechanisms related to diagnosis patterns rather than true incidence differences.

This cross-sectional neuroimaging study compared brain functional activity in 52 COVID-19 survivors (27 months post-infection) versus 35 healthy controls using resting-state fMRI. The study found persistent cognitive complaints and brain functional alterations in temporal lobe and parietal regions in long COVID survivors, but did not test any intervention or treatment.

This study examined vitamin D status in 681 COVID-19 survivors and its association with physical performance outcomes. While it found vitamin D deficiency was common in survivors and associated with poorer physical performance, it is a cross-sectional observational study without any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the trials meta-analysis.

A longitudinal cohort study following 176 COVID-19 survivors for one year post-infection to characterize long COVID symptoms and identify associated risk factors. The study found clinically significant declines in cognitive function and health-related quality of life, with severe initial infection and lower financial status predicting worse outcomes.

This study compares sex-related differences in cardiovascular complications in 274 post-acute COVID-19 syndrome patients followed over 6 months using echocardiography. Male patients showed more altered left ventricular systolic function while female patients had more impaired right ventricular function and diastolic dysfunction, with abnormalities improving over time.

Cross-sectional study of 347 women in Latin America examining sociodemographic and clinical factors associated with long-COVID-19 syndrome. Found anxiety to be the only significant independent factor associated with long COVID, while menopausal status had no significant influence.

Retrospective observational study of 30 critically ill COVID-19 patients with acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy during the first wave. Study focuses on acute phase mortality and renal outcomes at 6 months, not on long COVID or post-acute interventions.

Retrospective cohort study of 88 previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 3 months post-discharge to assess lung function recovery, inflammatory markers, and imaging findings. While arterial blood gas and inflammatory biomarkers normalized, imaging showed persistent interstitial lung involvement, and new symptoms (dyspnea on exertion, arthralgias) emerged at follow-up.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study assessing lung sequelae in 254 severe COVID-19 patients through CT scans and pulmonary function tests at 3-6 months post-discharge. Found persistent radiological abnormalities (72%) and pulmonary dysfunction (46%), particularly in patients with prolonged ICU stay and invasive mechanical ventilation.

Retrospective observational study of 30 critically ill COVID-19 patients with acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy during the first wave of the pandemic. Focuses on in-hospital mortality (63%) and acute renal outcomes, not long COVID sequelae or treatment interventions for post-acute disease.

topics: pulmonary function|quality of life|diagnostic tools|post-COVID sequelae
summary: A prospective follow-up study of 41 SARS-CoV-2 survivors at 6 months post-hospitalization examining the utility of the SF-12 quality of life questionnaire in identifying pulmonary sequelae. The study found SF-12 physical domain scores effectively detected patients with pulmonary function alterations (AUC 0.862) but did not test any intervention or treatment.

Descriptive cross-sectional study of 86 mild COVID-19 patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction lasting over one month, assessed using Sniffin' Sticks test. Found high prevalence of parosmia (70.9%), brain fog (46.5%), and pathological test results (72.1%), with significant associations between parosmia and cognitive symptoms.

Comparative imaging study of 8 long COVID patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction versus 2 healthy controls, using structural and functional MRI to assess brain changes. Found no morphological differences but significant functional differences in olfactory cortex activation, particularly absent entorhinal cortex activation in patients.

Retrospective-prospective cohort study following 201 severe COVID-19 patients at 90 days, 12 months, and 24 months post-discharge to assess neuropsychiatric symptoms and their predictors. Found high prevalence of insomnia (37.3%), anxiety (22.4%), and depression (21.4%) persisting over 2 years, with female sex, fatigue, and CRP as key predictors.

This descriptive observational study assessed the prevalence of persistent COVID-19 symptoms and their impact on physical, psychological, and neurocognitive domains in 85 patients 15 months after ICU discharge. The study found high rates of musculoskeletal disorders (44.7% arthralgia, 38.2% myalgia), cognitive impairments (52.9%), and psychological effects including anxiety and PTSD symptoms, with 22.2% of primary caregivers reporting significant caregiving burden.

Prospective longitudinal study of 443 COVID-19 survivors assessed at 10 and 36 months post-infection using the C19-YRS questionnaire to evaluate symptom prevalence, severity, and quality of life. Found that post-COVID symptoms improved over time (62.3% at 10 months to 54.9% at 36 months) with fatigue, dyspnea, and anxiety most prevalent, while overall quality of life remained stable compared to baseline.

Prospective cohort study examining post-intensive care syndrome one month after discharge in critically ill COVID-19 patients. While it describes persistent impairments in quality of life and functional domains, it focuses on acute COVID-19 ICU outcomes rather than long COVID as a distinct post-acute syndrome, and includes no intervention or treatment component.

A prospective cohort study of 254 individuals from Iran investigating the prevalence, manifestations, and risk factors associated with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome over time. The study found that 64.1% of participants reported symptoms in the post-acute phase, with neurological sequelae being the most frequent symptom (91.6%), and identified significant associations between underlying diseases, age, and acute phase symptoms with long COVID susceptibility.

This paper reports a longitudinal observational cohort study of 201 long COVID patients (190 analyzed) followed for up to 18 months with standardized clinical assessments and PET imaging. The study documents cerebral hypometabolism in regions associated with symptoms (70% of brain PETs abnormal) but provides no intervention or treatment, making it a descriptive natural history study rather than a treatment trial.

A prospective observational cohort study evaluating systematic cardiovascular assessment and follow-up in 124 post-COVID patients at 4, 12, 24, and 48 weeks post-infection using ECG, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, and biomarkers. The study found high prevalence of cardiac symptoms early post-infection (33% at week 4) that resolved by 12 months, with 20-29% abnormal imaging findings including myocarditis and pericarditis.

This study prospectively followed 190 long COVID patients over 12+ months with standardized, multidisciplinary assessments using validated questionnaires (SF36, Pichot, MRC, MoCA, SSPT) and clinical exams to develop a composite prognostic score. The researchers identified key risk factors for progression to long COVID (female sex, dyspnea, cognitive difficulties, psychiatric symptoms) and created a predictive model to estimate individual patient risk of evolving into chronic long COVID.

Retrospective cohort study examining COVID-19 disease outcomes and neuropsychiatric complications in 26,963 adults with MS compared to matched controls. Finds MS patients have higher risk for mortality, hospitalization, long-COVID diagnosis, and multiple acute and chronic neuropsychiatric complications.

This retrospective cohort study examines long-term MS disease activity and mortality in 1,633 patients with MS, comparing those with and without COVID-19 infection over 3.5 years. While it documents worse outcomes in MS patients post-COVID-19 (higher mortality, relapse, hospitalization), the study focuses on MS disease progression rather than long COVID syndrome itself.

Prospective cohort study evaluating psychiatric symptoms and sleep quality 3 months post-COVID-19 infection in 102 patients using standardized questionnaires and clinical interview. Found high prevalence of anxiety (34.3%), depression (22.5%), insomnia (34.3%), and sleep quality impairment (53.9%), with dyspnea associated with significantly higher insomnia scores.

This study assessed microvascular function in 33 long COVID patients and 30 healthy controls using flow-mediated skin fluorescence, with repeated measurements 3 months apart. Patients receiving cardioprotective therapy (ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers) showed significant improvement in hypoxia sensitivity, providing evidence that microvascular dysfunction in long COVID can recover with treatment.

Retrospective study examining protein-energy malnutrition in chronic hemodialysis patients during COVID-19 infection over 6 months. Found that malnutrition was a frequent complication with early onset and prolonged recovery; 20.9% of patients had COVID sequelae at 6 months, with older patients (>75 years) showing more severe weight loss and albumin decline.

Retrospective cohort study of 248 dialyzed patients infected with COVID-19, followed for a median of 180 days post-infection. While the study documents long-term complications (cardiovascular events, infections, cachexia), it is observational without any intervention assignment and represents passive follow-up of natural disease progression rather than evaluation of a treatment.

This retrospective cohort study examines long-term renal outcomes in 409 hospitalized COVID-19 patients with acute kidney injury (AKI), followed for 2 years post-discharge. While it reports long-term sequelae after acute COVID-19 infection, it does not study long COVID—rather, it focuses on acute COVID-19 hospitalization and subsequent renal complications in the general hospitalized COVID population, not the persistent symptoms characteristic of long COVID syndrome.

Cross-sectional case-control study comparing brain structure (via MRI/DTI) and cognitive performance between 56 long-COVID patients and 35 controls with normal recovery. Found minimal differences in white matter diffusivity on only one DTI metric and no significant differences in objective cognitive performance, despite patients reporting neuropsychiatric symptoms.

This study compares brain white matter microstructure and metabolite levels (glutamate, NAA) between 64 COVID-19 survivors and 33 healthy controls to investigate associations with cognitive impairment and brain connectivity. The findings suggest brain repair and remyelination processes may occur post-infection, but the study does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective single-center study evaluating cognitive function in 13 post-ICU COVID-19 patients at baseline and 3-month follow-up using standardized cognitive tests. All patients showed baseline cognitive impairment with significant improvement by 3 months on MMSE and FAB tests, suggesting short-term cognitive recovery similar to other post-intensive care syndromes.

Prospective observational cohort study assessing cerebrovascular health in 45 patients six months after hospitalization for acute COVID-19 using functional MRI, compared to 42 controls. Found chronic cerebrovascular impairment related to acute COVID-19 severity, associated with cognitive, mental, and physical health outcomes at follow-up.

Multi-center observational study following 60 NeuroCOVID patients for 6 months to evaluate functional outcomes and identify risk factors for neurologic sequelae. Found that 51.7% had residual disability, 68.9% had impaired cognition, and age was a predictor of QoL impairment, with persistent neuropsychiatric manifestations including memory complaints, smell/taste disorders, and anxiety/depression.

This prospective longitudinal study examines the relationship between fatigue-related brain functional connectivity abnormalities during acute COVID-19 and post-traumatic stress symptoms at 3-month follow-up in 106 patients. The findings show that disrupted brain topological metrics during acute infection are associated with chronic hyperarousal symptoms, but the study is observational without any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study evaluated cognitive impairments in 60 COVID-19 survivors 12 weeks after hospital discharge using neuropsychological tests and MRI imaging. The authors found widespread cognitive deficits (85% with impairments in at least one test), white matter lesions and cerebral atrophy in frontal/parietal regions, and significant correlations between specific cognitive test scores and neuroimaging findings.

A cross-sectional cohort study evaluating cognitive impairments and neuroimaging abnormalities in 60 COVID-19 survivors 12 weeks post-hospital discharge, comparing those who required invasive vs non-invasive mechanical ventilation. The study found high rates of cognitive deficits (85% showed impairments), white matter lesions, and cerebral atrophy in frontal/parietal regions, with significant correlations between neuroimaging findings and cognitive test performance.

Prospective cohort study following 76 COVID-19 patients with olfactory dysfunction for 6 months to assess the natural progression of taste and trigeminal alterations using psychophysical testing and questionnaires. While taste and trigeminal dysfunction improved over time, most patients did not achieve full recovery, highlighting the persistent nature of post-COVID chemosensory symptoms.

This cross-sectional study compared cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) performance in 77 long COVID patients versus 766 non-COVID controls with undifferentiated dyspnea, finding severe exercise limitation in the long COVID group. The study identifies physiologic abnormalities (mild pulmonary and autonomic impairment) underlying long COVID symptoms but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal cohort study examining the association between baseline socioeconomic status and post-COVID-19 symptoms in 3,912 patients from the Isfahan COVID Cohort. Found that low SES was associated with higher risk of post-COVID cardiovascular symptoms in hospitalized patients, but lower risk in non-hospitalized patients.

Prospective follow-up study comparing long COVID-associated symptoms between SARS-CoV-2 positive and negative individuals across outpatient and inpatient cohorts over 533 days. Found that long COVID symptoms were more frequent in hospitalized CoV(+) participants, while outpatients showed similar symptom rates regardless of infection status, suggesting low long COVID prevalence in non-hospitalized patients.

This cross-sectional study compared macular vessel density using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in 50 COVID-19 recovered patients versus 55 healthy controls. While the study found reduced vessel density in some retinal sectors in COVID-19 patients, it does not study long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks to months post-infection) and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study compared the incidence of various medical conditions in COVID-19 recovered patients versus matched non-infected controls using Israeli HMO data from 2020-2021. It found higher incidence of depression/anxiety, DVT, fibromyalgia, and sleep disturbance in the post-COVID group but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This longitudinal study followed 329 COVID-19 survivors for 12 months post-discharge to assess the development of PTSD symptoms and respiratory sequelae. PTSD prevalence decreased significantly over time (23.1% to 4.3%), with female gender and respiratory complications identified as risk factors for chronic PTSD.

Compares baseline neurocognitive and psychiatric data from 2015 (pre-pandemic) with 2021 follow-up data in 428 COVID-19 exposed participants to assess long COVID symptoms. Finds that subjective neurocognitive complaints increased post-infection but did not correlate with test performance, and depression increased compared to controls, though baseline data show similar complaints existed before infection.

Retrospective chart review of long COVID patients at an outpatient specialty clinic examining the prevalence of psychiatric symptoms, finding 44% required psychiatric referral predominantly for depression or anxiety. The study characterizes psychiatric comorbidities in long COVID but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective study followed COVID-19 survivors at 1 and 2 years post-discharge to examine brain structural changes using voxel-based morphometry. While it documents reduced gray matter volume in the cerebellum and temporal regions associated with immune-inflammatory markers, it is a natural history observational study without any treatment intervention and should be excluded from the treatment trials meta-analysis.

This two-year longitudinal cohort study examined post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS), depression, and anxiety in COVID-19 survivors compared to non-infected controls, with neuroimaging data collected at 6 months. Female survivors showed sustained PTSS and depression for up to 2 years, and neuroimaging revealed altered amygdala and hippocampus activity correlated with mental health outcomes and social support.

This retrospective cohort study uses propensity score matching on EHR data to compare stimulant prescribing rates between long-COVID patients and acute COVID-19 controls. It is excluded as a secondary analysis of existing EHR data without an intervention trial design.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes TriNetX data (33 million records, 2020-2022) to examine how substance use disorder exacerbates taste and olfactory disorders in long-COVID patients. The study identified epidemiological associations but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examines long-term renal consequences in COVID-19 patients who experienced acute kidney injury (AKI) during hospitalization, using data from the AP-HP health data warehouse. While the study follows patients longitudinally and documents renal outcomes, it is a secondary analysis of hospitalization data and does not involve testing or evaluating a specific treatment intervention.

This longitudinal study followed 70 post-acute COVID-19 patients over 6 months to investigate how trauma exposure influences psychological outcomes using standardized psychiatric assessment tools. Results showed that patients with trauma history had significantly worse psychological outcomes across multiple dimensions including anxiety and obsessive-compulsive difficulties, highlighting the importance of trauma assessment for tailored psychological interventions.

A 3-year prospective follow-up study of 100 COVID-19 survivors examining associations between baseline biochemical parameters and psychiatric outcomes, measuring HbA1c, electrolytes, and tau protein levels. Severe cases showed elevated p-tau and HbA1c levels, with baseline electrolyte imbalances predicting long-term depression, anxiety, and somatization symptoms.

This study recruited long COVID patients and controls to characterize predictors of brain fog using questionnaires and cognitive tasks, developing classification and regression models. While it identified biopsychosocial factors associated with brain fog and documented high non-remission rates (82.4%), it does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing neuropsychiatric outcomes in 50,805 hospitalized COVID-19 patients versus matched controls from the Veterans Health Administration. Found significantly higher rates of psychiatry-related hospitalizations, mental health visits, new-onset depression, and new-onset dementia in the COVID-19 group at 90-180 days, but this is an observational study without any treatment intervention.

A cross-sectional study comparing cognitive and reward processing in 24 post-COVID syndrome patients versus 24 healthy controls using fMRI and the Monetary Incentive Delay Task. The study found that post-COVID patients showed slower task performance and temporally altered brain activity in frontal regions, but normal reward circuit function, suggesting neural hypoarousal rather than reward system dysfunction.

A prospective cohort study of 109 COVID-19 ICU patients followed one year post-discharge to identify inflammatory biomarkers predictive of long-term functional outcomes. The study found that hyperinflammatory phenotypes and specific cytokine profiles predicted worse outcomes in psychiatric, cognitive, and health domains.

This prospective cohort study examined the association between physical activity and long COVID risk in 237 Brazilian adults who recovered from COVID-19. Physical activity during the pandemic was associated with reduced long COVID prevalence (PR: 0.83) and shorter symptom duration, with stronger protection for those maintaining activity from pre- to during pandemic.

Longitudinal cohort study following 516 COVID-19 patients at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months to identify long COVID prevalence and risk factors. Found 20% and 17% of participants reported persistent symptoms at 6 and 12 months respectively, with illness severity and hospitalization at diagnosis being significant risk factors.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study examining new-onset psychiatric complications in long COVID patients over 24 months, with prevalence ranging from 2.1-8.5%. Psychiatric complications were associated with COVID-related symptoms, organ system complications, hospitalization, and frailty.

This observational study examines the relationship between acute-phase cytokine levels and long-term cognitive impairment (anosognosia) in 39 post-COVID patients 6-9 months after infection. The findings show that elevated TNFα during acute infection predicts memory awareness deficits and altered limbic system connectivity, but no intervention or treatment was administered.

A prospective cohort study of 28,375 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Dubai followed for 90 days to identify risk factors for long COVID development. Found that 2.8% developed long COVID symptoms, with female gender, younger age, diabetes, asthma, and vitamin D deficiency as key risk factors, while pre-COVID vaccination and acute phase treatment with certain antivirals reduced long COVID risk.

Retrospective cohort study of 26,626 long COVID patients matched with 133,165 COVID-19 controls to identify predisposing factors for long COVID diagnosis. Found that social disadvantage, Black/Mixed ethnicity, multiple comorbidities, and repeated COVID infections increased long COVID risk, but does not test or evaluate any treatment.

This prospective observational study evaluated chest X-ray (CXR) findings in 119 COVID-19 patients at three months post-discharge to assess radiological sequelae and their relationship with clinical findings. The study identified predictive factors (oxygen saturation, hospitalization duration, previous CXR scores) for abnormal CXR at mid-term follow-up, highlighting the radiologist's role in long-term COVID-19 patient monitoring.

Longitudinal observational study examining systemic oxidative stress (measured by circulating free thiols) in non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients over 12 months and its association with post-COVID-19 syndrome development. Found that reduced serum thiols in the acute phase were associated with PCS development at 18 months, suggesting oxidative stress as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target.

This is a secondary analysis of the PAIN-COVID randomized controlled trial examining chronic and neuropathic pain in severe COVID-19 ICU survivors at 6 months post-discharge. While it involves COVID-19 survivors with long-term complications, it does not study a treatment intervention and is explicitly a secondary analysis of existing trial data.

A cross-sectional study of 116 COVID-19 patients discharged from hospital, examining the frequency of persistent symptoms at least 4 weeks post-discharge and their correlation with chest CT severity scores and laboratory findings. Found that 52.5% of patients had persistent symptoms (shortness of breath, fatigue, chest pain, etc.), which were associated with higher CT severity scores, elevated C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and female sex.

Prospective cohort study following COVID-19 hospitalized patients at 3, 6, and 12 months post-discharge to assess PTSD and health-related quality of life trends. While focused on post-hospitalization sequelae, this is a natural history study with no intervention, treatment, or experimental design—it passively follows outcomes without assigning any treatment.

This is a Japanese nationwide prospective cohort study of 1,066 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed at 3, 6, and 12 months post-discharge to characterize long COVID prevalence, symptom burden, and risk factors. The study documents symptom decline over time and identifies risk factors (female sex, middle age, oxygen requirement, critical illness) but does not test any treatment or intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 1,069 COVID-19 patients in Japan evaluating pulmonary function and chest CT abnormalities at 3 months post-discharge. Documents prevalence of persistent symptoms (muscle weakness 48.4%, dyspnea 29%, fatigue 24.7%) and finds disease severity correlates with impaired diffusion capacity, restrictive patterns, and CT abnormalities.

A cross-sectional survey of 170 COVID-19 survivors examining factors associated with chronic cough in post-COVID condition, conducted 158 days median post-recovery. Multivariate analysis identified gastrointestinal symptoms, sputum, and pre-existing chronic cough as significant predictors of cough-related outcomes.
