Prospective nationwide cohort study of 986 COVID-19 patients in Japan examining associations between long COVID symptoms and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-diagnosis. Long COVID symptoms including dyspnea, fatigue, headache, and muscle weakness were significantly associated with worse physical and mental HRQoL scores.

A prospective cohort study of 736 people experiencing homelessness in Toronto followed over 12 months to assess whether longitudinal symptom patterns can identify post-COVID-19 condition. The study found that self-reported symptoms are suboptimal for identifying potential PCC in this population due to high baseline symptom rates and recommends alternative approaches.

A multicenter prospective cohort study of 26 Japanese hospitals examining risk factors for dyspnea in long COVID patients during 12-month follow-up. COPD, asthma, and mechanical ventilation during acute COVID were identified as significant risk factors for prolonged dyspnea, but no intervention was tested.

This cross-sectional survey of 246 Japanese outpatients with mild COVID-19 during the Omicron wave identified risk factors for long COVID symptoms at 12 weeks post-infection. Age ≥40 years was significantly associated with respiratory and neurologic long COVID symptoms, while antiviral drug use was associated with reduced respiratory symptom risk.

Longitudinal CT study of 164 COVID-19 patients examining relationship between pneumonia severity at admission and long-term pulmonary and muscular sequelae at 3 months. Finds that extensive pneumonia on admission predicts reduced lung volumes and pectoralis muscle atrophy, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Observational study comparing post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) outcomes between COVID-19 patients who received advanced respiratory support (IPPV/HFNC) versus standard care, evaluated 3 months post-discharge. Findings show that respiratory abnormalities were more frequent in supported patients, particularly elderly individuals, though most symptom differences were attributable to initial disease severity.

The French SISCOVID cohort study followed 320 COVID-19 hospitalized patients for 3-6 months post-discharge to assess pulmonary impairment using clinical exams, PFTs, and CT imaging. At 6 months, over half had persistent dyspnea, 20% had severe DLCO impairment, and 40% showed fibrotic-like patterns, with worse outcomes in severe COVID-19 cases.

Prospective cohort study measuring respiratory muscle strength and pulmonary function in unvaccinated elite athletes before and after COVID-19 infection. Found persistent decrements in MIP and FVC up to 52 days post-infection despite mild disease, but no treatment intervention was evaluated.

Prospective cohort study following 478 COVID-19 survivors hospitalized in March-May 2020 with assessments at 4 and 16 months post-discharge. At 16 months, 68% reported symptoms including fatigue (53%), dyspnea (37%), and cognitive impairment (40%), with some patients developing new symptoms between assessments.

Retrospective cohort study of 454 long COVID patients from a Tunisian emergency department, documenting prevalence (64.1%) and characterizing residual symptoms. No intervention or treatment was evaluated; the study is purely descriptive/observational and therefore does not meet the criteria for screening as a treatment trial.

This study evaluated a multimodal rehabilitation program (respiratory therapy, exercise training, psychological support) for pulmonary impairment in both acute post-COVID and long-COVID patients. The program yielded marked improvements in pulmonary function, diaphragm dysfunction, and dysfunctional breathing patterns, with most patients achieving return to work.

Prospective cohort study evaluating long COVID sequelae in 478 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors at 4 months post-discharge. Found 51% reported new symptoms (fatigue 31%, cognitive symptoms 21%, dyspnea 16%) with significant CT chest abnormalities (63%) and psychological impacts, but lacked pre-COVID baseline and control group.

A retrospective cohort study of 454 acute COVID-19 patients admitted to a Tunisian emergency department that assessed the prevalence and risk factors for long COVID using WHO definition (symptoms 3+ months post-infection, lasting ≥2 months). Female sex and acute phase complications were identified as independent risk factors for long COVID development (prevalence 64%).

Prospective observational study of 100 long COVID patients with exertional dyspnea, assessing ventilatory efficiency via cardiopulmonary exercise testing at 18 and 36 months post-COVID-19 pneumonia. Found persistently reduced ventilatory efficiency correlating with acute-phase lung involvement, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

This cross-sectional study compared cardiorespiratory patterns and exercise capacity among 94 individuals with long COVID, 100 with resolved symptoms, and 70 healthy controls using 6-minute walk tests and oxygen uptake measurements. While the study found significant impairments in oxygen consumption, ventilatory efficiency, and exercise capacity in long COVID patients with minimal change over six months, it is an observational assessment study without an intervention or treatment component.

Prospective study evaluating long-term sequelae in 86 critically ill COVID-19 patients 6-9 months after hospitalization using standardized clinical assessments, pulmonary function tests, imaging, and psychological screening. Found high prevalence of fatigue (71%), weakness (48%), reduced diffusion capacity (64%), and psychological symptoms (depression 38%, anxiety 24%), with quality of life generally satisfactory.

This retrospective cohort study compares neuromuscular abnormalities (M-wave alterations) between 55 post-COVID patients and 62 ME/CFS patients with recent severe infections, examining symptom prevalence and exercise-induced muscle dysfunction. The study found similar frequencies of neuromuscular symptoms and M-wave alterations (~48% vs 41%) in both groups, suggesting post-COVID syndrome shares early neuromusculature pathophysiology with ME/CFS.

Prospective single-center cohort study evaluating persistent auto-immunity and pulmonary sequelae in 101 COVID-19 patients hospitalized for pneumonia, assessed 3-4 months post-symptom onset. Found 34.5% had detectable auto-antibodies with association between auto-antibodies and parenchymal lung abnormalities on imaging, but no treatment intervention was evaluated.

Post-hoc analysis of a prospective cohort evaluating a respiratory rehabilitation program (RRP) in 110 long COVID patients, with stratification by disease duration and clinical presentation. RRP produced significant improvements in dyspnea, 6-minute walk distance, respiratory pressures, and muscle strength, with benefits observed across disease duration and severity subgroups.

Prospective cohort study (ALCOVID) evaluating clinical, functional, respiratory, and neuropsychological sequelae 3-6 months post-COVID-19 in 100 patients across initial severity levels. Found persistent clinical signs in 50%, abnormal 6-minute walk test in 65%, reduced DLCO in 63%, and significant PTSD scores in 31% of patients.

Prospective cohort study evaluating a personalized rehabilitation program (outpatient, home-based, and self-administered modalities) in 101 post-acute COVID syndrome patients. The program significantly improved inspiratory muscle strength, muscle function, dyspnea, and exercise capacity at 3-6 months, though health-related quality of life improvements were limited to 3 months.

Prospective follow-up study of 33 hospitalized COVID-19 patients (not requiring mechanical ventilation) assessed 6 weeks post-discharge for pulmonary and extrapulmonary sequelae. Patients showed reduced exercise capacity and fatigue (45%), with mild impairment in diffusion capacity but no thromboembolic, cardiac, or significant pulmonary impairments.

This prospective observational study compares lung ultrasonography (LUS) and chest CT for evaluating respiratory outcomes in 38 COVID-19 survivors 3 months post-discharge. LUS demonstrated superior discrimination ability for identifying interstitial lung disease (AUC 0.94-0.95) compared to CT, suggesting it could be a first-line follow-up tool for post-COVID respiratory monitoring.

A longitudinal study of 39 long COVID patients receiving ambulatory respiratory rehabilitation over one year, with most patients presenting dyspnoea (90%) and fatigue (77%). Rehabilitation was associated with significant improvements in exertional dyspnoea, walking distance, and quality of life, with hyperventilation syndrome identified as a frequent contributor to persistent symptoms.

This single-center cohort study followed 126 severe COVID-19 survivors at three months post-hospitalization to assess respiratory sequelae through clinical evaluation, pulmonary function tests, and high-resolution CT imaging. While 25% reported dyspnea and 35% reported fatigue, with 45% showing decreased DLCO and 21% signs of fibrosis, this is a descriptive observational study documenting natural recovery outcomes rather than evaluating a treatment intervention.

This prospective observational study followed COVID-19 patients for 12 months post-infection to assess pulmonary function, imaging changes, and respiratory symptoms across different acute disease severity groups. Patients with more severe acute COVID-19 showed greater correlation between initial respiratory failure severity and persistent pulmonary impairment, though respiratory symptoms generally improved during follow-up.

This observational study examines lung function impairments in 128 COVID-19 hospitalized patients at 6 months post-discharge, stratified by race/ethnicity. It documents that ~22% of patients have persistent lung dysfunction across multiple domains, with non-Hispanic Black patients showing significantly lower diffusion capacity compared to White and Hispanic patients.

This observational cohort study tracked 21 recently hospitalized COVID-19 pneumonia patients using serial lung ultrasound, CT imaging, and physiological measures at discharge and follow-up timepoints (days 41 and 83). The study demonstrates that lung ultrasound can monitor early recovery of interstitial changes post-hospitalization, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

A prospective cross-sectional study of 440 long COVID patients examining the relationship between healthcare setting during acute COVID-19 and post-COVID mood disorders. Patients admitted to respiratory ICU showed higher incidence of mental alterations compared to general ICU patients, with female gender and specific post-COVID symptoms as additional risk factors.

This prospective observational study evaluated Galectin-3 blood concentrations as a predictive biomarker for post-COVID syndrome development in 437 patients. While Galectin-3 showed correlation with post-COVID outcomes and potential as a predictive marker, the study is observational/diagnostic only and does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal Q-SPECT/CT imaging study of 105 severe COVID-19 patients at baseline and 3-month follow-up to evaluate pulmonary perfusion defects and their correlation with symptoms. While the study mentions potential relevance to understanding long COVID mechanisms, it is an observational diagnostic study without any active treatment intervention—patients with perfusion defects received standard anticoagulation rather than an experimental treatment being tested.

A prospective cohort study evaluating respiratory follow-up protocols at 3 and 6 months post-acute COVID-19 in 168 patients. The study found minimal changes in pulmonary function tests and clinical variables during follow-up, concluding that intensive monitoring may not be necessary.

A non-randomized trial evaluating multidisciplinary rehabilitation outcomes in 95 post-COVID-19 patients, comparing 49 patients without preexisting comorbidities to 46 with underlying cardiorespiratory disease. Rehabilitation produced significant improvements in respiratory function, blood gases, and exercise capacity in both groups, suggesting multidisciplinary rehabilitation is effective regardless of preexisting cardiorespiratory comorbidity.

Prospective cohort study following 307 COVID-19 patients hospitalized during the first pandemic wave for up to 24 months post-discharge, assessing pulmonary phenotypes and recovery patterns using spirometry, lung volumes, DLCO, and chest CT. Identified three distinct phenotypes and four longitudinal recovery patterns, with persistent pulmonary symptoms and impaired lung function associated with longer hospitalization, more comorbidities, and severe acute disease.

Cross-sectional study of 417 COVID-19 survivors in Lebanon assessing post-COVID syndrome symptom prevalence and impacts on quality of life and mental health using SF-36 and HADS instruments. Found fatigue, dyspnea, and cough as most common symptoms, with severe acute infection associated with worse physical functioning and role limitations.

Prospective cohort study examining Long COVID as a predictor of myasthenia gravis (MG) exacerbation in 180 MG patients with COVID-19 co-infection, using machine learning for risk stratification. Found Long COVID was the strongest predictor of MG exacerbation (aHR=2.55), but this is observational epidemiology, not a treatment intervention trial.

Retrospective analysis of 213 patients hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia to identify predictive factors for long-term home oxygen therapy prescription. Study identifies advanced age, comorbidities, inflammatory syndrome, and extent of thoracic lesions as predictive factors but does not evaluate a specific intervention or treatment.

Retrospective analysis of 343 chest CT scans from patients over 40 years old comparing interstitial lung abnormality (ILA) prevalence in the post-COVID-19 era to pre-pandemic studies. Found 18% ILA prevalence (double the pre-pandemic ~7%), with increased fibrosing ILAs potentially linked to post-COVID lung changes, but this is an observational study without treatment intervention or control groups.

Prospective descriptive study of 150 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 3 months to assess prevalence and characterize persistent symptoms. 34.5% of patients retained persistent symptoms at 3 months, with fatigue (19%), dyspnea (19.9%), and arthralgia (11.8%) being most common.

This cross-sectional study assessed post-traumatic stress and psychological distress in 36 COVID-19 patients who had been intubated in ICU and were admitted to a respiratory rehabilitation center. While it documents long COVID sequelae (fatigue, dyspnea, anxiety, cognitive dysfunction), it is observational without any treatment intervention—patients were passively assessed during rehabilitation without being assigned to a specific treatment or intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 40 long COVID patients at 3 months post-infection, assessing persistence and types of symptoms. Found 70% had persistent clinical abnormalities, with fatigue (63%), headaches (48%), and neurocognitive dysfunction (38%) being most common; symptoms were more prevalent in women.

Prospective cohort study of 279 COVID-19 pneumonia patients followed at 1 and 3 months post-hospitalization to characterize post-COVID fibrosis clinical and radiological profiles. Identified 10 patients with post-COVID fibrosis and respiratory impairment who received corticosteroid treatment (0.5 mg/kg/day prednisone equivalent per SPLF protocol), with fibrosis associated with severe initial COVID-19 pneumonia and extensive parenchymal lesions.

Retrospective observational study examining the impact of systemic corticosteroid therapy during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection on respiratory sequelae at 3, 6, and 12 months follow-up in hospitalized patients. While patients receiving corticosteroids showed more ground-glass opacities at 3 months, no significant long-term functional differences were found between treatment groups.

Prospective study of 45 COVID-19 patients assessed 3 months post-infection with chest CT scans to characterize pulmonary sequelae and associated factors. Found parenchymal abnormalities in 75% of patients with regression in 91% of cases, most commonly ground-glass opacities, reticulations, and septal thickening.

Prospective observational study of 67 COVID-19 patients followed 3 months post-infection to characterize persistent clinical symptoms and identify risk factors. Found 61.8% retained >3 symptoms, with dyspnea, fatigue, and cognitive impairment as most common; no treatment intervention was tested.

The COMEBAC cohort study evaluated respiratory symptoms and radiological abnormalities in 478 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors at 4 months post-discharge, with detailed assessment of 177 who had ICU admission or persistent symptoms. New-onset dyspnea was present in 16.3% of patients, and pulmonary fibrotic lesions were detected in 19.3% of those reassessed, though their extent was typically minimal and rarely accompanied by both dyspnea and impaired diffusion.

This prospective cross-sectional study evaluated the prevalence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and its risk factors in 157 COVID-19 patients during acute hospitalization, using the PCL-5 questionnaire. PTSD was diagnosed in 36.9% of patients, with female sex and history of severe COVID-19 being significant risk factors.

Retrospective study of 423 COVID-19 patients assessing chest CT findings at admission and 3-month follow-up to evaluate prognostic factors and long-term sequelae. Demonstrates that initial CT extent of lung damage correlates with severe COVID-19 and subsequent imaging abnormalities at 3 months.

Retrospective cohort study of 300 COVID-19 pneumonia patients followed at 3 and 6 months post-discharge, with CT imaging in a subset (n=60 at 3 months, n=9 at 6 months) to assess radiological sequelae. At 6 months, 9 patients had persistent radiological lesions consistent with early pulmonary fibrosis; ground-glass opacities, bronchiolectasis, and septal thickening were most common, associated with older age, longer initial hospitalization, and ICU admission.

Descriptive observational study of 39 post-COVID patients with sleep disorders who underwent polysomnography testing in Madagascar from July 2020 to August 2021. Sleep apnea was diagnosed in 71.8% of patients, with significant correlation between Epworth sleepiness scale and apnea-hypopnea index, but no specific intervention or treatment was tested.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study of 155 hospital staff members with long COVID symptoms, following them over 2 years. Documents symptom persistence and prevalence across multiple organ systems (respiratory, neurological, cardiovascular, psychiatric), with most symptoms resolving by 6-12 months, and identifies need for multidisciplinary evaluation.

Prospective cohort study evaluating post-COVID-19 clinical manifestations and respiratory function in 96 Madagascar patients over 6 months across 3 consultations. Study documents persistent fatigue (50-68%), neurological symptoms (memory loss, insomnia, tremor), respiratory dysfunction, and socioeconomic impact, with 2/3 patient loss to follow-up limiting statistical analysis.

Retrospective cohort study of 77 patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia followed at 30 and 90 days post-discharge to identify predictive factors of persistent long COVID symptoms. Tobacco consumption emerged as a significant predictor of symptom persistence and worsening, while asthma history and advanced age correlated with symptom improvement.

Observational study of 20 patients admitted for respiratory and neuromuscular rehabilitation after acute COVID-19 hospitalization. Patients received physiotherapy interventions during acute phase recovery (not post-COVID/long COVID), showing improvements in 6-minute walk test and oxygen saturation.

Retrospective longitudinal study of 70 patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia followed at 3 months post-discharge to assess respiratory functional impairment. Found persistent diffusion abnormalities (DLCO reduction in 44.3%) and restrictive ventilatory patterns, with severity of initial lung involvement correlating with reduced FEV1.

This study follows 149 hospitalized and 141 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients for 18-30 months to assess long-term survival, functional dependency, and reinfection rates. It is a passive observational follow-up study with no treatment intervention tested, showing that functional dependency improved over time in both groups but reinfection rates were similar (~20%) regardless of initial severity.

Prospective study of 52 patients who had SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, re-evaluated 6 months post-infection with chest CT scans to characterize pulmonary sequelae. Found pathological CT findings in 44% of cases, most commonly ground-glass opacities, micronodules, and honeycombing patterns.

A prospective cohort study of 292 patients hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, followed at 3, 6, and 12 months post-infection to assess respiratory sequelae including DLCO impairment, persistent symptoms, and CT imaging findings. The study is observational with no intervention—it documents natural disease progression rather than testing a treatment.

Prospective analytical study of 1,124 mild COVID-19 patients (outpatient, no oxygen therapy) assessing predictors of persistent symptoms ≥12 months post-infection. Found 23.8% had persistent symptoms; obesity, comorbidities, and acute-phase symptom burden were significant predictive factors.

Retrospective study of 41 post-COVID-19 patients rehospitalized at a Moroccan pneumology service, examining clinical characteristics, inflammatory/coagulation abnormalities, imaging findings, and therapeutic interventions including oxygen therapy, corticosteroids, antibiotics, and anticoagulation. Most patients (70%) had favorable outcomes, though 24% experienced thromboembolic complications and 14% died.

This study examines the impact of long COVID on disease activity, disability, and quality of life in patients with inflammatory arthritis using data from RheumCARD, a prospective cohort study. The findings show that long COVID patients have significantly worse fatigue, pain, and quality of life compared to those without long COVID, but no treatment intervention is being tested or evaluated.

This study compares long-term functional disability and oxygen dependence between hospitalized and non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients at a Lebanese hospital, following 290 patients over 18-30 months. While it documents significant differences in functional disability outcomes, it is a secondary analysis of patient cohorts rather than a treatment intervention trial.

Prospective survey of 174 COVID-19 survivors with pre-existing systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases examining DMARD disruption, disease flare, and prolonged COVID-19 symptoms. Identifies hospitalization and initial symptom count as predictors of prolonged symptom duration (≥28 days) but does not test or evaluate any specific intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 29 COVID-19 participants with taste and smell assessments at baseline and 6-month follow-up using objective chemosensory tests and questionnaires. Study demonstrates significant improvement in olfactory function and modest improvement in taste intensity over 6 months post-infection.

This population-based cohort study examines long-term venous thromboembolism risk (pulmonary embolism and deep venous thrombosis) following COVID-19 hospitalization in Swedish citizens over 180+ days. While it documents elevated VTE risk as a post-COVID sequela, the paper is fundamentally an epidemiological study of disease complications rather than a treatment/intervention trial for long COVID patients.

This cross-sectional study characterized the prevalence and clinical features of persistent COVID-19 symptoms in 1,542 primary care patients, analyzing gender-specific differences in symptom clusters and functional status. While about long COVID, it is an observational characterization study that does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study from the ICOSS-2 collaboration assessed excessive daytime sleepiness and fatigue in 13,656 participants across multiple countries, comparing long COVID (LC), short COVID (SC), and COVID-negative groups. The study found that LC participants had significantly higher ESS and FSS scores and increased odds of severe fatigue and excessive sleep duration compared to SC and COVID-negative controls, highlighting sleep and fatigue as long COVID symptoms rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study surveyed 2,980 US adults at two time points during the COVID-19 pandemic to assess insomnia prevalence and its association with COVID-19 outcomes. Among the 149 participants who contracted COVID-19, those with insomnia reported significantly longer symptom duration (24.8 vs 16.1 sick days), suggesting insomnia is associated with more chronic COVID-19 symptoms.

This study examined respiratory and cardiovascular function in 87 young athletes (52 with prior mild COVID-19, 37 controls) during cycling ergometric testing at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. All athletes recovered fully with no significant functional differences by 6 months, indicating complete normalization of cardiorespiratory parameters post-infection.

Register-based cohort study examining socioeconomic disparities in long COVID diagnosis among ethnic minorities in Denmark, comparing COVID-19 cases (n=2,287,175) by income, education, and ethnicity. Found migrants with low income had higher long COVID risk than native Danes, and certain migrant worker occupations showed elevated risk.

This prospective cohort study followed 14,421 Japanese workers over one year to assess the impact of COVID-19 infection on work functioning. COVID-19 infected workers showed significantly higher incidence of new work functioning impairment (adjusted IRR: 2.18), demonstrating persistent post-acute infection symptoms affecting work capacity.

This prospective cohort study assessed endothelial dysfunction, coagulation activation, and inflammatory markers in 203 COVID-19 patients at 3 months post-infection compared to historic controls. The study found no macrovascular dysfunction but detected sustained inflammation, elevated endothelin-1, and coagulation abnormalities, highlighting vascular involvement in post-COVID recovery.

Population-wide cohort study examining arterial and venous thrombotic event risks following hospitalization for COVID-19, pneumonia, and influenza in 2.6 million Welsh residents. While the study covers post-hospitalization sequelae, it focuses on thrombotic complications rather than long COVID symptoms and does not evaluate any treatment interventions.

This prospective multicenter cohort study examined bleeding risk in pulmonary embolism patients receiving anticoagulation, comparing those with and without COVID-19 infection. While long COVID patients showed significantly higher bleeding rates, this is a secondary analysis of anticoagulation outcomes in PE patients rather than a treatment trial for long COVID itself.

Longitudinal prospective cohort study following 71 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors for up to 12 months to identify sequelae and associated factors. Found that 29.7% developed hypertension and 45.9% developed type 2 diabetes by 5 months, with cognitive dysfunction and memory loss persisting, though some metabolic changes reversed by 12 months.

Retrospective cohort study of kidney transplant recipients hospitalized with severe COVID-19, examining long-term graft function decline over 4 years. While it documents post-COVID renal complications in transplant patients, it does not study long COVID as a syndrome and does not test any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study evaluating whether SARS-CoV-2 vaccination improves symptoms in participants with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC). Found no significant difference in symptom improvement or full recovery between vaccinated and unvaccinated matched pairs over 3 months, with comparable antibody decay trajectories.

Retrospective analysis of 188 kidney transplant recipients with COVID-19 comparing outcomes between those whose immunosuppressive regimens were modified versus unchanged. The study found that immunosuppression minimization did not impact long-term kidney function, but 43.9% of patients reported persistent fatigue post-COVID, indicating long COVID sequelae in this transplant population.

This retrospective cohort study evaluates the relationship between COVID-19 vaccination status and the prevalence of post-COVID cardiac complications and persistent symptoms in 1,883 patients. Vaccinated patients showed significantly lower rates of cardiac injury (1.35% vs 4.11%) and persistent long-COVID symptoms (10.7% vs 18.3%) compared to unvaccinated patients.

This retrospective cohort study examined whether COVID-19 vaccination reduces the risk of developing post-COVID conditions in 84,464 Japanese participants. The study found that recent vaccination (14-149 days before infection) significantly lowered the 8-month incidence of 28 post-COVID conditions, but this is an observational analysis of vaccine effects on disease prevention, not a treatment intervention trial for patients with existing long COVID.

This study examines whether COVID-19 vaccination reduces long COVID risk among adolescents who were infected with SARS-CoV-2, using matched retrospective cohorts. The findings show vaccination reduces long COVID risk by 36%, but this is an observational secondary analysis of vaccine outcomes rather than a primary treatment trial for long COVID patients.

Retrospective observational study examining long COVID prevalence, risk factors, and vaccination status among 717 hospital-discharged COVID-19 survivors in Hong Kong. Study found that booster vaccination doses were associated with lower odds of long COVID symptoms, but this is an observational analysis without an assigned intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examines COVID-19 severity and long COVID incidence in 223 patients with inherited metabolic disorders at a single center. While 25.2% developed long COVID symptoms, the study does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it only characterizes disease outcomes and risk factors in this population.

This cross-sectional study investigates whether specific immune response plasma proteins measured ~39 weeks post-infection can predict Long COVID symptoms or fatigue severity assessed ~116 weeks later in 257 SARS-CoV-2 infected outpatients. While 9 proteins showed associations with Long COVID and 10 with fatigue severity before multiple testing correction, only SRPK2 and ITGA6 remained significant after FDR-adjustment, suggesting limited predictive value of individual plasma proteins.

This retrospective cohort study uses ultrasound shear wave elastography to assess liver stiffness in 30 post-COVID-19 patients compared to 100 controls at an average of 44 weeks post-infection. The study found COVID-19 infection is associated with increased liver stiffness (1.5 kPa increase, p=0.006), suggesting lasting hepatic injury, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

A prospective cohort study examining endothelial dysfunction in COVID-19 patients followed up to 6 months post-discharge, comparing acute and long-standing effects. While the study demonstrates persistent endothelial impairment in long COVID, it is observational without any treatment intervention being tested or evaluated.

This population-based cross-sectional study examined associations between social vulnerability and new-onset mobility disability among 4,295 adults with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in Michigan. Living in high social vulnerability counties was associated with 1.38 times higher odds of reporting new mobility disability post-COVID, but the study is observational without treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining the association between mRNA vaccination status and post-COVID condition (PCC) prevalence in 288 Thai patients with mild COVID-19. Vaccination was associated with reduced PCC risk (43.5% vs 67.3% unvaccinated), but this is an observational analysis of vaccination exposure rather than a treatment intervention trial.

This cross-sectional study of 651 German participants (DigiHero cohort) investigates molecular drivers of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), finding elevated IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF cytokine levels associated with persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, and cognitive dysfunction. The study suggests a self-sustaining pro-inflammatory feedback loop involving lung macrophages as a potential mechanism underlying PASC.

Ambidirectional cohort study of 1,733 COVID-19 survivors discharged from hospital, followed for 6 months to assess long-term health consequences and associated risk factors. Patients experienced fatigue/muscle weakness, sleep difficulties, and anxiety/depression; disease severity during hospitalization was associated with impaired pulmonary function and abnormal chest imaging.

A cross-sectional survey of 122 German healthcare workers infected during the first COVID-19 wave assessed long COVID prevalence and symptom characteristics in June/July 2021. The study found 67% reported persistent symptoms (29% met post-COVID criteria) and identified associations between acute symptoms and symptom persistence duration, but did not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

DigiHero is a digital epidemiology cohort study recruiting 318 long COVID patients in Germany to investigate molecular drivers of PASC through questionnaires, surveys, and blood biomarker profiling. The study found elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF) associated with long COVID symptoms that persist independently of post-infection vaccination.

Prospective cohort study of 291 long COVID patients in Nairobi followed for 12 months, measuring health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and economic burden (catastrophic expenditures/costs) at 3-month intervals. Found HRQoL significantly reduced up to 15 months post-infection, with older age, lack of vaccination, symptoms, and income loss associated with catastrophic expenditures.

This prospective population-based observational cohort study examined persistent somatic symptoms in 4,231 COVID-19 participants matched to 8,462 controls over 24 repeated measurements. The study identified 10 core symptoms substantially increased at 90-150 days post-COVID in 12.7% of patients after correcting for baseline symptom prevalence and population-level symptom dynamics, providing epidemiological evidence for post-COVID-19 condition without testing any intervention.

This cross-sectional study compares brain gray matter volume (GMV) in COVID-19 survivors versus healthy controls using MRI, finding significantly higher GMV in limbic and basal ganglia regions among survivors. The paper reports stronger correlations between GMV alterations and self-reported fatigue in COVID survivors, suggesting a link between structural brain abnormalities and fatigue symptoms, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This study compares major adverse cardiac events (MACE) at 6-month follow-up between COVID-19 positive and negative patients from early pandemic (March-April 2020). While it includes follow-up data, it focuses on acute COVID-19 infection outcomes rather than long COVID sequelae and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Registry analysis documenting the duration of dermatological manifestations in COVID-19 patients, including those with persistent symptoms (long-haulers defined as >60 days). This is a descriptive observational study tracking symptom duration, not an intervention trial.

A prospective multicentre cohort study investigating the relationship between sleep disturbance and respiratory outcomes (dyspnoea and lung function impairment) in COVID-19 hospital survivors. The study follows long COVID patients to understand how sleep disruption affects post-COVID respiratory symptoms.

Staggered cohort study examining whether COVID-19 vaccination prevents long COVID symptoms in data from the UK, Spain, and Estonia. This is an observational cohort study examining outcomes in vaccinated vs unvaccinated populations rather than evaluating a treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

This retrospective registry study examines COVID-19 sequelae prevalence and impact on survival in cancer patients who recovered from SARS-CoV-2 infection across 35 European institutions. While it documents long COVID symptoms (respiratory, fatigue) in 15% of cancer survivors, it is a secondary analysis of a cancer-oncology registry (OnCovid) and does not test or evaluate a specific long COVID treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study following 3,762 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for 1 year to characterize long COVID clinical features and inflammation profiles. Found that persistent symptoms at 12 months associated with elevated inflammatory markers and worse functional outcomes, with no specific intervention tested.

Retrospective cohort study examining rates of subsequent infections in 231,899 US veterans with positive COVID-19 tests versus 605,014 with negative tests between November 2021 and December 2023. Found that COVID-19 positive individuals had significantly increased risk of bacterial, viral, and fungal infections in the 12 months following infection, suggesting long-term immune system effects from SARS-CoV-2.

This is a 3-year longitudinal cohort study of COVID-19 survivors from Wuhan following disease trajectory naturally, without any intervention or treatment. The study found most long COVID symptoms were mild-to-moderate at 3 years, with higher reinfection rates and symptom worsening in those with baseline long COVID.

This prospective UK-wide multicentre MRI follow-up study (C-MORE) evaluates multiorgan abnormalities in 259 hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 5 months post-discharge compared to 52 non-COVID controls. The study documents higher prevalence of lung, brain, and kidney MRI abnormalities in COVID-19 patients but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This longitudinal cohort study followed 1,192 COVID-19 hospital survivors for 2 years post-infection, measuring symptoms, lung function, quality of life, and return to work. While symptoms improved over time, the study found persistent sequelae in 55% at 2 years and significantly worse health status compared to matched controls, highlighting the burden of long COVID but not testing any specific intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining whether molnupiravir treatment within 5 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection reduces the risk of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC/long COVID) in high-risk patients. Results show molnupiravir was associated with reduced risk of PASC (14% relative risk reduction) and 8 of 13 measured post-acute sequelae including fatigue, dysrhythmia, thromboembolism, and neurocognitive impairment.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between COVID-19 vaccination status and risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality in post-COVID-19 patients using Hong Kong electronic health records. The study found that vaccinated patients had lower CVD and mortality risk compared to unvaccinated patients, with a dose-response relationship.

Observational follow-up study across six countries examining mental health outcomes in COVID-19 patients up to 16 months post-diagnosis. Finds that severe acute illness (extended bedriddenness) is associated with persistent depression and anxiety symptoms, while non-severe cases show lower mental health morbidity than uninfected controls.

This retrospective cohort study of 1.3 million COVID-19 patients matched with respiratory infection controls examines 2-year neurological and psychiatric risk trajectories across age groups and variants. It is an observational epidemiological study comparing outcomes between groups but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examines whether early treatment with molnupiravir (within 5 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection) reduces the risk of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC/long COVID) in 229,286 US veterans with risk factors for severe COVID-19. Molnupiravir was associated with a 14% relative risk reduction for PASC, reduced mortality, and reduced risk of eight specific post-acute sequelae including fatigue, dysrhythmia, and neurocognitive impairment.

Prospective cohort study examining post-COVID condition prevalence and characteristics in patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases in the Netherlands. The study follows patients over time to assess long COVID outcomes in this vulnerable population.

A retrospective cohort study examining the association between nirmatrelvir-ritonavir treatment and post-acute sequelae outcomes in immunocompromised patients hospitalized with COVID-19 using Hong Kong Hospital Authority data. Among immunocompromised patients, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was associated with significantly lower risk of post-acute inpatient death (HR 0.58) and acute respiratory distress syndrome, though effectiveness on post-acute hospitalization outcomes was less pronounced than in immunocompetent patients.

A retrospective cohort study investigating associations between HLA alleles and severe COVID-19 outcomes, including PASC (post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection), using the All of Us dataset. The study aims to identify genetic risk factors for severe COVID-19 and PASC but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study followed 157 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in March-April 2020 and assessed them 12 months later for chronic pain and fatigue symptoms. The study found that 27.4% reported chronic fatigue, 25.5% met criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, and 15.3% experienced severe chronic pain, with women more affected than men.

Target trial emulation study comparing metformin users to controls (fluvoxamine, fluticasone, ivermectin, montelukast) using N3C data to assess metformin's effect on long COVID or death within 180 days post-infection. Metformin showed 53% risk reduction (aRR 0.47, 95% CI 0.25-0.89) compared to controls, with consistent results across subgroups and sensitivity analyses.

This retrospective cohort study examines the temporal relationship between new type 2 diabetes diagnosis and SARS-CoV-2 infection using nationwide EHR data from the RECOVER program. The study found that new diabetes diagnoses were paradoxically 83% lower in the 6 months post-infection compared to pre-infection, suggesting complex metabolic sequelae of COVID-19 rather than straightforward diabetes risk elevation.

A 2-year prospective cohort study following 230 COVID-19 survivors to assess prevalence of persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms and identify biobehavioral risk factors. Found that 39.1% had fatigue, 18.3% cognitive failure, and 11.3% depression at 2 years, with female gender, comorbidities, and acute phase severity as key risk factors.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes SARS-CoV-2 sequences linked to electronic health records to examine Long COVID incidence across viral lineages and identify conserved spike protein regions for vaccine development. While it characterizes Long COVID epidemiology by variant, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

A 12-month prospective cohort study of 144 SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals examining psychiatric sequelae using validated questionnaires (SPHERE, DMI, EQ-5D-5L) and inflammatory biomarkers at 6 timepoints. Long COVID status emerged as the strongest predictor of neuropsychiatric symptoms, with robust inverse associations found between inflammatory biomarkers and mental health outcomes.

This retrospective VA database study characterizes long COVID by analyzing new diagnoses in 316,782 COVID-positive veterans from 2020-2022, defining long COVID subtypes by organ system and identifying demographic risk factors. While it provides evidence for long COVID case definition and clinical characterization, it is a secondary analysis of existing EHR data without testing or evaluating any specific treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study examines how acute-phase oxygen saturation and body temperature predict long COVID symptoms (fatigue, depression, anxiety) in 120 LC patients and 36 controls 3-4 months post-infection. The study identifies an endophenotype class characterized by very low SpO2 and high body temperature associated with psychiatric and autonomic symptoms, but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

UK Biobank describes a large prospective cohort study (500,000 participants) repurposed to investigate COVID-19 and its long-term health effects through repeated blood samples, imaging, and data linkages. The paper outlines study protocols and sub-studies investigating long COVID sequelae but does not present results from completed interventions or treatments.

This multicenter study tracks trajectories of anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sleep quality over time in previously hospitalized COVID-19 survivors as part of the LONG-COVID-EXP-CM cohort. It is an observational follow-up study without intervention assignment, focusing on characterizing the natural course of post-COVID psychological and sleep symptoms.

Retrospective observational study of 146 COVID-19 patients with anosmia, tracking olfactory recovery rates and predictors of poor long-term restoration over a mean 5.6-month follow-up. Study found that 36.7% had persistent olfactory disorders, with prolonged anosmia duration as the only significant predictor of incomplete recovery, but no intervention was tested.

Retrospective cohort study examining associations between psychiatric disorders and long COVID diagnosis in 660,217 US veterans. Found that psychiatric disorders, particularly depression/anxiety, were associated with increased long COVID risk, though this is an observational analysis of existing health records rather than a treatment trial.

Longitudinal cohort study (PREDIMED-Plus) assessing the association between COVID-19 infection and long-term depression symptoms in 5,486 older Spanish adults with metabolic syndrome. COVID-19 was associated with significantly higher depression scores at a median of 29 weeks post-infection, particularly in women, but this is an observational study without any treatment intervention.

RECoVERED is a prospective cohort study following 235 participants for 24 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection to examine how biomedical, psychological, and social factors contribute to persistent symptoms (fatigue, cognitive complaints, depression, physical limitations). The study uses structural network analysis to explore associations between these factors and outcomes, finding that loneliness, fear avoidance, and illness perceptions are directly linked to persistent symptoms.

Prospective cohort study comparing long-term sequelae following SARS-CoV-2 infection across different variants, other respiratory infections, and uninfected individuals. Found that early SARS-CoV-2 variants had higher probability of long-term symptoms than recent Omicron sub-variants, which were similar to other respiratory infections.

A retrospective epidemiological study using primary care data from a Spanish rural village to describe COVID-19 spread, risk factors, and disease severity over 2.5 years. While it documents post-COVID illness in 23% of patients, it is an observational cohort study without any treatment intervention—it passively follows patients without assigning them to treatment.

A prospective cohort study examining the association between gastrointestinal symptoms during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and persistent GI symptoms or post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome (PI-IBS) at ≥45 days post-infection in 1,475 participants. The study found that participants with acute GI symptoms had 4-fold higher odds of persistent symptoms, with an average symptom duration of 8 months and 3.0% developing PI-IBS.

Descriptive cohort study assessing health-related quality of life in 559 former COVID-19 patients up to 2 years post-infection using PROMIS measures. Found significant impairments in fatigue, sleep, dyspnea, and cognitive function compared to non-infected controls, with depression, fatigue, and cognitive dysfunction as most commonly affected domains.

This cross-sectional study compares long COVID clinical phenotypes between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients, finding that vaccination status is associated with different symptom presentations rather than symptom prevention. The paper is excluded because it is observational without testing any intervention or treatment—it merely characterizes existing patients by vaccination status.

This paper describes the establishment and operation of Turkish Ministry of Health COVID-19 Follow-up Centers designed to monitor recovered COVID-19 patients for long-term complications. The centers tracked 11,288 patients over one year at multiple timepoints, finding declining symptom prevalence, but the paper presents operational/infrastructure details rather than formal treatment trial data or completed outcome analyses.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and depressive symptoms in a French population-based cohort. Findings show COVID-19 is associated with somatic complaints but not a direct impact on depression risk.

A cross-sectional post-discharge assessment of 767 COVID-19 survivors from Bergamo province conducted at median 81 days after discharge, documenting persistent symptoms (51.4%), psychological consequences (30.5%), lung impairment (19%), and thromboembolic markers. The study describes the complexity of long COVID sequelae and the need for multidisciplinary clinical approaches, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 1,234 long COVID patients from 3 to 6 months post-infection to identify factors associated with persistence or recovery. Found that pre-existing conditions and specific symptoms at 3 months predicted persistent long COVID at 6 months, with distinct clinical trajectories between those who recovered and those with minimal improvement.

Longitudinal study examining how COVID-19-related experiences during the peripartum period affect maternal depression and anxiety symptoms, with long COVID, partner support, and self-efficacy as moderators. This is an observational cohort study with no treatment intervention—it examines associations between experiences and outcomes without assigning or testing any therapeutic intervention.

This study assessed neuropsychiatric symptoms in 39 older COVID-19 survivors (~99 days post-discharge) using standardized screening tools, finding cognitive impairment in 18%, depressive symptoms in 23%, and anxiety in 15%. It is observational and descriptive with no treatment intervention or comparison group, making it ineligible as a treatment trial.

Observational study comparing 67 elderly dementia patients with COVID-19 to 41 controls without COVID, assessing changes in frailty, cognitive function, disability, and comorbidity over 12 months. COVID group showed significantly worse frailty progression and disability (ADL) compared to controls, suggesting COVID accelerates frailty trajectory in older adults with dementia.

This cross-sectional study compared 121 children with prior COVID-19 to 95 healthy controls, assessing persistent symptoms and cardiac findings. Results show 37.2% of cases had clinical symptoms persisting ≥1 month post-recovery, with significant differences in blood pressure and echocardiographic parameters between groups.

Retrospective study examining coronary artery changes in 157 non-hospitalized children with asymptomatic or mild acute COVID-19 using echocardiography. Found coronary artery dilation in 2.5% (4/157) of cases, but focuses on acute phase cardiac complications rather than long COVID sequelae.

A prospective cohort study tracking cognitive trajectories in 24 post-COVID-19 patients over 6 weeks using repeated neuropsychological testing. The study found improvements in cognitive fatigue (41.7%), processing speed, and memory, with older age and longer illness duration predicting faster recovery in select domains.

Retrospective chart review characterizing sluggish cognitive tempo (SCT) symptoms in 25 pediatric PASC patients and examining associations with ADHD, depression, anxiety, and functional impairment. Found elevated Sluggish/Sleepy and Low Initiation SCT subscales, with Low Initiation associated with depression/anxiety but not ADHD, suggesting depression/anxiety moderate the relationship between initiation problems and functional impairment.

This longitudinal study assessed cognitive impairment in 42 post-COVID syndrome patients with subjective cognitive complaints over ~15 months post-infection, comparing subjective reports to objective neuropsychological test results. The study found a ~40% discrepancy between reported and objectively measured cognitive deficits, with patients showing objective impairment reporting higher fatigue and reduced quality of life.

This cross-sectional study assessed cognitive dysfunction and cognitive complaints in 110 adults 12 months post-COVID-19 using neuropsychological testing and self-report questionnaires. While it characterizes long COVID cognitive sequelae and identifies predictors, it does not evaluate any treatment intervention—it is a natural history/observational study with no treatment assignment, so it is excluded from the intervention trial pipeline.

This study measured plasma protein levels in 74 COVID-19 patients at admission and 3 and 6 months post-infection to identify proteomic signatures of post-COVID conditions and associations with pulmonary function. The research found that lipid-related pathways increased while innate immune and vasoconstriction proteins decreased from acute to post-COVID stages, with distinct sex-based differences.

Population-based prospective cohort study (SHARE Corona Surveys) examining sex differences in the relationship between pre-pandemic BMI and Long COVID risk in 4,004 Europeans aged 50+. Finds linear BMI-Long COVID relationship in females and non-linear relationship in males, with females having higher overall Long COVID prevalence.

This retrospective cohort study examined whether molnupiravir treatment within 5 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection reduces the risk of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC/long COVID) in 229,286 Veterans Affairs patients. Molnupiravir was associated with reduced risk of PASC overall (RR 0.86) and eight specific post-acute sequelae including fatigue, neurocognitive impairment, and thromboembolism.

This retrospective cohort study of 34,489 COVID-19 hospitalized patients identifies acute severity markers (hospital stay >7 days, acute delirium, elevated monocyte count) that predict post-COVID new-onset psychiatric disorders over 2 years of follow-up. The study develops and validates predictive scores with good positive predictive values, though it is observational and does not test an intervention.

Retrospective cohort study using German primary care database examining prevalence and risk factors for post-COVID-19 condition in 6,568 children and adolescents diagnosed with COVID-19 between October 2020 and August 2021. Found post-COVID-19 condition rare (1.7% prevalence) with older age, anxiety disorders, somatoform disorders, and allergic rhinitis as significant risk factors.

Community-based cohort study of 1,000 COVID-19 survivors 20 months post-infection characterizing long COVID sequelae phenotypes across five organ systems using latent class analysis. Identified four clusters ranging from asymptomatic to severe, with predictors including age, comorbidities, hospitalization duration, and acute illness severity.

A case series studying therapeutic apheresis as a treatment for long COVID, analyzing biomarkers before and after treatment in patients who reported clinical improvement. The study found significant reductions in neurotransmitter autoantibodies, lipids, inflammatory markers, and fibrinogen in responders, suggesting potential objective biomarkers for monitoring treatment response.

This prospective cohort study identified three cognitive neurophenotypes in 205 post-COVID patients using neuropsychological testing and clustering analysis, with 6-month follow-up data on 79 participants. Most participants showed cognitive recovery or normal cognition, with the 25-30% showing impairment clustering into two distinct phenotypes (dysexecutive and amnestic) associated with different patient and disease factors.

Prospective longitudinal study comparing post-COVID-19 condition prevalence in 260 children with mild acute COVID-19, 60 with severe acute COVID-19, and 259 negative controls over 1-year follow-up. Found severe acute COVID-19 associated with higher PPCC prevalence (29.2% at 3 months) than mild cases (14.6%), with prevalence decreasing to 4.4% by 1 year, and identified risk factors including prior medical history, hospitalization, and persistent fatigue.

This study profiles humoral immune responses in children at acute presentation and 6-month follow-up after COVID-19 and MIS-C, tracking changes in antibody profiles and cytokine levels. While it documents post-COVID immunological changes, it is a passive observational follow-up study without any intervention or treatment being tested, and represents a secondary analysis of biorepository samples rather than a prospective trial design.

Prospective cohort study of 121 recovered COVID-19 patients at 1-year follow-up examining immune response persistence and functional recovery. Study documents long-term antibody levels, re-infection protection estimates, and persistent symptoms/abnormalities in severe patients (79% still symptomatic, 53% with imaging abnormalities), but is purely observational without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective study of 568 children with asthma and COVID-19 infection comparing clinical characteristics between asthmatic and non-asthmatic groups. Found that asthmatic children had higher frequencies of respiratory symptoms and that poor therapy compliance was a risk factor for long COVID, but this is an observational study that does not test or evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study uses electronic health records from 2.4M NYC patients to examine trends in clinical psychiatric diagnoses before and after COVID-19 infection between March 2020 and August 2021. While it documents increased psychiatric diagnoses in COVID-19 positive patients (relevant to long COVID sequelae), it does not evaluate any specific treatment or intervention for long COVID.

This cross-sectional study evaluated 608 COVID-19 survivors 6-11 months post-hospitalization to investigate whether subjective memory complaints are associated with objective cognitive impairment or psychiatric symptoms. The findings show that memory complaints are more strongly linked to depression and post-traumatic stress symptoms than to primary cognitive impairment.

Retrospective EHR study of 2.4M COVID-19 patients examining associations between non-psychiatric PASC manifestations and new-onset psychiatric disease. Finds significant associations between neurological, cardiovascular, and constitutional PASC features and psychiatric diagnosis; however, this is an observational analysis without testing any intervention or treatment.

Multicenter cohort study examining sex-specific risk factors for long COVID in 1,066 hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Calcium channel blocker use was significantly associated with reduced frequency of multiple long COVID symptoms (alopecia, memory impairment, sleep disorders, tinnitus) in female patients.

Prospective multicentric cohort study identifying an immunoglobulin (IgM and IgG3) signature that predicts risk of developing long COVID (PACS) in 215 COVID-19 patients followed up to one year, validated in 395 additional patients. The study aims to facilitate early identification of at-risk patients for targeted treatment research but does not itself test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study compared erectile dysfunction risk in men diagnosed with long COVID versus acute COVID using propensity score matching on TriNetX data from 2020-2023. Men with long COVID had significantly higher risk of ED or PDE5i prescription (3.63% vs 2.61%, RR 1.39) compared to acute COVID controls.

This study analyzes long COVID burden and risk factors using data from 10 UK longitudinal studies (6,907 participants) and 1.1 million individuals in electronic health records. It identifies associations between demographic and health factors (age, sex, ethnicity, mental health, obesity, asthma) and persistent symptoms lasting 12+ weeks, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study using Veterans Affairs healthcare databases quantifies the burden of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) across demographics and baseline health status. The study estimates PASC burden at 73.43 per 1000 persons at 6 months but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study compared the risk of erectile dysfunction following COVID-19 infection versus other acute viral infections using propensity-matched cohorts from a national claims database. COVID-19 was not specifically associated with elevated ED risk compared to other viral illnesses, suggesting a general inflammatory response to acute infection rather than a virus-specific effect.

A Scottish population cohort study comparing 33,281 confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases with 62,957 never-infected individuals, followed up at 6, 12, and 18 months to assess long-COVID prevalence and outcomes. Found that 6% of symptomatic infections had no recovery and 42% had partial recovery, with associations between non-recovery and hospitalization, age, female sex, deprivation, comorbidities, and 24 persistent symptoms.

A prospective observational cohort study comparing clinical and laboratory parameters in 42 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients with persistent moderate-to-severe fatigue to non-COVID myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome patients. The study identifies biomarkers associated with symptom severity and hand grip strength, suggesting low-level inflammation and hypoperfusion as potential pathomechanisms, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study comparing post-COVID complaints between Omicron and Delta variant infections across 1.3 million Norwegian participants. Finds similar acute/sub-acute burden but lower chronic musculoskeletal pain with Omicron at ≥90 days post-infection.

This paper uses longitudinal matched cohort data to characterize post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) conditions over time, comparing PCR-positive and PCR-negative populations while controlling for pre-existing conditions. It identifies PASC conditions occurring in acute/persistent (0-120 days) and late (30-120+ days) periods, finding increased risk of anosmia, cardiac dysrhythmia, diabetes, and other conditions in long COVID patients, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study analyzed gut microbiota composition in 133 COVID-19 patients followed for up to 6 months, identifying ecological clusters associated with disease severity and post-acute COVID-19 syndrome. The study did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention, but rather characterized microbial and host factors as prognostic biomarkers.

Population-based serological study examining the prevalence and risk factors of post-COVID syndrome in Swiss children and adolescents aged 6 months to 17 years. Found 9.1% prevalence of persistent symptoms in seropositive children (particularly adolescents), with identified risk factors including older age, lower socioeconomic status, and chronic health conditions like asthma.

Prospective e-cohort study tracking 968 long COVID patients over 5,350 person-months using daily symptom questionnaires to characterize disease natural history. Found that 85% of symptomatic patients at 2 months remained symptomatic at 1 year, with symptoms showing decreasing, stable, or increasing prevalence patterns over time.

This retrospective cohort study uses VA health databases to estimate the risks and 1-year burdens of gastrointestinal disorders in the post-acute phase of COVID-19, comparing 154,068 COVID-19 patients to contemporary and historical controls. The study found significantly increased risks of multiple GI disorders including motility disorders, acid-related disorders, and functional intestinal disorders across all severity levels of acute COVID-19.

This EHR-based cohort study from the RECOVER program examines the association between pre-COVID vaccination status and long COVID diagnosis using two definitions (clinical diagnosis and computational phenotype). It is an observational study analyzing existing health records data, not an intervention trial evaluating a treatment for long COVID.

This study uses electronic health records from two large Patient-Centered Clinical Research Networks (INSIGHT and OneFlorida+) to characterize long COVID diagnoses and medications through propensity score analysis. It identifies significantly elevated incidence of conditions like dementia, hair loss, dyspnea, chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, and fatigue in the 30-180 days post-infection window, highlighting heterogeneous PASC risks across different populations.

Population-based prospective cohort study following adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and PCR-negative controls at 6, 12, and 18 months post-infection to assess natural history and symptom progression of long COVID. Found 35% with persistent incomplete recovery, 12% improved, and 12% worsened, with most symptoms improving over time compared to never-infected controls.

This nationwide Danish register-based study examines the risk of neurological disorders after COVID-19 using all SARS-CoV-2 test results and hospitalization records from 2020-2021 with 22-month follow-up. While confirming increased neurological risk post-COVID, the study finds these risks are comparable to other severe respiratory infections and does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

A hybrid register and questionnaire study of 37,482 RT-PCR confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases and 51,336 test-negative controls examining post-acute sick leave as an indicator of societal burden. The study identifies risk factors (female sex, age 50-65, obesity, chronic lung disease, fibromyalgia) associated with substantial sick leave (>1 month) in the 1-9 months post-infection period, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Multinational cohort study of 856,840 COVID-19 cases and 3.1 million controls from Spain and UK examining the burden and patterns of persistent post-acute COVID-19 symptoms over time. Study characterizes symptom prevalence, compares cases vs controls, and tracks symptom trends across reinfections, but does not test any treatment interventions.

This Norwegian register-based study of 214,667 SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals identifies pre-infection risk factors for post-COVID condition, finding psychological, respiratory, and general health problems significantly increase risk. Using machine learning, the researchers achieved an AUC of 0.79 in predicting post-COVID complaints ≥3 months post-infection based on pre-infection characteristics and virus/vaccine information.

This nationwide population cohort study of 198,096 Scottish adults determines the true prevalence of long COVID symptoms attributable to SARS-CoV-2 infection, accounting for background symptom rates in never-infected controls. While 64.5% of infected individuals reported symptoms at 6 months, adjusted prevalence of infection-attributable long COVID was 6.6% at 6 months, 6.5% at 12 months, and 10.4% at 18 months.

IMPACC prospective cohort study tracking 590 COVID-19 patients from acute illness through one year post-discharge to identify long COVID phenotypes and associated acute-phase biomarkers. Identified 4 PRO-based clusters (minimal, physical, mental/cognitive, multidomain) and linked acute viral burden and immune markers to long COVID risk without testing any intervention.

A longitudinal case-control study (NCT05225688) examining the pathophysiology of post-exertional malaise in long COVID patients by comparing skeletal muscle structure, metabolism, and exercise capacity to controls. The study shows that muscle structure abnormalities, metabolic disturbances, myopathy, and amyloid deposits worsen after exercise-induced post-exertional malaise, revealing novel mechanisms underlying this distinctive long COVID symptom.

This study compares SARS-CoV-2 antibody and T cell immunity in 86 healthcare workers with mild/asymptomatic infection, stratified by presence or absence of persistent symptoms at 18 weeks and 1 year post-infection. The authors find no significant differences in adaptive immune responses between those with persistent symptoms and those without, concluding that differential SARS-CoV-2 immunity is unlikely to explain long COVID pathogenesis.

This retrospective cohort study examines the risk of long-term health consequences following SARS-CoV-2 infection across 1.17M patients stratified by vaccination status in Hong Kong. It is excluded because it is an observational analysis of vaccination's protective effect on natural disease progression, not a study testing a specific treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

Prospective 6-month follow-up study of mild Omicron BA.2 breakthrough infection convalescents examining immune recovery and metabolic outcomes using blood tests, proteomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing. Documents organ dysfunction recovery, durable neutralizing antibodies, and immunity-metabolism imbalance as potential contributors to long COVID development—but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This multinational cohort study examined the incidence of allergic diseases (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, food allergy) in patients with post-COVID-19 condition using claims-based data from South Korea, Japan, and the UK. The study found significantly elevated risk of developing allergic diseases beyond 30 days post-COVID, with the highest risk for asthma, and demonstrated protective effects of COVID-19 vaccination.

This observational study compares humoral and cellular immune responses between long COVID patients and recovered COVID-19 controls over 24 months, showing resolution of immune activation differences over time. The study does not evaluate a treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline despite being longitudinal and long COVID-focused.

Retrospective matched cohort study comparing post-COVID conditions (PCC) incidence in vaccinated vs. unvaccinated individuals following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Vaccination was associated with reduced risk of most PCC categories except mental health disorders.

Large population-based cross-sectional study comparing health outcomes and symptom profiles in 242,712 adults with ongoing post-COVID symptoms versus those who never had COVID or recovered. Finds that persistent symptoms are associated with worse mental health and quality of life, with 7.5% experiencing symptoms ≥12 weeks, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Population-based cohort study comparing respiratory complications in SARS-CoV-2 infected vs uninfected individuals in South Korea and Japan, using propensity score matching. Found significantly elevated risk of acute and post-acute respiratory sequelae in infected individuals, with protective effects of vaccination and risk diminishing but persisting beyond 6 months.

Prospective cohort study examining early viral and immune markers in 136 participants to identify biological predictors of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found that PASC patients had higher viral loads and lower Spike-specific IgG early in infection, but no treatment/intervention was tested.

This retrospective cohort study examined Long COVID risk in individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 during pregnancy compared to non-pregnant females using two U.S. healthcare databases (PCORnet and N3C). While the study found a high incidence of Long COVID in pregnant individuals, their adjusted risk was significantly lower than matched non-pregnant females, with Black race/ethnicity, advanced maternal age, and comorbidities identified as risk factors.

Retrospective cohort study using RECOVER Initiative data analyzing racial/ethnic differences in long COVID symptoms and conditions among 225,723 children and adolescents. Study found significant disparities in PASC manifestations across racial/ethnic groups, stratified by acute COVID-19 severity, but did not test any intervention or treatment.

Population-based retrospective cohort study examining cardiovascular disease risk following COVID-19 in 4.1 million Swedish adults aged 40-75, accounting for hospitalization status, vaccination, and social factors. Study demonstrates elevated cardiovascular risk even among mild COVID-19 cases, with strongest effects in vulnerable populations, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This UK Biobank cohort study examines associations between modifiable lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, BMI, physical activity, sleep, diet) and post-COVID multisystem sequelae, hospitalization, and death in 68,896 participants. A favorable lifestyle was associated with 36% lower risk of multisystem sequelae and 41% lower risk of post-COVID death, but the study is observational without testing any specific intervention.

Cross-sectional study comparing Post-COVID-19 Condition symptom prevalence between emergency department patients who tested positive vs negative for SARS-CoV-2, using WHO clinical case definition. Finds one-third of COVID-positive patients meet Post-COVID criteria at 3 months, but also 20% of test-negative patients report similar symptoms, highlighting diagnostic specificity challenges.

A nested case-control study comparing SARS-CoV-2 serological responses (anti-N and anti-S antibodies) between 394 people with post-COVID condition and 1,616 with acute-only infections from the Virus Watch cohort. The study found elevated anti-N antibody levels in PCC cases but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study of 3,659 RECOVER participants identified eight distinct longitudinal profiles of Long COVID symptom trajectories over 3-15 months post-infection, with 5% showing persistently high burden and 14% developing increasing symptoms. The research characterizes natural disease progression patterns to inform future clinical trial enrollment and treatment strategy development.

This retrospective cohort study evaluates the real-world effectiveness of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir in reducing short- and long-term cardiovascular complications in hospitalized COVID-19 patients using target trial emulation. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with significant reductions in cardiovascular mortality, major adverse cardiac events, and other cardiac complications over one year, while molnupiravir showed more limited long-term benefits.

This retrospective cohort study used EHR data from 19 U.S. children's hospitals to assess cardiovascular outcomes in 297,920 SARS-CoV-2-positive children and adolescents versus 915,402 negative controls during the 28-179 day post-infection period. The study found increased risk of multiple cardiovascular conditions (hypertension, arrhythmias, myocarditis, heart failure, etc.) in infected individuals but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between early SARS-CoV-2 virologic rebound and post-acute mortality/hospitalization among 13,859 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Hong Kong. Finds that virologic rebound is associated with significantly higher risk of post-COVID conditions, but the study observes outcomes in patients who had antiviral treatment rather than testing a specific intervention for long COVID.

Analysis of anonymized primary care data from a UK urban area examining demographic characteristics of long COVID patients and their referral patterns to secondary care services. Findings show that secondary care referrals were skewed toward older patients and UK-born individuals with comorbid anxiety, despite long COVID demographics broadly reflecting the multiethnic and socially disadvantaged population.

This study evaluates whether monovalent COVID-19 vaccination reduces long-COVID symptoms by inhibiting viral interference between SARS-CoV-2 and DNA viruses (EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19) in 252 long-COVID patients. Vaccinated patients showed significantly less fatigue, multiorgan symptoms, and lower DNA virus-related antibody titers compared to unvaccinated long-COVID patients.

This study analyzes plasma cytokine levels in 540 individuals with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) stratified by post-infection mRNA vaccination status and 20 uninfected vaccinated controls. The findings show that vaccinated PCC patients had lower IL-1β and IL-18 levels and reduced gastrointestinal symptoms compared to unvaccinated PCC patients, suggesting potential therapeutic benefit of post-infection vaccination in a subgroup with GI manifestations.

This retrospective cohort study using UK Biobank data examines long-term psychiatric outcomes and psychotropic prescriptions among COVID-19 survivors compared to uninfected controls. While it provides important epidemiological evidence of psychiatric comorbidities in long COVID, it is a secondary analysis of existing biobank data rather than a prospective trial evaluating a treatment intervention.

Commentary on the relationship between Long COVID and psychiatric outcomes, discussing design principles for patient-centered research. Not a primary empirical study—this is an editorial perspective piece by a Long COVID patient advocate.

A national surveillance study identifying 381 individuals with persistent SARS-CoV-2 RNA lasting ≥30 days and examining viral load kinetics and evolutionary dynamics. While the study documents an association between persistent infection and higher odds of long COVID self-reporting, it is an observational epidemiological study that does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study followed 214 COVID-19 patients for one year to identify early biomarkers of long COVID (PASC), including iron dysregulation, anemia, and altered immune responses. The study identifies mechanistic correlates of PASC but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This observational cohort study examined longitudinal brain imaging changes in 401 UK Biobank participants with SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to 384 controls, using pre- and post-infection MRI scans. The study found significant reductions in grey matter thickness, tissue damage markers, and global brain size in infected participants, along with greater cognitive decline, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.
