This epidemiological study analyzed 4,182 COVID-19 cases from the COVID Symptom Study app to characterize long COVID prevalence, identify risk factors (age, BMI, female sex, early symptom burden), and develop a predictive model to distinguish short from long COVID at 7 days post-infection. The model achieved 76% AUC and could identify individuals at risk for trials and inform rehabilitation planning, but does not itself test any intervention.

Analysis of INSPIRE cohort data examining symptom progression in 1,296 participants with COVID-like illness over 12 months, comparing those with positive vs. negative SARS-CoV-2 tests. Findings show no significant difference in persistent symptoms between groups at 12 months, suggesting many symptoms are not unique to post-COVID conditions.

This paper uses Veterans Affairs national healthcare databases to characterize 6-month post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 across multiple organ systems (respiratory, neurological, cardiovascular, metabolic, etc.). It is a retrospective observational analysis of health outcomes and medication use patterns rather than an intervention trial, and therefore is excluded.

Prospective cohort study of 159 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed 28-60 days post-discharge with multisystem imaging and biomarkers to characterize post-COVID syndrome pathophysiology. Found evidence of persistent cardio-renal involvement, myocarditis, reduced quality of life, and increased healthcare utilization compared to controls.

Population-based cohort study using Korean and Japanese national databases to investigate short- and long-term neuropsychiatric outcomes after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found elevated risks of conditions like cognitive deficit, anxiety, and mood disorders up to one year post-infection, with reduced risk associated with vaccination and mild COVID severity.

A prospective clinical study of patients 28-60 days post-COVID-19 hospitalization examining multisystem involvement through cardio-renal inflammation, lung function, and self-reported outcomes compared to controls. The study characterizes post-COVID sequelae but does not evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study uses US Veterans Affairs healthcare databases to characterize post-acute cardiovascular outcomes in 153,760 COVID-19 survivors compared to contemporary and historical controls. The study found increased risk of multiple cardiovascular conditions (heart disease, dysrhythmias, myocarditis, thromboembolism) in the year following acute infection, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective matched cohort study using UK primary care data identifying 62 symptoms significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection beyond 12 weeks and characterizing sociodemographic and clinical risk factors for long COVID development. Study reports symptom prevalence and risk factor associations but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study using VA healthcare databases examined post-acute sequelae following breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection in vaccinated individuals, comparing outcomes to multiple control groups. The study found that breakthrough infection was associated with increased risks of death and incident post-acute sequelae at 6 months, though these risks were lower than in unvaccinated infected individuals, suggesting vaccination provides partial but incomplete protection against long COVID.

This paper is a large cohort study of non-hospitalized adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection examining long COVID symptoms and risk factors. It identifies 62 persistent symptoms beyond 12 weeks and associated risk factors, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study followed 312 COVID-19 patients (247 home-isolated, 65 hospitalized) in Bergen, Norway to characterize long-term symptoms. At 6 months, 61% had persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, cognitive impairment, and taste/smell loss, with severity associated with initial illness severity and antibody titers.

A prospective observational cohort study examining cardiac pathology in 346 COVID-19 survivors with mild initial illness, using cardiac biomarkers and MRI imaging at baseline (~109 days post-infection) and follow-up (~329 days post-infection). Found that 73% of participants reported cardiac symptoms at baseline with evidence of diffuse myocardial edema and inflammatory involvement, and 57% had persistent symptoms at follow-up, with female gender and baseline myocardial involvement predicting persistent symptoms.

This retrospective cohort study uses VA healthcare databases to assess the incidence and burden of neurologic disorders at 12 months following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection in 154,068 COVID-19 patients compared to controls. The study found elevated risk of multiple neurologic sequelae (stroke, cognition disorders, movement disorders, etc.) but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational cohort study compares neurological outcomes in SARS-CoV-2 survivors versus uninfected contemporaries at 1-year follow-up. It documents increased risk of various post-acute neurological disorders as part of long COVID sequelae.

Prospective cohort study tracking 138,818 SARS-CoV-2-infected and 5.98 million uninfected individuals from the Veterans Affairs system for 2 years post-infection to assess mortality risk and 80 prespecified long COVID sequelae. Found that while many sequelae resolved by 2 years, hospitalized patients retained significant long-term health burden with substantial cumulative disability.

Three-year prospective cohort study of 135,161 COVID-19 patients from Veterans Affairs examining mortality and incident PASC over 3 years post-infection. Findings show declining but persistent risks of death and PASC-related disability burden in both hospitalized and non-hospitalized individuals through year 3.

This is a substudy of the NOR-SOLIDARITY randomized trial investigating pulmonary outcomes 3 months after COVID-19 hospitalization in 108 patients, examining associations with viral load, antibody response, and matrix metalloproteinase-9. The trial tested remdesivir and hydroxychloroquine efficacy, finding persistent respiratory symptoms and imaging abnormalities in ~30-40% of patients, with high viral load and elevated MMP-9 as predictors of worse pulmonary outcomes.

This prospective study investigates the prevalence and mechanisms of inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) in 200 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients, finding IST in 20% with reduced heart rate variability parameters suggesting cardiac autonomic nervous system imbalance. The study uses comparative analysis against recovered and non-infected controls to characterize the autonomic dysfunction underlying IST in long COVID patients.

Prospective cohort study following 200 COVID-19 hospitalization survivors at 12 months post-discharge to assess long-term sequelae including pulmonary function, motor performance, and psychological symptoms. Found high prevalence of persistent symptoms (39.5%), lung function impairment (49%), and motor dysfunction (25.8%), with respiratory decline but motor improvement over 4-12 month follow-up period.

This cohort study examined the prevalence and risk factors for acute and persistent symptoms in non-hospitalized PCR-confirmed COVID-19 patients in Denmark. Among 445 participants, 36% of symptomatic patients experienced persistent symptoms beyond 4 weeks, most commonly fatigue and cognitive difficulties, with female sex and higher BMI identified as significant risk factors.

This retrospective cohort study uses VA healthcare data to compare risks of death, hospitalization, and organ-system sequelae in individuals with one SARS-CoV-2 infection versus reinfection (two or more infections) versus uninfected controls. Reinfection significantly increased postacute sequelae risks across multiple organ systems (pulmonary, cardiovascular, neurological, etc.) at 6 months compared to single infection, demonstrating a cumulative burden effect.

This study examined retinal vessel changes in COVID-19 patients during acute infection and 6 months post-infection compared to unexposed controls. While it demonstrates persistent retinal vessel dilation in severe post-COVID patients suggesting vascular damage, it is observational without any treatment intervention and thus excluded from the intervention trials dataset.

Prospective cohort study following 248 COVID-19 survivors (69.4% hospitalized) for 6 months in Northwest Spain to document persisting symptoms. Found 48.0% had persistent symptoms at 6 months, with higher prevalence in hospitalized patients and women; identified COPD, female gender, and tobacco use as risk factors.

Retrospective cohort study examining pulmonary function, lung imaging, and inflammatory markers in 40 COVID-19 survivors (25 severe cases) at mean 249 days post-discharge. Severe cases showed persistent symptoms, DLCO impairment, and radiographic abnormalities correlated with acute illness severity and inflammatory markers.

This prospective cohort study followed 372 COVID-19 patients (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) at 2 and 6 months post-infection to characterize long COVID symptoms and their associations with demographic, clinical, and imaging variables. The study found gender differences in symptom presentation and that non-hospitalized patients experienced more severe fatigue and thromboembolic events.

summary: This observational study assessed the prevalence of post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) in 186 mechanically ventilated COVID-19 survivors at 3 months post-discharge across three hospitals. The study found 75% of survivors met PICS criteria with significant physical, cognitive, and psychiatric sequelae, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective cohort study assessing post-acute COVID-19 outcomes in hospitalized children and young people, with clinical assessments conducted 4+ weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found that 85% of children made full recovery, with only a small proportion experiencing symptoms lasting >4 weeks that mostly resolved by 3 months.

This study uses a representative U.S. population sample (n=308 COVID-infected individuals) to estimate long COVID prevalence and characterize new-onset persistent symptoms in the first year of the pandemic. It identifies that 23% experienced symptoms lasting >12 weeks and demonstrates associations between long COVID and obesity, hair loss, headache, and sore throat during acute infection, providing national prevalence estimates while accounting for pre-infection symptoms.

This prospective observational study compared balance function between 50 young adults recovered from mild COVID-19 and 50 matched healthy controls using force platform analysis and clinical tests. The study found statistically significant balance impairments in the COVID-recovered group, particularly in single-leg stance and eyes-closed conditions, suggesting that mild COVID-19 may lead to persistent balance problems.

Prospective cohort study following 767 SARS-CoV-2 positive participants at 7 and 15 months post-infection to characterize symptom chronification and associated outcomes. Found that 52.1% of symptomatic patients at 7 months had persistent symptoms at 15 months, with chronification associated with increased healthcare utilization, functional impairment, and reduced quality of life.

This cross-sectional study assessed post-viral symptoms in patients recovered from mild COVID-19, identifying prolonged symptomatology months after acute infection. The study found that 8 of 11 post-viral symptoms were notably more prevalent in female patients, validating long COVID as a recognizable post-viral condition.

Prospective cohort study following 413 hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 6 and 12 months post-discharge to assess long-term sequelae and symptom burden. Found that 30% had symptoms at 6 months and 25% at 12 months, with neurological symptoms and dyspnea being most common, particularly in patients who required mechanical ventilation.

Retrospective cohort study of 184 COVID-19 patients with severe ARDS admitted to ICU, followed up 6+ months post-discharge to identify risk factors for in-hospital mortality and long-COVID symptom development. Found extreme obesity (BMI >40) was the strongest independent predictor for both mortality and long-COVID symptoms, but this is an observational study documenting associations, not testing any intervention.

Longitudinal UK population survey investigating whether contracting COVID-19 in early 2020 was associated with poorer mental health outcomes (depression, anxiety, loneliness) measured at three follow-up timepoints through June 2021. Found that probable COVID-19 infection was associated with significantly worse mental health outcomes lasting up to 13 months post-infection.

Prospective cohort study following 81 adults for 12 months after mild COVID-19 infection, assessing quality of life, respiratory symptoms, and healthcare utilization. Found persistent respiratory symptoms in 42% at 1 year, associated with lower employment rates and increased primary care visits, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

This cross-sectional study examined cardiopulmonary function and quality of life in 60 COVID-19 survivors at 6 months post-discharge, comparing patients with and without fatigue. Fatigue was the most prevalent symptom and associated with worse quality of life and limited mobility, while subtle myocardial dysfunction (reduced GLS) was observed but did not correlate with fatigue presence.

Prospective single-center cohort study examining cardiac function and biomarkers in 227 post-COVID syndrome patients in relation to functional status and fatigue. Findings show most patients have normal cardiac function, with impaired cardiac function only observed in those with severe functional impairment or elevated troponin T.

This retrospective cohort study surveyed Swedish public employees to examine symptom severity, general health, and impairment in COVID-19 positive versus negative individuals at 4-12 weeks and >12 weeks post-infection. The study found symptoms were highly prevalent across all groups, with worse outcomes in the acute/subacute phases, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examined persistent liver injury in 7,595 hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute infection, identifying predictors of liver function recovery at discharge and 2 months post-discharge. Most patients recovered completely by 2 months, but the study focuses on acute COVID-19 hospitalization rather than long COVID syndrome.

This single-centre cohort study assessed pulmonary function in 257 COVID-19 survivors 3-5 months after hospital discharge, measuring lung volumes, respiratory strength, and diffusion capacity. The study found that 36% had reduced diffusion capacity and critically ill patients showed significantly worse outcomes, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Longitudinal prospective cohort study (CovILD trial) following 145 COVID-19 patients at multiple timepoints (60-360 days) to assess pulmonary recovery in relation to metabolic diseases. Finds that dysglycemia and dyslipidemia are associated with more severe acute COVID-19 and delayed early recovery, but do not impair long-term pulmonary recovery.

This prospective cohort study followed 669 COVID-19 patients to assess long-COVID symptom incidence and associated risk factors including vaccination status. The study found 41.6% incidence rates with higher risk in females, elderly, hospitalized patients, and unvaccinated individuals, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This is a prospective cohort study of 614 COVID-19 survivors followed 6-11 months post-hospitalization to assess the association between PASC symptoms and physical inactivity. While about long COVID, it is an observational study without any intervention—patients were not given a treatment; it merely documents the correlation between symptom presence and inactivity levels.

This retrospective cohort study compared long COVID symptom outcomes in 412 hospitalized COVID-19 patients stratified by vaccination status, finding that unvaccinated/incompletely vaccinated patients had higher symptom frequency 90 days post-discharge. While the paper studies long COVID outcomes, it does not test or evaluate a specific treatment intervention—it is an observational comparison study examining vaccination's association with long COVID risk, making it ineligible for inclusion in a treatment trials meta-analysis.

Prospective cohort study of 140 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed at 30 days and one year to identify risk factors for functional limitation using the Post-COVID Functional State Scale, Fatigue Severity Scale, and modified Borg scale. Found that 40.7% reported functional limitation at one year, with female sex, anxiety/depression diagnosis, persistent symptoms, and fatigue as significant predictors.

Population-based prospective cohort study of ~2.3 million Norwegian individuals comparing prevalence of long COVID complaints (pulmonary, neurological, fatigue) between COVID-19 positive and negative/untested persons at 5-6 months post-infection. Found modest differences in complaint prevalence between groups, with fatigue being the most common complaint, but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

This retrospective cohort study compared COVID-19 and non-COVID ARDS survivors to examine post-intensive care outcomes and pulmonary fibrosis. COVID-19 survivors showed higher rates of fibrotic changes on CT imaging (70% vs 43%), though functional differences were not statistically significant, highlighting the need for long-term follow-up in ARDS survivors.

Observational study of 97 long COVID patients with cognitive complaints examining sex and age effects on persistent neurological symptoms and cognitive outcomes. Found sex differences in presentation and cognitive outcomes, with females more likely to experience persistent short-term memory and executive dysfunction symptoms.

Prospective single-center study assessing health-related quality of life and psychological outcomes in COVID-19 survivors 3 and 12 months post-hospitalization, comparing ICU and non-ICU patients. Findings show persistent limitations in quality of life, depression, fatigue, and high stress levels, particularly in ICU survivors, but no intervention or treatment is tested.

This observational study characterized health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in 112 long-COVID patients from a post-COVID consultation clinic using validated questionnaires (SGRQ, EQ-5D-5L, SF-36). Long-COVID syndrome significantly impaired HRQoL particularly in physical health domains, with fatigue, concentration difficulties, and dyspnea being the most common symptoms.

This study examines cardiopulmonary fitness in elite athletes returning to high-intensity sport after SARS-CoV-2 infection using exercise testing. While it includes some athletes with minor post-COVID symptoms, the primary focus is on athletic performance recovery in asymptomatic individuals rather than treatment of long COVID.

A cross-sectional study examining metabolomic profiles and gut microbiome composition in 2,561 community-dwelling participants across the spectrum of COVID and non-COVID illness duration, including 180 with Post-COVID Syndrome. The study found that atherogenic-dyslipidemic metabolic profiles (fatty acids, cholesterol) were associated with longer illness duration in both COVID-infected and non-COVID participants, suggesting cardiometabolic dysfunction may contribute to prolonged symptoms.

This study prospectively evaluated autonomic nervous system function in 16 severely disabled long-COVID patients using clinical examination, Schirmer test, sudomotor evaluation, BP monitoring, and heart rate variability tests. 37.5% of patients showed abnormal autonomic test results, primarily affecting parasympathetic function, suggesting dysautonomia may contribute to long-COVID symptoms.

Retrospective study examining the relationship between T-cell immunity (measured by ELISPOT assays), cytokine levels, and persistent symptom counts in COVID-19 recovered patients in Japan. Found that patients with lower T-cell immune response (ELISPOT-low) had significantly more persistent symptoms, suggesting T-cell immunity is critical for symptom resolution.

A quasi-experimental study evaluating a 3-day micro-choice based rehabilitation program for 78 long COVID patients, with assessments at 7 days and 3 months. The intervention showed significant improvements in fatigue, functional levels, sick leave reduction, and exercise capacity, with no adverse events and 97.4% completion rate.

Longitudinal observational study of 900 healthcare workers in Switzerland comparing symptom prevalence and functional impairment in SARS-CoV-2 positive and negative individuals at baseline (July 2021) and follow-up (December 2021). Found increased reporting of fatigue, headache, insomnia, cognitive impairment, and other long COVID symptoms over time, with greater increases in the negative group and worsening quality of life and absenteeism.

Prospective cohort study following 132 adults with prior COVID-19 at 6, 12, and 24 months to assess long COVID prevalence and symptom persistence. Found 71.2% experienced long COVID symptoms at 24 months, primarily neuropsychiatric symptoms including fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and depression, with minimal impact from vaccination status.

This retrospective cohort study examines whether CNS biomarkers (GFAp, NfL, t-tau) measured in blood predict cognitive impairment and fatigue 3-6 months after ICU discharge in 57 critically ill COVID-19 patients. Elevated GFAp at follow-up was associated with mild cognitive dysfunction, while lower GFAp and NfL levels were associated with various dimensions of fatigue and reduced motivation.

Population-based cross-sectional study examining the prevalence and characteristics of post COVID-19 symptoms in young adults from a Swedish birth cohort (n=2,022). Found 16.5% of COVID-19-infected participants met post COVID-19 criteria, with altered smell/taste, dyspnea, and fatigue as most common symptoms.

Population-based study using electronic health data to assess prescription drug use and healthcare services during the 6-month post-COVID-19 period in 146,314 individuals. Found increased use of cardiovascular and psychotropic medications after COVID-19, with greater health impact in females and non-severe cases, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Cross-sectional study examining association between COVID-19 vaccination status and health-related quality of life outcomes in previously infected individuals in Israel. While addressing long COVID symptoms, this is a secondary analysis of vaccination outcomes rather than a study of a treatment intervention for long COVID.

A prospective cohort study following 153 COVID-19 patients with moderate-to-severe or mild disease with comorbidities for up to 1 year post-discharge to assess post-COVID syndrome prevalence, clinical features, and outcomes. Most post-COVID symptoms improved over the first few months, with disease severity and older age associated with persistent symptoms and transient cardiac dysfunction.

A prospective cohort study assessing body composition and cardiopulmonary fitness in 90 overweight COVID-19 survivors stratified by acute disease severity (mild, moderate, severe/critical), with measurements at baseline and 1-year follow-up. The severe/critical group showed improvements in lean mass and walking distance over 1 year, while all groups experienced long-term symptoms including memory deficit, fatigue, concentration difficulties, and dyspnea.

Prospective cohort study examining metabolic outcomes in 600 individuals with nonsevere COVID-19 at 1, 3, and 6 months post-onset. Found high prevalence of multiple metabolic abnormalities (41.3% at 6 months), particularly in high-risk individuals, with factors like female sex and vaccination associated with lower risk.

Longitudinal observational study of 6-month cognitive outcomes in Indonesian COVID-19 patients using CFQ, Fatigue Severity Score, and GAD-7 assessments. Findings show cognitive failure is multifactorial, associated with disease severity, vaccination status, age, and previous infection, but does not solely depend on acute COVID-19 severity.

A 2-year longitudinal follow-up study of Brazilian COVID-19 patients from the first pandemic wave, characterizing the clinical profile and prevalence of post-COVID condition symptoms. Long COVID patients were more likely to be female, previously hospitalized, and experienced varied symptoms including muscle pain and cognitive deficits.

This retrospective cohort study characterizes the clinical spectrum of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), a post-acute sequela of SARS-CoV-2 infection, using EHR data from 1,139 hospitalized children across 8 pediatric medical centers. Using latent class analysis, the study identifies three disease severity classes (severe, moderate, mild) and documents their temporal trends, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective chart review of 365 long COVID patients presenting to a dedicated Post-COVID-19 clinic in Texas, characterizing clinical presentation, symptoms, and cognitive/psychiatric burden. Study describes patient demographics and symptom burden but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 500 adults comparing nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment (n=250) versus no treatment (n=250) for reducing long COVID symptom development at 4 months post-infection. Overall nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was not associated with reduced long COVID risk (44% vs 49.6%, p=0.21), though it showed lower odds for brain fog and chest pain specifically.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing claims data to examine associations between pre-existing mental health diagnoses and post-COVID-19 condition development. Finds mental disorders, anxiety, depression, and somatoform disorders associated with increased PCC risk, but notes this association exists across all cohorts, not specifically in COVID-19 patients.

This cross-sectional study assessed handgrip strength (HGS), body composition, respiratory function, and 6-minute walk test in 113 long COVID patients 120 days post-acute COVID-19 to identify associations between dynapenia and functional impairment. The study found that patients with low handgrip strength had significantly worse functional outcomes and higher rates of ICU admission and mechanical ventilation during acute illness, suggesting HGS as a simple proxy indicator of functional impairment in long COVID populations.

Prospective cohort study of 97 chronically critically ill COVID-19 patients who required prolonged mechanical ventilation, followed at discharge and 3, 6, and 12 months post-discharge. Patients experienced persistent and high burdens of fatigue (55%), anxiety (42%), depression (40%), and reduced quality of life at 12 months, with minimal improvement over the follow-up period.

This cross-sectional study compares gut microbiota composition and gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with POTS and post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS) versus healthy controls using fecal DNA sequencing and symptom questionnaires. While it characterizes microbiota differences associated with PACS, it does not test or evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 121 long COVID patients for 24 months post-infection to characterize long COVID symptoms and assess the impact of COVID-19 vaccination. Found that 62% still experienced long COVID symptoms at 24 months, with fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and insomnia most common; vaccination status did not significantly affect symptom frequency.

This retrospective study examined 731 post-COVID patients to identify newly diagnosed alternative disorders that might explain their symptoms. Among the cohort, 6.8% were diagnosed with 52 new diseases, most commonly endocrine/metabolic and respiratory conditions, but the study does not test any treatment interventions for long COVID.

Prospective observational study of COVID-19 pneumonia survivors followed at 3 and 12 months post-discharge to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using SF-36 and pulmonary function tests in 130 patients. Minimal or mild pulmonary sequelae did not further deteriorate HRQoL, with medical care and pulmonary rehabilitation identified as effective tools for improving outcomes.

This study investigates molecular and metabolic changes in COVID-19 patients through a one-year follow-up period, examining inflammatory markers, amino acids, and micronutrients related to disease severity and physical recovery. The paper is an observational cohort study with no treatment intervention—it passively follows laboratory parameters and symptoms over time without administering any therapeutic intervention.

A prospective cohort study from the German DigiHero study examining early recovery factors in 5,098 SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals who developed early symptoms (4-12 weeks post-infection). The study identified that 48% achieved early recovery (symptom-free by 12 weeks) and found male sex, younger age, mild acute infection, Omicron variant infection, and non-help-seeking behavior as protective factors against symptom persistence.

This study analyzes long COVID outcomes in 643 CORE clinic patients versus 52,089 non-CORE COVID-19 patients to identify associations between health-related social needs (HRSNs) and symptom severity. Patients with unmet HRSNs experienced significantly worse long COVID symptoms, depression (PHQ-9), and anxiety (GAD-7) scores compared to those without unmet needs.

This prospective cohort study followed 271 COVID-19 pneumonia patients with CT imaging at 6 months post-hospitalization to assess pulmonary residual abnormalities and fibrotic-like changes. While the study mentions paxlovid as a predictor, it is an observational follow-up study without an assigned treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the treatment trials analysis.

Retrospective observational study of 609 nursing personnel assessing the relationship between post-COVID infection and work ability using the Work Ability Index. Long COVID was associated with significantly lower work ability compared to short COVID, with chronic diseases and low job control identified as key factors affecting work ability in long COVID patients.

Prospective observational study following 705 children and young people (aged 11-17) for 12 months after Omicron infection to assess long COVID prevalence and symptom profiles. By 12 months, 17.4% of first-infected and 21.9% of reinfected participants met the research definition of long COVID, with similar symptom profiles between groups.

This prospective observational study followed 45 working-age COVID-19 patients for 6 months post-discharge to assess autonomic nervous system dysfunction and its impact on work ability. The study found that one-third of participants developed new autonomic syndrome associated with reduced work capacity, but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 623 pregnant women comparing maternal and fetal complications across acute COVID-19, long-term COVID-19, and non-COVID-19 groups. Long-term COVID-19 in pregnancy was associated with increased risk of gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes mellitus, and fetal intrauterine growth restriction.

This study characterizes the cognitive profile, neuroimaging findings, and fluid biomarkers in 49 post-acute COVID-19 syndrome patients with cognitive complaints at a mean of 10.4 months post-infection. Participants underwent comprehensive neuropsychological testing, MRI, and biomarker analysis at baseline and follow-up, showing persistent attention-executive and verbal memory impairment without structural brain abnormalities or elevated neuronal damage markers.

This ecological analysis compares the epidemiological and economic burden of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) in Italy and the United States from 2020–2023, estimating incidence rates, quality-adjusted life years lost, and productivity losses. The study does not evaluate any treatment or intervention, making it ineligible for the clinical trials meta-analysis.

Population-based cohort study of all COVID-19 patients admitted to Hong Kong hospitals (2020), investigating associations between baseline viral load and long-term post-discharge outcomes including hospitalization and mortality. Study found higher baseline viral loads associated with increased risk of death, hospitalization, and cardiovascular complications during median 251-day follow-up, but is an observational analysis without testing any intervention.

A prospective cohort study examining the relationship between olfactory bulb volume (via MRI) and olfactory dysfunction in 233 individuals recovering from mild-to-moderate COVID-19, with follow-up assessments 1-2 years post-infection. The study found that reduced olfactory bulb volume is associated with persistent self-reported olfactory dysfunction and predicts objective olfactometric performance, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study examines the relationship between inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα) measured during acute COVID-19 infection and episodic memory performance at 6-15 months post-infection in 33 hospitalized patients. The study found that acute-phase cytokine levels predict long-term cognitive outcomes, but it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention—it is purely an observational follow-up study.

A 1-year longitudinal study investigating blood-brain barrier permeability in 102 COVID-19 patients by measuring astrocyte-derived biomarkers (EVs and S100B) at baseline, 4, 8, and 12 months post-hospitalization. The study found transient elevated BBB biomarkers at 4 months that returned to baseline by 12 months, with no correlation to long-term symptoms.

SETANTA is a prospective cross-sectional observational study examining symptom burden and cardiac abnormalities in patients 6-12 months post-COVID-19 infection in primary practice. The study found high prevalence of persistent symptoms (83%) and abnormal coagulation markers (elevated von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, D-dimer), with lower rates of CMR abnormalities compared to hospital-based cohorts.

Prospective cohort study examining persistent respiratory outcomes in COPD patients following COVID-19 infection of varying severity over 24.9 months. Patients with severe COVID-19 showed significantly increased risks of worsening dyspnea, COPD exacerbations, and respiratory mortality compared to uninfected COPD controls.

This sub-study of the ORCHESTRA cohort examined chemosensory impairment (smell and taste) in 1,187 post-COVID-19 patients, finding 47% with neurosensorial symptoms and assessing olfactory training outcomes. The study used psychophysical tests and SF-36 questionnaires to characterize the complex presentation of chemosensory dysfunction and its impact on quality of life.

Population-based longitudinal survey of 46,209 middle-aged and older Europeans assessing pandemic impact on well-being across 27 countries before summer 2021. Study found that COVID-19 infection and especially long COVID were associated with pronounced declines in well-being, but this is an observational survey without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing health problems, activity limitations, and participation restrictions in post-COVID syndrome patients, stratified by sex. While the study is about long COVID and uses a cohort design, it does not evaluate a treatment intervention—instead it is a descriptive epidemiological study characterizing the burden of disease.

This is a prospective observational follow-up study that tracked COVID-19 patients at 3 and 6 months post-infection to determine long COVID prevalence and clinical characteristics in Thailand. No treatment or intervention was tested; the study only passively followed patients and surveyed symptoms, making it ineligible for the trials pipeline.

Longitudinal observational study tracking 281 COVID-19 survivors over one year post-discharge to assess psychological and physical sequelae at multiple timepoints. Found that depression, anxiety, PTSD, and organ dysfunction decreased significantly from early to late stages, with male gender, age >50, severe COVID, and comorbidities as risk factors for prolonged sequelae.

This retrospective cohort study of 3,463 long COVID patients from British Columbia's post-COVID recovery clinics examines health-related quality of life using the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. The study identifies associations between social determinants of health (age, sex, employment, ethnicity) and quality of life outcomes, but does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study of 7,290 COVID-19 patients in Dubai comparing nirmatrelvir-ritonavir treatment versus no treatment for preventing disease progression and long COVID symptoms. Treatment was associated with reduced hospitalizations (HR 0.39) and fewer long COVID symptoms (HR 0.42) during the Omicron wave.

This prospective cohort study investigated the prevalence and risk factors of post-COVID fatigue in Parkinson's disease patients at 1 month and 12 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Fatigue was highly prevalent (75.89% at 1 month, 32.99% persistent at 12 months), with key risk factors including decreased physical activity, anxiety status, and antiviral drug use.

Retrospective cohort study examining the incidence and risk factors for new-onset gastrointestinal disorders in COVID-19 patients up to 3.5 years post-infection compared to non-COVID controls. Found COVID-19 patients had a 1.18-fold elevated risk of developing GID, but this is an observational study without treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study following 94 Post-COVID syndrome patients at two timepoints (median 9.4 months and 14 months after infection) to assess the course of neurological symptoms, fatigue, and cognitive function. While 47% reported symptom improvement and QoL increased in that group, 12% achieved full recovery, and significant fatigue and cognitive impairment persisted in over half the cohort.

A prospective observational study examining cardiac sympathetic nervous dysfunction in 33 recovered COVID-19 patients using 123I-mIBG SPECT/CT imaging. Increased cardiac sympathetic activity was found in 67.7% of patients at baseline and persisted in 70.4% at 6-8 months follow-up, suggesting long-term cardiovascular sequelae of COVID-19.

This retrospective cohort study compared the incidence of new-onset cardiovascular disorders in 56,400 COVID-19 patients versus 1,093,904 contemporary controls over 3.5 years post-infection. Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had significantly higher risk of MACE and other cardiovascular disorders, but the paper is an observational study without any intervention or treatment being tested.

Population-based prospective study following 960 individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in Hainan Province for 2 years to assess long COVID prevalence and risk factors. Found 12.5% experienced long COVID complications, with cough, fatigue, and hair loss being most common; independent risk factors included age over 65, moderate-to-severe infection, chronic diseases, and anxiety.

This retrospective cohort study examined 14,335 COVID-19 hospitalized patients to identify new clinical disorders developing 3.5 years post-infection, comparing those with and without hyperinflammatory syndrome (cHIS). Patients with cHIS showed significantly higher risk of cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and obesity, but not hypertension, diabetes, COPD, or asthma.

Longitudinal population-based cohort study following 789 pediatric participants over 2-4 years to assess the incidence of post-COVID syndrome (PCS) symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination. About 7% of participants experienced PCS-like symptoms persisting beyond 3 months, predominantly fatigue and exhaustion, with no significant difference in overall health status between infected and uninfected children.

This retrospective cohort study of 52,006 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examined whether remdesivir treatment during acute infection reduces the incidence of long COVID outcomes 90-270 days post-admission. Patients receiving remdesivir experienced significantly lower risk of developing long COVID (RR 0.96, p<0.001), with benefits observed in both immunocompromised and general populations.

This study measured inflammatory, fibrotic, and endothelial biomarkers (MMP2, MMP7, IL-6, angiopoietin-2, etc.) in 73 hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute illness and follow-up, with pulmonary function testing at follow-up. The results showed that biomarkers associated with fibrosis and endothelial injury remain elevated in COVID-19 survivors and correlate with impaired lung function, suggesting these mechanisms underlie post-COVID pulmonary sequelae.

A prospective cohort study of 137 convalescents investigating the relationship between anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody responses and long COVID development and phenotypes over one year post-infection. The study found that antibody responses were protective against vital organ-related long COVID symptoms but insufficient in preventing neurological, psychiatric, and pulmonary manifestations.

This retrospective cohort study of 64,000 COVID-19 patients examined the incidence and risk factors for new-onset hypertension up to 3 years post-infection using propensity-matched COVID-negative controls. The study found that hospitalized COVID-positive patients had significantly higher rates of hypertension development compared to controls, identifying COVID-19 as one of the five greatest risk factors for hypertension.

A prospective registry study of 56-63 long COVID patients undergoing hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), measuring outcomes at baseline, 3 months, and 1 year using SF-36, EQ-5D, and work ability assessments. Results show 56-63% achieved clinically relevant improvement in mental/physical component scores at 3 months, with cognitive symptoms showing the most improvement, though 13-19% experienced deterioration.

This cross-sectional study identifies baseline demographic, physical, and mental health characteristics associated with PASC development in 351 COVID-19 participants, 145 of whom experienced PASC. The analysis reveals depression, lower income, Hispanic ethnicity, younger age, and respiratory conditions as risk factors, and identifies two PASC subtypes with different symptom burden profiles.

This retrospective study developed a method to detect persistent physiological changes in long COVID patients using wearable device data from over 12,000 US military personnel. While the work demonstrates that wearable technology can objectively identify chronic physiological changes, it is not a treatment trial but rather a diagnostic/detection study with no intervention evaluated.

This retrospective cohort study examines herpes zoster reactivation as a post-viral complication in COVID-19 survivors and its association with cardiorenal outcomes using propensity score matching. While it identifies HZ as a risk factor for cardiovascular and renal complications in COVID-19 survivors, it is a secondary analysis of electronic health records rather than an intervention trial testing a treatment.

This retrospective cohort study followed 332 COVID-19 survivors (132 ICU, 200 medical ward patients) for up to 12 months to compare major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by disease severity. ICU patients experienced significantly higher MACE risk (HR 16.2), with severity of infection remaining independently associated with cardiovascular complications.

An observational longitudinal study comparing neuromuscular electrophysiological disorders and muscle architecture of the tibialis anterior and triceps surae in 70 participants (moderate-COVID, severe-COVID, and controls) assessed over 12 months. Severe COVID-19 was associated with higher prevalence of neuromuscular disorders and persistent echogenicity increases in lower limb muscles, suggesting polyneuromyopathy.

This cross-sectional study examined retinal microvascular abnormalities in 32 patients at various time points after COVID-19 recovery using OCT angiography and retinal oximetry. The study found no significant microvascular changes in the retina even among patients who had severe COVID-19 requiring mechanical ventilation or ECMO.

The CON-VINCE longitudinal cohort study (n=1,865) applied WHO post COVID criteria to distinguish post COVID from pandemic-related health effects in uninfected individuals. The analysis identified memory impairment with fatigue as a symptom cluster unique to post COVID patients, suggesting a potential biomarker for differential diagnosis.

This longitudinal cohort study followed 943 children and young people (ages 11-17) for up to 24 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection to characterize fatigue trajectories using the Chalder Fatigue Scale. While it documents that persistent fatigue is common and worsening over time in this population, it is an observational study with no treatment intervention—it passively follows patients without assigning them to any specific therapy or intervention.

This cohort study evaluated somatic neurological symptoms and examination findings in 708 COVID-19 survivors 6-11 months post-discharge using structured WHO-based protocols. Muscle weakness, gait impairment, and paresthesias were common long-term sequelae, with clinical diagnoses of neuromuscular disease, cerebrovascular disease, and epilepsy identified in subsets of patients.

Retrospective cohort study comparing long-term kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in CKD patients with and without COVID-19 over 24 months. While it studies post-COVID outcomes, it does not focus on long COVID syndrome specifically and does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective observational study examining subclinical cardiac abnormalities via transthoracic echocardiography in 343 individuals with mild initial COVID-19, compared to non-infected controls, at baseline and follow-up (median 327 days post-infection). The study found significant yet subclinical differences in systolic and diastolic cardiac function in COVID-infected individuals, with small magnitude changes unlikely to be clinically detectable at the individual level.

Prospective observational cohort study following 115 COVID-19 patients (inpatients and outpatients) for 24 months to assess post-COVID-19 condition prevalence, symptoms, lung function, and immunological markers. Found PCC prevalence declined from 51% at 3 months to 18% at 24 months, with risk factors including acute infection severity, sleep apnea, and obesity; symptom clusters showed associations with specific biomarkers (IL-6, hs-CRP, cortisol).

A prospective population-based study examining associations between health-related quality of life and 49 demographic/clinical variables in 3,475 participants at 9 and 26 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found that fatigue, remaining symptoms, perceived stress, and age explained most variance in quality of life, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This retrospective cohort study from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database examines the association between pre-existing back pain and the development of depression and anxiety following COVID-19 infection. The study finds that COVID-19 patients with back pain have significantly higher risk of developing depression and anxiety compared to those without back pain, but does not focus on long COVID or test any interventions.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed clinical and hospitalization records from over 675,000 Spanish patients to identify demographic factors, comorbidities, and symptoms associated with long COVID development and to build a predictive model. The study found that female sex, older age, and specific comorbidities increased long COVID risk, while COVID-19 vaccination—particularly mRNA vaccines—provided strong protective effects, achieving 73% balanced accuracy in their LC-19 prediction model.

This retrospective cohort study examined risk factors for moderate-severe dyspnea in COVID-19 survivors admitted to a university hospital between April 2020 and April 2021, analyzing the impact of medications used during critical care (neuroleptics, corticosteroids, etc.). The study found that neuroleptic dose and pre-existing comorbidities were independently associated with limiting dyspnea at 1 month, and persistent dyspnea was linked to depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life at 12 months.

This prospective cohort study examined risk factors for COVID-19 and its impact on diabetic peripheral neuropathy in 76 type 2 diabetes patients, with assessments before and ~11 months after COVID-19 infection. While 25.7% of COVID-exposed patients developed long COVID, the study found no evidence that COVID-19 affected neuropathy development or progression, though long-COVID patients showed significant changes in lipids and body weight.

Population-based case-control study comparing cognitive impairment prevalence 2 years post-infection between hospitalized COVID-19 survivors, hospitalized uninfected controls, non-hospitalized infected, and non-hospitalized uninfected groups. Found significantly higher cognitive impairment in both infected groups compared to matched uninfected controls.

This observational cohort study assessed physical activity levels in 105-95 COVID-19 ICU survivors at one year follow-up using standardized questionnaires. Longer ICU stays and diabetes mellitus were identified as predictors of physical inactivity, but the study does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Cross-sectional survey of 267 German dental team members assessing vaccination status and long COVID symptom prevalence. Found 22.6% of those with confirmed COVID-19 reported long COVID symptoms, with higher prevalence among dental auxiliaries, and noted vaccination may help protect against long COVID symptoms.

This matched cohort study compares COVID-19 and influenza patients from the TriNetX database to assess risk of advanced chronic kidney disease (stages 3-5) at 12-month follow-up in patients without initial acute kidney injury. COVID-19 patients showed higher risk of advanced CKD (HR 2.02) compared to influenza controls, with diabetes and hypertension as strongest predictors.

This three-year longitudinal study of 93 post-COVID-19 patients used machine learning to classify health status progression and identify predictive markers across clinical, neuropsychological, and laboratory measures. Key findings showed inflammatory markers, SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels, and neuropsychiatric measures were most predictive of disease stage, with improved classification accuracy over longer time intervals.

This pilot cohort study examines lipid profiles and inflammatory markers in COVID-19 patients at baseline and three months post-discharge, comparing them to diabetic and healthy controls. The study identifies persistent cardiometabolic abnormalities (elevated Lp(a), new-onset hypertension, dyslipidemia) and lipid biomarkers associated with mortality and long-term vulnerability in post-COVID recovery.

A retrospective cohort study of 126 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed at 3 and 12 months post-discharge to examine the frequency, severity, and risk factors for persistent physical, cognitive, and psychological symptoms. The study found 31-32% experienced moderate-severe physical symptoms, 26-27% had cognitive symptoms, and 14-18% had depression or PTSS at 12 months, with persistence associated with comorbidities, infection severity, and biopsychosocial factors.

This multi-national EHR study characterized post-acute COVID-19 sequelae (PASC) by comparing new-onset conditions in 414,602 COVID-19 patients versus 2.3 million controls across 277 hospitals. The study identified increased risk for cardiovascular, neurological, and metabolic complications but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational cohort study tracked COVID-19 symptom trajectories and physical activity in 121 non-hospitalized healthcare workers using smartphone apps and wearable devices. The study identified two distinct symptom duration patterns with 36% reporting persistent symptoms, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This 2-year prospective follow-up study of 295 Thai patients hospitalized for COVID-19 assessed long COVID prevalence, risk factors, and health-related quality of life impacts. While clearly about long COVID, the study is observational without treatment assignment—patients were simply followed over time to document symptom persistence and QoL decline, making it ineligible for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

This study tracked wearable sensor data (steps, resting heart rate, sleep) over one year in 279 people with Long COVID and 274 controls to characterize objective changes relative to pre-infection baseline. While the trial registration suggests planned follow-up, this appears to be a cross-sectional/observational characterization study without an intervention being tested, making it a natural history cohort rather than a treatment trial.

This cross-sectional study used wearable data from 20,815 individuals to characterize those with persistent fatigue and shortness of breath after SARS-CoV-2 infection, comparing physiological metrics (heart rate, step counts) and quality of life measures between long COVID cases and controls. The study found that persistent symptoms were associated with pre-existing lower fitness levels rather than being causally induced by infection, highlighting wearables as tools for tracking long COVID outcomes.

Observational cohort study documenting glycometabolic abnormalities, insulin resistance, and altered cytokine profiles in 551 hospitalized COVID-19 patients and recovered patients at 2-month follow-up. Reports that 46% of patients were hyperglycemic and abnormalities persist even in recovered patients, but does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study tracking cognitive changes in 1,245 older COVID-19 survivors and 358 uninfected controls over 2.5 years post-infection. Found 19.1% incidence of cognitive impairment at 2.5 years, with decline primarily in severe cases during the first year.

Retrospective cohort study of 88,818 Danish residents examining long-term sick-leave following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Uses machine learning to identify risk factors (age, BMI, depression, sex) associated with prolonged work absence due to post-COVID condition, but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Cross-sectional study examining persistent COVID-19 symptoms in 121 community-dwelling older adults from a population-based Canadian cohort, comparing symptom prevalence and duration to 23,636 non-COVID controls. Found that 60-73% of COVID-19 patients report symptoms persisting >1 month, with fatigue, cough, and muscle pain being most common, and identifies sex and multimorbidity as risk factors for longer persistence.

This N3C RECOVER EHR cohort study characterizes SARS-CoV-2 reinfections and Long COVID incidence in over 3 million patients from electronic health records. The study is a secondary analysis of existing cohort data examining associations between reinfection severity, initial infection severity, and Long COVID diagnosis rates rather than testing an intervention.

Retrospective cohort study using EHR data from two large clinical networks to identify risk factors and develop machine learning models for predicting Long COVID development. While methodologically sound, this is an observational epidemiology study that does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials meta-analysis.

A 24-month prospective cohort study of 12,632 English children and young people (11-17 years) examining the prevalence and impact of post-COVID-19 condition symptoms. The study found 7.2% consistently meet the Delphi PCC definition across all timepoints, with higher symptom burden in older children and more deprived populations, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective study evaluates symptom changes and immune responses to COVID-19 vaccination in 16 vaccine-naïve individuals with Long COVID, with surveys and immunological measurements at baseline and 2, 6, and 12 weeks post-vaccination. At 12 weeks, 10 of 16 participants reported improved health, with symptom improvement associated with specific plasma biosignatures including baseline sIL-6R elevation.

This longitudinal study characterizes immune profiles in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, comparing those with early persistent symptoms (EPS+) to those who recovered, with follow-up assessments at 3 months and 3 years post-symptom onset. While it identifies immune dysregulation markers associated with long COVID, it is an observational characterization study without any intervention or treatment evaluation, making it ineligible for the clinical trials meta-analysis.

This cross-sectional study compared health-related quality of life and mental health outcomes in 106 Dutch children with long COVID against reference cohorts of children with other chronic conditions and general population controls. Children with long COVID showed significantly impaired quality of life (84%) and higher rates of anxiety, depression, and sleep problems compared to both reference groups.

This population-based cohort study of 810,851 Swedish residents identifies demographic, clinical, and social risk factors associated with post-COVID-19 condition diagnosis. The study uses existing national register data to explore predictors rather than test any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes VA electronic medical records from 2021-2023 to identify risk factors for post-COVID conditions in US veterans, examining associations between pre-existing comorbidities, hospitalization severity, vaccination status, and PCC diagnosis. Results show COPD, chronic kidney disease, older age, female sex, and lack of full vaccination significantly increase odds of PCC diagnosis in both hospitalized and non-hospitalized cohorts.

This study uses sequence-symmetry analysis to examine the association between COVID-19 vaccination and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) diagnosis in 284,592 vaccinated individuals. It finds a possible association between vaccination and POTS incidence, though lower than post-infection POTS risk, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study using UK Biobank data examining the association between COVID-19 infection and new-onset vascular dementia (VaD) in adults ≥50 years, with propensity-score matching to uninfected controls. Found COVID-19 survivors had higher risk of VaD compared to controls, with pre-existing mental health conditions conferring additional vulnerability.

This prospective cohort study examines whether COVID-19 vaccination timing affects long COVID symptom reporting and quality of life in 4,809 Israeli participants followed for two years. Results show that receiving three vaccine doses before infection provides a 26.5% protective effect against long COVID, but the study observes outcomes rather than testing an intervention in long COVID patients.

Prospective study comparing cardiac MRI findings in 41 long COVID patients with persistent symptoms like dyspnea and fatigue versus 42 control subjects. Found no evidence that myocardial inflammation explains long COVID symptoms, contrary to prior hypotheses.

Retrospective analysis of 132 long COVID patients presenting to a post-COVID clinic at least 6 months after acute COVID-19, documenting symptom prevalence, quality of life impairment, and diagnostic findings. Most common complaints were persistent fatigue (82%) and dyspnea on exertion (61%), with reduced quality of life across all SF-36 domains.

Prospective observational study of 221 long COVID patients undergoing pneumological rehabilitation, measuring health changes from baseline to end of treatment. Rehabilitation produced significant improvements across all outcomes (effect sizes 0.76–1.30), with 76% of patients rating success as good to excellent; respiratory physiotherapy and endurance training were reported as most helpful.

This study analyzed sex differences in outcomes from a standardized 3-week pulmonary rehabilitation program in 233 post-acute COVID-19 patients. Females showed smaller improvements in lung function parameters but greater overall progress toward reference values compared to males, suggesting sex-specific rehabilitation requirements.

Observational study of long COVID patients treated with naturopathic complex therapy at a German natural medicine hospital, with whole-body hyperthermia as a central component. Early results from up to 6-month follow-up suggest patients improved with treatment, warranting further analysis.

Retrospective analysis of 132 long COVID patients presenting to a post-COVID clinic ≥6 months after acute COVID-19, characterizing persistent symptoms and diagnostic findings. Most common complaints were fatigue (82%), dyspnea on exertion (61%), and cognitive impairment (54%), with significantly reduced quality of life across SF-36 domains.

This paper reports on the treatment of long COVID patients at a hospital for naturopathic medicine (KfN) in Germany, which offers individualized treatment concepts combining classical naturopathic approaches, neural therapy, and homeopathy alongside conventional internal medicine care. The authors present a study evaluating the outcomes of their comprehensive treatment approach, aimed at symptom relief and improving patient energy levels.

A prospective observational study evaluating occupational outcomes in 173 long COVID patients undergoing pneumological rehabilitation, with follow-up assessments at baseline, end of rehabilitation, and 6 months post-intervention. Results show 85.5% returned to work at 6-month follow-up with significant improvements in work ability and reduced participation limitations, though 41.3% remained at risk for early retirement due to persistent cognitive symptoms and fatigue.

This cross-sectional study assessed olfactory and gustatory function in 48 long-COVID patients using validated tests (Sniffin' Sticks, 3-drop taste test) and self-reported ratings. The study found 90% of patients had pathological chemosensory diagnoses, but it is observational without any treatment intervention or control group.

This within-subjects study evaluated the effect of COVID-19 on the auditory efferent system by measuring transient evoked otoacoustic emissions and contralateral suppression before and after COVID-19 in 11 adults. The study found no significant difference in auditory efferent function between pre- and post-COVID measurements, though it notes that severe COVID-19 can affect cochlear and auditory efferent system function.

This cross-sectional study compared olfactory dysfunction (via U-sniff test) and subjective smell complaints across children with acute SARS-CoV-2, other URTIs, recovered COVID-19, and long COVID. The study found no significant between-group differences in hyposmia frequency (11-17%), but noted poor correspondence between objective test results and subjective complaints, particularly in the long COVID group.

This pilot study followed 110 pregnant women from the CRONOS registry who had SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy to assess long-term post-COVID symptoms and quality of life. The study found that 63.6% of women experienced symptoms lasting longer than 12 weeks, with fatigue being the most common symptom (88%), significantly impacting quality of life in affected women.

This prospective observational study examined diaphragmatic function using sonography in 54 post-COVID patients, stratifying them by presence or absence of dyspnea. Patients with dyspnea showed significantly reduced diaphragm thickness, mobility, and elasticity compared to those without dyspnea, suggesting diaphragm dysfunction as a potential mechanism underlying respiratory symptoms in post-COVID condition.

A multicentre longitudinal observational study comparing pulmonary rehabilitation outcomes in 172 long COVID patients versus 133 asthma/COPD patients over 12 months. Long COVID patients showed greater health improvements following rehabilitation and 89% returned to work, though persistent COVID symptoms remained at one year.

Prospective observational study examining hypogonadism and testosterone levels in male COVID-19 survivors at 3 and 12 months post-infection. Found 24.7% had low testosterone at 3 months, with 50% of affected subjects showing persistent low testosterone at 12-month follow-up, suggesting potential long-term endocrine sequelae of COVID-19.

A prospective observational study of 224 long COVID patients undergoing pulmonary rehabilitation, measuring patient-reported outcomes (dyspnea, quality of life, pain, fatigue, depression, anxiety) at baseline, end of rehabilitation, and at 3 and 6 months post-treatment. All outcomes improved significantly during rehabilitation, with improvements in dyspnea and quality of life persisting at 6-month follow-up, suggesting rehabilitation benefits both Post-COVID-19 syndrome and ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 subgroups.

This study evaluates the prevalence of persistent chemosensory symptoms in post-COVID patients across a cohort of 4,062 acutely infected individuals and 909 follow-up respondents at 14.5 months post-infection. The authors found that while subjective chemosensory complaints are common during and after acute infection, only 1.2% have objective quantifiable chemosensory damage and few seek specialized treatment, suggesting lower healthcare burden compared to other long COVID complications.

Prospective observational study investigating long-term persistence of olfactory disorders following COVID-19 infection. No intervention or treatment is tested; this is a descriptive follow-up study of natural symptom progression.

This study evaluates symptom progression in long COVID patients 3 and 6 months after inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation. The research follows patients post-rehabilitation to assess whether respiratory rehabilitation improves long-term outcomes in post-COVID sequelae.

This prospective study investigates late cardiac outcomes in children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C) associated with COVID-19 using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging at median 16-month follow-up. While the paper documents cardiac findings in a pediatric inflammatory condition linked to COVID-19, it does not address long COVID (post-acute sequelae in adults or children beyond acute inflammatory phase) and is not a treatment intervention study but rather a diagnostic imaging follow-up.

A population-based subgroup analysis of the COVIDOM study examining relationships between post-COVID syndrome symptom severity, resilience, and acute illness severity in long COVID patients. The study uses the PCS Score to assess symptom complexity and identifies resilience and acute symptom burden as key predictors of post-COVID outcomes.

This study examined pneumological post-COVID rehabilitation outcomes over one year (April 2020–April 2021), comparing patients with post-COVID syndrome to those with acute or ongoing symptomatic COVID-19. The research evaluated whether rehabilitation treatment effectiveness differed across these three COVID-19 disease phases.

This study compares subjective olfactory dysfunction reports with objective psychophysical testing results in COVID-19 patients, examining recovery patterns over time. The paper is observational and does not evaluate any treatment intervention, focusing instead on characterizing the natural course of olfactory impairment.

This retrospective cohort study compares medium-term outcomes and quality of life in hospitalized COVID-19 patients with acute venous thromboembolism across three pandemic waves (2020-2022). The analysis finds reduced prevalence and severity of post-COVID symptoms in later waves, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This cohort study follows 96 mother-infant pairs exposed to COVID-19 during pregnancy or birth, assessing physical, mental, and emotional well-being at 6 and 12 months postpartum. While it documents persistent stress in some mothers, the paper focuses on pregnancy/perinatal outcomes rather than long COVID syndrome (persistent sequelae weeks-to-months post-infection) and is excluded as outside the scope of long COVID treatment trials.

This prospective study evaluated late respiratory system findings, allergen sensitivity, and laboratory parameters in 105 children with a history of symptomatic or asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection (median 5 months post-infection). The study found that post-COVID respiratory symptoms (cough, shortness of breath, chest pain) occurred in a significant proportion of children regardless of initial infection severity, with no significant differences in laboratory or atopic markers between groups.

This study investigates the long-term persistence of taste disorders following COVID-19 infection, comparing subjective and objective measures of taste dysfunction. It documents the natural history and factors influencing recovery of taste disorders in long COVID patients.

Cross-sectional study examining the frequency of fatty liver disease (hepatic steatosis) in patients with post-COVID syndrome compared to controls. Investigates the potential association between chronic liver disease and post-COVID symptoms like fatigue.

Retrospective analysis comparing SARS-CoV-2 variants in hospitalized patients with focus on headache as a post-COVID symptom and its association with individual risk factors and other long COVID symptoms. The study examines prevalence and duration of headache across different viral variants but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A service evaluation of homeopathic treatment for long-COVID patients in the UK, using patient-reported outcome data. The study assesses the utility of homeopathy as a cost-effective intervention for long-COVID symptoms.

Prospective observational study following 39 long COVID patients with sleep complaints over 1 year to assess persistence of sleep disorders and cognitive symptoms. Found that 23% persisted with insomnia and 5% with central hypersomnia, with insomnia patients showing higher cognitive complaints.

Observational cross-sectional study examining neurological and cognitive symptoms in 124 children 6-12 months and 2 years after COVID-19 infection (positive vs negative controls). Found that acute symptoms (headache, anosmia, ageusia, myalgia) resolved within 6-12 months in most cases, with persistent functional difficulties in only 3% and behavioral symptoms remitting in most except those with prior involvement.

This cross-sectional study examined olfactory dysfunction in 221 long COVID patients and its association with APOE polymorphisms. The E4 allele was found to be a protective factor against persistent olfactory dysfunction, contrary to previous literature suggesting E4 association with worse COVID outcomes.

Retrospective cross-sectional survey of 109 hospitalized COVID-19 patients (1.5-2 years post-infection) characterizing otorhinolaryngological symptoms and long-term sequelae. Found that 40% of patients maintained persistent symptoms including smell/taste dysfunction and dizziness, with dyspnea, cough, and nasal obstruction being most common initially.

Large community-based cross-sectional study assessing objective cognitive function in 112,964 participants who completed online cognitive assessments, comparing those with resolved COVID-19, persistent symptoms, and uninfected controls. Found that participants with unresolved persistent symptoms had larger cognitive deficits (-0.42 SD) compared to those with short-duration or resolved symptoms, with memory and executive function most affected, but this is an observational assessment study without any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study comparing physical recovery and symptoms between 154 COVID-positive and 190 COVID-negative participants over one year in Western Australia. Found no between-group differences in physical function but higher fatigue, dyspnoea, and anxiety/depression in COVID+ group at 8 months, resolving by 12 months.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes Veterans Affairs health records to compare the cumulative incidence of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC/long COVID) across pre-delta, delta, and omicron eras from 2020-2022. It finds that PASC incidence decreased over the pandemic, with vaccination significantly reducing risk, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing thromboembolic outcomes over 2 years in 643 atrial fibrillation patients with and without prior COVID-19 infection. Found COVID-19 history was associated with increased thromboembolic events, but this is not a long COVID study as it focuses on AF complications rather than persistent post-COVID symptoms.

This cross-sectional study examines how GP registrars assess and consider long COVID in patients presenting with fatigue, based on 3193 consultations from 969 registrars during 2022-2023. The study is observational and does not evaluate any treatment or intervention, making it ineligible for the clinical trials meta-analysis.

Prospective observational study assessing hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysfunction in COVID-19 patients ≥3 months post-infection across severity groups. Found that 13.63% of subjects had adrenal insufficiency at follow-up, with most recovering spontaneously by 12 months.

This cross-sectional study assessed olfactory function in 91 COVID-19 recovered patients using validated olfactory tests (sniffin' sticks) approximately 8 weeks after symptom onset. While 45.1% of patients still showed objective olfactory impairment, the study only measures outcomes without testing any intervention or treatment.

Nationwide cohort study examining the prevalence of long-COVID symptoms in Israeli patients with mild or asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found that long-COVID is common after mild symptomatic infection (35.1% with decreased smell, 34.6% not returning to baseline health) and less common after asymptomatic infection, with female gender, symptomatic disease, and obesity as key risk factors.

This cross-sectional study examined 151 long COVID patients with persistent cough and dyspnea (>8 weeks post-infection) to investigate underlying chronic airway disease using bronchodilator reversibility testing. Results showed 26.5% had reversible airflow obstruction, 15.9% met asthma criteria, and 8.6% had non-reversible airflow obstruction, suggesting COVID-19 may trigger asthma pathogenesis.

This is a prospective observational study following 26 long COVID patients with olfactory dysfunction at 3 months post-infection to assess spontaneous improvement by 6 months using validated olfactory testing. The study found that 96% of patients showed significant improvement in smell function without any intervention being administered.

Retrospective study examining menstrual disturbances in 223 female long COVID patients from a Japanese clinic, comparing symptoms and endocrine markers between those with and without menstrual complications. Found 19.7% had menstrual symptoms associated with long COVID, with higher prevalence during Omicron phase and associations with fatigue, depression, and altered cortisol levels.

Longitudinal study following 20 hospitalized COVID-19 patients from discharge to three months post-discharge, assessing exercise capacity and occupational competence using standardized measures. While patients showed some improvement over time, the study is observational without any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline.

This prospective observational study compared mitochondrial function in isolated PBMCs from 27 long COVID patients versus 16 healthy controls using Seahorse flux analysis. The study found distinctive changes in ATP synthase function in long COVID cases that correlated with autonomic health, quality of life, and time since infection, but did not test or evaluate any intervention.

This registry-based cohort study examines pre-pandemic care-seeking patterns in 208,050 Swedish women and their association with subsequent post-COVID condition, post-viral fatigue syndrome, and exhaustion disorder diagnoses. The study is observational/analytical rather than an intervention trial, analyzing historical primary-care data to identify risk factors for symptom-based diagnoses.

Prospective cohort study of 84 elite football players assessing persistent performance deficits after SARS-CoV-2 infection, with 22 infections during follow-up. Found transient compromise in aerobic performance (elevated heart rate during exertion) 52 days post-infection, resolved by 128 days, with no deficits in anaerobic performance or strength.

This retrospective cohort study followed 365,354 individuals in Stockholm matched on age, sex, and baseline healthcare use to compare healthcare utilization in 2021/22 between those with SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity in 2020 versus seronegative controls. The study found no overall increase in healthcare use in the general seropositive population, with increased healthcare use restricted only to individuals hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2020.

This prospective cohort study investigates circadian rhythm alterations and sleep patterns in ME/CFS and post-COVID fatigue patients compared to healthy controls, examining associations with cardiovascular risk factors. While about long COVID, it is observational without any intervention—patients are monitored but not given a treatment, so it does not meet the inclusion criteria for treatment/intervention trials.

This comparative effectiveness study evaluates allied healthcare (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, etc.) versus no treatment for long COVID patients using data from two cohorts (ParaCOV n=1,451 with allied healthcare and LongCOVID n=1,427 controls) followed for 12 months. Allied healthcare showed significant improvements in physical functioning and quality of life, though between-group differences were not considered clinically relevant by pre-specified thresholds.

This observational cohort study evaluates vision-related symptoms and visual/oculomotor function in 38 non-hospitalised long COVID patients referred for neurocognitive assessment. The study validates clinical assessment tools (Developmental Eye Movement Test, Visual Motion Sensitivity Clinical Test Protocol) but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective observational study compares cardiovascular disease risk and mortality outcomes between hemodialysis patients with and without prior mild COVID-19 infection during the post-Omicron era.
