The study found no significant increase in long-term cardiovascular or non-cardiovascular mortality risk associated with mild COVID-19 in this population.

This study compared respiratory function, muscle strength, exercise capacity, and chronotropic response between post-COVID-19 patients with pulmonary involvement and healthy controls. Patients demonstrated significantly impaired respiratory function, exercise capacity, and chronotropic response, with most displaying sedentary lifestyle and elevated dyspnea; the authors recommend comprehensive pulmonary rehabilitation to prevent long-term impairments.

A cross-sectional survey of 12,000+ persons with HIV in Washington, DC that characterizes the prevalence (46%), symptom clustering, and risk factors for post-COVID conditions. The study found that asthma history and retired/disabled status were associated with post-COVID conditions, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational study assessed objective neurocognitive deficits in 133 COVID-19 patients five months after hospitalization using standardized neuropsychological tests (RBANS and CWIT). Findings showed 37% of patients had cognitive impairment below cutoff, with attention and memory deficits most common, though no clear associations with disease severity indicators were found.

This cohort follow-up study compares psychological impacts (anxiety, depression, PTSD) of COVID-19 on patients with and without chronic medical illnesses, with assessments at acute infection and 6-month follow-up. While it addresses long-term psychological sequelae, it does not test or evaluate any specific treatment or intervention for these conditions.

A prospective cohort study examining platelet function and activation markers in mild COVID-19 convalescents at 2-15 weeks and 6-10 months post-infection compared to matched controls. The study found increased platelet sensitization and elevated inflammatory mediators (S1P, MRP4) but no altered platelet aggregation or thrombin formation, suggesting a persistent pro-inflammatory state after convalescence.

Prospective cohort study following 34 COVID-19 hospitalized patients who received early rehabilitation, with 17 completing 12-month follow-up. While quadriceps strength and functional capacity improved significantly, the study focuses on acute COVID-19 recovery during hospitalization rather than long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks/months post-infection).

Prospective study evaluating the impact of an intensive, interdisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation program on 42 post-ICU COVID-19 survivors. The program resulted in significant improvements in muscle strength, respiratory function, fatigue, balance, exercise capacity, and ability to perform daily activities.

A prospective cohort study comparing psychological and biological assessments in 104 adults with tobacco use disorder before and four months after long COVID diagnosis. The study documents significant increases in depressive symptoms, anxiety, insomnia, and perceived stress, with decreased serum cortisol levels, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study examines immune response changes in 23 patients with cardiovascular disease during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and 3-month recovery, measuring monocyte phenotypes and cytokine profiles. The findings suggest persistent pro-inflammatory monocyte dysfunction post-infection, but the study focuses on acute infection rather than long COVID syndrome.

Prospective cohort study following COVID-19 ICU survivors in Congo for 2 years to assess kidney function decline and chronic kidney disease incidence, comparing patients with and without acute kidney injury. Finds that 23% experienced kidney function decline and 0.73% developed CKD, with prior AKI significantly increasing risk.

This is a secondary analysis from the COVID-19 RECOVERY STUDY II (CORES II) that performed cluster analysis on long COVID symptom phenotypes and their association with one-year psychosocial outcomes (anxiety, depression, PTSD, QOL) in 746 patients. The study identified five symptom clusters and found that multi-organ dysfunction and olfactory/gustatory disturbance phenotypes were associated with worse psychosocial outcomes, but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This case-control study compares psychological and neurological symptoms between 62 long COVID-recovered individuals and 36 healthy controls, identifying unrefreshing sleep as a significant predictor of attention and anxiety issues. The study is excluded because it is observational without an intervention—it characterizes symptoms and risk factors rather than testing any treatment.

This prospective observational study assessed thyroid dysfunction in 113 COVID-19 survivors two months post-infection, finding thyroid dysfunction in 61.1% of patients, predominantly subclinical hypothyroidism. The study documents the long-term effects of COVID-19 on thyroid function but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective database analysis of work absence claims among US employees with COVID-19 from 2018-2022, examining disability benefit utilization, claim duration, and costs. Findings show COVID-19 caused significant work loss extending beyond acute infection, ranking as the second most common reason for short-term disability claims during the study period.

Retrospective cohort study using French primary care EHRs to assess healthcare resource utilization and costs among 30,122 adults with long COVID between 2020-2023. Found that long COVID patients incurred €2,443 per patient per year in healthcare costs, with 97.3% using GP services and 62.4% using nursing care.

This retrospective cohort study quantifies healthcare resource utilization and direct medical costs for children with mild-to-moderate long COVID in France using primary care electronic health records. Among 27,537 children with COVID-19, 3,888 (14.1%) developed long COVID with mean first-year costs of €823 per patient, representing an incremental increase of €98 compared to non-long COVID controls.

Cross-sectional comparison of neuropsychological functioning between long COVID patients with persistent severe fatigue/concentration difficulties and those without complaints, assessed median 23 months post-infection. No significant cognitive impairment was found on most tests, with only minimal differences in processing speed.

This cross-sectional study evaluates performance validity testing (PVT) in 247 long COVID patients undergoing neuropsychological evaluation, examining the relationship between PVT failures, external incentives (disability claims), and cognitive performance. Results show that external incentives are associated with PVT failures, but this is an observational assessment study without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between COVID-19 vaccination status and long COVID incidence and healthcare resource utilization in UK primary care data from 2022-2023. Vaccination was not associated with long COVID incidence, though some subgroup-specific benefits in specialist referrals were observed.

Prospective cohort study of non-hospitalised COVID-19 patients across 11 European countries followed for 12 weeks to assess long-COVID prevalence, symptom characteristics, and risk factors. Found 52% developed long-COVID with fatigue as the most common lingering symptom; no treatment intervention was tested.

This cross-sectional study compared psychological functioning in 201 long COVID patients versus 102 post-concussion syndrome patients using the Personality Assessment Inventory, finding similar patterns of emotional distress and psychological symptoms between groups. The study suggests psychological treatment strategies used for PCS may benefit long COVID patients but does not test or evaluate a treatment intervention.

A retrospective cohort study evaluating the prevalence of post-COVID-19 syndrome and associated risk factors in 463 healthcare workers followed for 18 months. Female sex and obesity were identified as statistically significant risk factors, with fatigue (32.5%) and memory disorders (21.5%) being the most common persistent symptoms.

This pre-registered controlled study compared auditory function between 57 hospitalized COVID-19 patients and 40 matched non-COVID controls using comprehensive behavioral, physiological, and self-report measures. The study found no significant differences in auditory function between groups, concluding that COVID-19 infection does not have a significant long-term impact on hearing.

Longitudinal neuropsychological assessment of 46 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors at 1 and 2.5 years post-infection, examining objective cognitive functioning across multiple domains. Found no consistent objective cognitive deficits or major cognitive disorders in the majority of cases, with stable performance over time except for improvement in phonemic fluency.

This prospective cohort study followed 291 SARS-CoV-2 positive individuals in Kenya for up to 16 months to characterize long COVID symptoms and recovery patterns. The study found that half had lingering symptoms at 6 months and a third at 12 months, with slower recovery in older adults, women, and those with comorbidities, but does not test any interventions or treatments.

This retrospective cohort study compares lung perfusion scintigraphy findings between 30 post-COVID patients with persistent dyspnea and 30 controls without prior COVID-19. The study investigates diagnostic imaging markers rather than evaluating a treatment intervention, making it a diagnostic/observational assessment study excluded from the trial analysis.

Cross-sectional study comparing chest CT airway and vascular measurements in females with long-COVID, COPD, and ex-smokers. Found significant differences in airway lumen area, wall thickness, and pulmonary vessel volume in long-COVID patients but no evidence of pulmonary vascular remodeling.

Prospective cohort study of 327 long COVID patients receiving SPA (spa water therapy) rehabilitation, examining dyspnea and fatigue outcomes in relation to pulmonary function, obesity, and comorbidities. SPA therapy showed benefit for alleviating fatigue and improving well-being in selected subgroups, particularly those with chronic respiratory conditions, though not in patients with impaired DLCO and obesity.

This cross-sectional study compares neural mechanosensitivity and peripheral nerve function between 33 long COVID patients and 31 healthy controls using standardized clinical assessments and neurodynamic tests. Long COVID patients showed significantly worse neural mechanosensitivity, functionality, and quality of life, but the study does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

A prospective observational cohort study assessing long-term consequences of severe COVID-19 hospitalization at 4-5 months post-discharge in 128 patients. Findings show high prevalence of fatigue, dyspnea, and cognitive dysfunction with impaired quality of life and lung function (45% with reduced diffusing capacity), but no intervention was tested.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing pre- and post-COVID medication and disease burden in older adults using health system data from 2020-2024. Finds significant increases in diagnoses and medication use post-COVID, with disparities by age, race, and gender, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study examining depression and PTSD symptoms in COVID-19 critical illness survivors at 1 and 12 months post-ICU discharge. Found that 29-32% had depression and 31-36% had PTSD symptoms, with mechanical ventilation predicting symptom persistence, but no intervention was tested.

Longitudinal metagenomic study of 142 COVID-19 patients tracking antimicrobial resistance genes in gut microbiota from acute infection through 6 months post-viral clearance, with intervention groups receiving antibiotics or probiotics. Probiotics (synbiotic formula SIM01) significantly reduced antimicrobial resistance gene burden compared to antibiotic treatment, with expanded resistome associated with increased post-acute COVID-19 syndrome prevalence.

Retrospective observational study evaluating post-COVID health status in 123 recovered patients using the EuroQol-5D-5L scale at discharge and 4-8 weeks post-discharge. Found significant improvements over time in anxiety/depression and other dimensions, with smoking associated with reduced activity levels at 4 weeks.

This is a prospective follow-up study of lung function in COVID-19 ICU survivors at 4 months, 1 year, and 2 years post-discharge. While it documents persistent pulmonary deficits in post-acute COVID-19, it does not focus on long COVID per se and contains no treatment or intervention component—it is purely observational follow-up of ICU survivors from acute COVID-19.

Prospective observational cohort of 34 long COVID patients receiving 12 weeks of telerehabilitation based on the STOP-REST-PACE approach, assessing post-exertional malaise (PEM), quality of life, respiratory symptoms, and return to work outcomes. Despite therapy, PEM persisted in 19/30 completers; respiratory symptoms improved significantly, but fatigue, quality of life, and return to work showed minimal improvement.

A cross-sectional study comparing symptom trajectories in 278 long-COVID patients over ~21.7 weeks against 502 ME/CFS patients using standardized questionnaires. The study documents natural symptom evolution (improvement in most domains, worsening in neurocognitive) but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This cross-sectional study from the SHARE survey examined associations between preexisting depression and COVID-19 vaccination uptake, SARS-CoV-2 infection risk, and long COVID development in 31,115 middle-aged and older Europeans. Depression was associated with reduced vaccination odds (OR=0.72), increased infection risk (OR=1.15), and increased long COVID risk (OR=1.21), with associations strengthening with depression severity.

This study examines changes in thyroid function in hypothyroid patients during acute COVID-19 infection in Shanghai, comparing pre-infection baseline to 1-month and 3-month follow-up. It is not a long COVID study as it focuses on acute infection effects in a specific patient population rather than persistent post-COVID sequelae.

This 1-year longitudinal study tracks immune responses (antibodies, B cells, T cells) in 65 COVID-19 convalescents, finding that 48% retain post-acute sequelae symptoms and all maintain immune memory components. The study documents kinetics of SARS-CoV-2 immunity but does not test or evaluate any treatment or intervention for long COVID.

A prospective cohort pilot study evaluating stellate ganglion block (SGB) treatment in 10 patients with Long COVID/ME/CFS. Results showed significant improvements in post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment, orthostatic intolerance, and quality of life measures, with objective resolution of POTS symptoms.

Prospective cohort study following 155 COVID-19 survivors for 2 years post-infection to assess persistent symptoms and health outcomes. Found that 36.6% had long COVID symptoms, 35.0% had psychological symptoms, and 50.7% had radiographic abnormalities, but no treatment intervention was tested.

A prospective cohort study following 20,000+ COVID-19 patients in Shanghai for one year to assess long COVID prevalence and impact. Found 8.89% with self-reported long COVID symptoms at 6 months, with 68.5% achieving symptom resolution by 12 months; no treatments were administered.

Prospective cohort study of 6,412 Omicron COVID-19 patients in Shanghai followed from November 2022 to February 2023, examining long COVID sequelae and reinfection rates. Found 9.4% experienced sequelae (primarily fatigue and mental symptoms) and 12.1% experienced reinfection; hybrid immunity with vaccination reduced reinfection risk and was associated with higher neutralizing antibody titers.

This observational study using target trial emulation compared nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir versus no antiviral treatment for post-COVID-19 outcomes among 140,477 and 96,030 outpatients respectively in Hong Kong. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir significantly reduced post-acute mortality and all-cause hospitalization at 31-180 and 181-360 days, while molnupiravir showed only short-term mortality benefit with no protective effect on long-term post-COVID outcomes.

Retrospective cohort study of 1,530 COVID-19 patients examining the predictive role of baseline chest radiograph severity on short- and long-term outcomes. Found that CXR severity (Brixia score) was a significant independent predictor of mortality and presence of long-term residual symptoms at 5-6 month follow-up, with 36% of survivors symptomatic.

This retrospective cohort study of 50,438 COVID-19 patients examines whether complete COVID-19 vaccination modifies the protective effect of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir treatment on post-acute mortality and rehospitalization outcomes. The study found a significant additive interaction between nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and complete vaccination on post-acute rehospitalization, with greater antiviral benefits in fully vaccinated individuals, particularly among older adults and females.

This cross-sectional study examined 305 healthcare workers at least 12 weeks post-COVID-19 to identify characteristics and predictors of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PCS). Female sex and increasing age were identified as statistically significant predictors of PCS, with fatigue, shortness of breath, and muscle/joint aches being the most common symptoms.

Prospective cohort study of 154 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients examining long-term symptoms and health-related quality of life over time. Found that ~10% developed long-term symptoms with significant negative impact on EQ5D-VAS scores, but this is an observational study with no treatment intervention—patients were passively followed, not actively treated.

A prospective cohort study of 102 COVID-19 patients assessing clinical and immunological features associated with persistence of post-COVID-19 syndrome at six months follow-up. The study identified that pro-inflammatory markers (IL-1α, IP-10, elevated CD57 expression in CD8+ T cells) and obesity were independently associated with symptom persistence.

This retrospective cohort study compared cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max) measured via repeated cardiopulmonary exercise tests in 40 healthcare workers who had COVID-19 versus 87 controls over a mean interval of 762 days. COVID-19 survivors showed a statistically significant decline in VO2 max (3.12 mL/kg/min reduction) compared to controls, indicating that mild-to-moderate COVID-19 persistently reduces cardiorespiratory fitness even months after infection.

A 30-month nationwide French cohort study of 63,990 COVID-19 hospitalized patients matched to 319,891 controls, examining excess risks of death and organ-related hospitalizations. Findings show persistent increased risks for neurological, respiratory, and psychiatric disorders up to 30 months post-discharge, but this is an observational study with no treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 1,666 COVID-19 survivors hospitalized in Italy followed for 12 months to identify factors associated with persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnoea, insomnia, and mental confusion. Female sex and older age were independently associated with symptom persistence, while greater acute severity markers paradoxically predicted symptom improvement over time.

This prospective/retrospective cohort study enrolled 223 long COVID patients (89 female, 134 male) to characterize sex-related differences in persistent symptoms at 5-month follow-up. Women were significantly more likely to report dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, and palpitations, but the study does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

A retrospective cross-sectional study developing machine learning models to predict COVID-19 outcomes (hospitalization, ICU admission, long COVID) using viral sequencing and clinical data from 4,450 individuals. The study identifies risk factors and predictors but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational study compared neurocognitive function and language performance in 47 COVID-19 survivors (12 weeks post-infection) versus 51 healthy controls, assessing associations with disease severity, BMI, and inflammatory markers. While the study documents significant cognitive deficits in long COVID patients, particularly in processing speed and memory, it does not test or evaluate any specific treatment or intervention—making it an observational assessment rather than a treatment trial.

Retrospective analysis of 157 COVID-19 pneumonia patients evaluated at a Post-COVID clinic at 4 months follow-up, comparing pulmonary function and exercise capacity between males and females. Findings show women had more severe alveolar diffusion impairment and reduced exercise tolerance than men despite similar acute illness severity.

Prospective cohort study following 81 hospitalized COVID-19 patients over 12 months to track changes in pulmonary function, imaging, and patient-reported outcomes. Found pulmonary function improved between 3-6 months with plateauing thereafter, while 60% continued reporting abnormal quality of life at 12 months, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

This retrospective cohort study using TriNetX data compared thyroid dysfunction risk in COVID-19 patients versus matched controls over 12 months. The study found a significant 2-fold increased risk of thyroid dysfunction (both thyrotoxicosis and hypothyroidism) in COVID-19 patients, with higher risk in older adults and females.

This cross-sectional study compared spleen size and T lymphocyte counts in 76 COVID-19 recovered patients versus 55 healthy controls. While it found reduced spleen size and decreased T lymphocytes in recovered patients, it addresses acute COVID-19 sequelae during the recovery phase, not persistent long COVID symptoms weeks-to-months post-infection, and does not study any treatment intervention.

This observational cohort study examined whether daily emotional exertions (stress, worry, rumination) are associated with symptom severity in 376 UK Long COVID patients using intensive daily smartphone assessments. Results showed stress and worry are distinct factors linked to same-day and next-day symptom fluctuations, with implications for stress management in Long COVID self-care.

This cross-sectional study assessed post-COVID-19 symptoms and functional capacity in 394 hospitalized and nonhospitalized survivors using tele-assessment methods at 1-6 months post-infection. The study found high prevalence of anxiety (47.7%), fatigue (46.7%), and muscle pain (45.7%), with significantly reduced functional capacity in the hospitalized group, highlighting the need for comprehensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation programs.

Real-world analysis comparing post-COVID-19 condition risk in older patients (≥65 years) with influenza survivors using the TriNetX network. COVID-19 survivors showed significantly higher risk of multiple post-COVID conditions including abnormal breathing, fatigue, anxiety/depression, and cognitive symptoms, with age-related differences in cognitive symptom incidence.

This cross-sectional study examined associations between acute-phase bed rest duration and grip strength in 49 post-COVID-19 patients reporting ongoing symptoms and fatigue. Findings showed that each additional day of bed rest during acute illness was independently associated with lower grip strength (~150g per day), highlighting the importance of early mobilization during acute COVID-19.

This retrospective cohort study follows 360 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for six months after discharge to assess longer-term outcomes including readmissions, mortality, and changes in residential status. While it documents significant post-discharge morbidity and mortality, it is an observational study without any treatment intervention and therefore does not meet criteria for inclusion in a treatment trials meta-analysis.

A prospective cohort study of 30 older Irish adults who received inpatient geriatric rehabilitation following acute COVID-19 infection, with follow-up assessment at six months post-discharge. Patients regained pre-admission functional ability but experienced persistent symptoms and reduced quality of life compared to baseline.

Population-based cross-sectional analysis of 4,004 Europeans aged 50+ from the SHARE Corona Survey examining the prevalence of Long COVID and its association with multimorbidity and socioeconomic factors. Found 71.6% of COVID-19 survivors reported at least one Long COVID symptom, with significant cross-country variation and associations with education, employment, and age, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining the incidence of long COVID symptoms 12-20 weeks post-diagnosis in a large US ambulatory care database of 916,894 COVID-19 patients. Identifies risk factors associated with long COVID development but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Retrospective cohort study using Oracle EHR data comparing thyroid disease risk (hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism) in 1.8M COVID-19 patients versus 3.7M matched controls from 2019-2024. COVID-19 was associated with significantly elevated risk of both conditions, with severity-dependent increases up to 9.87x for ECMO-dependent patients, and additional risk in long COVID-19 and reinfection cases.

Population-based cohort study comparing six-month post-COVID symptom risk between the first and second COVID-19 waves in France before vaccine rollout. Finds higher post-COVID risk during the first wave (14.6%) vs second wave (7.0%), with risk factors including baseline physical/mental conditions, female sex, and acute symptom severity.

Retrospective cohort study comparing risk of geriatric syndromes (cognitive impairment, depression, pressure injury) in older adults (65+) with and without COVID-19 using propensity score matching from US TriNetX data (2020-2022). The study found significantly elevated risk of multiple geriatric syndromes in COVID-19 survivors but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study examining the association between pre-infection binge alcohol use and functional outcomes (mental and physical) among COVID-19-positive individuals measured at 3 and 6 months post-infection. Binge drinking showed statistically significant but clinically irrelevant associations with improved function at 3 months that were not sustained at 6 months.

This cross-sectional study evaluated grip strength and associated factors among 93 post-COVID-19 older adults (mean age 73) recruited at an average of 55 days after hospital discharge. The study found that 74.2% had low grip strength, with age, hospital stay duration, and comorbidity burden as significant negative correlates, highlighting the need for rehabilitation monitoring in this population.

A cross-sectional study assessing cumulative neuropsychological deficits in 121 post-COVID patients using validated test batteries and Monte-Carlo simulation methods. Finds that moderate and severe COVID-19 cases show significantly greater long-term cognitive deficits (memory, executive function, perception, reasoning) compared to normative populations, while mild cases do not.

This study examined executive functioning and processing speed changes in 9 older adults with mild cognitive impairment who contracted COVID-19 between two assessment timepoints. Results showed significant decline in one cognitive measure post-infection, but the paper focuses on acute COVID-19 infection effects in MCI patients, not long COVID syndrome or treatment interventions.

Retrospective analysis of 205 long COVID patients using factorial analysis and hierarchical clustering to identify distinct clinical forms and patient clusters. Study identifies three clinical phenotypes (long, persistent, post-viral syndrome) associated with different pathophysiological mechanisms but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study examines cognitive performance validity test (PVT) failure rates in 323 long COVID patients receiving care at a specialized clinic, finding that failure on both PVTs was uncommon (6.3%) and unrelated to COVID severity or cognitive complaints. The paper characterizes patterns of validity test failure rather than evaluating a treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of acute COVID-19 inpatients (not long COVID patients) examining neurological symptoms and cerebral glucose metabolism in the subacute stage of active infection. Study focuses on acute COVID-19 pathophysiology, not persistent post-COVID syndrome or interventions for long COVID.

Retrospective cohort study examining the risk of psoriatic arthritis and uveitis in patients with psoriasis after COVID-19 infection using propensity score matching. The study is not about long COVID treatment or management; instead, it investigates whether acute COVID-19 increases the risk of dermatological complications in psoriasis patients.

This retrospective audit compares the incidence of chronic fungal sinusitis at a UK tertiary center before and after the COVID-19 pandemic (2018-2022). While it observes a higher post-pandemic incidence, the paper does not study long COVID specifically—it examines an opportunistic fungal infection that may have increased during the pandemic, not a persistent symptom or sequela of COVID-19 infection itself.

Prospective cohort study examining humoral immune responses to SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses in 112 infected individuals, comparing those who developed neuroPASC (n=18) versus those who did not (n=94). Finds that neuroPASC patients show attenuated anti-SARS-CoV-2 responses but expanded responses to other coronaviruses, suggesting immunologic imprinting as a pathogenic mechanism, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study used electronic health records to compare cognitive outcomes in epilepsy patients taking phenytoin versus other anticonvulsants at the time of COVID-19 infection, testing whether phenytoin's receptor-interacting protein kinase inhibition could prevent post-COVID cognitive deficits. Patients on phenytoin had significantly lower risk of cognitive deficits in the 6 months post-infection compared to those on levetiracetam or valproate, suggesting potential protective effects of this drug class.

This study compares white matter changes and cognitive function in 22 recovered COVID-19 patients at 1-year follow-up versus 21 healthy controls using advanced diffusion imaging techniques. While white matter abnormalities were detected in COVID-19 patients (particularly in those with ICU admission), no significant decline in cognitive function was found, and the paper does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational case-control study compared brain white matter microstructure in 16 long COVID patients versus 16 matched controls using advanced diffusion MRI techniques. The study found widespread white matter abnormalities in the patient group indicative of vasogenic edema, demyelination, and axonal damage, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study investigated limbic system damage and emotion recognition abilities in 105 long COVID patients at 6-9 months post-infection, stratified by acute respiratory severity. Moderate and severe patients showed impaired emotion recognition compared to mild cases, with findings linked to decreased episodic memory and anosmia rather than psychiatric symptoms.

Prospective cohort study measuring plasma biomarkers of nervous system injury (neurofilament light, GFAP, tau) in hospitalized COVID-19 survivors at 6 months and 1 year post-discharge. Found no robust associations between biomarkers and acute COVID-19 severity or post-acute neuropsychiatric symptoms, suggesting ongoing symptoms are not due to ongoing neural injury.

International prospective cohort study of 6,862 hospitalized COVID-19 patients tracked for up to 12 months to assess post-acute neurological sequelae (PANSC) and sex differences in symptom resolution. Found that ~70% had multiple neurological symptoms at follow-up, with fatigue and myalgia most common; females experienced longer symptom resolution times than males, and ICU admission was associated with prolonged recovery.

This retrospective observational cohort study compared structural and functional brain integrity in 65 healthcare workers with mild COVID-19 at 9-month follow-up versus pre-pandemic healthy controls using comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and MRI. The study found specific executive function impairments, white matter hyperintensities, thalamic volume loss, and altered functional connectivity in the mild COVID-19 group, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Swedish national register-based cohort study examining the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequent demyelinating diseases, including multiple sclerosis. While the study identifies elevated risk in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, it focuses on acute infection consequences rather than long COVID syndrome or any treatment interventions.

Longitudinal observational study tracking brain imaging, clinical symptoms, and biomarkers in 51 post-COVID patients over 3 years compared to healthy controls. Study documents slow clinical improvement and brain recovery patterns with structural stabilization and increased connectivity, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examined the association between COVID-19 infection and inflammatory dermatoses in 204,241 patients using electronic health records. The study found significantly elevated risks for several dermatological conditions (atopic dermatitis, acne, rosacea, alopecia areata, seborrheic dermatitis) following COVID-19 infection, but did not evaluate any treatment interventions.

This retrospective cohort study compared neurological manifestations of long COVID between patients with pre-vaccination and breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infections, evaluating 1,300 Neuro-PASC patients at a neuro-COVID clinic. The study found that vaccination prior to infection does not significantly affect neurologic symptoms or cognitive outcomes, though breakthrough infection patients had higher comorbidity burden.

This prospective cohort study assessed olfactory dysfunction in COVID-19 patients at 6 months post-infection using both self-report and psychophysical testing. The study found persistent smell dysfunction in 60% of participants despite many self-reporting normal smell, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

A longitudinal observational study of 180 nonhospitalized COVID-19 patients in the Faroe Islands tracking symptom persistence over ~4 months. Found 53.1% reported persistent symptoms at mean 125 days post-infection, with fatigue, anosmia, and arthralgias being most common.

This study conducted a comprehensive multidisciplinary assessment of 124 COVID-19 patients 3 months post-discharge, evaluating lung function, imaging, exercise capacity, body composition, and mental/cognitive health. Findings revealed persistent pulmonary abnormalities in 91%, fatigue in 69%, functional impairment in 64%, and cognitive problems in 36% of patients, highlighting substantial long-term health sequelae across multiple domains.

This cross-sectional study evaluated late olfactory bulb morphometry changes in COVID-19 patients 129±68 days post-infection using 3T-MRI and olfactory function testing. Although it demonstrates SARS-CoV-2 is associated with persistent olfactory bulb atrophy regardless of symptom status, it is an observational assessment study without any intervention or treatment being evaluated.

This cross-sectional study assessed 118 individuals 3-4 months post-COVID-19 diagnosis using symptom surveys, work productivity measures, and 6-minute walk tests. The findings demonstrate significant persistent functional impairment and symptoms even in non-hospitalized patients with uncomplicated COVID-19.

A matched-cohort study using administrative healthcare data comparing 27,589 inpatient and 46,857 outpatient COVID-19 cases to matched controls over 4 months. Found that 7-7.7% of COVID-19 patients developed post-COVID conditions including pulmonary embolism, chest pain, fatigue, headache, and respiratory/neurological/circulatory/gastrointestinal symptoms within 31-120 days post-diagnosis.

Prospective cohort study tracking COVID-19 symptom trajectories in 342 patients over 12 months post-illness. Finds that 40.7% continue reporting symptoms at 12 months, with female sex and obesity associated with slower recovery.

Prospective cohort study following 96 COVID-19 patients from 5 to 12 months post-infection to characterize persistent symptoms and their associations with laboratory markers. At 12 months, 77% remained symptomatic with reduced exercise capacity, fatigue, and neurocognitive symptoms most common; elevated ANA titers were associated with higher neurocognitive symptom frequency.

Prospective multicenter cohort study of 3,334 healthcare workers assessing frequency and risk factors for long COVID symptoms 3+ months post-infection. Found that infected HCWs reported more long COVID symptoms than controls (73% vs 52%), with acute viral symptoms and lower physical activity as risk factors.

Prospective cohort study of 548 non-hospitalized COVID-19 cases followed for 6 months in England, measuring health-related quality of life using EQ-5D and comparing to SARS-CoV-2-negative controls. Found that 16.8% reported persistent physical symptoms at 6 months with significant quality-of-life losses, but this is an observational study without any intervention or treatment being tested.

This retrospective cohort study examines the association between COVID-19 vaccination and long COVID referral rates at a UK teaching hospital clinic. The authors report a 79% reduction in long COVID referrals correlating with vaccination uptake, suggesting vaccines may reduce long COVID incidence.

Multicenter prospective cohort study comparing prevalence of prolonged symptoms 3 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection across three variant periods (pre-Delta, Delta, Omicron). Found that pre-Delta infections were associated with more severe fatigue and multiple prolonged symptoms, but these differences were not significant after adjusting for vaccination status.

Prospective cohort study comparing symptom profiles in adults with positive vs negative SARS-CoV-2 tests at baseline and 3 months follow-up. While the study confirms long COVID symptoms exist, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 1.36 million COVID-19 patients examining the association between initial COVID-19 severity and subsequent cardiovascular events >30 days post-infection. Patients requiring ICU or hospitalization had significantly higher risk of cardiovascular events compared to outpatient cases (aHR 1.80 for ICU, 1.28 for non-ICU hospitalization).

This cohort study investigates the relationship between glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and COVID-19 infection severity in an Israeli healthcare population. While it identifies long COVID as an outcome, the study does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it is purely observational epidemiology examining disease association.

This Danish nationwide cohort study examined whether SARS-CoV-2 infection increases susceptibility to non-COVID-19 infectious disease hospitalizations in adults aged ≥50 years during the postacute phase (≥29 days post-infection). The study found no evidence of increased risk of infectious disease hospitalization following SARS-CoV-2 infection, with an overall IRR of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.88-0.92).

Observational study of 1,293 healthcare workers examining risk factors for developing long COVID, finding that longer duration of SARS-CoV-2 positivity increases risk while BNT162b2 vaccination provides protection. This is a secondary analysis of infection/vaccination data rather than an intervention trial testing a treatment for long COVID patients.

This study compares the prevalence of post-COVID symptoms 12 weeks after Omicron infection versus negative controls in vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. It is an observational cross-sectional assessment without any intervention or treatment evaluation.

Prospective observational study examining the relationship between SARS-CoV-2 viral clearance rates during acute infection and subsequent long COVID development in 172 participants. Slower viral clearance and higher acute symptom burden were associated with increased long COVID risk, particularly in women.

Retrospective cohort study examining cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and thrombotic complications in COVID-19 survivors during the Delta wave in Singapore, comparing 106,012 infected cases to 1.68 million test-negative controls followed for ~300 days. Found increased risk of new-incident cardiovascular/cerebrovascular complications among infected individuals, with risks attenuated by vaccination and boosting.

Prospective cohort study of 1,967 household members examining prevalence and risk factors for ongoing symptoms 90 days after SARS-CoV-2 or influenza infection. Found SARS-CoV-2-infected participants had nearly twice the odds of ongoing symptoms compared to influenza-infected participants, with underlying conditions and COVID-like acute symptoms increasing risk.

Population-based study examining the prevalence of post-COVID conditions (PCCs) and their association with return to pre-COVID health using state-level case reporting and patient surveys. Found 29.9% prevalence of PCCs with 77.2% of affected individuals not returning to baseline health within 8-60 weeks, identifying symptom clusters and risk factors but not testing any intervention.

This EHR-based retrospective cohort study estimates long COVID incidence across three nationwide research networks using different classification algorithms, comparing SARS-CoV-2-infected patients to COVID-negative and historical controls. The findings show 4-10-26% incidence depending on phenotype, but the paper is observational surveillance research without any treatment intervention or control group assignment.

This study uses Veterans Health Administration records to compare cumulative incidence of post-COVID conditions and mortality between SARS-CoV-2 infected and uninfected veterans across different viral eras (WT, Alpha, Delta, Omicron) and vaccination status. It found elevated post-COVID burden persisted 31-180 days post-infection, with lower burden in Omicron era and among vaccinated individuals, but does not test any treatment intervention.

Analyzes INSPIRE registry data to compare long-term symptom outcomes between individuals with single vs. repeated SARS-CoV-2 infections across different variant periods. Finds that reinfection effects on long-term symptoms vary by variant timing, with Omicron reinfections associated with higher risk of persistent symptoms.

Retrospective cohort study examining increased pneumonia risk in COVID-19 patients compared to controls in a large urban health system from 2020-2024. While it studies post-COVID sequelae, it is not about long COVID (focuses on acute infection consequences for pneumonia) and does not test any treatment intervention.

A retrospective cohort study using target trial emulation evaluating metformin's effectiveness in preventing post-COVID-19 condition in overweight/obese adults in UK primary care data (2020-2023). Early metformin treatment (within 90 days of COVID-19 diagnosis) was associated with a 64% risk reduction in post-COVID condition at 1 year (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.32-0.41).

Retrospective cohort study of 248 maintenance hemodialysis patients with COVID-19, followed for a median of 180 days post-acute infection. Documents long-term complications including cardiovascular events, infections, gastrointestinal bleeding, and post-COVID-19 cachexia (13% of patients), highlighting persistent sequelae beyond the acute phase.

This retrospective cohort study examined the association between ACEI/ARB use and kidney disease/mortality outcomes in 18,168 long COVID patients and 181,680 matched non-long COVID controls from October 2021 to October 2023. ACEI/ARB treatment did not increase CKD or AKI risk in either group, though long COVID itself was associated with increased CKD and all-cause mortality.

This study examines the association between HIV status and long COVID risk using data from two large electronic health record databases (PCORnet and N3C) with over 4.6 million SARS-CoV-2 infected patients. The analysis found a modest increased risk of long COVID in people with HIV when using a computed phenotype definition, but no association using ICD-10 codes.

This study uses NMR-based molecular phenotyping on a longitudinal cohort of 200+ SARS-CoV-2 positive individuals to identify biomarkers and predict long COVID outcomes based on lipoproteins, amino acids, and metabolic parameters. The work characterizes disease mechanisms and patient stratification but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This prospective cohort study uses UK Biobank data to evaluate the short- and long-term cardiovascular and mortality risks associated with COVID-19 infection, comparing infected patients to matched uninfected controls over 18 months. The study found significantly elevated CVD risk and all-cause mortality in both acute and post-acute phases, with persistent elevated risk in long COVID patients, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective population-based cohort study of 516 Danish patients with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease who developed COVID-19, comparing outcomes to the general COVID-19 population. Found higher hospitalization and ICU admission rates in IBD patients, with 43.7% experiencing persistent symptoms at 5-month follow-up, though no specific treatment intervention was tested.

Population-based prospective cohort study of 319 UC and 197 CD patients with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19, examining whether IBD disease activity correlates with COVID-19 severity and long-term sequelae. Found no association between IBD activity and adverse/severe COVID-19 or long-term outcomes, but this is a secondary analysis focused on IBD outcomes rather than long COVID treatment or intervention.

This study evaluates vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19 and long COVID using a test-negative design in healthcare workers, comparing vaccinated versus unvaccinated individuals. It is an epidemiological analysis of existing vaccination and laboratory data rather than a treatment trial, and does not study an intervention administered to long COVID patients.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed a 3-year population-based database of 31,764 COVID-19 patients matched against pre-pandemic controls to assess the incidence and risk of major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events following SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study found that COVID-19 patients had significantly elevated cardiovascular and cerebrovascular event risk throughout the 3-year follow-up period, with the highest incidence in the first year post-infection.

Danish population-based prospective cohort study investigating long-term health consequences of COVID-19 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (UC and CD). Found high prevalence of post-COVID-19 sequelae (42-46% with symptoms ≥12 weeks) including fatigue, anosmia, and ageusia, with associations to immunosuppressive therapy discontinuation and COVID-19 severity.

Retrospective cohort study examining Long COVID incidence in IBD patients treated with immunosuppressive medications in the VA Healthcare System. Found that COVID-19 hospitalization, ICU admission, and pre-existing COPD were associated with Long COVID risk, but IBD medications did not impact Long COVID development.

Population-based cohort study using Danish national registers comparing risk of PASC in 25,889 patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) versus 51,778 matched controls without IMIDs. Found significantly increased PASC risk in IMID patients (HR: 1.51), particularly in spondylarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and psoriasis.

This retrospective cohort study compares fecal calprotectin levels in IBD patients who had COVID-19 versus those who tested negative, measured 30-365 days post-infection. While it does examine post-COVID effects, it is not a long COVID study—it focuses on IBD biomarker changes in a disease-specific population rather than studying long COVID as the primary condition or testing a treatment for long COVID patients.

This prospective observational study examines troponin elevation in acute COVID-19 patients and its association with in-hospital and long-term mortality outcomes. While it does track patients post-discharge, it focuses on acute COVID-19 complications and biomarker prognostication rather than long COVID persistent symptoms or treatment interventions.

Retrospective comparison of acute coronary syndrome presentations in a cardiology department during (2020-2021) vs before (2018-2019) the COVID-19 pandemic. Study found higher frequency of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and spontaneous coronary artery dissection in post-COVID patients but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective analysis of 524 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients with 24-hour Holter monitoring to assess cardiac autonomic function and the role of dysautonomia in inappropriate sinus tachycardia. Found significant differences in heart rate variability indices and autonomic nervous system activity between IST and non-IST groups, suggesting dysautonomia contributes to IST in PCS.

An observational study of 40 acute COVID-19 patients with mild pneumonia evaluated myocardial performance index via echocardiography at acute infection and ~28 days after clinical recovery. The study found reversible left ventricular dysfunction at the acute stage that resolved after recovery, with no long-term follow-up or treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study of 104 recovered COVID-19 patients undergoing stress myocardial perfusion CMR imaging at median 131 days post-infection. Found no evidence of reduced global myocardial blood flow compared to risk-factor-matched controls, though regional perfusion defects were identified in some patients.

Longitudinal echocardiography study comparing cardiac function in 80 COVID-19 patients during acute hospitalization and at 3-month recovery. Right ventricle parameters improved significantly, but 25% of patients still had left ventricle systolic dysfunction at follow-up, suggesting subclinical cardiac involvement may persist during recovery from COVID-19.

This study examines cardiac involvement in 53 pediatric patients with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, comparing left ventricular function to healthy controls at least 3 months post-infection. While the paper mentions potential long-term outcomes, it focuses on acute/early post-infection cardiac changes in children during their acute illness phase rather than long COVID sequelae or treatment interventions.

Prospective echocardiographic study evaluating serial cardiac changes in 1000 COVID-19 patients from hospital discharge through 3-month follow-up. While the study does examine post-acute cardiac dysfunction following COVID-19, it focuses on acute infection outcomes and natural disease progression rather than long COVID patients or treatment interventions.

This study compared left heart echocardiographic parameters in COVID-19 pneumonia patients at 3 months and 1 year post-discharge to assess long-term cardiac changes. The findings show worsening of left ventricular strain and changes in cardiac volumes from 3 months to 1 year, despite improved ejection fraction.

This prospective cohort study followed 116 COVID-19 pneumonia patients with echocardiographic assessment at 3 months and 1 year post-discharge to evaluate long-term cardiovascular effects. Results showed dynamic changes in right ventricular parameters over time, including decreased RV diameter and area but increased RV sphericity indices, suggesting ongoing cardiac remodeling in the post-COVID period.

Prospective observational study of 43 ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients evaluated at follow-up for long-term cardiovascular impacts, finding subclinical left ventricular dysfunction detected by global longitudinal strain despite preserved ejection fraction. Study does not evaluate a treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the clinical trials pipeline.

Prospective observational study following 66 COVID-19 patients at 6 and 12 months to investigate persistent dyspnea and subclinical cardiac dysfunction via echocardiography. Found that 34.8% reported exertional dyspnea at one year, with reduced myocardial performance (GCW and GWI) associated with dyspnea symptoms.

This cross-sectional study examined cardiac structure and function in 220 long COVID patients using echocardiography and cardiac MRI at 3 and 12 months post-infection. Despite normal ejection fraction, patients showed decreased global longitudinal strain and new-onset hypertension, indicating subclinical left ventricular dysfunction.

This pilot study investigates whether baseline left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS) predicts changes in cardiopulmonary performance (VO2 peak) over 12 months in 48 post-COVID athletes. While baseline LV-GLS showed a significant association with VO2 peak after adjustment for confounders, this relationship was attenuated when controlling for sex, age, and BMI.

This cross-sectional study compared cardiac function between 58 COVID-19 survivors (6 months post-infection) and 20 healthy controls using echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers. Findings showed no significant differences in ventricular or atrial function between groups, suggesting uncomplicated COVID-19 survivors do not develop long-term cardiac sequelae.

Prospective multicenter cohort study following 200 patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19 for up to 30 months post-discharge, assessing cardiopulmonary impairments through imaging, function tests, and clinical evaluations. While most cardiopulmonary abnormalities resolved over time, 49% of patients still reported long COVID symptoms at 30 months despite functional/structural improvement.

Multicentre case-control study comparing cardiac structure and function via echocardiography in 679 post-COVID syndrome patients vs 475 recovered controls at 1.5 years post-infection. PCS patients showed small but statistically significant reductions in left ventricular strain and diastolic function, though values remained within normal clinical ranges.

This interrupted time series analysis examined the incidence and prevalence of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) before and after COVID-19 using TriNetX database data from 65 million patients across 64 healthcare organizations. The study found a significant increase in POTS incidence post-COVID (from 1.42 to 20.3 per million per year), but does not evaluate any treatment interventions.

Echocardiographic study of 92 COVID-19 hospitalized patients examined 3 months after discharge to assess left and right ventricular function. Found normal traditional cardiac parameters in all patients, with subtle ventricular dysfunction detected in approximately one-third by sensitive methods, mostly attributable to pre-existing conditions rather than COVID-19 infection.

This study used transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess long-term cardiac structure and function in 40 COVID-19 survivors (median 308 days post-infection) versus 12 matched controls. No significant differences were found in cardiac imaging parameters between survivors and controls, suggesting absence of long-lasting myocardial damage.

Prospective cohort study examining cardiac arrhythmias 3-4 months after COVID-19 hospitalization in 201 Norwegian patients using 24-hour ECG monitoring. Found arrhythmias in 27% of participants, primarily ventricular premature contractions and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, with associations to pre-existing cardiovascular disease and elevated cardiac troponin levels.

Prospective cohort study examining cardiac dysfunction in 50 patients with chronic heart failure following COVID-19 infection with lung involvement. Found worsening heart failure features including increased pulmonary artery pressure, ventricular dilation, valvular regurgitation, and left ventricular diastolic dysfunction one month post-infection.

This observational study evaluates cardiovascular sequelae in COVID-19 survivors with elevated biomarkers using advanced echocardiography. The study found minimal cardiac abnormalities in survivors without pre-existing cardiovascular disease and did not support routine screening programs post-discharge.

A prospective follow-up study assessing cardiopulmonary exercise capacity at 6 months post-hospitalization in 40 COVID-19 patients, comparing outcomes between those who received oxygen therapy versus those who did not. The study found no statistically significant differences in long-term cardiopulmonary limitations between groups, though 7.5% of patients showed asymptomatic cardiopulmonary limitations.

Prospective observational cohort study evaluating cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) findings in 389 patients recovered from COVID-19, with 77% experiencing ongoing cardiovascular symptoms (long COVID). CMR findings of myopericardial inflammation, elevated native T1/T2, and pericardial changes were associated with long COVID status and symptom severity, but no differences in cardiac function were observed.

This is an interim analysis of an ongoing prospective multicenter registry study examining long-term cardiopulmonary effects in 65 COVID-19 patients at 6 months post-discharge. The study documents persistent symptoms (fatigue 40%, dyspnea 36%) and imaging abnormalities (ground glass opacities 45%, cardiac MRI findings 11-19%) but reports no results yet, making it a protocol/interim analysis without complete trial data.

Cross-sectional observational study measuring endothelial dysfunction, coagulation markers, and inflammatory cytokines in 203 patients 3 months after COVID-19 infection compared to historical controls. Found sustained thrombo-inflammation (elevated ET-1, vWF:Ag, proinflammatory cytokines) but no macrovascular dysfunction.

Prospective observational cohort study of 105 COVID-19 patients (63.5% with postcovid syndrome) evaluated ~107 days post-infection using cardiac imaging (echocardiography, ECG monitoring) and blood markers. Study found cardiac impairment is rare despite high symptom burden, with only 4 patients requiring cardiac intervention and no evidence of ventricular dysfunction.

This study examines inflammatory markers and cardiac function in 63 patients (26 without CVD, 37 with CVD) at 3 months after COVID-19-associated pneumonia. It is a passive observational follow-up study without any intervention, measuring associations between inflammation biomarkers and ventricular systolic function rather than testing a treatment.

This study follows COVID-19 reconvalescents at 2-5 months post-discharge to assess coagulation abnormalities and endothelial function. The findings show suppressed clot formation but enhanced fibrinolysis compared to controls, with no thrombotic complications observed.

Prospective analysis comparing inflammatory, endothelial, and hemostasis parameters in COVID-19 pneumonia patients with and without type 2 diabetes, assessed at baseline and 3 months post-hospitalization. Found elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, homocysteine) and thrombophilia indicators at 3 months, particularly in diabetic patients, suggesting increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events during the post-COVID recovery period.

This retrospective cohort study examines the risk of incident diabetes in long COVID patients using Veterans Health Administration data, comparing 181,280 COVID-19 survivors with contemporary and historical controls. The study found a 40% increased risk of new-onset diabetes and 85% increased risk of antihyperglycemic medication use in COVID-19 patients at 12 months follow-up.

This study develops a prognostic score (HOPE-2) for predicting long-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in 2,575 COVID-19 patients using multivariable regression analysis on retrospective registry data. The score stratifies patients into low, intermediate, and high-risk groups based on clinical factors, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 70 COVID-19 survivors (41 with persistent dyspnea, 29 asymptomatic) evaluated at 3 months post-hospitalization using cardiopulmonary exercise testing, imaging, and functional assessments. Symptomatic patients showed reduced peak oxygen consumption and potential ventilatory inefficiency compared to asymptomatic patients, with >50% of survivors experiencing functional impairment regardless of hospitalization history.

This study evaluates atrio-ventricular mechanics using speckle-tracking echocardiography in 157 children 4-5 months after asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared to 107 healthy controls. Results show subtle subclinical left ventricular systolic dysfunction in 60% of post-COVID children despite normal ejection fraction, with worse impairment in those infected during the second pandemic wave.

Prospective longitudinal study investigating cardiac impairment in 534 long COVID patients using cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging at baseline and 12-month follow-up. Found that 19% had cardiac impairment at baseline, persisting in 58% of those with paired 12-month data, but this is a natural history/observational study with no intervention.

Prospective observational study of 488 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients without comorbidities followed for 3 months to identify predictors of long COVID. Found that severe acute COVID course, higher BMI, and arthralgia during acute phase were independent risk factors for developing long COVID symptoms.

Cross-sectional study comparing right ventricular function via echocardiography in 263 CKD patients, with 168 post-COVID-19 and 95 controls, measured at mean 2.2 months post-infection. Found statistically significant differences in TAPSE, Tei index, and RVFWLS between groups, suggesting cardiovascular sequelae in CKD populations post-infection.

A prospective observational study of 158 COVID-19 survivors assessed at 3 months post-infection using cardiac imaging (ECG, echocardiography) and pulmonary function tests. Found no significant differences in cardiac or left/right ventricular function parameters across disease severity groups, arguing against significant cardiac sequelae.

Multicenter retrospective registry comparing cardiovascular outcomes in 3,578 COVID-19 patients vs. 849 controls at 1-year follow-up across 17 Spanish and Italian centers. Found no increased CV death but higher rates of VTE, major bleeding, and cardiac arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients.

This study investigates cardiac and vascular abnormalities in 25 COVID-19 patients at 1 and 6 months post-hospitalization, measuring ventricular-arterial coupling (VAC), arterial stiffness, and left ventricular function. Results show significant impairment in post-COVID patients compared to controls at both timepoints, with correlations between VAC and inflammatory markers (IL-6, CRP).

This study evaluated 246 post-COVID patients using a stepwise cardiac diagnostic sequence to determine the prevalence of de novo cardiological alterations at least 30 days after discharge. While 25% had cardiac findings, only 6.5% were clinically relevant and the paper focuses on diagnostic prevalence rather than testing any intervention or treatment.

This case-control study compared coronary microvascular function between patients with prior COVID-19 infection and matched controls without prior infection using PET imaging. The study found higher rates of coronary microvascular dysfunction in post-COVID patients, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective cross-sectional study examining the prevalence of cardiac dysrhythmias in 87 long COVID patients using echocardiography and Holter monitoring. Found that 90.8% had normal sinus rhythm, but 80.5% had atrial premature beats and 57.5% had ventricular premature beats, with 8% presenting sustained atrial dysrhythmias.

A prospective cohort study of 140 COVID-19 survivors at one-year follow-up examining cardiac dysfunction in long COVID patients using myocardial work parameters (GWI and GCW) on echocardiography. The study found that reduced myocardial work indices were independently associated with long COVID diagnosis, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective multicenter registry study following 150 COVID-19 hospitalized patients (~6 months post-discharge) with comprehensive cardiopulmonary assessments including echocardiography, cardiac MRI, CT imaging, and lung function tests. Found 75% met long COVID criteria with persistent symptoms, identified cardiac (reduced GLS, pericardial effusion, myocarditis) and pulmonary abnormalities (ground glass opacities, fibrosis), and determined independent predictors of long COVID including disease severity markers and elevated biomarkers.

Prospective follow-up study of 34 COVID-19 hospitalized patients examining heart rate variability (HRV) at 1 and 6 months post-discharge compared to age/sex-matched controls. Found reduced SDNN (autonomic dysfunction marker) in COVID-19 group with partial recovery at 6 months, and lower SDNN values in patients with long COVID symptoms, suggesting a link between autonomic dysfunction and long COVID.

Prospective observational study comparing acute coronary syndrome presentation and outcomes in patients with prior COVID-19 infection versus uninfected and vaccinated patients. Finds that prior COVID-19 infection is associated with higher rates of coronary ectasia, thrombosis, and thrombectomy requirement, but does not study treatment of long COVID.

This single-centre retrospective cohort study examined 169 COVID-19 patients to determine whether late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI predicts long-term outcomes including mortality and cardiovascular events. The study found no significant association between the presence of myocardial scarring and adverse outcomes over 2-3 years of follow-up, suggesting larger multicentre studies are needed.

Prospective observational study comparing viral IgG/IgM titers (EBV, CMV, HSV, VZV, Parvo-B19) in 105 long COVID patients versus 105 healthy controls. Found significantly elevated EBV IgG and Parvo-B19 IgM in long COVID patients, suggesting viral reactivation linked to symptom domains (EBV with respiratory, Parvo-B19 with cardiovascular), but no intervention or treatment was administered.

A case-control study comparing 1,195 female long-COVID patients with 718 controls to identify age-independent predictors of long-COVID occurrence. Found that HDL cholesterol and 24-hour pulse pressure are independent predictors in younger women, while cardiovascular abnormalities and severe acute COVID-19 course are associated with long-COVID in all females.

A prospective cohort study of 252 post-COVID-19 patients followed for up to 428 days examining associations between socioeconomic deprivation and illness trajectory using imaging, biomarkers, and patient-reported outcomes. Greater deprivation was associated with worse health status, more lung/cardiac/renal imaging abnormalities, higher anxiety/depression, and more secondary care referrals.

Population-based Swedish cohort study examining long-term venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk after COVID-19 in hospitalized and non-hospitalized patients. Hospitalized COVID-19 patients retained elevated PE and DVT risk for >180 days post-infection, while non-hospitalized individuals had similar risk to unexposed controls.

Prospective registry study following 200 severe COVID-19 patients at 6 and 18 months post-discharge to assess cardiopulmonary impairment through clinical examination, imaging, and functional testing. Study is excluded because it does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment—it is a passive observational follow-up study documenting natural recovery patterns without assigning patients to treatment groups.

This observational study compares long COVID symptom prevalence and cardiovascular complications between healthy women and men without comorbidities at 12 weeks and one year post-COVID. It finds women more frequently reported long COVID symptoms (63% vs 59%) and specific symptoms like fatigue and hair loss, while men showed more ECG abnormalities.

Longitudinal observational study assessing the prevalence of cardiovascular symptoms in 643 patients at 3 and 12 months following COVID-19 infection. Found that 65.7% had at least one post-COVID symptom at 12 months, with cardiovascular symptoms present in 60.1% at 3 months and 33.9% at 12 months; female sex and severe infection were predictive of persistent symptoms.

This retro-prospective study evaluated 793 long COVID patients to assess the incidence of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and other autonomic dysfunction symptoms, finding a 1.5% incidence of autonomic dysfunction and 0.1% incidence of POTS. The study identified elevated C-reactive protein as an associated factor and fatigue and orthostatic intolerance as the most common symptoms.

A prospective cohort study following 1,474 COVID-19 hospitalized patients across 16 countries at 3 months post-discharge to assess persistent long COVID symptoms, cardiovascular complications, and mortality. The study found 38% reported long COVID symptoms (primarily fatigue, cognitive impairment, and anxiety) and a 3% mortality rate, mostly from cardiac arrest and other severe complications.

Prospective cohort study following 2,504 COVID-19 hospitalized patients from 16 countries at 1, 3, 6, and 9-12 months post-discharge to assess long-term sequelae and burden of disease. Found persistent symptoms in 63% at 1 month declining to 28% at 9-12 months, with 12% mortality by one year primarily due to cardiovascular events, highlighting significant post-COVID complications requiring preventive strategies.

This prospective registry study followed 200 patients hospitalized for severe COVID-19 at 6, 18, and 30 months post-discharge to assess cardiopulmonary long-term effects and symptom burden. While long COVID prevalence decreased over time (73% at 6 months to 49% at 30 months), structural and functional abnormalities persisted, though at lower rates than reported symptoms.

This 2-year retrospective cohort study of 17 million individuals in England examines the association between COVID-19/influenza vaccinations, cardiovascular drugs, and hospitalisation/mortality outcomes in both COVID-19 and Long COVID populations. The study finds that COVID-19 vaccination (≥2 doses), influenza vaccination, and cardiovascular preventive therapies (particularly anticoagulants) significantly reduce mortality and hospitalisation risk, with greatest benefits in those with prior cardiovascular disease.

This study evaluates pericoronary adipose tissue attenuation as a marker of vascular inflammation in post-COVID patients using ultra-high-resolution CT imaging. The abstract indicates this is a study protocol describing enrollment and methods, with results presented only as baseline data and preliminary findings.

Prospective observational follow-up study comparing long COVID symptoms and cardiovascular outcomes between vaccinated and unvaccinated COVID-19 hospitalized patients across 16 countries at 1, 3, 6, and 9-12 months post-discharge. Study found unvaccinated patients had higher rates of long COVID symptoms (fatigue, palpitations, anxiety), MACE, and mortality, but does not test a specific intervention—it passively compares outcomes by pre-existing vaccination status.

This cross-sectional study examines myocardial injury in young adults (ages 18-44) 2-6 months after COVID-19 recovery using cardiac MRI and inflammatory biomarkers, comparing them to two control groups. One-third of COVID-19 patients with cardiovascular risk factors showed myocardial damage (interstitial edema and/or fibrosis), with correlations found between biomarkers and imaging findings.

This prospective multicentric cohort study investigates accelerated vascular ageing in COVID-19 survivors across 2,390 participants in 16 countries, measuring carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity as a biomarker of large artery stiffness. The study finds that COVID-19 survivors, particularly women with persistent symptoms, show significantly higher PWV indicating early vascular ageing compared to controls, though PWV stabilizes or improves at 12-month follow-up.

A prospective observational study of 101 long COVID patients with persistent dyspnea that assessed the incidence of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD) and identified associated risk factors. Found 8% CTEPD rate with history of DVT/PE as the strongest independent predictor, and elevated NT-proBNP and reduced exercise capacity associated with CTEPD diagnosis.

Retrospective cohort study of 863 ICU COVID-19 survivors followed for median 4.1 years to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Study found age, dementia, and COPD were significant mortality predictors, but myocardial injury and classical cardiovascular risk factors were not.

Observational study comparing coronary ectasia prevalence in acute coronary syndrome patients before (2017-2019) and after (2020-2023) COVID-19 pandemic, finding increased ectasia rates post-pandemic (62% vs 12%). Study documents a post-COVID cardiovascular complication but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective longitudinal study examining long-term cardiovascular consequences of COVID-19 using cardiac MRI and exercise testing in 138 individuals 3+ years post-infection. The study identifies native T1 as an independent predictor of reduced aerobic capacity (VO2max) in post-COVID patients, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study examines how pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) affects symptoms, quality of life, and functional outcomes in 668 long COVID (PASC) patients in Australia. The study finds that while prior CVD does not worsen PASC symptoms or functional capacity, it is associated with elevated blood pressure and cardiac troponin levels, and significantly impairs quality of life in long COVID patients.

This cross-sectional study characterizes and compares clinical and hemodynamic profiles among 270 long COVID patients diagnosed with POTS, IST, or dual pathology using tilt testing and ECG monitoring. The findings show distinct phenotypes with different clinical presentations, particularly highlighting that IST patients have higher hypertension and resting blood pressure, while POTS and dual pathology patients experience more presyncope/syncope and cognitive impairment.

This observational cohort study assessed long-term cardiac arrhythmias in 63 patients 6 months after severe COVID-19 infection using 24-h Holter monitoring. The study identified new diagnoses of atrial fibrillation in 4.8% of patients, asymptomatic bradycardia in 18%, and moderate-to-severe sleep apnea in 53%, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective multicentre cohort study of 155 post-COVID-19 patients undergoing serial assessments with plasma proteomics and multisystem imaging to identify dysregulation of catecholamine pathways. The study identified a distinct proteomic cluster characterized by heightened catecholamine activity and oxidative stress, associated with heightened illness perception and reduced cardiorespiratory function despite absence of objective imaging abnormalities.

This study evaluated cardiac involvement in patients recovered from COVID-19 using echocardiography, comparing 41 COVID-19 patients (15 hospitalized, 26 home-treated) with 13 healthy volunteers at median 5.9 months post-infection. Hospitalized patients showed significant right ventricular dysfunction compared to non-hospitalized patients and controls, while left ventricular function remained similar across groups.

This prospective follow-up study assessed functional capacity using cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) in 198 COVID-19 survivors at 3 months post-discharge. The study found that 42% of patients had dyspnea, and among those tested, 61% showed reduced peak VO2, but this is a descriptive observational assessment study with no treatment intervention evaluated.

A prospective/retrospective cohort study of 160 COVID-19 patients followed for a median of 5 months post-infection, examining cardiac structural and functional changes using echocardiography and imaging. The study found that COVID-19 differentially impacts right and left ventricular function, with pneumonia severity affecting the right ventricle and inflammatory status affecting the left ventricle.

Prospective/retrospective cohort study comparing long COVID symptom patterns between 89 female and 134 male patients at 5-month follow-up. Females reported significantly higher rates of dyspnoea, fatigue, chest pain, and palpitations compared to males, suggesting sex as an important determinant of persistent symptoms.

Prospective observational study using cardiovascular magnetic resonance to characterize myocardial injury in COVID-19 patients with elevated troponins during hospitalization, followed up ~169 days post-diagnosis. Found evidence of myocarditis-like injury in 28.6% of patients but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective follow-up study of 230 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors assessing cardiovascular sequelae at 2 months and 1 year post-discharge. Found 16% with persistent or delayed cardiovascular involvement and 45% with persistent symptoms at long-term follow-up, but this is an observational study without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study of 170 COVID-19 ICU patients identifying acute pericarditis in 32.2% (60 patients), with 21 pericarditis patients receiving 7 weeks of cardiac rehabilitation. Cardiac rehabilitation showed significant improvement in 6-minute walk test distance (352m to 498m, 41% increase, p<0.03) in long-COVID patients.

Cross-sectional assessment of myocardial function in 64 recovered SARS-CoV-2 patients with persistent symptoms using echocardiography and strain analysis. Found evidence of diastolic dysfunction and subtle myocardial changes in all patients, with 4 patients showing left ventricular dysfunction, but this is a diagnostic study without treatment intervention.

Prospective follow-up study of 45 COVID-19 patients with severe pneumonia requiring high-flow oxygen, assessed 382 days post-discharge for long-term respiratory and quality-of-life outcomes. Found persistent radiological alterations in 61%, reduced lung function in 38%, and widespread quality-of-life impairment (62% fatigue, 62% dyspnea), but no treatment intervention was tested.
