The asthma and allergic disease PRS were significantly associated with severe COVID-19 and post-acute symptomatology, suggesting genetic factors influence COVID-19 severity and long COVID risk.

This study compares circulating monocyte abundance and immune profiles in long COVID patients with and without persistent pulmonary fibrosis, using single-cell RNA-sequencing and immunostaining on blood samples collected at one timepoint and six-month follow-up. The findings identify reduced monocytes as a potential biomarker distinguishing patients whose post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis resolves versus persists, but the study does not test any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing EHR data from the RECOVER program to assess whether pre-COVID-19 vaccination is associated with reduced long COVID risk. Found that vaccination was protective against long COVID development in breakthrough infections.

This study characterizes clinical subphenotypes of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) using a large retrospective cohort from 8 pediatric centers, identifying three severity classes (severe, moderate, mild) based on organ involvement and laboratory markers. While MIS-C is a post-acute sequela of COVID-19, the paper focuses on acute post-infection inflammatory syndrome in children rather than long COVID (chronic persistent symptoms weeks-months post-infection in adults), and it is descriptive/observational without testing any specific treatment intervention.

A mobile health study using commercial fitness wearables and self-reported questionnaires to identify long COVID cases based on persistent physiological changes and symptoms lasting 12+ weeks. Found that wearable-detected changes in heart rate, sleep, and activity can differentiate long COVID patients, and identified prior activity levels and depression as risk factors.

Matched cohort study examining the incidence of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) following SARS-CoV-2 infection using UK primary care data. Found a 22% increased risk of IMIDs post-COVID, particularly T1DM, IBD, and psoriasis, but does not study treatments or interventions for long COVID.

Retrospective cohort study examining whether nirmatrelvir treatment during acute COVID-19 reduces the risk of developing post-acute sequelae (long COVID). Treatment with nirmatrelvir was associated with significantly reduced risk of PASC overall and 10 of 12 specific post-acute sequelae outcomes including cardiovascular complications, fatigue, neurocognitive impairment, and reduced post-acute mortality.

This EHR-based cohort study from the RECOVER program identifies contextual and spatial risk factors for post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection using electronic health data from New York City and Florida. The analysis reveals associations between environmental factors (air toxicants, pollutants, neighborhood deprivation, built environment) and increased risk of various PASC symptoms across multiple organ systems, with risk factor profiles varying by geographic region.

This study analyzed 4,040 participants from the UK COVID Symptom Study App to identify risk factors and symptom clusters associated with long COVID. It found that female sex, pre-existing poor health, and worse initial illness predicted long COVID with 76% accuracy, but did not identify consistent symptom subtypes.

This prospective cohort study examines how different symptom selection criteria affect long COVID prevalence estimates in a population of COVID-19 survivors followed longitudinally. The authors demonstrate that prevalence estimates vary widely (39.6% to 80.6% at 12 months) depending on which symptoms are included in the case definition, highlighting the need for harmonized diagnostic criteria.

A retrospective case series examining transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) as a treatment for psychiatric and physical symptoms in long COVID and post-vaccination patients. Results showed significant improvements in depression, anxiety, and other symptoms after 10 TMS treatments, though improvement was reduced in patients with severe fatigue.

This prospective cohort study tracked 166 unvaccinated, previously uninfected adults who contracted SARS-CoV-2 during Omicron or Delta waves, monitoring acute and post-acute symptoms over 48 weeks. The study found that Omicron infections resulted in significantly lower rates of post-acute symptoms (79% reduction) compared to Delta, but this is an observational natural history study without any therapeutic intervention.

EHR-based retrospective cohort study characterizing SARS-CoV-2 reinfection patterns and long COVID development using N3C RECOVER data. Analyzes incidence, timing, and biomarkers associated with reinfection but does not test any intervention or treatment.

A population-based internet survey tracking post-COVID-19 condition remission rates across 16 waves from August 2020 to November 2022. The study identifies sociodemographic and clinical correlates of spontaneous symptom remission (31% remission rate) but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This observational cohort study evaluated whether nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection reduces long COVID symptom development in vaccinated, non-hospitalized individuals from an online cohort. Treatment with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was not associated with lower prevalence or severity of long COVID symptoms.

Analysis of UK ONS Coronavirus Infection Survey data examining how long-COVID prevalence and severity vary across industries and occupations. Finds that public-facing sectors (teaching, healthcare, social care) have highest odds ratios for long-COVID, with prevalence ranging 7.7-11.6% by industry.

A hybrid register and questionnaire study examining self-reported sick leave following SARS-CoV-2 infection in 37,482 cases and 51,336 controls from Denmark. The study identifies risk factors (female sex, age ≥50, pre-existing conditions like fibromyalgia) associated with substantial sick leave (>1 month) 1-9 months post-infection, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of professional soccer players examining the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and muscle injury risk during the 2019-2021 seasons. While the study documents increased muscle injuries in infected players, it is not about long COVID—it focuses on acute post-infection complications in athletes rather than persistent long COVID symptoms, and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study surveyed 1,731 Australian children and adolescents 12 weeks after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (Delta variant) to assess prevalence and burden of long COVID symptoms and functional impairment. Among clinically reviewed responders, 37.9% (64/169) were diagnosed with post-COVID condition, with 21 meeting the UK consensus definition for long COVID, demonstrating a spectrum of severity warranting population-level attention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir treatment vs. no treatment in vaccinated patients with COVID-19 to assess prevention of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC). Treatment was associated with reduced PASC symptom development at 30-180 days and 90-180 days post-infection using broad and narrow clinical definitions.

Prospective population-based study measuring serum brain injury biomarkers (sNfL and sGFAP) in 146 individuals before, during, and after mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection, with follow-up at 5 and 10 months to assess associations with neurological symptoms and Long-COVID status. Found that neurological symptoms were not associated with brain injury markers, though sGFAP showed a significant increase in Long-COVID patients without correlation to symptoms.

Randomized trial evaluating convalescent plasma (CCP) versus control plasma in 883 COVID-19 patients, with biomarker and symptom follow-up through day 90. Early CCP treatment showed a trend toward reduced post-COVID conditions, with elevated baseline IL-6 associated with PCC development; female sex and older age were significant risk factors.

Retrospective analysis of U.S. Medicare claims data characterizing long COVID incidence, demographics, and comorbidities among beneficiaries. Found 0.6% of beneficiaries had post-COVID diagnoses with higher rates in nursing home residents, and identified certain diagnoses (myopathies, interstitial pulmonary diseases) disproportionately associated with long COVID.

This retrospective cohort study uses UK primary care data to estimate the incremental costs of GP and allied health consultations associated with long COVID. The study found that non-hospitalised adults with long COVID incur significantly higher primary care consultation costs (£2.44-£5.72 per patient per year) compared to matched controls without COVID history.

This paper compares self-reported long COVID cases in UK longitudinal population studies with coded diagnoses in electronic health records over 10-22 months follow-up. It is a secondary analysis of existing linked data rather than a prospective or intervention study, and does not test or evaluate any treatment.

This retrospective cohort study of 2 million Medicare patients compares the incidence and characteristics of long COVID versus 'long Flu' using WHO diagnostic criteria applied to administrative claims data from 2018-2021. The study found long COVID affected 16.6-29.2% of COVID-19 patients with higher rates of dyspnea, fatigue, and neurocognitive symptoms compared to long Flu, and associated with greater healthcare utilization.

This large-scale population-based cohort study from UK Biobank examines the long-term risk of digestive diseases in COVID-19 survivors compared to control groups. The study found significantly elevated risks of multiple gastrointestinal conditions including GERD, functional GI disorders, and liver disease, with risks increasing with acute COVID-19 severity.

This community-based cohort study from the UK COVID-19 Infection Survey examined the risk of new-onset long COVID following reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 compared to first infection. The study found that the risk of long COVID after second infection was significantly lower than after first infection in adults (aOR 0.72), though some risk remained (~1 in 40 adults reporting long COVID after reinfection).

A cross-sectional survey of 11,697 COVID-19 patients in Western Australia assessed the prevalence of long COVID symptoms 90 days post-infection during the Omicron wave. The study found 18.2% prevalence of long COVID with associated healthcare utilization and work/study impacts, but did not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study followed long COVID patients and matched controls over 24 months to characterize immune responses and health-related quality of life changes. The study is a secondary/observational analysis of existing cohorts rather than testing a specific intervention or treatment.

This case-crossover retrospective cohort study of 367,148 VA patients empirically derives a long COVID case definition by identifying 323 ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes significantly increased post-infection. The study characterizes long COVID subtypes and risk factors (severe COVID, comorbidities) but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes the effect of COVID-19 vaccination status on the risk of developing Long COVID symptoms or receiving a Long COVID diagnosis using data from 2021-2022. While the paper is about Long COVID, it does not study a treatment or intervention given to long COVID patients—it is an observational analysis comparing vaccination outcomes in people who developed long COVID, making it ineligible for the trials pipeline focused on interventions tested in long COVID populations.

Longitudinal cohort study comparing cognitive performance in 276 COVID-19 patients and 217 controls using pre- and post-pandemic data (2015 onwards). Found significant cognitive decline in processing speed and visual working memory in COVID-19 patients, particularly those with PASC, equivalent to 10.6 years of normal aging.

Population-based cross-sectional study comparing prevalence of long COVID-associated symptoms in 7,683 German adults with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found 12 of 19 symptoms significantly more prevalent in infected participants (fatigue 27.5% vs 18.3%, concentration problems, dyspnea, smell/taste disorder), with small attributable excess prevalence of 3.8% for symptoms impacting work ability.

Population-based observational study comparing long-term symptom profiles in 10,203 UK adults following SARS-CoV-2 infection, non-COVID-19 acute respiratory infections, or no infection. Identifies symptom clusters and demonstrates higher prevalence of taste/smell problems and hair loss in long COVID versus other ARIs, but does not test any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study measured SARS-CoV-2 plasma antigens in 171 post-acute COVID-19 patients and 250 pre-pandemic controls at multiple timepoints (3-14 months post-infection) using single-molecule array detection. The study found significantly elevated antigen prevalence in infected individuals compared to uninfected controls, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study analyzes routine primary care electronic health records from the OpenSafely platform to assess the uptake and consistency of Post-COVID syndrome diagnosis and referral codes following NICE guidelines. The analysis of 45 million patients found low overall coding rates (0.15% diagnosed, 0.15% referred) with substantial gaps between diagnosis and referral coding, suggesting inconsistent implementation of diagnostic pathways.

This retrospective cohort study examined vaccine effectiveness against long COVID in children aged 5-17 using EHR data from 17 US health systems. While it shows vaccination provides moderate protection against long COVID (35-42% effectiveness at 12 months, waning over time), it is an observational study without any treatment intervention—it only compares vaccination status between groups without testing or evaluating any therapeutic intervention for long COVID patients.

Comparative cross-sectional study examining pulmonary features of post-acute COVID-19 sequelae (PASC) in vaccinated vs unvaccinated patients presenting with dyspnea after mild COVID-19. Found vaccination associated with reduced imaging abnormalities but no difference in lung function, bronchiolitis, or autoantibodies.

A prospective cohort study (RECoVERED) that followed 101 long COVID patients and reference controls for 6 months, collecting serum samples and symptom data to characterize longitudinal immune trajectories. The study identified elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, TNF-α, IP-10) associated with PASC and reduced pulmonary function, with early IL-1β as a potential predictor of long COVID development.

OpenPROMPT is a UK cohort study measuring the impact of long COVID on health-related quality-of-life using Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) collected via smartphone app. The study found that 24.7% of 6,070 participants self-reported long COVID and experienced substantial losses in quality-of-life, with long COVID associated with an 0.37 QALM loss.

This retrospective cohort study examined performance validity test (PVT) patterns in 177 long COVID patients with cognitive complaints, comparing rates of invalid responding to an MS sample. The study found that 7% of the long COVID sample had invalid VSVT scores, significantly lower than MS patients, suggesting most long COVID patients produce credible neuropsychological test results.

This retrospective cohort study using TriNetX data compared the risk of erectile dysfunction (ED) between men diagnosed with long COVID versus acute COVID-19 only. The study found that long COVID was associated with a higher risk of ED diagnosis or PDE5i prescription (3.63% vs 2.61%, RR 1.39) compared to acute COVID alone, with no significant increased risk among those requiring vasopressors or hospitalization.

Multicentre observational study measuring prevalence of orthostatic intolerance (OI), postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (PoTS), and orthostatic hypotension (OH) in 277 long COVID patients using standardized NASA Lean Test. Found 52% developed OI symptoms during testing and 15% had abnormal test results, with 7% meeting PoTS criteria and 8% meeting OH criteria.

Longitudinal survey examining the association between psychological distress and prolonged PASC symptoms over 1-year follow-up in 1,674 Japanese individuals with PASC. Found that psychological distress at baseline was associated with higher odds of persistent symptoms at 1-year follow-up, particularly general and respiratory symptoms.

Observational study of 506,903 patients with depression analyzing whether SSRI use during acute COVID-19 infection reduces the risk of developing long COVID over 12 months. Found that SSRI users had significantly lower long COVID risk (adjusted RR 0.90), supporting a serotonin-mediated mechanism in long COVID pathogenesis.

Descriptive analysis of 149 calls to a Long-COVID consultation service (RACE line) in British Columbia over 11 months, documenting types of symptoms physicians inquired about. Respiratory symptoms (shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, fevers) were most commonly reported, with results intended to inform resource allocation rather than evaluate any intervention.

Prospective multicentre cohort study of 264 critically ill COVID-19 survivors followed at 3 and 12 months post-ICU discharge, assessing functional outcome and health-related quality of life using Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended and SF-36v2. Functional outcome improved significantly from 35% to 64% with good outcomes, and physical HRQoL improved between timepoints, with shorter mechanical ventilation duration associated with better outcomes.

This prospective multinational cohort study examines socio-demographic predictors of quality of life in long COVID patients across Norway, the UK, and Russia. It identifies educational attainment, employment status, and sex as independent predictors of QoL that are not fully explained by clinical comorbidities, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective observational cohort study of 403 long-COVID patients from a University of Iowa clinic, with 129 respondents providing symptom data over time. Finds that 51.2% of patients reported subjective improvement over the course of their illness, with pulmonary symptoms more persistent than neuromuscular symptoms, but notes significant recall bias as a limitation.

This paper describes implementation and evaluation of an app-based remote monitoring system for acute and post-acute COVID-19 patients in primary care, with patients measuring vital signs and symptoms daily. While feasibility is demonstrated through patient satisfaction surveys, the study does not test or evaluate a specific treatment intervention for long COVID.

Network cohort study using electronic health records from multiple countries to assess the risk of autoimmune and inflammatory post-acute COVID-19 conditions compared to test-negative controls. Observational study comparing disease incidence rates rather than testing a treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 172,136 children aged 5-20 years examining the association between pre-infection BMI and post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) risk. Found that overweight, obesity, and severe obesity were associated with significantly increased PASC risk in a dose-dependent manner (4.7%, 25.4%, and 42.1% higher risk, respectively).

This cross-sectional study compared post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) between COVID-19 patients with and without post-COVID conditions using the Impact of Event Scale-Revised (IES-R). Results showed elevated PTSS in patients with PASC compared to those without, and trait resilience was associated with lower PTSS; however, this is an observational study that does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study of over 1.2 million children from the RECOVER consortium examined post-acute cardiovascular outcomes after SARS-CoV-2 infection with at least 6 months follow-up. The study found that children and adolescents with and without congenital heart defects had significantly elevated risks for multiple cardiovascular conditions including arrhythmias, myocarditis, heart failure, and thrombotic disorders, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study compared EEG signatures among COVID-19 survivors, close contacts, and normative controls using quantitative and source-density analysis. The paper characterizes neurobiological differences in long COVID patients but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study comparing SARS-CoV-2 antibody trajectories in people with post-COVID condition versus acute-only infections using data from the Virus Watch community cohort. Found elevated and persistent anti-nucleocapsid antibodies in post-COVID patients but no differences in vaccination-related antibody responses between groups.

This multinational prospective cohort study followed 651 post-acute COVID-19 patients to assess mortality risk and evaluate urinary peptide markers as prognostic tools. The study identified 201 peptides associated with mortality and developed a predictive classifier (DP201) that, combined with age and BMI, significantly predicted death in post-COVID-19 survivors.

summary: Prospective registry of 232 long COVID patients receiving hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) with outcome measures at baseline, post-treatment, and 3-month follow-up. Results showed 65% of patients had clinically relevant improvements in mental/physical quality of life (SF-36), with cognitive symptoms showing the most improvement, though 15% experienced deterioration.

Retrospective cohort study examining the relationship between SARS-CoV-2 viral clearance kinetics during acute infection and subsequent long COVID development in 7,361 community-dwelling participants. Found that slower viral clearance rates and longer time to viral clearance were associated with increased risk and severity of long COVID symptoms.

This prospective cohort study evaluates the clinical and cost-effectiveness of diverse post-hospitalization healthcare pathways for COVID-19 patients using data from 1,013 participants at 12-month follow-up from the PHOSP-COVID cohort. Comprehensive services providing assessment, rehabilitation, and mental health support were more clinically effective and cost-effective (£1,700 per QALY) compared to minimal or no services, supporting proactive, stratified follow-up care for hospitalized COVID-19 patients with long COVID.

Retrospective cohort study examining post-acute and chronic kidney outcomes in children and adolescents after COVID-19 infection using EHR data from 19 US hospitals (n=1,864,637). Found increased risk of CKD progression and adverse kidney outcomes in the post-acute phase (28-365 days), particularly in those with pre-existing CKD or acute kidney injury.

A follow-up survey of 526 long COVID patients assessing the prevalence and severity of autonomic dysfunction using the COMPASS-31 scale and its impact on function and quality of life. The study found that 71.9% of patients had moderate to severe autonomic dysfunction with a median symptom duration of 36 months, and 40.5% were newly diagnosed with POTS after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

This prospective cohort study analyzes viral reactivation of latent viruses in 1,154 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 12 months as part of the IMPACC study. Multi-omic analysis reveals that persistent Anelloviridae reactivation during convalescence is associated with PASC symptoms, particularly physical dysfunction and fatigue, and identifies immune and metabolomic biomarkers of viral reactivation.

This study retrospectively mapped existing data from two COVID-19 recovery cohorts onto ME/CFS diagnostic criteria to determine the prevalence of ME/CFS symptom overlap in long COVID patients. No intervention was tested; it is a secondary analysis of cohort data examining diagnostic overlap between conditions.

Retrospective cohort study assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms in 162 long COVID patients at a South Texas clinic using validated screening tools (PCL-5, PHQ-9, GAD-7, SWL). Found high burden of neuropsychiatric symptoms (cognitive impairment 79%, headache 74%, insomnia 58%) significantly correlated with symptom severity, but this is a descriptive/observational study without a treatment intervention.

Retrospective analysis of 948 long COVID and ME/CFS patients using the Visible app to examine associations between symptom severity, menstrual cycle phase, and hormonal contraception use. Findings show worsened symptoms during menstruation and significant symptom reduction in users of combined hormonal contraception compared to non-users.

Prospective community cohort study examining post-COVID condition (PCC) risk across deprivation levels, migration status, and ethnic minority groups in England using Virus Watch data. Finds increased PCC probability in deprived populations and certain migrant/ethnic minority subgroups, driven by infection risk and post-infection determinants rather than treatment intervention.

This household cohort study followed 143 non-hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals during the D614G variant period, measuring daily symptoms, viral loads, and antibody responses. While the paper identifies that higher day 28 antibody levels predict later PASC symptoms, it does not test or evaluate any intervention—it is a prospective observational study of natural disease progression and immune response.

Longitudinal study of 799 outpatients examining gut microbiome signatures during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection as predictors of long COVID development. Uses machine learning to show microbiome composition predicts LC risk better than clinical variables alone, identifying four symptom clusters linked to microbiome alterations.

This retrospective cohort study examines six-month functional outcomes, hospitalization rates, and mortality in 23,632 long COVID cases in US skilled nursing facilities, primarily affecting adults over 65 years old. The study evaluates functional status (ADLs) across seven medications used to treat COVID-19 in this population.

This cross-sectional cohort study of 71 long COVID patients investigates how acute COVID-19 severity and biomarkers predict long COVID symptom domains. The study identifies that affective, fatigue, respiratory, and neurological symptoms form an intercorrelated phenotype predicted by acute-phase dyspnea, RT-PCR values, and reduced antioxidant/nitric oxide levels.

Retrospective cohort study comparing frailty characteristics in 106 long COVID patients versus 97 geriatric patients with multimorbidity at a Veterans Affairs Medical Center. Finds that long COVID patients develop a distinct 'post-viral frailty' phenotype characterized by higher rates of exhaustion and low activity compared to age-related frailty, which presents more with weakness and slowness.

Real-world prospective cohort study (n=106, 220 person-years follow-up) comparing anticoagulant (Asaflow + Clopidogrel) vs. antiviral (Paxlovid) treatment in long COVID patients, measuring clinical recovery and neurodamage markers. Antiviral treatment (Paxlovid) was the strongest predictor of clinical recovery and showed rapid decline in CNS damage markers (GFAP/NFL), supporting viral persistence as a therapeutic target.

Target trial emulation study evaluating nirmatrelvir-ritonavir effectiveness in 34,870 US adolescents with SARS-CoV-2 infection, comparing 2,923 treated within 5 days to 31,947 untreated controls. Treatment reduced acute illness severity and healthcare utilization but showed no association with reduced long COVID diagnosis risk.

Cross-sectional study examining oral health manifestations of long COVID across racial/ethnic groups, finding higher rates of periodontal disease and persistent viral markers in COVID-19 positive subjects. Study characterizes the oral cavity as a long-term SARS-CoV-2 reservoir but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This study analyzed hundreds of immunological and virological biomarkers in 270 mild and 188 severe COVID-19 patients 6-9 months post-infection to identify markers associated with post-acute sequelae (PASC). Patients with PASC showed altered CD4+ and CD8+ memory T-cell subsets with elevated TEMRA phenotype and SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells, achieving >80% classification accuracy in a random forest model.

This 3.5-year prospective follow-up study tracked 207 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors to document the persistence and natural recovery of short-term memory loss, one of the common long COVID symptoms. The study found memory loss in 11.5% of patients, with variable recovery patterns (25% fully recovered, 37.5% improved, 29% showed minimal progress) but no specific intervention was administered or evaluated.

Retrospective cohort study using N3C data examining how rare diseases affect COVID-19 severity, reinfection, and long COVID outcomes, and evaluating the effectiveness of vaccination and antiviral treatments. Finds that vaccination and antiviral combination therapy reduces acute severity and reinfection risk, but impact on long COVID prevention is limited, particularly in rare disease patients.

Retrospective cohort study comparing post-acute sequelae (PAS) risk between COVID-19 and influenza patients in a large healthcare system (74,738 COVID-19 and 18,790 influenza cases). Findings show similar PAS frequency between non-severe cases but higher severe PAS requiring hospitalization in COVID-19 patients.

Retrospective cohort study using All of Us Research Program data to examine associations between pre-infection symptoms, functional status, and long COVID risk in 65,464 U.S. adults. Found that greater pre-illness symptom burden and lower self-rated mental health increased odds of developing long COVID, but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study from the RECOVER consortium analyzed 465,717 children under 21 to compare PASC risk after reinfection versus initial SARS-CoV-2 infection during the Omicron period. Reinfection was associated with significantly increased risk of overall PASC diagnosis and 24 specific conditions across multiple organ systems, but the study does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study of 627 COVID-19 patients comparing those with and without long COVID using propensity score matching to identify risk factors. Identified key risk factors including age, BMI, ethnicity, smoking status, comorbidities, and biomarkers (fibrinogen, serum sodium), with fatigue and dyspnea as most prevalent symptoms.

A prospective cohort study of 2,046 COVID-19 patients in Nepal followed up to 12 months post-infection to characterize long COVID prevalence and risk factors across SARS-CoV-2 variants (Delta vs Omicron). The study found higher long COVID prevalence in Delta-infected individuals (>40% by symptom criteria) with sex, comorbidity, and vaccination status as key risk factors, while Omicron cases showed age-related differences.

Retrospective cohort study of 10,500 Quebec healthcare workers examining long COVID risk and severity following first infection versus reinfections using electronic and telephone surveys conducted in 2023. Finds ~15% long COVID risk with first infection (three-fold higher than reinfections), identifies seven symptom clusters, and demonstrates that long COVID is common and disabling among workers.

This retrospective cohort study uses electronic health records from the RECOVER initiative to examine whether COVID-19 reinfection increases the risk of developing long COVID. The study found that reinfection resulted in a 35% increased risk of long COVID incidence compared to non-reinfected controls, though it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing EHR data from 1.5M patients to evaluate whether COVID-19 vaccination timing affects risk of developing long COVID after acute infection. Found vaccinated patients had 16% lower long COVID risk than unvaccinated, but no significant difference based on vaccination timing relative to acute infection.

This retrospective study analyzed 41,694 long COVID cases across 1,063 U.S. counties using N3C data to characterize spatiotemporal patterns and associations with sociodemographic factors. The study found increased long COVID incidence after Omicron emergence and identified spatial clustering in economically vulnerable inland regions, demonstrating the need for targeted public health interventions.

This prospective community cohort study from Virus Watch examined how socioeconomic deprivation, migration status, and ethnicity influence specific functional limitations (work, concentration, self-care, activities) among 776 adults with post-COVID condition in England. Findings showed that socioeconomic deprivation was the primary driver of functional limitations, with individuals in the most deprived areas experiencing 2.2–2.85-fold higher odds of limitations, while migration status and ethnicity showed no significant associations.

This retrospective cohort study examined post-acute dyslipidemia and abnormal BMI in children and adolescents with COVID-19 using EHR data from 25 US hospitals (384,289 COVID cases vs 1,080,413 controls). Children with documented COVID-19 showed higher risks of new-onset dyslipidemia and abnormal BMI in the post-acute period compared to uninfected peers, but the paper does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal study of elderly subjects examining whether COVID-19 infection is associated with differential decline in cognitive or motor function compared to age-related changes. Found no significant differences in cognitive impairment conversion or motor decline between COVID-19 exposed and unexposed groups; only 1 subject reported long COVID, limiting generalizability to the long COVID population.

CHASING COVID Cohort study identifying symptom clusters and phenotypes in 511 long COVID patients followed for ≥12 months post-infection. Study characterizes three burden clusters (highest, moderate, lowest) and identifies demographic/clinical risk factors but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed health records from 23 million U.S. patients to examine associations between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS), COVID-19 infection, and Long COVID development. The study found that patients with hEDS were significantly more likely to develop Long COVID, particularly those with overlapping conditions like autonomic dysfunction and chronic fatigue, but it does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This prospective community-based cohort study (CHASING COVID) uses target trial emulation to compare the natural history of long COVID symptoms in 1,055 newly infected versus 52,310 uninfected individuals over 12 months. The study found that SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with elevated risk of new-onset long COVID symptoms (22.6% vs 11.3% at 4-8 months), but does not evaluate any specific treatment or intervention.

Target trial emulation examining whether a third COVID-19 vaccine dose reduces long COVID incidence at 6 and 12 months in a community cohort. Found no meaningful reduction in long COVID incidence with third dose vaccination compared to primary series only.

This study examines the association between pre-infection COVID-19 vaccination and long-COVID-associated mental fatigue using longitudinal data from the Johns Hopkins COVID Long Study cohort. It is excluded as a secondary analysis of an existing cohort study rather than a treatment intervention trial.

This prospective matched cohort study from the Arizona CoVHORT examines the association between long COVID and food insecurity among 2,415 participants with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections. The study finds that individuals with long COVID have 47% higher odds of experiencing food insecurity compared to matched controls without long COVID.

This study analyzes mobility patterns of COVID-19 infected versus uninfected individuals in Wuhan using smartphone location data from 2019-2020. It finds that infected individuals showed higher mobility during the pandemic and slower recovery of mobility patterns post-infection, suggesting long-term behavioral impacts of COVID-19.

Retrospective longitudinal study of 276 COVID-19 survivors evaluating exercise therapy adherence and symptom progression over 32 months post-discharge. Early exercise initiation and adherence were associated with reduced symptom burden, particularly dyspnea, with day-21 symptom status serving as a prognostic marker for recovery.

Cross-sectional assessment of 201 Indian adults at least six months post-COVID using standardized cognitive and mental health tests. Found pronounced working-memory deficits in moderate-to-severe cases but no robust differences in depression/anxiety, highlighting that hospitalization is inadequate for assessing disease severity.

This nationwide population-based study examined the incidence and risk of chronic urticaria, vitiligo, alopecia areata, and herpes zoster in COVID-19 patients versus matched controls using Cox proportional hazard analyses. COVID-19 infection was associated with significantly higher rates of these dermatological and infectious conditions, even after adjusting for confounders.

A retrospective cohort study examining the relationship between pre-pandemic autonomic function and COVID-19 clinical course in 30 young adults. The study finds that baseline parasympathetic reactivity predicts COVID severity and post-COVID symptoms, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

A retrospective service evaluation comparing speech and language therapy (SLT) needs and service delivery across two NHS Long COVID multidisciplinary services. The study describes the clinical presentations, intervention approaches, and workforce requirements for managing SLT needs (voice, swallowing, communication, upper airway difficulties) in Long COVID patients.

This study evaluates the clinical and cost-effectiveness of plasmapheresis and hemoperfusion treatments in COVID-19 survivors followed for 6 months post-discharge. While these interventions improved some clinical outcomes at discharge, they showed worse long-term results compared to controls and exceeded cost-effectiveness thresholds, suggesting limited economic justification for their use.

A retrospective cohort study of 70 ICU patients with critical COVID-19, examining recovery of coagulation biomarkers and complete blood count at 6 months post-hospitalization. Most biomarkers normalized but 21% of patients showed persistent abnormalities; FVIII and D-dimer elevation correlated weakly with reduced diffusing capacity.

topics: post-ICU sequelae|quality of life|functional outcomes|psychological health
summary: Prospective cohort study following 113 COVID-19 ICU survivors for 5 months post-discharge to assess long-term functional and psychological outcomes across different ventilation support types. Most survivors reported impaired quality of life with high rates of psychological symptoms, reduced exercise capacity, and lung function deficits, with similar outcomes between invasive and non-invasive ventilation groups.

Prospective multicentre cohort study of critically ill COVID-19 survivors followed at 3 and 12 months post-ICU to assess functional outcome and health-related quality of life. While the paper studies long-term recovery, it is not about long COVID specifically—it focuses on recovery from critical acute COVID-19 requiring ICU admission rather than persistent post-acute symptoms weeks to months after infection onset.

This study examines 60-day mortality and post-discharge health outcomes in Swedish ICU patients with acute COVID-19 during the first pandemic wave (March-June 2020). While survivors reported declined general health at 4-month follow-up, the paper primarily focuses on acute ICU management and mortality during active infection, not long COVID sequelae or interventions for persistent post-COVID symptoms.

Prospective follow-up study of 326 Danish ICU patients with COVID-19 assessed at 6 and 12 months for cognitive function, frailty, quality of life, and fatigue. Found persistent cognitive impairment in up to 26% at 6 months, frailty in 20%, and fatigue in ~50% of survivors, demonstrating long-term sequelae in ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients.

Prospective longitudinal study of 173 COVID-19 patients examining T-cell recovery and immune function up to 12 months post-infection using flow cytometry and mass cytometry. Found T-cell lymphopenia recovery by 6 months but persistent CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation at 12 months, with a subset of severe COVID patients showing persistently low CD8+ counts and dysregulated immune responses.

Large matched cohort study (641,704 COVID-19 patients vs 1,907,992 controls) examining new-onset atopic dermatitis in the post-COVID period (3-15 months after infection). Findings show a 33% increased risk of developing atopic dermatitis in COVID-19 patients compared to matched controls, with consistent elevation across age groups and sex.

Retrospective and prospective cohort study examining asthma phenotypes and their association with COVID-19 severity and long-term symptoms in 6,976 SARS-CoV-2-positive patients. Finds asthma is not a risk factor for severe disease, but observes that over 50% of patients report ongoing respiratory symptoms 3 months post-infection.

Longitudinal observational study examining immune system changes in non-vaccinated subjects at 10 weeks and 10 months post-COVID-19 infection compared to matched controls. Found reduced immune cell counts, antibody decline, and shift from Th1 to Th2 cytokine profiles in convalescent patients, suggesting an immunological mechanism for long-term COVID sequelae.

A prospective observational study examining gastrointestinal barrier disruption and immune markers in post-COVID syndrome patients with fatigue and related symptoms. Found associations between pre-existing GI complaints and PCS development, with elevated inflammatory markers and evidence of intestinal barrier leakage in affected patients.

This is a national cohort study examining 1-year functional recovery (measured by sick leave) in working-age COVID-19 patients from Swedish registries, comparing ICU patients, hospital patients, and matched population controls. While it addresses long COVID sequelae, it is a secondary analysis using existing registry data without testing any intervention, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline.

Cross-sectional assessment of persistent symptoms in pediatric COVID-19 patients at 120+ days post-infection, finding >50% reported at least one persisting symptom (fatigue, joint pain, headache, insomnia, respiratory problems, palpitations) with 42.6% experiencing functional impairment. Highlights long-term impact of COVID-19 in children including asymptomatic cases.

Observational study of 348 pregnant women with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection examining the development of long COVID and associated risk factors. Found 27% developed long COVID, with vaccination reducing risk by 62% and preexisting respiratory disease/pneumonia increasing risk.

This cross-sectional study examines the prevalence and characteristics of persistent symptoms in Swedish children hospitalized with COVID-19. The authors assess symptom duration and burden in pediatric long COVID cases to clarify the magnitude of this condition in children, which remains understudied compared to adults.

This study evaluates urogenital involvement in 74 male recovered COVID-19 patients by assessing SARS-CoV-2 presence in body fluids and measuring semen quality and hormonal profiles. The findings show no direct urogenital involvement or viral detection, but slight declines in semen quality compared to healthy controls, with worse outcomes in patients with longer recovery times (≥90 days).

A descriptive study of 201 pediatric COVID-19 patients followed for up to 13 months documenting acute and long-term symptoms in mostly outpatient populations. Reports persistent long COVID symptoms including fatigue, muscle weakness, dyspnea, chest pain, cough, and anosmia lasting more than four weeks post-illness.

Observational study examining laryngotracheal pathologies in COVID-19 survivors ≥12 months after critical care intubation, comparing tracheotomized and long-term intubated patients. Finds high incidence of visible pathologies (58%) associated with tracheostomy tube size and duration, with symptom-pathology associations for voice and swallowing.

A Czech national multicentre study evaluating respiratory symptoms and functional outcomes in 39 children with persistent respiratory issues >12 weeks after COVID-19. The study found exertional dyspnoea and cough as dominant symptoms with a median recovery time of 4 months and generally favourable prognosis.

Multicentre retrospective study of 451 Spanish children with COVID-19, comparing prolonged symptom prevalence to a control group without COVID-19 history. Found 14.6% symptomatic beyond 12 weeks with higher odds in children aged ≥5 years, hospitalized, admitted to PICU, and those with symptomatic relatives.

Prospective follow-up study of 1,243 children with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection assessed at 3-6-12 months post-infection to evaluate long COVID symptom persistence by infecting variant (Omicron vs pre-Omicron). Children infected with pre-Omicron variants (Alpha, Delta, wildtype) had significantly higher rates of symptom persistence at 3 and 6 months compared to Omicron, with non-Omicron variants showing 4-10 fold increased odds of persistent symptoms.

A day care-based cross-sectional study comparing long-term symptoms in children who were infected versus not infected with SARS-CoV-2 during COVID-19 outbreaks. The study found no significant differences in long-term symptoms between the two groups, providing evidence on post-acute symptom burden in young children.

Prospective study tracking haematology patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome from pandemic start, monitoring mortality and symptom persistence across SARS-CoV-2 variants. Demonstrates declining mortality (42% to 2%) and post-COVID-19 syndrome prevalence (46% to 14%) over time, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This cross-sectional study from the Isfahan COVID Cohort examines the association between obesity status (BMI and waist circumference) and long-COVID symptoms in 4,008 COVID-19 patients. Higher BMI and abdominal obesity were significantly associated with increased risk of cardiovascular and respiratory long-COVID symptoms.

A prospective observational study measuring platelet activity in COVID-19 patients up to 40 days post-admission using a haematology analyzer. The study demonstrates that platelet hyperactivity persists after acute inflammation subsides, potentially contributing to thromboembolic complications in post-COVID patients, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Longitudinal observational study of 66 long COVID patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction (>6 months post-infection) assessing chemosensory function and recovery factors at two timepoints. Found that younger age and absence of parosmia were associated with better olfactory recovery, but the study does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study characterizes sympathicotonia (overactive sympathetic nervous system) in 17 post-COVID condition patients versus 18 healthy controls using 14-day electrodermal activity monitoring via smart ring. While EDA did not identify PCC itself, individuals with orthostatic test-identified sympathicotonia showed heightened EDA, particularly during late night, suggesting long-term EDA monitoring may objectively detect sympathicotonia independent of self-reported symptoms.

Prospective cohort study of 187 ICU patients with critical COVID-19 infection, examining the association between ventilatory support type (HFNO/NIV vs invasive ventilation) and long-term pulmonary outcomes at 6-month follow-up. While 74% had residual lung changes, the extent of pulmonary impairment was similar across ventilation groups, though invasive ventilation patients had lower total lung capacity.

This retrospective cohort study examines acute COVID-19 outcomes in solid organ transplant recipients during the initial infection period (March 2020–November 2021), focusing on readmission, graft dysfunction, and mortality within 6 months of infection. The study does not address long COVID or post-acute sequelae; it documents outcomes of acute COVID-19 infection in an immunocompromised population.

This Danish nationwide cohort study examines post-acute COVID-19 hospitalizations and mortality risk in diabetic patients who were hospitalized with COVID-19 versus unexposed diabetics. Among type 2 diabetes patients, those hospitalized with COVID-19 had significantly higher risks of subsequent respiratory infections, other infections, and death compared to unexposed diabetics.

Retrospective cohort study of 2,649 COVID-19 hospitalized patients in Moscow assessing prevalence and risk factors for persistent symptoms at 6-8 months post-discharge. Found 47.1% reported persistent symptoms (fatigue, shortness of breath, cognitive issues), with female sex and certain comorbidities associated with increased risk.

This cross-sectional survey of German psoriasis patients examined SARS-CoV-2 infection prevalence and symptom characteristics in 4,818 registry participants. While 231 patients (31.4% of those infected) reported longer-lasting symptoms after acute COVID-19, the study does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment—it is purely observational and epidemiological in nature.

This study examined immune repertoire abnormalities in COVID-19 convalescent patients at 6+ months post-discharge and assessed whether post-hospitalization rehabilitation alleviates these immune system changes. Patients who received rehabilitation showed attenuated immune repertoire abnormality compared to those without rehabilitation, suggesting rehabilitation may correct long-term immunological impairment from COVID-19.

This retrospective cohort study examines long-term effects of COVID-19 on diabetes complications and mortality in 2,456 UK and 80,546 Hong Kong diabetic patients with COVID-19 compared to matched uninfected controls. The study found COVID-19 infection was associated with significantly increased risks of cardiovascular disease, microvascular disease, and all-cause mortality at 18-28 months follow-up.

This retrospective cohort study examines the incidence of new hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and diabetic ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes patients with and without COVID-19 infection up to 40 months post-infection. While it studies post-COVID sequelae, it focuses on comorbidities in a specific diabetes population rather than long COVID syndrome itself, and is observational without treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examines the association between obesity and the risk of postacute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in 2,839 patients followed for a median of 8 months after acute COVID-19. The findings show that moderate and severe obesity are associated with significantly higher risks of hospital admission and need for diagnostic tests during the PASC period, but this is an observational study tracking outcomes without testing any intervention.

This cross-sectional study compared myocardial performance index (MPI) measurements between 200 long COVID patients with cardiac symptoms and 182 healthy controls, finding significantly elevated MPI and prolonged isovolumetric relaxation time in the patient group. The study is observational without intervention and does not test a treatment, making it ineligible for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

This cross-sectional study assessed left ventricular function using echocardiography in 134 COVID-19 recovered patients 30-45 days post-infection. The study found subclinical cardiac dysfunction in ~30% of patients but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study assessed cardiac involvement in COVID-19 recovered patients using cardiac MRI, comparing 30 symptomatic post-COVID patients to 20 healthy controls. The research found abnormal CMR findings in 53.3% of patients, with persistent abnormalities in 25% at 6-month follow-up, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational study evaluated myocardial dysfunction in 546 recovered COVID-19 patients using echocardiography and clinical follow-up to identify imaging markers associated with persistent cardiovascular symptoms at 12 months. While it identifies strain parameters predictive of symptom persistence, it is an observational study without any treatment intervention being tested or evaluated.

A prospective observational study following 385 unvaccinated patients for up to 12 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection to characterize inflammatory biomarkers in long COVID patients versus asymptomatic controls. The study found elevated neutrophil degranulation markers (MMP-8, MPO), endothelial dysfunction markers (L-selectin, P-selectin), and metabolic dysfunction (leptin) in long COVID patients, without testing any intervention.

A retrospective cohort study examining whether circulating haematopoietic stem/progenitor cell (HSPC) levels at COVID-19 hospital admission predict 1-year mortality and long-COVID development in 100 hospitalized patients. While the study found HSPCs predictive of mortality, it was not designed to evaluate a treatment intervention and does not test or evaluate any therapeutic approach for long COVID.

Prospective cohort study of 480 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors (moderate vs severe) followed for 1 year with echocardiography and biomarker assessment. Severe COVID-19 survivors showed progressive right ventricular dysfunction, with FeNO and ET-1 serving as prognostic biomarkers for mortality and disease severity.

This prospective longitudinal study assessed cognitive performance in COVID-19 survivors using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment at multiple timepoints before and after infection. The study found that COVID-related cognitive decline observed at 6 months post-infection spontaneously improved by 18 months, suggesting cognitive sequelae may not be permanent.

Prospective multicentre cohort study following COVID-19 survivors for neurological outcomes at 3 months and 1 year post-infection, assessing cognitive deficits and olfactory dysfunction. Documents natural history of neurological sequelae rather than evaluating a specific intervention or treatment.

Longitudinal follow-up study of 76 COVID-19 hospitalized patients assessing cognitive function at 5 and 12 months post-discharge. Found persistent cognitive deficits in processing speed, visuospatial and verbal memory after 1 year, with associations to acute illness severity and sensory symptoms, but no treatment intervention tested.

This international cohort study prospectively and retrospectively enrolled 971 neuro-COVID patients across 19 European countries to assess short- and long-term outcomes and identify predictors of functional status. While it documents persistent neurological symptoms in 29.4% of hospitalized patients at 6-month follow-up, it is an observational study without any treatment intervention and should be excluded from the intervention trials pipeline.

Retrospective study examining cardiac involvement via MRI in 100 young COVID-19 patients post-recovery, finding cardiac abnormalities in 49% of cases with significant associations between cardiac involvement and symptoms. This is an observational study that does not evaluate any treatment intervention, only characterizes post-COVID cardiac pathology.

Prospective cohort study following 110 COVID-19 recovered patients for 28 months to assess the prognostic impact of subclinical myocardial dysfunction on long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Found that subclinical myocardial dysfunction (detected in 34% of patients) was independently associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, but long-COVID condition itself had no prognostic significance.

This study examines anti-apolipoprotein A-1 autoantibodies (AAA1) in 193 COVID-19 survivors over 12 months, finding that AAA1 predicts persistent respiratory symptoms independently. The work is mechanistic/biomarker research assessing correlations between autoimmune markers and symptom persistence rather than testing a treatment intervention.

This matched-control study compares long-term COVID-19 outcomes in people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) to matched pwMS without COVID-19, following 211 cases for ≥6 months. While the paper documents persistent symptoms (fatigue, hyposmia, dyspnea) in a minority of pwMS post-COVID, it does not evaluate any treatment intervention—it is a purely observational comparison of untreated natural recovery.

Multicentre prospective cohort study examining structural brain abnormalities and neuropsychological consequences in COVID-19 ICU vs general ward survivors 8-10 months post-discharge. ICU survivors showed higher prevalence of cerebral microbleeds but similar cognitive dysfunction and psychological symptoms, with cognitive complaints and severe fatigue frequently reported across both groups.

This prospective observational study follows patients with neurological long COVID symptoms over 18 months to track symptom progression and recovery patterns. While it identifies natural recovery in 50% of patients and suggests vaccination may accelerate recovery, it is a passive observational follow-up study with no treatment intervention assigned to participants.

This paper describes a systematic diagnostic registry of 156 long COVID patients presenting with neurological symptoms to a specialized outpatient clinic. The study found fatigue, cognitive impairment, and headache as the most common persisting complaints, with minimal structural neurological findings on comprehensive diagnostic workup.

Prospective cohort study following 732 COVID-19 patients for 24 months to characterize new-onset persistent headaches in long COVID. Found that 16.2% of headache-naïve patients developed de novo persistent headaches, with 64.8% meeting migraine-like headache criteria, demonstrating elevated migraine incidence compared to general population.

This retrospective observational cohort study examines the incidence, clinical characteristics, and diagnostic timeliness of long COVID in North West London using primary care records from 2.7 million patients. The study identifies disparities in long COVID diagnosis rates across demographic groups and pre-existing conditions, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective observational cohort study examines hospital care intensity and continuity for long COVID patients in an English healthcare system, analyzing changes in secondary care utilization before and after LC diagnosis. The study found increased healthcare utilization after diagnosis but reduced hospital-level continuity of care, indicating fragmented care pathways.

This retrospective cohort study examines long-term outcomes (up to 3.5 years post-infection) in Parkinson's disease patients who had COVID-19 compared to PD patients without COVID-19. The study found that PD patients with COVID-19 had significantly higher risks of mortality, cardiovascular events, dyspnea, fatigue, and falls, suggesting that COVID-19 has lasting adverse effects on this vulnerable population.

This longitudinal cohort study examines the bidirectional relationship between migraine and COVID-19 in 1,085 women from the MECH-HK cohort. Women with migraine had greater COVID-19 symptom burden and elevated PASC risk (aOR 1.87), while COVID-19 infection was associated with increased migraine attack frequency during the first 3 months post-infection.

Observational study of 97 mildly symptomatic COVID-19 patients examined sinonasal symptoms and smell/taste dysfunction during acute infection. Smell/taste dysfunction affected 25.6% of patients and recovered completely in 81% at three months, with no intervention tested.

NHS service evaluation examining the effectiveness of person-centred experiential counselling for depression (PCE-CfD) in 31 long COVID patients, using routine outcome measures (PHQ-9, GAD-7, WSAS) with pre/post comparisons. Results showed significant reductions in depression (d=2.1) and anxiety (d=1.2) symptoms, with 83.87% of treated patients reaching recovery status.

Retrospective cohort study examining factors associated with persistent symptoms in 315 COVID-19 patients at 1-month follow-up in a chest diseases clinic. Study identifies elevated D-dimer, CRP, hospitalization, and comorbidities as predictors of symptom persistence but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective comparative study examining lung tissue morphology in long COVID patients undergoing tumor resection, finding increased vascular and parenchymal lesions compared to controls. This is a secondary analysis of archived tumor resection specimens rather than a prospective treatment trial or observational cohort study.

Prospective longitudinal observational study tracking 339 recovered COVID-19 patients over 12 months to investigate long COVID symptom prevalence and types. Found 66.8% reported symptoms at 3 months and 44.8% at 12 months, with fatigue as the most common symptom and pain increasing over time; vaccination showed protective effect.

A prospective cohort study comparing symptom persistence and recovery in 48 COVID-19 survivors versus 97 uninfected controls in New Zealand, assessed ~10 months post-infection. COVID-19 survivors showed significantly higher rates of fatigue (63%), dyspnoea (27%), and chest pain (21%), with delayed return to normal activity, though anxiety and overall quality of life were similar between groups.

Multicenter observational cohort study examining the relationship between obesity and short-term complications and post-acute sequelae in 216 hospitalized pediatric COVID-19 patients. Obesity was significantly associated with severe acute outcomes (ICU admission, ventilatory support) and post-acute sequelae (dyspnea, muscle weakness), but no treatment intervention was tested.

Prospective cohort study assessing associations between persistent COVID-19 symptoms at 6-11 months post-infection and health status, quality of life, and psychological distress in 436 mild COVID-19 patients. Higher symptom burden was significantly associated with poorer health outcomes and increased psychological distress.

This multi-center longitudinal study followed 715 COVID-19 survivors from Wuhan for a median of 225 days post-discharge to characterize the prevalence and risk factors for mid-term clinical sequelae. The study found that 29.9% of survivors experienced at least one sequela, with fatigue (19.2%), respiratory symptoms (22.7%), and cardiovascular symptoms (5.0%) being most common, associated with disease severity and mechanical ventilation use.

Prospective cohort study tracking 292 long COVID patients over 24 months to identify symptom trajectories and their association with illness perception using group-based trajectory models. Found four distinct symptom trajectories with little overall fluctuation in symptom burden but individual symptoms developing and resolving over time, with negative illness perception correlating with higher symptom burden.

Prospective cohort study of 203 adults hospitalized with acute COVID-19, examining in-hospital factors (delirium, remdesivir use, family visits) associated with 12-month cognitive, PTSD, and depression outcomes. This paper focuses on acute COVID-19 hospitalization outcomes, not long COVID sequelae occurring weeks to months post-infection.

Retrospective cohort study examining how acute COVID-19 infection affects blood pressure variability and cardiovascular outcomes in hypertensive patients over 2 years. While the paper studies post-infection effects, it focuses on acute/immediate cardiovascular complications in hypertensive populations rather than persistent long COVID sequelae, and does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

A 2-year prospective cohort study of 1,389 COVID-19 survivors examining associations between monocyte count trajectories and long COVID symptoms, lung function, and exercise capacity. High monocyte trajectories were associated with increased odds of smell disorder, reduced 6-minute walking distance, impaired lung function, and rehospitalization.

Longitudinal observational study examining viral load and cytokine dynamics in hospitalized individuals with and without long COVID, using nasopharyngeal swabs and plasma samples collected within 55 days of SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis. Found that long COVID patients had delayed viral clearance, delayed cytokine normalization, and distinct patterns in IL-18, MIG, and IP-10 levels, suggesting these markers could serve as early signatures of long COVID development.

This retrospective cohort study of 3 million matched pairs examines amputation risk in COVID-19 survivors using Japanese insurance claims data, finding a 2.33-fold increased risk of amputation persisting beyond 2 years post-infection. The elevated risk was particularly pronounced in individuals with higher comorbidity burden, highlighting the need for long-term vascular monitoring in COVID-19 survivors.

This cross-sectional study evaluates the prevalence and predictors of long-term olfactory dysfunction in COVID-19 patients hospitalized during acute infection. The study examines associations between age, cognitive impairment, and persistent olfactory dysfunction as part of the Neuro Covid Next Study Group.

Retrospective cohort study of 245,857 US veterans examining frailty as a risk factor for developing post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) during the Delta and Omicron waves. Found that frailty and pre-frailty were associated with 41% and 15% increased risk of PASC respectively, while vaccination reduced PASC risk by 27-33%.

Longitudinal population-based study examining hand grip strength changes in community-dwelling older adults before and after SARS-CoV-2 infection. SARS-CoV-2 seropositive individuals showed greater HGS decline (1.72 kg) compared to seronegative controls (0.57 kg), with more pronounced effects in those infected >8 months prior, suggesting chronic skeletal muscle damage.

Retrospective cohort study of 171 nursing home residents (90 COVID-positive, 81 non-COVID) examining functional and cognitive trajectories following SARS-CoV-2 infection. COVID-19 infection caused significant ADL decline persisting 9 months post-infection, but the study passively observes patients without testing any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing Long COVID symptom recovery rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated COVID-19 survivors across 478 patients over a median 10-month follow-up. Vaccinated patients showed significantly better recovery rates for all ten common symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, forgetfulness) compared to never-vaccinated patients.

Retrospective cohort study comparing frailty changes in older Veterans with COVID-19 versus matched uninfected controls over 12 months. Found COVID-19 survivors accrued significantly more new frailty deficits, with fatigue, anemia, and muscle atrophy being most common.

Cross-sectional study examining the association between long COVID symptoms and physical function/ADLs among older women in the Women's Health Initiative cohort. After adjusting for pre-COVID functional status, the association between long COVID and lower functioning became nonsignificant, suggesting pre-existing functional decline is a major confounding factor.

Prospective cohort study of 1,019 older adults hospitalized with COVID-19, examining how persistent post-discharge symptoms (fatigue, myalgia, dyspnea) predict functional decline, falls, and ED visits over 1 year. Finds that patients with ≥2 persistent symptoms had significantly higher risk of mobility/IADL decline and unplanned healthcare events, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Prospective observational study of 131 COVID-19 ICU survivors assessing post-traumatic stress symptoms 6 months after discharge using the Impact of Event Scale-6. Found 22.5% reported PTSD symptoms, with female gender, younger age, and high respiratory rate as predictive factors.

Multicenter follow-up study assessing health-related quality of life in 311 COVID-19 patients at 3 months post-discharge, finding persistent physical symptoms and reduced HRQoL compared to population norms. Study identifies risk factors (female sex, older age, physical symptoms) but does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

A longitudinal cohort study following 102 nonhospitalized COVID-19 patients from 3 months to 6-7 months post-infection to assess changes in quality of life, psychological state, cognition, and pulmonary/physical function. The study found persistent impairment in quality of life and physical/cognitive function in 29-55% of participants, identifying predictors of poor long-term outcomes, but did not test any treatment intervention.

Prospective observational cohort study following 200 COVID-19 survivors for 12 weeks to characterize post-COVID syndrome manifestations and their correlation with acute disease severity. Found fatigue (23.5%), hair loss (12.5%), and dyspnea (9%) as main persistent symptoms at 12 weeks, with acute severity being an independent predictor of post-COVID outcomes.

This observational study examines age-related differences in Long COVID symptom frequency and patterns using the RECOVER-Adult cohort, comparing community-dwelling participants aged ≥60 years to younger adults. Findings show that aging alters both the prevalence and clustering of reported Long COVID symptoms, with reduced discriminatory value for certain symptoms like fatigue and pain in older adults.

This observational cohort study examines whether hospitalization during acute COVID-19 is a risk factor for long COVID severity. The study found that hospitalization is associated with worse pulmonary complications but does not increase overall long COVID severity compared to non-hospitalized patients.

A longitudinal descriptive study following 66 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for up to 3 months post-discharge to characterize emotional, mental health, and physical symptoms. Found that 96% experienced ≥1 COVID-related symptoms at 1 month and 85% at 3 months, with fatigue, dyspnea, and cognitive dysfunction being most prevalent.

This is a secondary analysis from the NOR-Solidarity trial examining the association between gut microbiota alterations and respiratory dysfunction 3 months post-COVID-19. The study found reduced microbial diversity and altered bacterial composition in patients with respiratory dysfunction, but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Population-based study in Lombardy using administrative data to assess healthcare resource utilization in 48,932 COVID-19 survivors over 6 months post-infection, comparing to the same period in 2019. Found significantly increased rehospitalizations, emergency visits, and diagnostic imaging/medications in previously hospitalized patients, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study of 414 hospitalized COVID-19 patients investigated whether T-cell exhaustion markers (sTim-3) persist and associate with prolonged respiratory dysfunction and mortality. The study found elevated sTim-3 levels 3-12 months post-hospitalization were associated with pulmonary radiological pathology and 60-day mortality, but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 337 COVID-19 patients (mild, moderate, severe) assessed 3-6 months post-infection for respiratory impairment using spirometry, DLCO, and exercise tests. Findings: reduced DLCO was most common in severely hospitalized patients (20% vs 4% in nonhospitalized), breathlessness was prevalent (40.6%), and DLCO reduction did not correlate with physiological responses to exertion.

Population-based cohort study of 204,805 SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals in Stockholm examining the occurrence of post COVID-19 condition (PCC) diagnosis and associated healthcare use 90-360 days after infection, stratified by acute infection severity. Found PCC diagnosis rates of 1% (nonhospitalized), 6% (hospitalized), and 32% (ICU-treated), with female sex and prior mental health disorders/asthma as risk factors, and elevated outpatient care use persisting 1 year post-infection.

This retrospective cohort study examines the symptom trajectory and predictors of long COVID in hospitalized COVID-19 survivors. The paper characterizes the natural history and course of persistent symptoms in recovered hospitalized patients.

Retrospective observational study examining whether preexisting symptoms increase the risk of developing long COVID. Found that individuals diagnosed with long COVID had significantly higher prevalence of relevant symptoms before the pandemic compared to those without long COVID (OR 2.28-2.32 after adjustment).

Prospective seroepidemiological study in a large Danish working population examining SARS-CoV-2 antibody dynamics across three timepoints (baseline through 12-month follow-up) and risk factors for infection and long COVID symptoms. Found ~33% of seropositive individuals reported persistent symptoms (anosmia/ageusia 17.5%, fatigue 15.3%), but the study is observational without testing any interventions or treatments.

Register-based cohort study of 1.5 million Swedish individuals examining healthcare utilization changes before and after COVID-19 infection. Found increased healthcare contacts in a small proportion of the population post-COVID, primarily in primary care, but this is an observational health services analysis without treatment intervention.

Follow-up study of 58 hospitalized children with COVID-19 to assess symptom persistence at 13+ months post-admission. Found low prevalence of long COVID symptoms (10%) with most resolving over time, representing a descriptive natural history assessment rather than a treatment intervention study.

This Swedish matched cohort study examines long-term cardiovascular risk in COVID-19 patients up to 365+ days post-infection, comparing hospitalized and nonhospitalized cases with non-COVID comparators. While it addresses post-COVID sequelae, it is an observational epidemiological study measuring disease outcomes rather than testing a treatment intervention.

Cross-sectional survey study examining nightmare frequency and suicidal ideation across 16 countries during the COVID-19 pandemic, comparing participants with long-COVID vs short-COVID and pre-pandemic baseline. Found higher suicidal ideation (21.1%) and nightmare frequency (18%) in long-COVID patients, but this is an observational study with no treatment intervention tested.

This cross-sectional study examines the association between probable post-COVID-19 condition and changes in sleep quality and quantity in 2,445 non-hospitalized adults. Patients with post-COVID condition reported significantly greater decreases in sleep hours and higher odds of perceiving worsened sleep quality, but the study is observational without any intervention or treatment being tested.

Observational study measuring D-dimer and coagulation markers in 150 COVID-19 convalescent patients at a median of 80.5 days post-infection. Found elevated D-dimer in 25% of patients, associated with prior hospitalization and age >50, but no treatment was tested or evaluated.

This study investigates pathophysiological mechanisms of long COVID by examining VWF-ADAMTS-13 axis imbalance, endothelial activation, and immune dysfunction in 50 convalescent COVID-19 patients compared to healthy and acute COVID controls. It is an observational biomarker study that does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining the association between self-efficacy and health-related quality of life in mechanically ventilated COVID-19 ICU survivors over 2 years. Finds that higher self-efficacy at 3 months post-discharge is associated with better long-term quality of life outcomes, but does not evaluate an intervention.

This retrospective cohort study evaluated quality of life at work and chronic fatigue syndrome symptoms in 283 COVID-19 hospitalization survivors across multiple time points (4, 4-12, and >12 weeks post-infection). The study identifies fatigue, sleep disturbance, and headache as predictors of decreased work-related quality of life but does not evaluate any specific treatment or intervention.

This controlled cohort study compared gastrointestinal and somatoform symptoms in 164 SARS-CoV-2 infected patients versus 183 controls at 5 months post-infection. Infected patients showed significantly increased risk of loose stools, chronic fatigue, and somatization, suggesting persistent functional gastrointestinal and somatoform disorders may share a common biological origin after COVID-19.

Post hoc mediation analysis of a multicenter cohort study examining how COVID-19 exposure leads to post-COVID-19 IBS through psychological and clinical mediators. The study identifies dyspnea, GI symptoms, and depression as key mediators but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This study followed 1,304 Chinese COVID-19 patients to assess gustatory dysfunction as a long COVID symptom, with 6-month follow-up on 216 cases. While it documents that 20% developed long COVID-related taste loss and identifies risk factors for persistence, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study tracking 79 long COVID patients over 2 years using MRI and neuropsychological assessments. Found persistent brain changes in brainstem and limbic regions with partial recovery of fatigue symptoms, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This study examined gastrointestinal and somatic symptoms in children 3 months after COVID-19 testing using questionnaires and medical records. While it follows patients post-infection, it does not study long COVID specifically—it focuses on acute post-infectious symptom changes in the immediate 3-month period without assessing the persistent, chronic nature of long COVID or testing any intervention.

Retrospective chart review of 101 pediatric SARS-CoV-2 patients examining clinical and demographic markers associated with severe acute disease and chronic complications (symptoms >4 weeks). Found that pulmonary comorbidity and obesity were associated with severe disease markers, while pulmonary comorbidity and acute severity predicted long-term sequelae.

This retrospective cohort study evaluates liver function abnormalities in 595 COVID-19 patients during acute infection and their evolution at follow-up in 153 patients. The study finds that persistent abnormal liver function tests are common but mostly reflect metabolic fatty liver disease rather than viral hepatitis, with no correlation between acute and follow-up liver abnormalities.
