summary: Prospective cohort study following 114 COVID-19-associated ARDS survivors at 3, 6, and 12 months post-ICU discharge to assess physical, cognitive, and mental health outcomes. Found persistent impairments in handgrip strength and fatigue, with cognitive and mental health symptoms largely unchanged over the follow-up period.

This retrospective cohort study examines risk factors for fibrotic-like radiographic abnormalities 4 months after severe COVID-19 hospitalization, comparing mechanically ventilated and non-ventilated patients. The study identifies severity of illness, mechanical ventilation duration, and leucocyte telomere length as independent risk factors, finding fibrotic-like changes correlate with lung function and frailty but not dyspnea.

Prospective cohort study evaluating lung injury in 118 COVID-19 pneumonia patients at 6-month follow-up using chest CT imaging. Found that 72% of patients showed fibrosis-like changes and baseline imaging metrics could predict late pulmonary sequelae.

This secondary analysis of a prospective multicenter cohort study examined chest CT abnormalities 1 year after COVID-19 pneumonia in 91 participants. Over half (54%) showed persistent CT abnormalities, with older age and critical COVID-19 severity being significant predictors of findings, indicating long-term pulmonary sequelae in a subset of recovered patients.

Prospective cohort study of 114 severe COVID-19 survivors followed up at 6 months with chest CT imaging to assess long-term pulmonary sequelae. Found fibrotic-like changes in 35% of patients, with older age, ARDS, prolonged hospitalization, and higher initial CT scores as independent predictors.

The PHENOTYPE study prospectively followed 80 COVID-19 survivors with serial CT scans and symptom assessments at 3 months and 1 year post-discharge. The study documented persistent pulmonary abnormalities (ground-glass opacification, bands, fibrosis signs) and associated risk factors, with radiologic improvement in most participants by 1-year follow-up, but did not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This prospective observational study used MR spectroscopy to assess mitochondrial function in 41 long COVID patients with fatigue versus 29 healthy controls. Participants with long COVID showed differences in phosphocreatine recovery rate and mitochondrial capacity compared to controls, but these measures did not correlate with fatigue severity.

Prospective study comparing cardiac MRI findings between 41 patients with chronic COVID-19 syndrome (persistent fatigue and dyspnea) and 42 healthy controls, ~103 days post-infection. Found no signs of active myocardial injury or inflammation in the CCS group, with comparable MRI parameters between groups except for a non-significant trend toward more late gadolinium enhancement in CCS patients.

This study compares cardiopulmonary exercise capacity between long COVID patients with persistent symptoms, those who have recovered, and healthy controls at 5 months post-infection. It is a descriptive observational study that does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Comparative study of cardiovascular risk factors, arterial stiffness, and physical functioning in nonhospitalized COVID-19 patients versus controls at 6 months postinfection. Found one in three patients reported residual symptoms (notably fatigue) but no objective differences in cardiovascular risk or arterial stiffness between groups.

This study compares chest CT imaging and pulmonary function in 100 ambulatory, hospitalized, and ICU-level PASC patients versus 106 healthy controls, measuring ground-glass opacity and air trapping. It documents quantitative pulmonary structural abnormalities in post-acute COVID-19 but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This case-control study compared cardiopulmonary fitness and endothelial function in immunocompromised youth 6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection versus matched controls. Patients showed impaired exercise capacity and endothelial dysfunction, but the study is observational without any intervention or treatment evaluation.

Prospective cohort study of 154 COVID-19 ARDS patients measuring alveolar fibroproliferative biomarkers during hospitalization and following up at 3 and 12 months post-discharge. Found that elevated fibroproliferative response was associated with increased mortality but not with long-term fibrotic lung sequelae in survivors.

This observational cohort study followed 64 PASC patients over ~97 days to determine whether cardiovascular autonomic abnormalities persist over time using hemodynamic testing. The findings show that autonomic abnormalities (most commonly Initial Orthostatic Hypotension and POTS) remain prevalent at follow-up, with no significant improvement, suggesting these complications are chronic rather than transient.

A follow-up comparative study evaluating the effect of an 8-week selective yoga regime on pulmonary function in 82 COVID-19 survivors with deranged lung function. The intervention showed significant improvements in most PFT parameters, suggesting yoga may be effective for long-term pulmonary recovery in post-COVID patients.

Longitudinal observational study examining optic nerve head parameters and peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thickness changes in 18 COVID-19 recovered patients using OCT imaging at baseline, 1-month, and 3-month follow-up. Found localized peripapillary nerve fiber layer thinning in the nasal lower sector and decreased cup volume, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Longitudinal observational study following 88 military-trained individuals (hospitalized and community-managed) for up to 12 months post-COVID to assess cardiopulmonary exercise function, fatigue, and mental health. Found persistent fatigue (48-46%) and dyspnea (52-43%) in symptomatic groups at 12 months, with reduced work capacity and high rates of medical non-deployability.

Controlled follow-up study comparing 206 COVID-19 patients seven months post-infection with matched controls, measuring hospitalization rates, physical performance, and quality of life. Found similar hospitalization and exercise capacity but significantly reduced quality of life and functional status in COVID-positive subjects.

This 16-week observational cohort study examined the relationship between clinical biomarkers, symptom profiles, and functional status in 35 long COVID patients from UK clinics. While 63% of participants had abnormal biomarker values, these were not significantly correlated with symptoms or functional outcomes, suggesting that routine clinical investigations alone are insufficient for long COVID diagnosis and that condition-specific assessments are needed.

This study compares clinical features, laboratory findings, and imaging results between 52 long COVID patients coinfected with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and 77 with long COVID alone. The findings show that M. pneumoniae coinfection is more common in females and associated with typical chest CT findings, but no specific treatment intervention was tested.

Retrospective cohort study examining cardiac hemodynamic changes in stroke patients with versus without SARS-CoV-2 infection. While the study mentions potential long-term cardiac effects of COVID-19, it focuses on acute/concurrent infection in stroke patients rather than long COVID sequelae, and does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective study of 29 long COVID patients examining chest radiograph and CT findings in relation to pulmonary function tests and clinical characteristics during post-acute phase. Found associations between moderate/severe CT involvement and abnormal spirometry, and between radiological severity and hospitalization history, but this is an observational study without intervention or treatment evaluation.

This case-control study examines whether type 2 diabetes patients who had COVID-19 are at greater risk of developing new hypertension and chronic kidney disease compared to COVID-negative controls. The findings indicate that T2D patients with prior COVID-19 have elevated risk for new cardiovascular and renal complications, suggesting COVID-19 may accelerate metabolic and organ dysfunction in this vulnerable population.

This EHR-based retrospective cohort study from the RECOVER program examines associations between SARS-CoV-2 infection and T1D disease trajectory in children, measuring healthcare utilization for DKA/severe hypoglycemia and HbA1c changes. While the study finds a trend toward worse outcomes post-COVID (greater HbA1c declines beyond 180 days), results were not statistically significant, and no treatment interventions were administered to participants.

This retrospective cohort study characterized immune system heterogeneity in 106 COVID-19 patients by measuring inflammatory markers (HBP, SAA, IL-6, CRP) during acute infection and convalescence, with follow-up >1 month post-discharge. The study found persistent elevation of HBP, CRP, and IL-6 at long-term follow-up and identified four distinct inflammatory phenotypes, suggesting ongoing inflammatory responses may contribute to long-term COVID symptoms.

This retrospective cohort study from the NIH RECOVER Initiative compares circulating milieu-mediated endothelial function in PASC+ vs PASC- patients at baseline and 6 months post-infection. The study found reduced acetylcholine-stimulated nitric oxide production in PASC+ patients at 6 months, suggesting circulating factors contribute to endothelial dysfunction in long COVID.

Prospective follow-up study of 71 COVID-19 ICU patients assessed 3 months post-discharge for cognitive impairment and fatigue using standardized assessments (MoCA, MFI-20). Found 30% had cognitive impairment and elevated fatigue scores, but no significant differences related to ICU length of stay or intubation status.

This prospective cohort study examined the association between cancer history and COVID-19 outcomes among 35,623 older postmenopausal women from the Women's Health Initiative. Cancer history was not significantly associated with COVID-19 positivity, hospitalization, symptom severity, or long COVID risk.

Retrospective study of lymphoma patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 in 2020, examining the incidence of prolonged COVID-19 symptoms (>30 days hospitalization) and risk factors. While the paper discusses persistent symptoms during acute infection, it does not study long COVID as a post-acute sequela and is primarily focused on acute COVID-19 outcomes in an immunocompromised population.

Retrospective cohort study examining whether serological biomarkers measured at hospital admission predict long-term post-COVID fatigue and dyspnea. While some biomarkers differed between patients with and without post-COVID symptoms, they explained only 4.5% of variance and could not meaningfully explain long-COVID development.

Prospective multicentre cohort study following 312 patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19 pneumonia for 6 months post-discharge to characterize pulmonary sequelae. Found DLCO impairment (46%) and chest X-ray abnormalities (25%) as most sensitive markers, with minimal dyspnea symptoms reported despite objective findings.

Cross-sectional study examining long-term effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 medications (favipiravir, hydroxychloroquine) on male reproductive function in 29 recovered patients 3-8 months post-infection. Found no significant differences in semen parameters or serum hormone levels before and after COVID-19, concluding that infection and treatment did not affect spermatogenesis.

Prospective observational cohort study of 253 COVID-19 patients followed for 2 years to assess prevalence and recovery of olfactory and gustatory dysfunction. Most patients experienced favorable recovery, with 79.3% achieving complete resolution, though 7.9% had persistent qualitative symptoms at 24 months.

This multicentre cross-sectional study assessed fatigue, dyspnoea, and functional limitations in 1,142 COVID-19 survivors 7 months after hospitalization from 4 Madrid hospitals. The study found 70% of survivors had fatigue and/or dyspnoea with 45% experiencing functional limitations, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective observational cohort study of 58 long COVID patients undergoing 6-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation, showing significant improvements in 6-minute walk distance (62.9 m increase), functional status, dyspnea, fatigue, and quality of life. Results suggest pulmonary rehabilitation is effective for improving exercise capacity and symptom burden in long COVID patients, though further controlled trials are needed.

Retrospective study of 737 COVID-19 patients examining whether early antiviral or monoclonal antibody treatment reduces long COVID risk. Both vaccination and mAbs/antivirals independently reduced long COVID occurrence (11% vs 34% in propensity-matched analysis, p=0.001).

Prospective follow-up study of 100 COVID-19 pneumonia patients assessed with pulmonary function tests and HRCT imaging at 3 and 15 months post-infection. Found that 8% developed post-COVID interstitial lung disease, with aging and acute infection severity as risk factors; does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 584 COVID-19 patients for 12 months to assess lung function recovery and radiological abnormalities. Severe COVID-19 patients showed persistent lung function impairment (lower DLCO, minimal oxygen saturation, total lung capacity) compared to non-severe patients at 12 months, though both groups improved over time.

This prospective cohort study investigates cardiopulmonary function in post-COVID patients with versus without myocardial scars detected by CMR imaging at ~6 months post-infection. The study found no significant associations between minor myocardial scars and cardiopulmonary function or longitudinal changes over 12 months.

This observational study evaluated respiratory, mental, and physical sequelae in 58 children (aged 5-18) 1-6 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection using spirometry, exhaled breath condensate analysis, and functional tests. Most children were asymptomatic or mild cases with gradually diminishing emotional symptoms and no significant pulmonary sequelae detected by objective measures.

This retrospective cohort study followed COVID-19 patients hospitalized with acute kidney injury (AKI) for 9.6 months post-discharge to investigate the relationship between kidney recovery and mortality. While it examines long-term outcomes after acute COVID-19, it focuses on acute kidney injury sequelae rather than long COVID syndrome, and is observational without any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study assessed cognitive impairment prevalence in 34 post-COVID-19 hospitalized patients using TMSE and MoCA assessments at 2-week follow-up, comparing results to 22 healthy controls. The study found 61.76% prevalence of cognitive impairment but no statistically significant difference between post-COVID patients and healthy controls, suggesting cognitive dysfunction may not be directly attributable to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Retrospective study of 549 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examining predictors of long COVID and differences in persistent symptoms, chest imaging findings, and pulmonary function between ICU and non-ICU patients at 6-month follow-up. Identifies female gender, myocardial infarction, OSAS, low PCO2, and longer hospital stay as risk factors, with no specific intervention tested.

A follow-up study of 1,164 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors assessed the persistence of brain fog 11 months post-infection through phone interviews. The study found that 2.2% reported long-lasting brain fog, which was significantly associated with ICU admission during acute illness.

A case series of 134 post-COVID patients with dyspnea evaluated bronchodilator responsiveness during pulmonary rehabilitation, finding increased prevalence of obstructive airway defects and elevated bronchodilator response compared to historical controls. The study suggests post-COVID patients may benefit from adapted β2-inhalation therapy.

Prospective observational study of 133 COVID-19 patients with pulmonary embolism followed for 2 years to assess incidence of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD) and CTEPH. Found 18% had persistent thrombotic defects and 0.75% developed CTEPH, with right ventricular dysfunction at PE diagnosis as the independent risk factor.

A 24-month prospective observational study of severe COVID-19 patients following hospital discharge, measuring pulmonary function and chest CT imaging to assess long COVID respiratory sequelae. Found that 16-41% of patients at 24 months had reduced lung function, with fibrotic changes and persistent dyspnea, but no intervention was tested.

Prospective observational study of 133 COVID-19 patients hospitalized with pulmonary embolism, followed for 2 years to assess incidence of chronic thromboembolic disease and pulmonary hypertension. While studying post-COVID sequelae, this is specifically about acute PE complications during COVID-19 infection, not long COVID syndrome, and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study assessed intestinal inflammation and permeability in 86 long COVID patients using fecal calprotectin and zonulin measurements, correlating findings with gastrointestinal symptoms and quality of life. The study found that long COVID GI complaints are unlikely to be driven by local inflammatory mechanisms, with no significant differences in intestinal permeability between symptomatic and asymptomatic groups.

Retrospective study of 85 patients with preexisting neurological conditions who experienced long COVID symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found high prevalence of neurological, systemic, and cardiopulmonary symptoms, with anxiety, depression, and fatigue significantly associated with long COVID presentation and perceived worsening of baseline neurological conditions.

Prospective cohort study examining whether pre-existing perceived chronic stress predicts persistent symptoms one month after COVID-19 infection. Found that higher pre-infection stress levels (OR: 1.08) and pre-existing symptom burden significantly increase odds of ongoing symptomatic COVID-19.

Prospective observational study of 20 neonates infected with SARS-CoV-2 during early pandemic, assessed at 18-24 months corrected age using Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development. Found developmental delays in 45% of children (predominantly expressive language, fine motor, receptive language), but this addresses acute COVID effects in newborns rather than long COVID syndrome in post-acute patients.

This retrospective cohort study examines associations between nutritional intake during ICU admission for severe COVID-19 and long-term outcomes including post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and post-COVID conditions at 1-year follow-up. While the paper addresses long COVID sequelae, it is a secondary analysis of nutritional data from acute COVID-19 hospitalization rather than a prospective intervention trial testing a nutritional therapy treatment.

A longitudinal observational study following 48 post-COVID-19 patients after intensive care discharge, assessing lung function, voice quality, and quality of life at 4 and 8 months post-discharge. While the study documents improvements in pulmonary function and persistent dysphonia, it is an observational follow-up study without any intervention or treatment assigned to participants.

Prospective multicenter cohort study (PoCoRe, N=1,028) evaluating how post-COVID rehabilitation modulates psychological symptoms and functional health in long COVID patients. Depression improved significantly with rehabilitation (d=0.50), while fatigue remained largely unchanged, suggesting these are independent symptoms with different treatment responsiveness.

A prospective cohort study of COVID-19 ICU survivors assessed at 3 and 6 months post-discharge using pulmonary function tests, cardiopulmonary exercise testing, and quality of life questionnaires. While participants showed improved exercise capacity, persistent ventilatory deficiencies and significantly compromised health-related quality of life remained, with worsening mental health concerns and dyspnea.

This cohort study evaluates small fiber neuropathy (SFN) occurrence in 18 long COVID patients with neuropathic pain using multimodal assessment including skin biopsy, quantitative sensory testing, laser evoked potentials, and electrochemical skin conductance. While 82% showed abnormal skin biopsy and symptoms persisted beyond 6 months, the study is purely diagnostic/observational and does not test any treatment intervention.

Cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of lung function abnormalities in 936 post-COVID syndrome patients from the COVIDOM cohort, examining the relationship between dyspnea, small airway dysfunction, and PCS severity. While oscillometry measures differed between dyspneic and non-dyspneic groups, no intervention or treatment was tested, making this a descriptive mechanistic study rather than a treatment trial.

A cross-sectional study comparing clinical and epidemiological features of COVID-19 acute infection versus long COVID symptoms in 108 patients. The study describes symptom persistence in long COVID (fatigue, headache, shortness of breath, sleep disorders) but does not test any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study followed 302 SARS-CoV-2-positive participants in Zambia from July to September 2020 to assess persistent symptoms at two months post-infection. At median 54-day follow-up, 17% of symptomatic participants had not returned to pre-COVID health status, with cough, headache, and chest pain being most common persistent symptoms.

An ambidirectional cohort study examining the association between post-COVID-19 syndrome at 6 months and health-related quality of life at 6 and 12 months post-hospital discharge in 189 patients. Post-COVID syndrome was associated with quality of life impairment and anxiety/depression at 6 months but not at 12 months.

This prospective cohort study evaluates quality of life, sarcopenia, and proteinuria in 253 individuals with mild to moderate COVID-19 at 6 and 12 months post-infection. The study documents worse functional capacity, pain, and muscle strength in the moderate group at 6 months, with some improvements but persistent dysfunction at 12 months, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study using TriNetX data comparing cardiovascular and renal outcomes between long COVID patients and COVID-19 patients without long COVID. Finds increased prevalence of cardiovascular complications (DVT, PE, stroke, heart failure, IHD, hypertension) in long COVID patients but no significant association with myocardial infarction or renal outcomes.

This retrospective cohort study examined 27 COVID-19 pneumonia patients to assess psychological characteristics (optimism/pessimism) 6-12 months post-discharge using the Life Orientation Test-Revised. The study found that optimism levels decreased significantly with increasing pneumonia severity, with group III patients showing 26.2% lower optimism and higher pessimism compared to controls.

A cross-sectional study of 134 COVID-19 recovered patients (30-45 days post-recovery) assessing subclinical left ventricular dysfunction using speckle tracking echocardiography. Found subclinical LV dysfunction in 29.9% of patients with correlation to disease severity and inflammatory markers, suggesting persistent cardiac effects in post-COVID recovery.

Cohort study comparing cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) findings in 77 long COVID patients versus 766 non-COVID patients with undifferentiated dyspnea on exertion at Mayo Clinic. Long COVID patients showed significantly lower functional aerobic capacity and peak VO2, with higher rates of central nervous system changes during exercise, suggesting systemic exercise limitation rather than primary pulmonary dysfunction.

A retrospective cohort study of 454 patients from a Tunisian emergency department evaluating the prevalence and risk factors for long COVID symptoms following acute COVID-19 infection. The study found an 84.8% prevalence of long COVID and identified female sex as a significant risk factor, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Cross-sectional study assessing medical and health-related quality of life outcomes in 2,646 COVID-19 patients at median 142-day follow-up using questionnaires and blood investigations. Found 22% of participants felt worse than before, with common symptoms including anosmia, abnormal taste, and fatigue, and hospitalized patients showing more biochemical and hematological abnormalities.

This retrospective cohort study measures gamma' fibrinogen (GPF) levels in 52 COVID-19 patients and associates elevated GPF with mortality and thrombotic events. While it notes that 70% of long COVID patients have elevated GPF 6 weeks post-infection, the study does not test or evaluate any intervention—it is purely a biomarker observational study.

Prospective cardiopulmonary exercise testing study in 417 COVID-19 survivors across 5 UK/European centers, stratified by acute disease severity and post-acute symptoms. Found that post-acute symptoms (dyspnea, muscle pain) rather than acute disease severity were associated with reduced peak oxygen consumption and lower cardiac/pulmonary function parameters.

Retrospective cohort study comparing major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in older adults hospitalized for COVID-19 during the Omicron era versus Pre-Omicron era and historical influenza. Finds MACE risk declined in Omicron era but remains elevated compared to influenza controls.

This study uses UK Biobank data to examine long-term cardiovascular risk (>1000 days post-infection) in COVID-19 cases compared to controls, finding that hospitalization represents a coronary artery disease risk equivalent with genetic interactions via ABO blood type. It is a secondary analysis of existing cohort data without testing any treatment intervention.

This is a prospective cohort study (LIINC) examining cardiopulmonary pathophysiology in long COVID patients >1 year post-infection using exercise testing, cardiac imaging, and inflammatory biomarkers. The study found that early inflammatory markers and reduced exercise capacity are associated with long COVID symptoms, but it does not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

Prospective observational study of 18 PASC patients with persistent tachycardia and/or dyspnea on exertion, examining vascular resistance via aortic vascular impedance and autonomic function through ambulatory monitoring and tilt-table testing. Found elevated vascular resistance and orthostatic intolerance in most patients, suggesting COVID-19 vascular injury leads to abnormal autonomic signaling.

This study uses cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to assess myocardial injury and cardiac dysfunction in 30 COVID-19 recovered patients compared to 20 healthy controls. While it identifies persistent cardiovascular sequelae in recovering COVID-19 patients, it is observational and does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes electronic health records from 4,274 vaccinated individuals in Alabama to compare post-acute SARS-CoV-2 sequelae (PASC) and mortality rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals with breakthrough infections. While the study is about long COVID, it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it is a purely observational epidemiological analysis of PASC incidence and outcomes.

A cross-sectional observational study evaluating 113 COVID-19 survivors in Brazil to identify sociodemographic and clinical variables associated with post-acute COVID syndrome (PACS). The study found that severe acute infection, ICU admission, and supplementary oxygen use were associated with higher PACS prevalence, along with specific sequelae patterns including cough, gait issues, dysgeusia, and anosmia.

A prospective observational study examining echocardiographic changes in 83 long COVID patients at 3, 6, and >12 months post-infection. Found that right ventricular size increases over time and several cardiac structural parameters (posterior wall thickness, left atrium size, diastolic dysfunction) correlate with initial infection severity.

This retrospective cohort analysis from the ACTIV SARS-CoV-2 international registry examines cardiovascular disease (CVD) as a risk factor for adverse outcomes in the first 3 months after COVID-19 hospitalization across 7 Eurasian countries. The study found that 79.8% of 3,099 patients required unscheduled medical care post-recovery, with CVD significantly increasing mortality risk (OR 4.93), predominantly through cardiovascular events and complications.

This observational cohort study compares cardiometabolic risk factor changes (BMI, blood pressure, LDL) over time between COVID-19 infected and unexposed groups using health records data from OneFlorida+. The study found that SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with weight retention and rising blood pressure, but does not test any specific intervention or treatment.

Retrospective chart review of 144 PASC-CVS patients at a dedicated post-COVID cardiology clinic examining predictors of symptom improvement time. Found that time to presentation, dyspnea, and chest pain were significant predictors, with earlier care-seeking associated with faster symptom resolution.

This study evaluates subclinical left and right ventricular dysfunction in 189 COVID-19 recovered patients using speckle tracking echocardiography at baseline, 6 months, and 1 year. While the study demonstrates some improvement in cardiac function over time, it is a purely observational follow-up study with no treatment intervention tested.

IMPACT-COVID-19 is a prospective longitudinal cohort study investigating the prevalence, risk factors, and diagnostic biomarkers for acute myocarditis and pericarditis in long COVID patients with cardiac symptoms. The study found 30% prevalence of myocarditis/pericarditis, with prior ER visit during acute infection as a risk factor, and elevated ESR as a potential diagnostic marker.

Prospective registry study following 200 patients hospitalized for severe COVID-19 at 6, 18, and 30 months post-discharge to assess long-term cardiopulmonary symptoms and structural impairments. Long COVID prevalence decreased over time (73% at 6 months to 49% at 30 months), with fatigue as the most common symptom, though structural abnormalities (cardiac and pulmonary) were less frequent than reported symptoms.

This study examines LEF1-AS1 blood levels as a biomarker to predict neurological and cardiovascular outcomes in COVID-19 patients at 12-month follow-up using the PrediCOVID cohort. It is a secondary analysis of prognostic associations rather than a treatment trial, and therefore excluded from the intervention trials pipeline.

A prospective cohort study following 63 COVID-19 survivors with prior severe pneumonia requiring hospitalization to assess risk factors for post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis at 1- and 6-month follow-up. The study found that longer hospitalization during acute COVID-19 was associated with increased odds of traction bronchiectasis on follow-up CT scans, but is excluded as it is observational without testing any intervention or treatment.

This prospective cohort study investigates the prognostic value of cardiac CT delayed enhancement (CTDE) imaging in individuals with suspected cardiovascular post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC). While it is a legitimate long COVID study, it does not test or evaluate a treatment—it merely uses imaging to assess cardiovascular risk in PASC patients, making it ineligible for the treatment trials pipeline.

A prospective cohort study of 127 long COVID patients in Colombia assessing cardiopulmonary symptoms, pulmonary function, and physical performance at 6 months post-infection. The study found significant sex disparities, with women experiencing greater functional impairment including lower FEV1/FVC and reduced exercise capacity, suggesting vulnerable populations need tailored recovery strategies.

This longitudinal observational study examined cardiorespiratory fitness changes in 3,532 participants from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study, comparing those with SARS-CoV-2 infection (including long COVID cases with symptoms ≥3 months) to uninfected controls. The study found no significant differences in fitness decline across groups over 2.8 years, suggesting COVID infection does not accelerate age-related declines in cardiorespiratory fitness.

This retrospective cohort study compares cardiovascular outcomes between COVID-19 and influenza patients using propensity score matching on TriNetX data from 2020-2021. While it identifies higher arrhythmia risk in COVID-19 patients (suggesting long COVID sequelae), it is a secondary analysis of existing registry data rather than a treatment intervention study.

Retrospective analysis of 130 pediatric myocarditis cases comparing pre-COVID-19 and post-COVID-19 eras at a Pakistani hospital. While the study mentions post-COVID-19 changes in treatment patterns, it is not focused on long COVID as a primary condition but rather on myocarditis as a post-COVID complication in isolation, and the comparative analysis does not constitute a treatment trial.

Retrospective cohort study of 51 patients with COVID-19-related myocarditis examining sex differences in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) recovery. While 63% of patients with reduced LVEF recovered, this paper focuses on acute myocarditis as a direct COVID-19 complication rather than long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks to months post-infection), and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective study of 467 symptomatic long COVID patients assessing the prevalence and clinical characteristics of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Found POTS in 31% of patients, associated with younger age, predominantly female presentation, lower physical activity, and reduced exercise capacity compared to non-POTS long COVID patients.

Population-wide cohort study of 48 million adults examining arterial and venous thrombotic disease incidence following acute COVID-19 infection in 2020. While the paper studies post-COVID sequelae, it focuses on acute infection outcomes and vascular complications rather than long COVID syndrome, and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This case-control study compares cardiovascular and vascular phenotypes in COVID-19 hospitalized patients versus non-COVID controls at ≥12 weeks post-discharge. It is a secondary analysis of hospitalized acute COVID patients (not a treatment intervention study) and does not test any therapeutic intervention for long COVID.

This binational population-based cohort study examines the long-term cardiovascular outcomes after SARS-CoV-2 infection in South Korea and Japan using existing health insurance and medical databases. It finds that SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events up to 18 months post-infection, though absolute risks remain low.

Prospective observational cohort study comparing plasma biomarkers of endothelial function, thrombosis, and renal injury between post-COVID syndrome (PCS) patients and recovered controls at 3-36 months post-infection. Found elevated thrombotic markers and evidence of renal stress in post-hospitalized PCS patients but no significant biomarker differences in non-hospitalized cohorts.

This matched cohort study uses wearable data and EHR records from the All of Us Research Program to examine changes in physical activity and sleep patterns in individuals with high probability of long COVID versus matched controls. The study found that high-probability long COVID participants showed sustained reductions in physical activity and increased sleep irregularity at 330-360 days post-diagnosis, suggesting LC impacts health behaviors; however, this is an observational study without intervention and does not screen for treatment trials.

This prospective cohort study examines the relationship between myocardial injury during acute COVID-19 hospitalization and longer-term outcomes including post-acute sequelae at 6-12 months. The study is observational without intervention and represents a secondary analysis of hospitalization data rather than a treatment trial.

Retrospective cohort study examining cardiovascular disease risk >30 days after COVID-19 diagnosis using insurance claims data from 23.8 million adults. Finds significantly elevated CVD risk regardless of diabetes status, but this is a secondary analysis of claims data without an intervention component.

This study evaluates vascular and cardiac autonomic function in long COVID patients using a cross-sectional design (Study-1: 90 COVID-19 patients vs 180 controls) and a longitudinal follow-up component (Study-2: 41 patients followed for 27 weeks). It finds that COVID-19-related arterial stiffening is partially resolved over time but remains elevated compared to controls at 48 weeks.

This prospective cohort study compared cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction between Long COVID-19 patients with POTS and primary POTS patients using standardized autonomic testing. Long COVID-19 POTS patients showed significantly higher autonomic symptom burden despite having similar autonomic reflexes, but this is a diagnostic/descriptive study with no intervention or treatment provided.

This case-control study compared 34 COVID-19 survivors (median 4.6 months post-infection) with 103 matched controls using cardiac positron emission tomography to assess coronary flow reserve. The study found impaired myocardial blood flow reserve in COVID-19 survivors, suggesting long-term vascular complications, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective observational cohort study followed 37 COVID-19 recovered and 60 control participants over 12 months to investigate vascular consequences and blood pressure trajectories post-COVID-19. The study found significant increases in systolic/diastolic blood pressure and decreases in flow-mediated dilation in the COVID-19 group, but it is an observational study without treatment intervention, studying natural disease progression rather than testing a therapeutic intervention.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes cardiovascular outcomes following COVID-19 hospitalization in relation to social vulnerability using Medicare claims data linked with a cardiovascular registry. While it follows patients post-hospitalization, the focus is on acute COVID-19 hospitalization outcomes and cardiovascular complications rather than long COVID syndrome or any treatment intervention for persistent symptoms.

Retrospective cohort study examining long-term left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) decline in COVID-19 survivors compared to controls from 2016-2024. Found that both hospitalized and non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients had increased risk of LVEF decline, with more severe declines in hospitalized patients, but the study does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective observational cohort study of 40 COVID-19 ICU survivors with mechanical ventilation, assessing dyspnea persistence and emotional impact at 6 months post-discharge. Finds 62.5% with persistent dyspnea and common associated negative emotions (fear 60%, anxiety 57.5%), but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

Retrospective study of long-term neurological outcomes and quality of life in COVID-19 patients treated with ECMO for acute respiratory distress syndrome. While the paper mentions 'long term' outcomes, it focuses on acute COVID-19 hospitalization and ECMO management, not persistent long COVID symptoms occurring weeks/months after infection.

Prospective observational study of 49 severe COVID-19 ICU survivors assessing long-term cognitive, psychiatric, and physical impairments consistent with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) at a critical care recovery center. Results show substantial rates of cognitive impairment (23-38%), depression (33%), and reduced quality of life, highlighting the need for targeted follow-up and rehabilitation in COVID-19 ICU survivors.

Retrospective chart review of 52 COVID-19 ICU survivors seen in a Post ICU Recovery Clinic, describing the incidence and characteristics of Post Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS) including cognitive, psychological, and functional impairments two months post-discharge. This is a descriptive observational study with no intervention or treatment evaluation, making it ineligible for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

Retrospective follow-up study examining changes in sleep quality one month after acute COVID-19 hospitalization in 20 patients using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. The study documents worsening sleep quality post-infection but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining the association between pre-COVID cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and post-COVID CRF changes in 4,005 participants from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study. Findings show that individuals who developed long COVID had lower baseline CRF but COVID did not accelerate age-related CRF decline, with the authors noting few participants had severely disabling long COVID.

Prospective cohort study following 98 COVID-19 patients 4-12 weeks post-infection to characterize persistent symptoms and pulmonary/radiological abnormalities by initial disease severity. Found that 90.8% had residual symptoms (primarily dyspnea and fatigue) regardless of initial severity, with minimal objective abnormalities on spirometry or imaging.

Retrospective follow-up study of 25 severe COVID-19 survivors evaluated at 7 months post-discharge for pulmonary function, chest imaging, and inflammatory markers. Findings show radiological and functional impairment in a subset of survivors, associated with disease severity and inflammation levels, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Prospective registry study following COVID-19 survivors at 1, 3, and 6 months post-recovery to assess pulmonary function and exercise capacity. No intervention is given; this is a natural history/survivorship study designed to characterize sequelae rather than test a treatment.

This is a conference abstract describing a cross-sectional clinical assessment of 25 long COVID patients without comorbidities at a COVID-19 recovery clinic, documenting persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, cough, and gastrointestinal issues. The study presents no treatment intervention or outcomes evaluation, only baseline symptom documentation.

Retrospective study of 142 COVID-19 patients evaluating persistent CT findings 3 months after symptom onset, comparing imaging features to disease severity at presentation. Found residual opacities in 70% of patients, with ground-glass opacities and atelectasis most common; signs of fibrosis observed in only 12%.

Retrospective study of 15 severe COVID-19 patients (with ARDS) treated with high-dose pulsed methylprednisolone during acute infection, followed at 3 months post-discharge for pulmonary outcomes. While the study examines post-acute outcomes, it focuses on acute severe COVID-19 infection during hospitalization rather than long COVID syndrome (persistent symptoms weeks-to-months after infection).

Prospective observational study tracking pulmonary function and persistent symptoms in 30 COVID-19 recovered patients at 2 and 4 months post-symptom onset. Found significant improvements in most symptoms and pulmonary function parameters between visits, with median symptom count decreasing from 4 to 2.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study comparing inflammatory biomarkers and physical function in COVID-19 ALI/ARDS survivors versus pneumonia survivors over 3 years. Finds persistently elevated GDF-15 and lower 6-minute walk distance in ARDS survivors, but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

A prospective observational study examining post-COVID lung fibrosis in 200 severe COVID-19 patients and 118 controls, using CT imaging and inflammatory marker correlation at 10-12 week follow-up. The study found elevated inflammatory markers (LDH, ESR, CRP, ferritin) predicted fibrosis development and persistent exertional dyspnea in 54% of patients.

This cross-sectional study describes the organization and characteristics of pediatric long-COVID care programs across 13 countries, analyzing 431 long-COVID patients from 11 dedicated clinics. While it documents multidisciplinary care approaches and symptom patterns in children with long COVID, it is a descriptive analysis of existing care programs without testing any specific therapeutic intervention.

This study examines associations between acute COVID-19 hospitalization biomarkers (D-dimer, inflammatory markers) and CT imaging findings with reduced pulmonary diffusion capacity at 2-3 month follow-up. It is a secondary analysis of existing patient data without testing any treatment intervention.

International multicenter prospective follow-up study of 354 COVID-19 ICU survivors assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months post-discharge for functional, pulmonary, psychological, and cognitive status. The abstract indicates this is preliminary analysis with comprehensive pre-ICU evaluation still underway, suggesting incomplete data collection.

The UKILD post-COVID-19 study examined residual lung abnormalities in 3,700 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors using CT imaging within 240 days of discharge. The study estimated that up to 11% of discharged patients had moderate to very high risk of residual lung abnormalities, with risk factors including abnormal chest X-ray, reduced DLCO, and severe admission requiring ventilation.

summary: CANCOV is a Canadian multi-center prospective cohort study following 381 critically ill COVID-19 ICU survivors and their caregivers for up to 5 years, with detailed 2-year outcomes data. The study documents persistent multidimensional disability, cognitive dysfunction, respiratory impairment, and high healthcare utilization at 24 months post-ICU discharge, with significant variation across respiratory support modalities (ECMO, mechanical ventilation, HFNC, NIV/O2).

A study of 297 long COVID patients at New Cross Hospital evaluated the impact of tailored interventions (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychological support, dietary changes) on fatigue severity measured by the Fatigue Severity Score (FSS). Results showed 91 of 102 engaged patients reported improved fatigue with an average FSS decrease of 16.86, with better outcomes in patients without comorbidities.

This observational study examined chest CT scans from 1,712 long COVID patients in the RECOVER cohort to assess coronary artery and aortic calcification as cardiovascular risk markers. Non-radiologists identified calcification in 36.1% for coronary arteries and 34.8% for aortic arch, with prevalence increasing by CVD risk category, demonstrating that opportunistic imaging can supplement existing risk assessment.

This prospective cohort study examined rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) measures of blood coagulation in 93 COVID-19 ALI/ARDS survivors at 15-month follow-up to investigate associations between subclinical hypercoagulability and PASC phenotypes. Greater clot strength in fibrin-based assays was directly associated with PASC positivity, post-exertional malaise, and fatigue, suggesting fibrinogen dysregulation may underlie physical symptoms of long COVID.

A prospective cohort study comparing hospitalized COVID-19 patients with and without GI symptoms to examine in-hospital outcomes and long-term post-COVID sequelae. The study found that GI symptoms were associated with better in-hospital outcomes (lower oxygen requirements, higher complete recovery rates) but similar long-term post-discharge symptoms between groups.

Prospective follow-up study of COVID-19 patients who received ECMO for acute respiratory distress syndrome, assessing physical and mental health outcomes at 6 and 12 months post-discharge. While the study documents long-term sequelae, it focuses on acute COVID-19 complications (ARDS requiring ECMO) rather than post-acute sequelae/long COVID, and does not test any treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

Prospective cohort study of acute COVID-19 inpatients assessing muscle strength, malnutrition, and sarcopenia during hospitalization and at Day 30 post-discharge. Focuses on acute phase hospitalization outcomes rather than long COVID sequelae months after infection.

Prospective cohort study of 135 COVID-19 pneumonia patients followed at 2 and 12 months post-discharge to identify biomarkers of pulmonary fibrogenesis. Found that early periostin levels predict fibrotic changes, with 29.4% of patients showing persistent fibrotic changes at 12 months despite functional improvements.

Prospective cohort study of 61 individuals with persistent respiratory symptoms after COVID-19, examining pulmonary function tests and plasma biomarkers across different COVID-19 severity groups. Identified three biomarkers (LCN2, MMP-7, HGF) associated with impaired lung function that may serve as therapeutic or prognostic targets.

This study characterizes functional and transcriptomic changes in monocytes from COVID-19 patients across acute and convalescent phases. It is an observational immune profiling study with no intervention tested, making it ineligible for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

This observational cohort study of 617 COVID-19 patients tracked symptom resolution over one year, finding that 40% had symptoms at six months. The study identified anti-nucleocapsid antibody levels and pre-existing lung disease as predictors of prolonged symptom duration, but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

This retrospective cohort study of 929 long COVID patients with persistent pulmonary symptoms characterizes pulmonary impairment using longitudinal pulmonary function testing and CT imaging. The study identifies diffusion impairment and restriction as key features of pulmonary long COVID but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This longitudinal neuroimaging study followed 34 COVID-19 patients without acute neurological symptoms for 10 months post-discharge, measuring dynamic changes in brain gray matter, cerebral blood flow, and white matter using MRI. The study found that while some cortical changes were reversible, subcortical and white matter abnormalities persisted, suggesting long-term brain effects even in patients without acute neurological manifestations.

Observational study examining associations between chronic viral coinfections (EBV, CMV, HIV) and long COVID symptom development in a cohort of 280 SARS-CoV-2 infected adults. Findings show EBV reactivation correlates with fatigue and neurocognitive dysfunction, while prior CMV infection is protective against neurocognitive long COVID.

This cross-sectional study examined brain microstructure and cerebral blood flow changes in 51 COVID-19 patients (19 mild, 32 severe) 3 months post-discharge compared to healthy controls. The authors found more severe decreases in cortical thickness, cerebral blood flow, and white matter microstructure in severe COVID patients, with changes correlating to inflammatory markers.

A prospective longitudinal study examining neurological, neurocognitive, and neuropsychiatric sequelae in 67 COVID-19-convalescent individuals compared to 20 COVID-19-free controls, measuring biomarkers (LPS, kynurenine, quinolinic acid) at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-infection. The study found significantly higher rates of asthenia, olfaction/taste alterations, headache, memory dysfunction, and systemic symptoms in the convalescent group, with decreased kynurenine levels correlating with cognitive impairment.

This study investigates immune signatures in 50 COVID-19 patients with prolonged symptoms (>30 days) versus rapid recovery (<20 days), measuring SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell and antibody responses. Findings show that sustained symptom duration is associated with maintained antigen-specific immune responses and increased IgG avidity, suggesting persistent viral antigens as a potential etiology.

Retrospective descriptive study of 100 long COVID patients characterizing neuropsychiatric symptoms and cognitive impairment, finding fatigue, brain fog, and attention/executive dysfunction as prevalent outcomes. No intervention or treatment was tested; this is a passive observational characterization of symptoms in a cohort.

Retrospective cohort study estimating the prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition (≥90 days symptoms) in a tribal community on the Tule River Reservation, finding 21% prevalence and 37% reporting increased functional limitations. Study highlights health inequities in AI/AN populations and the need for inclusion in long COVID research, but is observational with no treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining changes in oral and maxillofacial disorders before and after COVID-19, finding increased mucormycosis and Sjögren's syndrome prevalence post-pandemic. Study focuses on acute COVID-19 infection effects on oral pathologies in Iraq, not persistent long COVID symptoms or interventions.

Prospective follow-up study of 1,354 recovered COVID-19 patients assessed 3 months post-discharge via telehealth to characterize persistent symptoms and clinical outcomes. Found fatigue (39.7%), stress/anxiety (27.6%), and new-onset diabetes/hypertension in some patients, with comorbidities and illness severity as independent risk factors for symptom persistence.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study following 536 long COVID patients over 12 months to assess prevalence and persistence of multi-organ impairment. Found that organ impairment persisted in 59% at 1-year follow-up, with common symptoms including breathlessness, cognitive dysfunction, and reduced quality of life.

A retrospective population-based cohort study of 201,799 UK participants examining socioeconomic inequalities in Long COVID risk, finding that participants in the most deprived decile had 46% higher odds of Long COVID (11.4% vs 8.2%) compared to the least deprived. The study identifies disparities by sex and occupation but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study derived and validated a prediction model to identify risk factors for developing long COVID in a large Scottish population. The study identified predictors including older age, higher BMI, severe COVID-19 infection, female sex, and deprivation, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This population-based cohort study analyzes healthcare utilization and costs in 282,080 individuals with long COVID over two years using matched controls and UK electronic health records. It demonstrates that LC patients have substantially higher healthcare utilization and costs across primary, secondary, and emergency care compared to multiple control groups, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Longitudinal descriptive study following 37 COVID-19 hospitalized patients for up to 12 months post-discharge to characterize their long COVID symptom experiences. Found persistent physical symptoms (87% at 12 months) with fatigue as most common, and significant quality of life impact despite overall normal PROMIS scores.

A multinational retrospective cohort study examining the risk of clinical sequelae across multiple organ systems over short-, medium-, and long-term periods (up to 2 years) after COVID-19 infection. The study found elevated risks for respiratory, cardiovascular, dermatological, and endocrine complications in the short-term, with most risks subsiding by medium- and long-term follow-up except for cardiovascular and endocrine complications.

Prospective observational cohort study following 141 COVID-19 patients for 90 days post-hospital discharge to assess symptom persistence and quality of life using SF-36. Found that 75.9% had persistent symptoms (fatigue, joint pain, dyspnea most common) with significantly lower QoL scores, but no intervention was tested.

Retrospective pre-post cohort study evaluating the impact of cognitive functioning and fatigue on rehabilitation treatment outcomes in 66 COVID-19 hospitalized patients. Results showed significant improvements in disability levels after rehabilitation, with mechanical ventilation patients benefiting most, regardless of baseline neuropsychological functioning.

Retrospective cohort study assessing hand grip strength, walking speed, functional mobility, and postural control at 1-year follow-up after ICU admission for COVID-19. Found functional impairments in 45% of participants, with longer ICU stay and diabetes as risk factors, suggesting need for long-term rehabilitation follow-up.

A prospective cohort study of 33 mild COVID-19 patients followed for 12 months post-discharge, assessing pulmonary function, exercise capacity, and mental health outcomes. Findings show persistent impairments in these domains up to 1 year, supporting the need for long-term rehabilitation monitoring in post-COVID patients.

A 2-year prospective follow-up study of 19 COVID-19 patients who survived ECMO therapy, assessing cardiopulmonary, neurocognitive, psychological, and functional outcomes. While cardiopulmonary status improved, significant long-term impairments persisted in cognition, mood, and social functioning.

A prospective cohort study evaluating a virtual multidisciplinary rehabilitation program for 36 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients using a within-subject design with waiting period control. The program significantly reduced symptoms (C19-YRSm and MFIS scores) after 6 weeks of intervention compared to baseline, with no improvement during the waiting period.

Multicenter ambisective study following 905 COVID-19 patients with acute headache over 9 months to characterize the long-term trajectory of post-COVID headache. Found that while median headache duration was 2 weeks, approximately 19% had persistent headache at 3 months and 16% at 9 months, with higher acute intensity predicting longer persistence.

A retrospective cohort and nested case-control study examining factors associated with supplemental oxygen requirement and persistent symptoms 1 year after severe COVID-19 infection in 135 ICU patients. The study identified female sex and high comorbidity burden as risk factors for prolonged oxygen requirement and documented high prevalence of persistent dyspnea, myalgia, and other post-COVID symptoms, but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective follow-up study of 103 ICU survivors from acute COVID-19 hospitalization tracked long-term outcomes (>6 months post-discharge), including persistent symptoms, organ function recovery, and mental health complications. While it documents long COVID sequelae in critical illness survivors, it is a passive observational study with no treatment intervention tested.

This retrospective cohort study examines associations between COVID-19 symptom severity and cognitive impairment (memory and executive function) in older adults using National Health and Aging Trends Study data. The study finds that moderate-to-severe COVID-19 symptoms and cardiovascular comorbidities are associated with increased risk of poor cognitive outcomes, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective observational study of 113 severe COVID-19 survivors treated in ICU, assessing health-related quality of life 4 months after admission using EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. Found significant impairment in anxiety/depression (46%), usual activities (37%), and mobility (29%), with worse outcomes in patients with longer respiratory support and hospital stays.

Prospective cohort study following 132 ICU survivors of severe COVID-19 at 6 months post-discharge to assess long-term health outcomes and quality of life using validated instruments. Most patients achieved positive outcomes similar to general population, though physical function was significantly worse and substantial minority reported PTSD and loneliness.

Prospective cohort study following 74 ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients at discharge, 30 days, and 90 days post-discharge to assess cognitive and functional recovery. Participants showed significant functional improvement by 90 days with 96% achieving independence, but cognitive changes were minimal and quality-of-life scores remained below normal in several domains.

This study examines ICU memory recall in acute COVID-19 survivors who were critically ill, evaluating the relationship between deep sedation and delusional memories. While the paper studies COVID-19 patients, it focuses on acute critical illness sequelae (ICU delirium and memories) rather than long COVID, which is defined as persistent symptoms weeks to months post-infection in non-critically ill populations.

Prospective multicenter cohort study following 262 critical COVID-19 survivors from Swedish ICUs at 3 and 12 months post-discharge, assessing fatigue and mental health symptoms using validated scales. Fatigue improved from 50% to 40% between timepoints, but mental illness symptoms remained stable; worse functional outcomes and reduced sleep were identified as risk factors for long-lasting symptoms.

Retrospective EHR study analyzing symptom patterns and risk factors for developing long COVID (PASC) in 2,153 PCR-confirmed COVID-19 patients. Identified PASC prevalence at 11%, characterized five symptom clusters, and found that female sex and specific early symptoms predicted PASC development.

Prospective cohort study of 24-week follow-up in moderate to severe COVID-19 cases from India to estimate long COVID prevalence and identify associated risk factors. Reports prevalence rates (35-87.4%) and symptom profiles including respiratory dysfunction, cognitive impairment, fatigue, chest pain, and psychological symptoms.

This cross-sectional study compared functional capacity and work performance in 30 healthcare workers who had mild COVID-19 one month prior versus 30 matched healthy controls. Healthcare workers with COVID-19 showed significantly worse functional outcomes and work performance despite mild disease severity, with 77% experiencing persistent symptoms including fatigue, myalgia, and respiratory symptoms.

Retrospective cohort study describing the prevalence and characteristics of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) symptoms in 132 patients at a tertiary-care academic center. The study identifies fatigue, dyspnea, and cognitive dysfunction as the most common PASC symptoms and reports higher prevalence in women, Caucasian individuals, and middle-aged patients, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Retrospective cohort study describing a post-ICU recovery clinic model and outcomes for COVID-19 ICU survivors during April-December 2020. While the study documents cognitive, psychiatric, and functional impairments in ICU survivors, it focuses on acute ICU complications (post-intensive care syndrome) rather than long COVID, which is defined as persistent symptoms weeks to months after acute infection in non-critically ill patients.

summary: A prospective 12-month longitudinal observational study of 92 hospitalized COVID-19 patients tracking residual symptoms, organ function, and quality of life outcomes post-discharge. While documenting that 15.5% of patients experienced persistent symptoms at 12 months including 'brain fog,' the study is observational without intervention and does not evaluate any treatment.

This observational study examined whether SARS-CoV-2 vaccination alters clinical presentation in 477 post-COVID patients at Mayo Clinic, comparing vaccinated (51.4%) and unvaccinated subjects. Vaccinated patients reported significantly fewer symptoms including abdominal pain, anosmia, parosmia, chest pain, dizziness, numbness, dyspnea, tremors, and weakness, suggesting vaccination may reduce post-COVID symptom burden.

Retrospective study of 33 home health care patients infected with Omicron COVID-19, comparing hospitalization and survival outcomes by comorbidity profiles and nursing care environment. While post-COVID syndrome symptoms (appetite/weight loss) were observed and associated with IL-6 inflammation, no treatment intervention was tested or evaluated.

Retrospective cohort study of 19 patients with inflammatory demyelinating diseases treated with anti-CD20 who developed COVID-19-associated organizing pneumonia. While 13 patients experienced long COVID, this is a secondary complication analysis, not a treatment intervention trial for long COVID itself.

A prospective cohort study following 178 COVID-19 patients hospitalized with significant pulmonary involvement for 3 months post-discharge to assess cardiac, pulmonary, and laboratory recovery. Study found persistent pulmonary changes (reticulation, fibrosis), decreased cardiac abnormalities, significant improvements in inflammatory markers, but lingering symptoms like myalgia and taste loss.

Prospective cohort study evaluating functional impairments and limitations in 53 long COVID patients across three time points over 12 months using the ICF framework. Found significant increases in disabilities (mental, sensory, pain, movement, cardiovascular, immunological, respiratory functions) and activity limitations from baseline to 6-12 months, with specific symptom-disability associations identified.

Retrospective multicenter observational study of COVID-19 ICU survivors examining new medical conditions and medication changes at hospital discharge. While focused on post-acute outcomes in ICU survivors, the paper does not specifically address long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks to months post-infection) and does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Cross-sectional survey of MS patients examining overlap between PASC symptoms and MS manifestations using the NIH RECOVER PASC score. Found lower than expected PASC prevalence (1.5%) in MS patients and similar symptom proportions across infection groups, complicating PASC assessment in this population.

This pilot study investigated interferon-gamma-mediated metabolic pathways (tryptophan catabolism, neopterin, tyrosine, nitrite) in 31 hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute infection and 60-day follow-up. While it documents persistent symptoms (neurological: 17.2%, fatigue: 51.7%, sleep disturbance: 34.5%) in long COVID reconvalescence, it is a mechanistic biomarker study with no treatment intervention tested.

Retrospective single-center study of 42 post-COVID-19 patients examining the clinical features and prevalence of fatigue and associated comorbidities. Found that fatigue (90.5% prevalence) was the most prominent symptom and was associated with daytime sleepiness and depressed mood, but not with COVID-19 severity or demographic factors.

This study uses data from a population-based birth cohort to examine whether confirming COVID-19 infection status influences Long COVID symptom reporting, testing for a potential nocebo effect. The analysis found no evidence of a nocebo effect or moderation by sex or anxiety in Long COVID symptom reporting.

This retrospective cohort study compared long-term health outcomes in dementia patients with and without prior COVID-19 infection using electronic health records from a large health system. COVID-19 survivors with dementia had significantly higher risks of mortality, cardiovascular events, dysphagia, dyspnea, fatigue, sleep disturbances, and falls compared to non-infected controls.

A cross-sectional study of 2,646 randomly selected COVID-19 patients assessed symptom persistence and health-related quality of life at median 142 days follow-up. Found 22% felt worse than pre-COVID, with hospitalized patients showing more biochemical/haematological abnormalities and higher symptom burden.

This 12-month prospective cohort study examined nonlinear EEG parameters in 83 long COVID patients during rest and cognitive/motor tasks to characterize brain electrical activity patterns. The study found task-dependent changes in EEG activity and complexity over time but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study comparing vascular parameters (intima-media thickness, arterial velocities, inflammatory markers) in 72 post-COVID-19 patients versus 11 controls over 12 months. Found increased IMT and altered arterial velocities in post-COVID patients with no DVT instances, suggesting potential atherosclerotic changes warranting further investigation.

Prospective observational study comparing brain activity via EEG and cognitive function in 53 COVID-19 patients and 30 controls over one year post-infection. Found reduced brain activity at rest and during cognitive tasks in COVID-19 group at 6-12 months, with long-term changes in cognitive function, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Retrospective analysis of 205 medical records from Vietnamese inpatients with long COVID, describing the prevalence and characteristics of clinical and subclinical manifestations. Most common symptoms were fatigue (59%), dyspnea (53%), and cough (43%), with 80% experiencing respiratory symptoms and 42% reporting neurological symptoms including sleep disturbance.

A prospective cohort study following 756 hospitalized COVID-19 patients over 2-3 years to identify risk factors for chronic pain and fibromyalgia-like symptoms in post-COVID syndrome. Key predictors included anxiety/depression severity, sleep disruption, and reduced handgrip strength, highlighting modifiable targets for early intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 317 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) assessing pulmonary function (DLCO) and quality of life (SF-36) at 3 and 6 months post-discharge. While physical functioning improved by 6 months, non-physical QoL domains declined across all severity groups, and diffusion capacity remained decreased in severely affected patients.

This retrospective cohort study followed 410 hospitalized Omicron patients at 6 months and 1 year post-discharge to identify mortality predictors and symptom trends. The study found that 86% experienced persistent symptoms at 6 months, with elevated CRP (≥15.38 mg/L) as a predictor of symptom persistence, but no intervention was tested or evaluated.

This cross-sectional study evaluates clinical and imaging findings in 110 patients with post-COVID olfactory dysfunction compared to 50 COVID-negative controls using endoscopy, smell testing, and MRI. The study identifies increased olfactory bulb dimensions and edema as key mechanisms of COVID-related olfactory dysfunction, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective follow-up study examined the prevalence of PTSD symptoms among 903 COVID-19 patients 3 months after discharge from hospitalization. The study found that 23.5% of patients screened positive for clinically significant PTSD, with key risk factors including multiple clinical symptoms at disease onset and residual respiratory symptoms post-discharge.

This retrospective cohort study uses linked patient data from UK primary and secondary care to compare healthcare utilization in the 3 months before and after COVID-19 diagnosis across 7,791 individuals. The study documents increased non-elective admissions, GP attendances, and mental health contacts post-COVID, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study compared cytokine (IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα) and cortisol serum levels across four groups: never infected, infected without PASC, resolved PASC, and ongoing PASC patients. The study found no significant differences in these biomarker levels between groups, suggesting they may not be reliable markers for PASC identification.

Retrospective follow-up study of 565 severe/critical COVID-19 patients evaluating post-acute symptoms persisting 4+ weeks after symptom onset. Found 62.6% had persistent symptoms (pulmonary and neuropsychiatric most common), with obesity, ICU admission, and mechanical ventilation as risk factors.

Longitudinal observational study tracking 4,670 COVID-19 patients discharged from a Mexico City hospital over 90 days to identify symptom clusters and risk factors for long COVID. Found that neurological, dermatological, and mood disorder symptoms persisted in >30% of patients, with women and those requiring mechanical ventilation at higher risk.

Retrospective cohort study of 128 COVID-19 hospitalized patients followed in an outpatient clinic, documenting long-term symptoms and laboratory abnormalities at follow-up. Study describes prevalence of respiratory, constitutional, GI, and neurological symptoms but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 112 severe/critical COVID-19 survivors for 6 and 12 months post-discharge to assess pulmonary function, chest imaging, and quality of life outcomes. Most clinical parameters improved over 12 months despite persistent radiological findings, with diffusion capacity remaining impaired.

This study evaluated oral zinc and steroid treatment in 71 long COVID patients with olfactory and gustatory dysfunction, using standardized smell and taste tests at baseline, 2-4 months, and ~10 months follow-up. Most patients showed persistent olfactory dysfunction despite treatment, with 91.2% reporting subjective improvement at 10 months follow-up, though objective testing showed continued hyposmia in 71-77% of patients.

This prospective longitudinal study followed COVID-19 patients over 12 months to identify predictors of clinically meaningful declines in health-related quality of life. The study found that shortness of breath, lower BMI, and history of anxiety were significant predictors of worsening HRQoL, but did not evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

A retrospective observational study characterizing persistent COVID-19 symptoms in 1,542 primary care patients in Spain between December 2020 and May 2022. The study documents symptom prevalence (12.39% at 90 days), affected systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, psychoneurological), and average symptom duration (178 days), but does not test any intervention or treatment.

A prospective observational feasibility study of Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) delivered via telehealth to 61 patients with COVID-19-related symptoms, documenting clinical encounters, symptom outcomes, and treatment patterns. Results showed 49 patients reported symptom resolution sufficient to complete treatment, with good recruitment and retention supporting feasibility for a future randomized trial.

Follow-up study of 329 vaccinated individuals tracking late disorders 6 months post-booster vaccination, identifying conditions possibly linked to vaccination (73.1%), long COVID (0.8%), or both (26.8%). The study does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention but rather characterizes and differentiates adverse outcomes between vaccination and long COVID.

This cross-sectional study analyzes cytokine profiles in 390 long COVID patients stratified by SARS-CoV-2 variant epoch, comparing pro-inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) across early versus later variant periods. The study found that early-epoch long COVID patients had persistently elevated peripheral cytokine levels compared to later epochs, though symptom clusters remained similar across all variants.

Retrospective longitudinal study comparing functional outcomes (ADLs, cognitive function, clinical care needs) in 1,310 LTC home residents with COVID-19 versus 2,301 without COVID-19 over seven months post-infection. Found initially greater deterioration in ADLs and clinical care needs in COVID-positive residents, but trajectories converged over time with similar overall outcomes.

Describes a novel three-tier integrated multidisciplinary NHS rehabilitation pathway in Leeds for managing long COVID in the community, comprising specialist MDT assessment, community therapy teams, and self-management support. Reports on the service model development and implementation using standardized outcome measures including the C19-YRS.

Community-based prospective cohort study investigating short-term impacts of COVID-19 on depressive symptoms and cognitive decline in the BRAVE cohort (n=1,012). Found no significant associations between COVID-19 infection and depressive symptoms or cognitive decline at 3-4 months post-infection.

A 2-year longitudinal cohort study of 968 healthcare workers infected with SARS-CoV-2 across three pandemic waves, tracking post-infection complications and the impact of vaccination. The study found that fully immunized personnel had lower hospitalization and complication rates, with documented post-COVID complications including neurological, cardiovascular, and pulmonary sequelae.

Retrospective cross-sectional study comparing neuropsychological and cardiopulmonary outcomes in 321 long COVID patients stratified by acute infection severity (outpatient vs inpatient). Found that functional sequelae in mild-disease patients were comparable to severe-disease patients, with insomnia and activity limitations prominent in outpatients despite worse cognition in inpatients.

This retrospective cohort study examines characteristics and healthcare utilization patterns among 10,265 U.S. primary care patients with an ICD-10-CM diagnosis code for Post-COVID-19 Condition between 2021-2023. The study documents symptom prevalence across body systems and identifies potential diagnosis gaps, particularly in rural and economically disadvantaged populations, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective observational follow-up study tracking 83 Indian patients with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 at 2, 6, and 12 weeks post-acute infection to characterize recovery trajectories and post-COVID syndrome incidence. Found 50% had complete symptom resolution by 6 weeks, while 45 patients (54%) developed persistent symptoms consistent with post-COVID syndrome.

This prospective cohort study examined how COVID-19 infection affects seminal fluid analysis parameters in 44 male participants followed over 6 months. While it demonstrates temporary reductions in semen quality in the first 3 months post-infection with recovery by 6 months, the study is not about long COVID but rather acute post-viral effects on male reproductive health.

This pilot observational study evaluated the feasibility of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) to assess Integrative Medical Group Visits (IMGV) as an intervention for long COVID patients. Results showed improvements in stress (PSS), anxiety (GAD-2), and symptom interference (MYMOP), supporting the use of these measures for future controlled efficacy trials.

Retrospective study of 540 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examining functional status at discharge and two months later using the PCFS scale. Identifies age and admission NEWS2 score as independent risk factors for functional impairment, though multiple clinical and laboratory factors were associated with worse outcomes.

Retrospective propensity-matched cohort study using EHR data to evaluate long-term thromboembolic risk in PASC patients compared to non-PASC controls over up to 5 years.
