Found significantly elevated risk of thrombotic events (17.4% vs 10.0%) in PASC cohort, but this is an observational epidemiological study without treatment intervention.

This study compared transcriptomic profiles of peripheral blood leukocytes in 162 COVID-19 convalescent plasma donors versus 40 healthy controls, examining gene expression changes during the post-acute period. Results identified persistent alterations in inflammatory pathways and T-cell activation/exhaustion markers for months after infection, with the most marked changes occurring 120-150 days post-diagnosis.

This cross-sectional study investigates thrombotic markers in 276 post-COVID syndrome patients, finding that an elevated von Willebrand factor/ADAMTS13 ratio is present in nearly one-third of patients and is 4 times more likely in those with impaired exercise capacity. The findings suggest a prothrombotic state and microvascular/endothelial dysfunction in long COVID pathogenesis, indicating a potential role for antithrombotic therapy.

Prospective cohort study of 518 children previously hospitalized with COVID-19, followed up 256 days post-discharge to assess persistent symptoms and risk factors. Found 24.3% experienced persistent symptoms, with older age and allergic diseases as risk factors, but the study is observational without any treatment intervention.

This study examines angiopoietin-2 as a biomarker to predict mortality and pulmonary outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute infection. While the authors mention angiopoietin-2 blockade as a potential treatment, this is a prognostic biomarker study of acute COVID-19 hospitalization, not a long COVID treatment trial.

Population-based registry study examining acute COVID-19 severity and mortality outcomes in 1,166 Spanish patients with hematologic malignancies between February 2020 and February 2021. The paper documents high mortality (33%) and post-acute persistent symptoms in 1 in 6 patients but does not evaluate any treatment intervention for long COVID.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study following 728 COVID-19 survivors with residual lung abnormalities at 6 months, 12 months, 2 years, and 3 years post-discharge. Most patients showed improvement in radiological abnormalities and pulmonary function over time, but over one-third continued to have persistent lung abnormalities at 3 years associated with respiratory symptoms and reduced diffusion capacity.

This study measured circulating anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) in COVID-19 survivors at 3, 6, and 12 months post-infection and assessed their association with long COVID symptoms (fatigue, cough, dyspnea). The findings show that persistent ANAs and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β) correlate with symptom severity, but this is an observational biomarker study with no intervention tested.

A prospective multicentre cohort study following 485 severe-to-critical COVID-19 survivors for up to 12 months post-discharge to describe respiratory recovery trajectories and health-related quality of life. While pulmonary function improved modestly over 12 months, approximately 41% of patients had significant radiological sequelae at final assessment, with multiple factors predicting impaired diffusing capacity at 3 months.

This UK national surveillance and cohort study evaluates the incidence of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) as a potential long-term complication following COVID-19-associated pulmonary embolism. The study found that CTEPH is a rare post-COVID complication (1.2% of cases) and that simple risk scoring can effectively identify high-risk patients for further investigation, but it is excluded as it does not study a treatment intervention.

Population-based case-control study (n=23,452) using prospective app-based symptom logging to examine whether pre-infection symptoms affected long COVID duration. Found that individuals with baseline symptoms had longer illness duration and increased odds of long illness (≥8 weeks), though two-thirds of long illness cases were asymptomatic before infection.

Prospective cohort study describing pulmonary outcomes (dyspnea, lung function, CT findings) in 103 COVID-19 patients 3 months after hospital discharge. No intervention was tested; this is a passive observational follow-up study of post-acute COVID recovery, not a treatment trial.

Prospective follow-up study of 647 COVID-19 survivors at 3 months post-discharge evaluating pulmonary function and persistent symptoms. Found abnormal diffusing capacity in 54% of patients, with severity associated with initial CT findings and ARDS, but this is a passive observational study with no intervention tested.

Prospective observational study following 84 severe COVID-19 survivors over 12 months to assess pulmonary sequelae using spirometry, diffusing capacity, walking tests, and chest imaging. Found persistent lung abnormalities and exercise-induced desaturation at 12 months despite gradual functional improvement over time.

Prospective multicentre observational study following 145 COVID-19 patients at 60 and 100 days post-diagnosis with comprehensive cardiopulmonary assessments including lung function, imaging, and echocardiography. Found persistent symptoms in 41% at day 100 (mainly dyspnea), impaired lung function in 21%, and CT abnormalities in 63%, with significant improvement over time.

This study followed 20 COVID-19 ICU survivors who received a 3-week intensive multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation program, assessing their functional status 18 months post-rehabilitation using the PCFS scale. At 18-month follow-up, 70% achieved complete functional recovery (grade 0), with the remainder showing only negligible to mild functional limitations, suggesting pulmonary rehabilitation improved long-term outcomes in severe COVID-19 survivors.

This prospective cohort study assessed exercise tolerance using incremental shuttle walk tests in 378 COVID-19 survivors at 5 and 12 months post-hospital discharge. The study found no significant improvement in exercise tolerance between the two timepoints, highlighting the persistent exercise limitation in post-COVID patients.

COVIDOM is a population-based cohort study that developed and validated a PCS severity score based on 12 long-term symptom complexes in German COVID-19 survivors at 6-12 months post-infection. The score correlates with quality of life, inflammatory markers, D-dimer levels, and lung function impairment, with early predictors including acute symptom burden, resilience, and anxiety.

This study characterizes monocyte migration profiles and immune dysfunction in acute COVID-19 and long COVID patients compared to other respiratory viral infections. It identifies distinct monocyte signatures associated with specific long COVID symptoms (lung injury and fatigue) but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective follow-up study evaluated the long-term lung effects of C21 (angiotensin II type 2 receptor agonist) treatment in COVID-19 survivors, using CT scans 90-170 days post-treatment. C21-treated subjects showed a nearly 50% relative reduction in CT disease severity score compared to placebo, suggesting potential for reducing long-term lung injury in post-COVID patients.

Prospective cohort study following 128 COVID-19 survivors over 1 year to characterize long COVID symptoms, spirometric abnormalities, and natural history. Found 67% had persistent symptoms at baseline, declining to 42% by year-end; female gender and acute dyspnea predicted long COVID development.

This cross-sectional study assessed fatigue and pulmonary function in 218 patients 3-6 months after COVID-19 hospitalization, stratified by disease severity. Fatigue was most prevalent in patients with short hospital stays and normal lung function, suggesting paradoxical symptom burden independent of acute infection severity.

Population-based survey of 1,895 long COVID patients in the Czech Republic describing clinical characteristics, symptom profiles, and pulmonary findings in relation to acute COVID-19 severity. No intervention or treatment was tested; this is a descriptive epidemiological study only.

A cross-sectional assessment of 443 post-COVID-19 patients from a specialist clinic evaluating respiratory outcomes including spirometry, 6-minute walk test, and chest imaging. Abnormal spirometry (FVC <80%) was found in 47% of patients and was associated with older age, longer initial hospitalization, and oxygen desaturation during functional testing.

Prospective cohort study following 94 post-COVID-19 patients (63 hospitalized, 31 non-hospitalized) over ~1.5 years to assess quadriceps muscle strength recovery using isometric dynamometry. Quadriceps strength modestly improved in the first 7-9 months but plateaued thereafter, with approximately half of both groups remaining weak at final assessment.

Prospective observational study of 89 COVID-19 patients with chest CT imaging at 3 and 6 months to assess long-term pulmonary sequelae. Found persistent parenchymal changes in 88.5% at 3 months and fibrotic-like changes in 52% of patients, with age >65 years, prolonged hospitalization, and initial CT severity as predictors of fibrosis.

Retrospective cohort study of 38 COVID-19 patients followed at 90 days post-onset to assess persistent respiratory symptoms and functional impairment. Found high rates of spirometry abnormalities (73%) and reduced exercise capacity in those with severe pneumonia, with dyspnea and restrictive defects being most common.

A longitudinal study evaluating the effects of inpatient disease-specific rehabilitation on neuropsychological symptoms in 49 long COVID patients, mostly healthcare workers. Rehabilitation produced significant improvements in depression, anxiety, and processing speed over a 3-week treatment period.

Prospective cohort study following 61 COVID-19 hospitalized patients one month after discharge to assess persistent symptoms. Found 77% reported dyspnea and 24.5% had hyperventilation syndrome, with symptoms associated with age and comorbidities.

Retrospective analysis of 70 long-COVID patients who underwent inpatient rehabilitation, investigating the prevalence of sleep-related breathing disorders (SRBD) via polysomnography/polygraphy. Found 37% SRBD prevalence overall, higher than population average, with SRBD patients showing greater need for respiratory support during acute COVID hospitalization.

This longitudinal observational study evaluated a subacute rehabilitation program (respiratory and physical therapy) on work ability in 38 healthcare workers who acquired COVID-19 at their workplace. The Work Ability Index showed significant but modest improvement after mean rehabilitation duration of 30 days, though most patients remained poorly able to work post-intervention.

This cross-sectional study assessed fatigue and functional capacity in 148 post-COVID patients at 12 months post-discharge, stratified by treatment setting (home, hospital ward, ICU). The study found fatigue was clinically relevant across all groups and significantly correlated with functional capacity measures, but did not test any intervention or treatment.

This cross-sectional study enrolled 309 long COVID patients stratified by respiratory support intensity during acute COVID-19 to identify clinical phenotypes and outcomes. Patients with no respiratory support had less fatigue and mood disorders, while hospitalization severity was associated with different inflammatory markers and neuropsychiatric sequelae.

Prospective follow-up study of 198 COVID-19 survivors at 3 months post-discharge, assessing functional capacity via cardiopulmonary exercise testing, pulmonary function tests, and 6-minute walking test. Found 42% of patients presented with dyspnea at 3 months post-discharge, independent of initial disease severity.

This observational cohort study from the Swiss COVID Lung study examined the association between airway microbiota composition and lung function impairment 3-12 months after severe COVID-19 in 72 hospitalized patients. Patients with reduced total lung capacity showed distinct microbiota profiles with lower bacterial diversity and different phylum composition compared to those with normal lung function, suggesting microbiota may play a role in respiratory recovery.

Prospective cohort study following 161 COVID-19 patients from the first pandemic wave in the Netherlands, assessing long-term symptom burden one year after infection using the ABCoV tool. Identifies smoking, high BMI, and lack of exercise as risk factors for persistent Post-COVID symptoms, with 12% of patients reporting substantial symptoms at one-year follow-up.

This observational cohort study assessed small airways disease prevalence in 40 patients 1 year after COVID-19 hospitalization using forced oscillometry testing. Small airways dysfunction was found in 28% of patients, though it was not associated with self-reported breathlessness, cough, ventilatory status, or markers of inflammation.

Retrospective case note review of 1,285 referrals to a regional Long COVID service analyzing employment status and occupational impact. Study documents that 30% of long COVID patients were unemployed or on long-term sick leave, with healthcare workers disproportionately affected, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 137 COVID-19 hospitalized survivors comparing 94 with long COVID to 43 asymptomatic controls. Identified female sex, obesity, respiratory comorbidities, and prolonged hospitalization as predictive factors for persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, and joint pain.

Prospective cross-sectional study of 108 healthcare workers examining the incidence of post-COVID syndrome (PCS) at 3 months post-infection and its correlation with SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibody levels. PCS was detected in 63% of participants, with higher IgG levels associated with PCS symptoms, suggesting immunological mechanisms in PCS pathogenesis.

This cross-sectional study assessed psychological burden and health status in 99 long COVID patients using standardized scales (anxiety, depression, PTSD, fatigue, quality of life). The study found significant gender differences, with females reporting higher rates of anxiety and asthenia compared to males, but did not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study assessing pulmonary function, exercise tolerance, and muscle strength in 93 long COVID patients 3+ months post-infection. The study characterizes the consequences of SARS-CoV-2 on respiratory and muscular function but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 88 long COVID patients referred to pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) in the UK, evaluating adherence rates and outcomes. PR improved symptoms in over half of patients, but 35% were unable to complete the program due to various health and personal factors.

Observational study measuring physical activity levels and pulmonary/physical function in 49 patients 1 year after hospital discharge for severe COVID-19. Finds that 65% of patients retained low PA levels (<7500 steps/day), with PA positively associated with exercise capacity but not with lung function metrics.

This prospective cohort study followed 93 critically ill COVID-19 patients for up to 12 months post-discharge to assess long-term lung function impairment and recovery. No treatment was administered; this is a passive observational follow-up study documenting natural recovery of respiratory parameters rather than evaluating an intervention.

A prospective cohort study of 194 long COVID patients examined the prevalence of exercise-induced oxygen desaturation (EID) and its relationship to exertional dyspnea and pulmonary function tests at 6-month follow-up. The study found that 17% of patients showed persistent EID during 6-minute walking tests, which correlated with reduced walk distance and diffusing capacity but not dyspnea severity.

This cross-sectional study assessed the frequency of acute and persistent COVID-19 symptoms in 697 children aged 0-18 years following SARS-CoV-2 infection. While 79.2% experienced acute symptoms, 26.8% reported persistent symptoms at 30 days and 10.2% at 90 days; risk factors for persistence included being overweight/obese, female sex, and acute-phase asthenia.

Observational case-control study comparing cognitive function (anxiety, depression, memory, concentration) in 455 long COVID patients versus 451 matched controls one year post-infection. Found significant cognitive impairment in long COVID group but no treatment intervention was tested.

Prospective cohort study evaluating the 1-minute sit-to-stand test as a diagnostic tool for long COVID, comparing physiological parameters (heart rate, SpO2) in 32 post-COVID patients with and without long COVID criteria. The study identifies lower heart rate at 60 seconds as a potential diagnostic marker but does NOT test any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 254 post-COVID patients assessing persistent dyspnea at 4 weeks post-infection and identifying predictive factors. Found dyspnea in 53% of patients, correlated with initial severity, female sex, cough, asthenia, hyperventilation, and PTSD, but not with imaging severity.

This observational case-control study compared pain characteristics in 455 long COVID patients one year post-infection to 451 age- and gender-matched controls using standardized pain assessment tools (MPQ, BPI, PROMIS-PI). Long COVID patients showed significantly worse affective and sensory pain characteristics, greater pain intensity, and greater pain interference compared to controls.

This prospective study followed 89 COVID-19 pneumonia patients with thoracic CT scans 4 months post-acute infection to identify factors influencing radiological evolution. Male sex was the only significant factor associated with persistent parenchymal lung damage, though the overall evolution of long-term COVID-19 remains poorly understood.

Prospective cohort study of 84 hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessing long-term sleep disturbances and related symptoms 6-9 months post-discharge. Sleep quality, insomnia, sleepiness, depression, and pain were all significantly worsened compared to baseline, with poor sleep increasing from 15.5% to 48.8%.

This observational study compared activity levels and health-related quality of life in 455 long COVID patients versus 451 matched controls one year post-infection using IPAQ and EQ-5D-5L assessments. Long COVID patients showed significantly lower activity levels and quality of life across all measured dimensions, highlighting the need for tailored treatment interventions.

Prospective cohort study of 56 long COVID patients followed over 16 weeks with assessments of quality of life, functional status, and symptom profiles. While functional status improved slightly, quality of life remained severely impaired and this is a descriptive study without treatment intervention.

This observational study followed 19 COVID-19 survivors with reduced exercise capacity at 6 months post-discharge and reassessed them 2 years later using cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET). The study found significant improvement in exercise capacity and anaerobic threshold at longer follow-up, supporting the hypothesis that exercise impairment after COVID-19 is reversible.

Longitudinal cohort study following 51 non-hospitalized adults with post-COVID condition at baseline (median 9 months post-infection) and 20-month follow-up. Study documents natural disease trajectory showing modest improvements in physical function and breathing capacity but persistent impairments in quality of life without any intervention being tested.

This is a prospective follow-up study of hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessing pulmonary function, CT imaging, and respiratory symptoms at 6-8 months post-discharge. It documents natural recovery patterns without testing any intervention, making it observational rather than a treatment trial.

Retrospective observational study of 6,000 post-COVID patients in a tertiary care setting documenting the prevalence and characteristics of long COVID manifestations. While the study characterizes long COVID symptoms and associated complications, it does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention and is primarily descriptive epidemiology rather than a treatment trial.

Prospective follow-up study evaluating clinical, functional, and radiological outcomes in 68 COVID-19 pneumonia patients at 3-month post-discharge, comparing ICU-admitted versus non-ICU groups. No intervention was tested; this is a passive observational study of disease sequelae without treatment assignment, presented as a conference abstract without results publication.

Multicenter observational study of 314 post-COVID-19 subjects from 19 respiratory clinics across India assessing long-term sequelae and symptom presentation. Study found 75% of patients presented after 12 months with respiratory symptoms being most common, but is observational without any treatment intervention.

Retrospective study of spirometry outcomes in lung transplant recipients following SARS-CoV-2 infection, examining lung function changes at 3, 6, and 12 months post-infection. While the paper studies COVID-19 in a vulnerable population, it does not focus on long COVID syndrome or test any treatment intervention for long COVID patients.

Prospective multicentre cohort study following 695 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors at 3 and 12 months post-discharge, assessing clinical recovery, lung function, muscle strength, and quality of life. While many survivors showed improvement by 12 months, about one-third continued experiencing fatigue, dyspnea, or cognitive impairment, with severe disease predicting worse functional outcomes.

Prospective 2-year follow-up study examining exercise response and cardiopulmonary function in post-COVID patients using exercise testing. Demonstrates that most patients show improvement in oxygen utilization and ventilatory efficiency over time, with exercise testing identifying candidates for rehabilitation.

PHOSP-COVID is a prospective cohort study characterizing post-COVID-19 breathlessness in 1,226 UK adults hospitalized for COVID-19, identifying risk factors including socioeconomic deprivation, pre-existing depression/anxiety, and female sex. The study is observational and does not test any treatment intervention, instead examining prevalence and predictors of persistent breathlessness at 5-month follow-up.

Multicenter prospective cohort study following 492 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for up to 12 months to assess persistence of long COVID symptoms. Physical and respiratory symptoms declined gradually over time, while fatigue and cognitive symptoms persisted through 12 months.

Retrospective cohort study using English primary care data to assess whether blood biomarkers and biological age differ across long COVID phenotypes. Found that respiratory and broad spectrum phenotypes show elevated biomarkers and accelerated biological aging compared to controls, but this is a secondary analysis of clinical database records without an intervention.

This prospective study evaluated the impact of a multidisciplinary post-COVID care programme on health-related quality of life and symptom resolution in 730 severe COVID-19 survivors. Patients attending the programme showed significant improvements in SF-12 scores and greater reductions in fatigue, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, neuropsychiatric, and respiratory symptoms compared to non-attendants.

This is a prospective follow-up study of long COVID patients from online support groups, assessing symptom burden, functional status, and quality of life at 3 and 6 months post-infection. It documents the natural recovery trajectory without testing any intervention, making it an observational study of disease progression rather than a treatment trial.

Prospective observational cohort study characterizing functional respiratory complaints (FRCs) among 177 post-COVID-19 patients, finding FRCs in 20.9% with significant associations to dyspnea severity, reduced exercise capacity, and psychological symptoms. The study is descriptive/diagnostic rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

A prospective longitudinal observational study following 108 COVID-19 patients for 12 months to characterize recovery trajectories and identify risk factors for persistent symptoms. The study found that 65% of participants had persistent symptoms at 12 months, with three distinct recovery clusters ranging from almost complete recovery to post-COVID syndrome with impaired mental health.

A prospective cohort study following long COVID patients at 4 and 8 months post-infection to assess symptom persistence and quality of life. The study found that a significant proportion of patients had persistent symptoms with no significant improvement between the 4- and 8-month follow-up assessments.

This prospective cohort study evaluated inspiratory muscle strength and functional outcomes in 50 COVID-19 ICU survivors at 3 and 6 months post-discharge. While survivors showed recovery over time, impaired inspiratory pressure persisted in nearly half at 3 months, and dyspnea and reduced functional capacity remained common, highlighting the long-term sequelae of critical COVID-19.

The COMEBAC cohort study evaluated 478 long COVID patients 4 months post-hospitalization for respiratory symptoms and radiological abnormalities. 16.3% reported new-onset dyspnea and 19.3% had fibrotic lung lesions, with more severe cases and ICU admissions among symptomatic patients.

This longitudinal cohort study examines 1-year health outcomes in COVID-19 patients who received systemic corticosteroids during acute hospitalization, comparing HRQoL between treated and untreated groups using propensity weighting. The analysis finds no significant difference in long-term HRQoL outcomes between corticosteroid-exposed and non-exposed groups, suggesting treatments targeting persistent post-COVID impairment are needed.

This prospective study evaluated 87 post-COVID-19 survivors hospitalized for moderate-to-severe/critical disease to characterize the mechanisms of exercise intolerance through comprehensive cardiopulmonary assessment and exercise testing. The findings showed that reduced peak oxygen consumption was independently predicted by elevated dead space fraction and decreased resting forced vital capacity, suggesting pulmonary microcirculation injury and ventilatory impairment as key drivers of aerobic capacity reduction.

Prospective observational cohort study following 138 COVID-19 hospitalization survivors for 28 months to assess long-term respiratory disabilities and clinical outcomes. Patients showed improvement in lung function parameters and most symptoms by 28 months, with persistent asthenia and dyspnea as primary residual complaints.

A prospective cohort study following 262 COVID-19 patients at 3 and 12 months post-hospital discharge to assess pulmonary outcomes including dyspnea, lung function, and chest CT findings. The study found overall improvement in objective pulmonary function measures (DLCO, total lung capacity) between 3-12 months with no progression of fibrotic-like findings, though self-reported dyspnea remained unchanged.

This study assessed 2,113 COVID-19 patients (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) from Facebook groups and a patient registry in the Netherlands and Belgium to evaluate symptom persistence ~79 days after infection onset. The research documents that multiple symptoms persist in a substantial proportion of patients at 3 months, establishing evidence for a post-COVID-19 syndrome with unmet healthcare needs, though it does not evaluate any specific treatment.

Prospective cohort study assessing diaphragm function in 28 COVID-19 survivors during hospitalization and 1-year follow-up using ultrasound. Found significant improvements in diaphragm thickening fraction from admission to 12-month follow-up, suggesting prolonged diaphragm recovery in post-COVID syndrome.

Analysis of sleep disturbance and fatigue in long COVID patients using validated questionnaires from a large UK cohort study. The study is observational without any intervention or treatment testing, making it ineligible for the trials meta-analysis.

This retrospective study examines domiciliary supplemental oxygen (DSO) therapy outcomes in 65 COVID-19 survivors discharged from a VA Medical Center, tracking DSO duration and development of post-acute sequelae (PASC) over 6 months. The study finds that most patients discontinued DSO within 8 weeks despite lack of formal reassessment, and 46% developed PASC, highlighting gaps in monitoring and evaluation protocols.

Observational study of 248 long COVID patients attending a post-COVID clinic examining sick leave duration and factors associated with longer absences from work. Finds median sick leave was 53 days, significantly longer than standard viral pneumonia recovery time, with dyspnea being a key factor in work disability.

This longitudinal cohort study followed 615 COVID-19 hospitalized patients with pre-existing airway diseases (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis) and compared their long-term recovery to those without airway disease at 5 months and 1 year post-discharge. Patients with pre-existing airway disease experienced worse outcomes including lower perceived recovery rates, reduced quality of life, impaired mobility, and higher symptom burden at 1 year follow-up.

This is a retrospective cohort study using France's National Hospital Discharge database to compare chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) incidence between COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients hospitalized for pulmonary embolism over 2 years. The study does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention, only compares natural disease outcomes between groups.

UKILD is a prospective multicentre observational cohort study assessing the prevalence of residual lung abnormalities (RLA) in non-hospitalised long COVID patients using CT imaging at least 3 months post-infection. Preliminary analysis of 90 scans found RLA in 36% (predominantly ground glass opacity and consolidation), with no intervention or treatment being tested.

This prospective cohort study investigates neuro-inflammatory markers in post-COVID-19 patients with new or worsening headaches, comparing serum levels of inflammatory cytokines and microglial activation markers across four headache phenotype groups. The study identifies associations between pro-inflammatory profiles and headache severity but does not evaluate or test any specific treatment intervention.

The P4O2 cohort study describes baseline characteristics of 95 long COVID patients recruited from 5 Dutch hospitals at 3-6 months post-COVID, assessing pulmonary function, imaging, and clinical symptoms. This is a prospective cohort describing patient characteristics and outcomes without assigning any treatment intervention.

This prospective observational cohort study assessed 56 severe COVID-19 survivors at 4-6 weeks post-discharge, examining the utility of chest radiography in monitoring recovery and documenting persistent symptoms. Despite radiographic resolution in 87%, patients showed high rates of persistent breathlessness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and psychological symptoms (PTSD, anxiety, depression), with physiological impairment evident on functional testing.

This retrospective cohort study using TriNetX database examines the association between long COVID diagnosis and new-onset uveitis risk across vaccinated and unvaccinated populations. The study observes that unvaccinated long COVID patients have increased uveitis risk, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study evaluating blood pressure changes in 5,355 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients at one-year follow-up. Found significant increases in systolic and diastolic BP post-COVID, with 16% developing new-onset or exacerbated hypertension, but this is an observational study with no treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study examining sex differences in post-COVID-19 illness, investigating multiorgan injury and patient-reported outcomes in COVID-19 survivors during convalescence. Found that women had more myocardial inflammation and worse psychological outcomes, though lower cardiovascular hospitalization rates than men.

This prospective observational study evaluated residual pulmonary alterations detected by lung ultrasound in asymptomatic post-COVID patients undergoing surgery and their association with postoperative complications. While the paper mentions post-COVID patients, it is primarily focused on surgical perioperative risk assessment rather than studying treatments for long COVID symptoms.

Retrospective cohort study of 233 long COVID patients assessed at a cardiovascular clinic 1+ year post-infection, documenting prevalence of dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, and palpitations. This is an observational study documenting symptoms without testing any intervention or treatment, so it does not meet criteria for the trial pipeline.

This cross-sectional study evaluated cardiopulmonary exercise capacity and heart rate responses in 101 long COVID patients with varying symptoms at a mean of 12.7 months post-infection. The study is diagnostic/observational in nature without testing any intervention or treatment; it identifies subgroups with dysautonomia or chronotropic incompetence but does not evaluate therapeutic outcomes.

This prospective observational cohort study assessed prescribing errors in 98 post-COVID-19 patients 3 months after hospitalization. While it addresses long COVID sequelae, it does not evaluate any treatment intervention but rather documents medication safety issues as a secondary outcome of previous acute hospitalization.

This retrospective data-linkage study examines cardiovascular mortality outcomes in 51,346 patients during 6-9 months following COVID-19 hospitalization in Iran, finding 3.32% cardiovascular-related deaths. The study characterizes the incidence and clinical characteristics of fatal cardiovascular outcomes but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This longitudinal observational study characterizes respiratory burden in 85 long COVID patients over 6 months, identifying four distinct phenotypic clusters based on symptom severity and lung function. The study found that symptom improvement correlates with reduced systemic inflammation and decreased anti-SS-B/La autoantibodies, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Comparative cohort study examining the frequency and persistence of long COVID symptoms in general practice patients up to 42 months post-infection, with 204 infected cases and 119 uninfected controls followed for 12 months. Found significantly higher symptom prevalence in infected patients (55-79% vs 43%), with persistent symptoms in earlier variant cases but decreasing trend in Omicron cases, and identified fatigue as a key driver of daily life impairment.

This study assessed liver fibrosis in acute COVID-19 patients and post-COVID patients (3-6 months after recovery) using serum biomarkers (hyaluronic acid and FIB-4 index) and ultrasound elastography. While it includes a post-COVID group and documents long-term liver changes, it is purely observational with no treatment intervention evaluated.

Retrospective observational study examining risk factors for post-COVID irritable bowel syndrome in 571 hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Identifies nausea and diarrhea during acute hospitalization as predictive factors for subsequent IBS development (2.1% incidence).

This study compares oral bacterial and fungal microbiota composition in 23 COVID-19 recovered patients versus 29 healthy controls. While it demonstrates microbial changes persist 12 months post-recovery, it is an observational characterization study with no intervention or treatment evaluated.

Prospective cohort study of 106 older COVID-19 hospitalized patients followed 6 months post-discharge to assess changes in health-related quality of life and functional status. Over half reported decline in QoL, with 66% experiencing negative changes across EQ-5D-5L dimensions; no intervention or treatment was evaluated.

Multicentric cohort study comparing mortality and functional status 18 months after hospitalization in geriatric patients (aged 75+) hospitalized for COVID-19 versus other diagnoses. COVID-19 positivity was not associated with excess mortality, and functional outcomes did not differ between groups at 18 months.

A prospective observational cohort study of 198 COVID-19 survivors over 75 years old followed for 3 months post-discharge to assess functional decline, frailty transitions, and long-term symptoms. Found that 36% experienced functional decline, 49% reported long-term symptoms, and 26.8% showed increased frailty, with severity of acute infection and comorbidities as key predictors.

Prospective UK cohort study comparing specialist care referral patterns between emergency department attendees and hospitalized patients with long COVID symptoms at ~6 weeks post-acute infection. Finds post-ED patients receive higher physiotherapy and mental health referrals despite lower symptom burden, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective study of discharged COVID-19 patients in Lagos, Nigeria describing persistent symptoms and investigating risk factors. Found 40.9% experienced persistent COVID-19 symptoms, with fatigue, headaches, and chest pain most common; moderate disease severity was a predictor of persistent symptoms.

Prospective telehealth study evaluating functional performance, frailty, quality of life, and mental health trajectories in 109 adults over 18 weeks following COVID-19 hospitalization. Found that functional performance improved over the follow-up period, with age, sex, and pre-hospitalization frailty status influencing recovery trajectories.

Follow-up study examining serum cholesterol and laboratory values in 107 COVID-19 patients at 3-6 months post-discharge, comparing mild vs severe/critical cases. While findings indicate a long-term recovery process and potential for sequelae like pulmonary fibrosis, this is an observational cohort study with no treatment intervention.

A community-based cohort study examining the resolution of smell and taste loss in people with and without SARS-CoV-2 antibodies at 4-6 week follow-up. The paper identifies risk factors for persistent smell loss (female sex, age >40, distorted perception) but is registered as a clinical trial protocol without reporting intervention outcomes.

This longitudinal biorepository study enrolled 119 COVID-19 survivors and collected multi-matrix samples over 6 months to characterize post-acute sequelae (PASC) across patient phenotypes. While 49% of participants developed PASC with fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and anosmia as leading symptoms, this is a descriptive observational cohort study rather than an intervention trial—it establishes a resource for future research to identify targeted treatments.

Observational cross-sectional study examining the relationship between sleep quality (measured by PSQI) and long COVID symptom prevalence in 4,781 older adults (age 60+). Poor sleep quality was associated with increased risk of various long COVID manifestations including cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and neurological symptoms, but this is an epidemiological risk factor study without testing any intervention or treatment.

A retrospective observational study of 95 COVID-19 survivors assessing functional status at 6-month follow-up using the post-COVID-19 functional status scale. The study found that 70.5% achieved complete functional recovery, with muscle/joint pain at onset associated with incomplete functional recovery.

This retrospective cohort study uses UK primary care database data to estimate the economic costs of consultations associated with long COVID in non-hospitalised adults. The study finds that long COVID diagnosis and symptom reporting are associated with substantial increases in primary care consultation costs, but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

A prospective follow-up study of self-reported olfactory and gustatory dysfunctions in COVID-19 patients from the Foggia district, Italy, assessing symptom evolution up to one year post-infection using the SNOT-22 questionnaire. The study found that approximately 30% of patients with paucisymptomatic-to-mild COVID-19 experienced persistent sensory dysfunction at 12 months, with recovery rates increasing over the first 90 days.

This prospective cohort study followed 236 non-hospitalized Brazilian COVID-19 patients to characterize persistent symptoms and mental health complaints during the long COVID phase (5-8 months post-infection). The study found high prevalence of fatigue, headache, memory complaints, depression, anxiety, and sleep problems, with memory complaints significantly associated with sleep disturbance and depressive mood.

A prospective survey of 241 COVID-19 recovered patients at 12 months post-infection assessed persistent symptoms, clinical characteristics, and quality of life using EQ5D scores. The study found that 52.7% still experienced long COVID symptoms (primarily cognitive dysfunction, fatigue, and neuropsychiatric manifestations), with older age, female sex, and greater initial disease severity as risk factors.

This case series describes 29 long COVID patients with persistent symptoms ≥4 weeks post-infection who received antiviral treatment on a compassionate use basis. Detectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA was found in plasma/stool/urine in 51% of patients, and the treatment group showed significant clinical improvement compared to untreated patients (p=0.01).

Prospective cohort study examining post-infection functional gastrointestinal disorders (PI-FGID) in 190 COVID-19 patients and 160 healthy controls followed for 6 months. Found higher incidence of new-onset FGIDs in COVID-19 patients (8.9%) versus controls (3.1%), with GI symptoms at COVID onset as a risk factor, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This prospective observational cohort study followed 361 hospitalized COVID-19 patients to characterize post-COVID conditions (PCC) using a multidisciplinary screening approach across five symptom categories. At follow-up, 67.3% remained symptomatic, with 44% developing new symptoms; male gender, ICU admission, and discharge symptoms were independent predictors of persistent PCC.

A prospective observational study of 414 South Indian patients following breakthrough COVID infections to characterize long COVID incidence and develop a predictive risk scoring system. The study identified age, hypertension, and asthma as significant predictors of long COVID at 12 weeks post-infection, but did not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Survey of 221 hospital employees with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection to assess the frequency, duration, and risk factors for long-term COVID-19 symptoms. Found that 47.1% experienced persistent symptoms >90 days, with breathlessness, low initial Ct value, and anosmia/ageusia as significant predictive factors for prolonged illness.

Prospective multi-centre cohort study examining symptom clusters in 417 long COVID patients, comparing those infected pre- and post-Alpha variant emergence. Found that later infection timing (VOC group) was associated with lower frequencies of palpitations and chest pain, with effects mediated by variant introduction rather than vaccination status.

Longitudinal cohort study of 8,238 Belgian adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection followed for 3 months post-infection to assess association between viral variants (Alpha, Delta, Omicron) and post-COVID-19 condition (PCC). Found that Alpha and Delta variants had significantly higher odds of PCC (OR=1.61 and OR=1.73 respectively) compared to Omicron, with differences in symptom patterns across variants.

This prospective cohort study measured circulating calprotectin levels in 192 COVID-19 patients (post-ICU and non-ICU) four months after infection across two Swiss hospitals. Post-ICU patients had significantly elevated calprotectin levels compared to non-ICU patients, with a negative correlation between calprotectin and lung function markers (DLCO and FVC).

This cross-sectional study examined post-COVID syndrome (PCS) prevalence and investigated whether EBV reactivation is causative in individuals with asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study found 18% developed PCS symptoms but found no evidence of EBV reactivation or persistent antiviral immune response in PCS patients, suggesting EBV is not a causal mechanism for post-COVID syndrome in otherwise healthy individuals.

Retrospective cohort study comparing standard of care alone versus standard of care plus antivirals in 142 Vietnamese patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 breakthrough infection. Antivirals were not significantly associated with lower risk of residual respiratory symptoms or long COVID-19 diagnosis.

Prospective cohort study of 1,451 COVID-19 patients in Tunisia followed for 3 months to estimate post-COVID syndrome (PCS) incidence and identify risk factors. Found 44% PCS incidence with fatigue and cognitive impairment as primary symptoms; identified female gender, comorbidities, hospitalization, and multiple COVID episodes as significant risk factors.

Descriptive cross-sectional study of 905 long COVID patients in primary care in Catalonia characterizing symptom patterns, sex differences, and symptom clustering over time. Identifies five symptom clusters with varying prevalence and stability, finding major sex differences in dermatological, olfactory, and neurocognitive symptoms.

This retrospective cohort study uses EHR data from 43 PCORnet sites to compare the occurrence of specific symptoms and conditions 31-150 days post-SARS-CoV-2 infection between positive and negative test groups (3.1M adults, 676K children). The study establishes associations between SARS-CoV-2 infection and increased risk of PASC symptoms and conditions but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study compared self-reported health and disability outcomes among outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19-like illness who tested positive vs. negative for SARS-CoV-2 during the pre-Delta period (Sept 2020–Feb 2021). At 2–7 months post-illness, no significant differences in global health, physical function, fatigue, or dyspnea were detected between groups in multivariable analysis.

The RESPIRA cohort study compared 641 PCR-confirmed COVID-19 cases with 947 matched controls to assess long-term health-related quality of life and symptomatology at 6 months post-infection. Cases showed significantly higher prevalence of joint pain, chest tightness, and skin manifestations, with reduced quality of life across all dimensions, particularly in moderate/severe cases and women.

Prospective observational study of 212 veterans examining prevalence and risk factors for post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) nested within the national Airborne Hazards and Open Burn Pit Registry. Found 70% met PASC criteria but military-specific exposures (airborne hazards, burn pits) did not augment risk for PASC.

This study assessed long-term cardiovascular effects of COVID-19 in 37 college students >2 months post-infection, measuring endothelial function and arterial stiffness using non-invasive vascular assessment. Results showed significantly impaired flow-mediated dilation (endothelial dysfunction) but improvement in arterial stiffness over time, with increasing blood pressure trends.

Longitudinal investigation of 134 adults and children infected with SARS-CoV-2 B.1.1.7 in Norway, with follow-up at 2 and 7 months post-infection. Study documents symptom persistence rates and identifies fatigue and insomnia as common long-term complications, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study followed 825 COVID-19 survivors from Italy for at least 12 weeks post-infection to examine how pre-existing socioeconomic status affects recovery outcomes including persistent symptoms, quality of life, PTSD, and lung function. The study found that disadvantaged socioeconomic status was independently associated with lower health-related quality of life, particularly in physical health dimensions, though no association with other outcomes was observed.

This paper follows 96 severe COVID-19 survivors at 3-6 months post-hospitalization to identify predictive factors for long COVID symptoms using Graphical Chain Models. It is a retrospective observational analysis of existing clinical data without any treatment intervention or randomization.

Historical cohort study comparing long COVID symptoms in 141 Iranian children hospitalized with COVID-19 to 141 matched controls. Found 32.6% developed long COVID with fatigue, concentration impairment, and anxiety as most common symptoms; older age and tobacco smoke exposure identified as risk factors.

This study examines erectile dysfunction in male kidney transplant recipients across four time periods, including pre- and post-COVID-19. While the paper mentions post-COVID effects on ED prevalence, it does not focus on long COVID as a primary condition and does not test any treatment for long COVID patients.

Retrospective cohort study of 2,524 Malaysian adults examining whether nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment reduces post-COVID condition (PCC) and improves health-related quality of life over 180 days during the Omicron wave. The study found no significant difference in PCC symptoms between treated and control groups at 3 and 6 months, though nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with reduced negative emotions at 3 months but increased walking limitations.

This prospective observational study assessed pulmonary function patterns in 198 mild-moderate COVID-19 recovered individuals 6-8 months post-infection using spirometry, comparing them to 102 healthy controls. The study found restrictive respiratory patterns in 35.5% of recovered patients and identified an association between higher viral loads (CT ≤20) and these abnormal patterns, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This bidirectional prospective cohort study followed 300 COVID-19 survivors in Thailand to estimate post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) incidence, identify risk factors and biomarkers, and classify clinical phenotypes. The study found 47% developed PCS, identified alkaline phosphatase (ALP) as a significant biomarker, and revealed four distinct clinical phenotypes ranging from mild to severe symptoms with varying quality of life impacts.

Population-based cohort study comparing the frequency and persistence of post-viral symptoms between COVID-19, influenza, and uninfected controls using German healthcare data over 18 months. Finds post-viral symptoms more frequent in COVID-19 than influenza or controls, with similar persistence between COVID-19 and influenza, but does not test any treatment interventions.

This retrospective cohort study uses primary care electronic health records to assess the association between COVID-19 vaccination status and long COVID incidence and healthcare resource utilization in England (2021-2022). The study finds that vaccination reduced long COVID risk but represents a secondary analysis of observational health data rather than a treatment intervention trial.

This observational study compares long COVID symptom incidence between COVID-19 patients with and without chronic hepatitis B virus infection using clinical records and surveys. While it documents higher long COVID rates in the HBV+ group, it is an epidemiological comparison study with no treatment intervention, making it outside the scope of intervention trial screening.

This retrospective cohort study of 1,012 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examined long COVID incidence and clinical manifestations over 19 months of follow-up, analyzing risk factors including vaccination status and viral variants. While it identifies vaccination as protective against long COVID symptoms, it is a retrospective observational analysis that does not test or evaluate any intervention—vaccination status was simply recorded during hospitalization and analyzed post-hoc.

A prospective cohort study following 120 COVID-19 patients (ICU and non-ICU) for one year to evaluate PASC incidence and identify predictive biomarkers. Found 32.8% developed post-COVID conditions at one year, with C-reactive protein, lactate-dehydrogenase, ferritin, and albumin as predictive markers.

Retrospective cohort study examining cardiac symptoms in 1,080 long COVID patients 3-6 months post-infection from the STOP-COVID registry. Found that 54.3% had persistent cardiac symptoms (predominantly fatigue at 38.9%), with palpitations associated with increased ventricular extrasystoles and higher anxiety/depression scores.

This propensity score-matched cohort study evaluates remdesivir (RDV) in formerly hospitalized post-COVID patients (N=94 per group), comparing RDV+standard care vs standard care alone. RDV was associated with significantly faster patient-reported symptom resolution and better sleep quality, though no differences were found in functional outcomes.

This cross-sectional study examines serum sST2 as a biomarker in COVID-19 patients with coronary artery disease, comparing 75 COVID-19 patients to 68 non-COVID-19 controls. The study identifies sST2 as an independent risk factor for COVID-19 patients with coexisting CAD but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Observational study of 85 German children/adolescents with long COVID assessing neurocognitive and psychiatric symptoms through standardized assessments and clinical evaluations. Found high prevalence of fatigue (82.4%), attention deficits (71.8%), and mood changes, with post-COVID adjustment disorder being the most common diagnosis, but no treatment intervention was tested.

A retrospective cohort study of 319 COVID-19 patients followed via telehealth in Brazil examining the persistence of cognitive symptoms from acute infection through 24 weeks post-onset. Found that 27.9% had persistent cognitive symptoms, with female sex and infection during the second COVID wave as significant risk factors, but no active treatment intervention was tested.

Population-based cohort study in Italy examining the incidence of outpatient care utilization within 24 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection using administrative healthcare data. Found increased rates of outpatient visits and diagnostics starting 2 months post-infection, peaking at month 4 (IRR=2.05), with higher increases in severe acute COVID-19 patients and those without comorbidities.

This pilot observational study evaluated MYPplus, an herbal formulation, in 50 long COVID patients with fatigue and brain fog over 4 weeks. All measured parameters including fatigue scales, brain fog VAS, and quality of life significantly improved, with no safety concerns reported.

This prospective cohort study followed 853 post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients for up to 26 months to investigate symptom trajectories and factors associated with PCC persistence. The study found that PCC burden decreased at 7 months post-infection, but one-third of patients experienced long-lasting symptoms including fatigue, respiratory sequelae, brain fog, and chronic pain.

Prospective cohort study following 555 long COVID patients for up to 24 months to identify symptom trajectories and their determinants. Identified two distinct trajectories (mild/fast resolution vs elevated/persisting symptoms) but no treatment intervention was tested.

Longitudinal study of 411 COVID-19 patients who received monoclonal antibody treatment at a Federally Qualified Health Center, tracking symptom burden and post-COVID condition development at baseline, 14 days, and 28+ days. Time to mAb infusion was not significantly associated with PCC development, though most symptoms decreased over the follow-up period and 69% of patients met PCC criteria at final follow-up.

Retrospective chart review of 984 patients at three U.S. post-COVID clinics describing clinical characteristics, symptom prevalence, comorbidities, and healthcare utilization patterns. Study documents high rates of shortness of breath, fatigue, brain fog, and post-exertional malaise, with 64% referred for subspecialty care and 38% for rehabilitation therapy.

Retrospective cohort study of 319 COVID-19 patients examining prevalence and risk factors for post-COVID symptoms over 6+ months of follow-up. Study identifies male sex, fever, and taste disorders during acute infection as independent risk factors for symptom persistence, with 80-81% reporting improvement by 6-12 months.

Population-based study of 3,372 participants from the COVIDOM cohort examining subdomains of post-COVID syndrome using an expanded dataset and Classification and Regression Tree analysis. The study identifies distinct PCS symptom clusters predicted by acute COVID severity and individual resilience, proposing two novel refined PCS scores for clinical assessment.

Retrospective cohort study of 1,803 Portuguese COVID-19 hospitalized patients examining cardiovascular events occurring ≥30 days post-infection. Found 7.9% experienced cardiovascular events (34.65 per 1,000 person-years), with higher risk in those with pre-existing cardiovascular disease and lower risk in vaccinated individuals.

Population-based longitudinal study examining long COVID symptom profiles in older European adults, comparing those with and without pre-existing depression. Found that participants with pre-existing depression had 16% increased risk of additional persistent symptoms and higher prevalence of headaches, joint pain, and confusion.

This prospective observational study of 2,989 Brazilian adults analyzed long COVID symptom phenotypes following Omicron infection using machine learning clustering, identifying three distinct phenotypic presentations (cognitive symptoms, fatigue/respiratory, severe multi-symptom). The study found significant differences in health-related quality of life across phenotypes, with the severe phenotype having substantially lower utility scores, but conducted no intervention evaluation.

Retrospective cohort study examining 30-month longitudinal changes in glucose metabolism, endocrine, and renal functions in COVID-19 survivors stratified by vaccination status. While the study shows improved metabolic outcomes in fully vaccinated individuals, it is a passive observational analysis of vaccination records rather than an intervention trial, and does not test or evaluate a specific treatment given to long COVID patients.

This retrospective cohort study compared serum RAAS component levels (ACE, ACE2, Ang1-7, AngII) between healthcare workers with and without long COVID at 3-6 months and 12 months post-infection. No statistically significant differences in RAAS markers were found between LC cases and controls, suggesting RAAS disruption is not a significant contributor to LC pathophysiology.

A four-year prospective cohort study in Saudi Arabia following 816 COVID-19 patients to identify risk factors and predictors of long COVID-19 and recovery patterns. Female sex and diabetes were strong predictors of long COVID development and delayed recovery, with persistent fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction being most common.

A retrospective study of 24 long COVID patients that used 3D voxel-based morphometry brain imaging to measure cortical grey matter volume depletion at median 85 days post-infection. The study found statistically significant CGM volume reduction but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention—it is a descriptive neuroimaging study of disease correlates.

Prospective cohort study characterizing sleep disorders in 189 long COVID patients, finding insomnia in 22.2% and excessive sleepiness in 3.17%. The study documents the prevalence and types of sleep symptoms as part of the long COVID clinical spectrum but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective case-control study examining macular vessel density and foveal avascular zone (FAZ) enlargement in recovered COVID-19 patients with and without fatigue using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA). Found significantly enlarged FAZ in non-ICU patients and fatigue groups compared to controls, suggesting retinal microvascular alterations may be associated with long COVID fatigue.

A patient-engaged cohort survey study of 11,328 COVID-19 hospitalized patients in Rio de Janeiro assessing long COVID prevalence 6-24 months post-discharge. The study found 71.3% reported persistent symptoms and 39.3% self-reported long COVID, with fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive impairment being most common.

Retrospective cohort study estimating long COVID prevalence and symptoms among 6,846 quarantined adults in Germany, finding 14.6% prevalence with fatigue, cognitive impairment, and dyspnoea as most common symptoms. Identifies chronic diseases and acute infection severity as significant risk factors but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study of 105 children with confirmed COVID-19 followed for 24 weeks to characterize acute disease course and long COVID outcomes. Found 15.2% developed long COVID symptoms (fatigue, hair loss, concentration issues, abdominal pain), with older children (11-16 years) and those with ongoing symptoms at 4-6 weeks at higher risk.

This study used a mobile application (NCRCC) to track daily symptom evolution in 63 Neuro-PASC patients over 12+ months post-COVID onset, classifying them as Improvers or Non-Improvers based on subjective recovery trajectories. Key findings include that women and patients with anosmia/dysgeusia were less likely to improve, and Improvers showed greater fluctuations in recovery perception with modest improvements in processing speed and sleep disturbance at 3-month follow-up.

This study examined long COVID symptoms in an Italian pediatric cohort of Tourette Syndrome patients with and without SARS-CoV-2 infection via questionnaire and clinical assessments at baseline and 3-month follow-up. While it documents the prevalence of long COVID symptoms (38.5%) and their association with worsening tics and behavioral/mood symptoms, it is observational without any intervention or treatment being tested.

A prospective longitudinal observational study assessing retinal structure and microvasculature changes in long COVID patients using swept-source OCT imaging at baseline, 1 month, and 1 year post-infection. The study documents retinal alterations but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 1,038 medical staff examining how acute-phase COVID-19 symptom trajectories predict anxiety and depression 2 years post-infection. Found that moderate and severe acute symptom trajectories were associated with significantly higher anxiety and depression risk at 2-year follow-up.

This multicenter cohort study assessed the prevalence of anxiety and depression symptoms one year after ICU admission for COVID-19 in Swedish patients during the first pandemic wave. The study found high rates of anxiety (38.1%) and depression (35.2%), with female sex identified as a predictor of depression, highlighting the need for long-term mental health support in COVID-19 ICU survivors.

Longitudinal study of 1,581 UK adults examining whether pre-infection health behaviours (exercise, sleep, smoking) are risk factors for developing long COVID. Found that poor sleep quality and smoking increased odds of long COVID, while meeting physical activity guidelines reduced difficulty with self-care.

Registry-based cohort study analyzing sick leave patterns in 11,955 Swedish COVID-19 patients over 4 months, examining predictors of prolonged sick leave and long COVID occurrence. Findings show 13.3% experienced long COVID-related sick leave, with inpatient care, prior sick leave, and older age as key predictive factors.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed medical claims data from over 1.37 million COVID-19 survivors to identify long-term health effects and their associations with social determinants of health. The study identified 36 ICD-10 codes significantly increased in the post-COVID period and found age and gender were commonly associated with long-term effects, but it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed 130,010 pediatric COVID-19 cases from a database to compare Emergency Department utilization between children with and without long COVID symptoms (defined as symptoms occurring 30-180 days post-infection). Children with long COVID symptoms had significantly higher odds of ED visits (OR: 2.52), with chest pain and electrolyte disturbances showing the strongest associations.

Registry-based cohort study examining recurrent sick leave patterns in 11,955 Swedish COVID-19 patients during the first pandemic wave (March–August 2020). Found that 2.0% experienced recurrent sick leave, with older age and female sex as risk factors, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

A longitudinal cohort study of 5,727 Belgian adults followed from SARS-CoV-2 infection to three months post-infection, assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. The study found significant HRQoL decline during acute infection and persistent decline at three months specifically among those reporting post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), with fatigue, headache, and memory problems as the main symptom drivers.

Prospective matched cohort study examining the prevalence and burden of long COVID among sheltered people experiencing homelessness in Seattle between September 2020–April 2022. Found that 77% of COVID-19-positive cases reported symptoms 30–59 days post-infection, with fatigue and rhinorrhea most common, though few accessed medical care; risk of symptoms was 5.4 times higher in COVID-19 cases versus controls.

Population-based cohort study comparing health outcomes in 350 individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection to 4467 uninfected controls at ~1.5 years follow-up. Infected individuals showed significantly higher rates of persistent symptoms (smell/taste disorders, shortness of breath, fatigue, myalgia), incident diseases (liver, lung, cardiovascular), and worse quality of life measures.

This study examined immune and endothelial biomarkers in 112 participants from Riverside County across healthy controls, moderate infection, severe infection, and recovery groups to identify factors associated with COVID-19 severity and long-term outcomes. Results showed infection-related changes in immune cells, cytokines, and endothelial markers, with long COVID symptoms persisting up to 11 months post-infection, though pulmonary function recovered.

This retrospective cohort study evaluated the frequency and patient-reported effectiveness of symptomatic therapies in 200 post-COVID patients at a German specialty center, with 82.5% follow-up response rate. Beta-blockers showed highest effectiveness (31.5% strong improvement), followed by antibiotics (29.6%), while plasmapheresis was perceived as strongly effective by 33.0% of users.

A 2.5-year prospective cohort study of 130 non-hospitalised adults with post-COVID-19 condition assessing physical function, activity levels, and mental health outcomes. The study identified risk factors for low self-rated health but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Population-based longitudinal study (n=5,422) tracking work ability and sick leave 2 years post-SARS-CoV-2 infection in Southwest Germany. Findings show 1.1% remained continuously on sick leave due to fatigue, neurocognitive impairment, and mental health symptoms; age and working task type were key effect modifiers.

This prospective observational study followed 39 patients with acute SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia for 3 months, assessing radiological, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes. While it documents medium-term sequelae of acute COVID-19 infection, it does not address long COVID (persistent symptoms beyond 3-4 weeks post-infection) and is primarily focused on acute disease recovery rather than long COVID syndrome.

Retrospective cohort study examining the association between Post-COVID Syndrome (PCS) and self-stigma among 759 Israeli adults who tested positive for COVID-19. Found that 25.2% met PCS criteria and individuals with PCS reported significantly higher levels of COVID-19-related self-stigma (p < 0.001), with OR = 2.5.

Population-based surveillance study in Kenya evaluating the burden and risk factors for long COVID among 832 previously SARS-CoV-2 infected participants. Found 20.9% had respiratory symptoms, 20.8% reported non-recovery, and identified underlying medical conditions and female sex as significant risk factors, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This study evaluates long-term pulmonary function, exercise capacity, and radiological findings in patients 6 months after critical COVID-19 requiring ICU treatment. It is an observational cross-sectional assessment without any treatment intervention or control group, documenting persistent lung impairment and radiological abnormalities but not testing a therapeutic approach.

Post hoc analysis of a prospective cohort comparing pulmonary function tests, diffusion capacity, blood gas analysis, and CT imaging between long COVID patients with and without persistent respiratory symptoms. Found that 71% of patients reported long-lasting symptoms with 58% having respiratory symptoms; patients with persistent symptoms showed significantly lower FVC, TLC, and diffusion capacity compared to asymptomatic patients.

This study follows 257 convalescent COVID-19 patients from acute infection through post-discharge recovery, characterizing four distinct trajectory subgroups based on pneumonia lesion progression and lymphocyte counts. The focus is on acute disease severity and recovery trajectories during the active infection phase, not long-term post-COVID syndrome or treatment interventions.

Observational study of 146 patients recovering from mild COVID-19 assessed lung function via spirometry and DLCO testing 34 days post-diagnosis. Found 30% had impaired DLCO and 20% had restrictive spirometric patterns, with fatigue, cough, and dyspnea being prevalent symptoms.

This prospective cohort study assessed respiratory function in 86 COVID-19 patients approximately one month after hospital discharge using pulmonary function tests, arterial blood gas analysis, and exercise testing. Patients showed residual respiratory impairment including reduced diffusing capacity and exercise tolerance, with greater impairment in those with more severe initial respiratory failure.

Prospective single-center study evaluating cardiopulmonary function 12 months post-hospitalization for severe COVID-19 in 60 ICU patients using exercise testing, lung function assessment, and CT imaging. Found most patients had normal peak oxygen uptake but showed ventilatory inefficiency during exercise, with dyspnea more pronounced in those with elevated dead space ventilation.

A 1-year prospective follow-up study of 33 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors examining dyspnea persistence and regional ventilation distribution using pulmonary function tests and electrical impedance tomography. The study found that 45% of patients reported new-onset dyspnea at 1 year, associated with increased regional ventilation inhomogeneity despite normal standard pulmonary function tests.

Retrospective observational study examining the utility and safety of bronchoscopy as a diagnostic procedure in 45 patients with suspected post-acute COVID-19 sequelae in Italy. Bronchoscopy was used diagnostically to evaluate tracheal complications and persistent parenchymal infiltrates, not as a treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study following 61 hospitalized COVID-19 pneumonia patients at 3 and 10 months post-discharge to assess health-related quality of life and pulmonary outcomes. Patients showed anxiety/depression correlations with severity, persistent radiological abnormalities (41% at 3 months, 28% at 10 months), and gradual lung function improvement (FVC and DLCO) by 10 months.

A prospective cohort study following 94 COVID-19 patients with severe pneumonia for 12 months post-discharge to characterize respiratory sequelae and functional recovery. Most patients showed improvement in dyspnea, quality of life, and exercise capacity by 12 months, though pulmonary fibrotic-like changes persisted in some patients.

An ambispective cohort study of 104 post-COVID-19 patients with chronic cough comparing outcomes between those receiving inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment (n=51) and controls (n=53) over 60 days. ICS treatment improved pulmonary function parameters but did not significantly impact symptom management of post-COVID-19 chronic cough.

Prospective 12-month study comparing physiological recovery and health-related quality of life in COVID-19 survivors versus historical SARS survivors using spirometry, 6-minute walking distance, and imaging assessments. COVID-19 survivors showed similar recovery in lung function and exercise capacity to SARS survivors but exhibited different patterns of psychological recovery over time.

Prospective cohort study following 76 COVID-19 hospitalization survivors for 12 months to characterize post-COVID dyspnea prevalence, severity, predictors, and associated outcomes. Found clinically meaningful dyspnea in ~46-49% at 12 months, associated with worse sleep, mood, and quality of life, with early dyspnea and depression predicting persistent symptoms.

Observational cohort study of 286 critically ill COVID-19 survivors examining pulmonary function outcomes 6 months post-ICU discharge, comparing those who received corticosteroid treatment versus those who did not. Corticosteroid treatment was associated with lower diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide but no difference in health-related quality of life.

Prospective cohort study assessing pulmonary function (spirometry, DLCO, LCI) in 110 non-hospitalized adults and children 4-12 weeks post-mild COVID-19 infection. Found impaired lung function in 50% of adults and 85% of children, with most recovering by 5 months, but no intervention or treatment was tested.

This study evaluates the effects of pulmonary rehabilitation on functional and psychological outcomes in 55 PASC patients, measuring improvements in 6-minute walk test, chair rise repetitions, dyspnea scales, and anxiety/depression scores. Results demonstrate significant improvements across multiple physical and mental health indices following PR, though comorbidities and certain pharmacologic treatments were associated with poorer response to rehabilitation.

Longitudinal study following 32 post-COVID subjects at 6 and 34 months post-discharge to assess the persistence of exercise ventilatory inefficiency (EVin) and its association with cardiorespiratory health. Found that a significant subset exhibited persistent EVin correlated with unfavorable cardiovascular responses, suggesting prognostic value for long-term post-COVID monitoring.

This retrospective cohort study examines 24-month radiologic trajectories and corticosteroid treatment strategies in hospitalized COVID-19 patients with pre-existing interstitial lung disease (ILD). While it analyzes treatment outcomes, the study focuses on acute COVID-19 in an ILD population rather than long COVID syndrome, making it outside the scope of long COVID trials.

This retrospective, multi-center observational study compares the prevalence and characteristics of post-COVID-19 (PC) in fibromyalgia (FM) patients versus patients with other rheumatic diseases. The FM group showed similar PC prevalence (79.5%) to the rheumatic disease group (66.1%), but experienced more PC symptoms and greater severity of fatigue, cognitive impairment, and sleep disturbance.

Retrospective cohort study of 1,946 women examining the relationship between COVID-19 infection and menstrual changes. Found 37% of infected women experienced menstrual cycle irregularities compared to uninfected controls, with chest pain and dyspnea associated with higher odds of menstrual changes.

Follow-up study comparing asthma control in Hong Kong patients with and without COVID-19 history across different viral variants (BA.2 to XBB). Found no significant worsening of asthma control in patients with more recent COVID-19 infection (2023), unlike earlier findings with BA.2 variant.

This retrospective cohort study examined healthcare utilization and medical expenditures for 250,514 COVID-19 patients over 6 months post-diagnosis using claims data. It found that COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with significantly increased healthcare visits and monthly costs, with effects persisting longer in older age groups, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study used German health insurance claims data to compare healthcare costs and mortality between COVID-19 patients and matched controls from 2020-2021. While it documents that post-COVID syndrome patients incurred significantly higher costs and mortality, it does not evaluate any intervention or treatment—it is a purely observational cost-effectiveness and epidemiological analysis.

This retrospective cohort study uses Ontario health administrative data to estimate incidence of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) following introduction of a diagnostic code in January 2023, and compares demographic characteristics and healthcare utilization between individuals with and without the PCC code. The study found 7,343 individuals received a PCC code, with substantially increased healthcare utilization post-diagnosis (100.61 vs 14.59 encounters per person-year pre-pandemic), but identifies underrepresentation of PCC cases in the coding system.

Prospective cohort study examining financial hardship outcomes 18 months after COVID-19 infection among US Veterans, comparing those with and without COVID-19 history. While the study includes long COVID patients, it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it is a purely observational epidemiological study of socioeconomic consequences, not a treatment trial.

This prospective cohort study tracked 4,721 NHS healthcare workers at 12 and 32 months post-baseline to examine COVID-19-related sickness absence and predictors of long-term absence among those with long COVID symptoms. The study found that healthcare workers with self-reported LC symptoms or formal LC diagnosis reported significantly greater sickness absence (median 14 days at 12mo vs 9.5 days without LC symptoms), with predictors including pre-existing respiratory illness and age 41-50 years.

Retrospective observational study following 797 COVID-19 hospitalized patients for 6 months after discharge to identify and quantify long-term sequelae. Found 63.9% reported persistent symptoms, most commonly respiratory (42%), systemic (36.1%), and neurological (20.8%) manifestations, with identified risk factors for emergency readmission.
