This matched cohort study examined post-acute healthcare expenditure in 10,380 COVID-19 hospitalized patients versus 26,270 non-COVID hospitalized controls in Belgium during 2021, and identified socioeconomic factors associated with costs. While it follows COVID-19 patients post-hospitalization, it focuses on healthcare utilization and cost patterns rather than long COVID-specific symptoms or treatment interventions.

Retrospective EHR cohort study identifying phenotypes associated with past SARS-CoV-2 infection in 96,000 non-hospitalized patients. While it clearly addresses long COVID, it is an observational study without treatment intervention, so it does not meet the inclusion criteria for the treatment trials meta-analysis.

This longitudinal study of 1,300 German health and social services workers examines determinants of work ability among those with work-related COVID-19 infection, with 75.2% reporting post-COVID symptoms. The study identifies risk factors for reduced work ability (obesity, memory/concentration problems, post-COVID symptoms, psychological conditions) and suggests rehabilitation and workplace adjustments as needed interventions.

Prospective cohort study assessing the prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) in hospitalized adults and children at 6 and 12 months post-discharge in Moscow. The study documents symptom decline over time and identifies risk factors (female sex, pre-existing hypertension in adults; neurological comorbidities in children) but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study comparing persistent symptoms 12 months after discharge in 453 COVID-19 hospitalized patients versus 453 non-COVID controls across 4 hospitals in Spain. Found similar overall symptom prevalence (36.1% vs 35.3%) but COVID-specific symptoms like pharyngeal symptoms, memory loss, and anxiety were significantly more prevalent in the exposed cohort.

This study characterizes peripheral immune system changes in 69 COVID-19 convalescents (including 21 with long COVID) at 12, 16, and 24 weeks post-infection through immunophenotyping, RNA sequencing, and serological analysis. It identifies significant perturbations in innate and adaptive immune populations and gene expression patterns that persist up to 6 months post-infection, with differences between those who developed long COVID symptoms and those who recovered.

Prospective cohort study (RECoVERED) in Amsterdam comparing health-related quality of life (SF-36) among 269 persons with initial mild, moderate, or severe/critical COVID-19 at 1 and 12 months post-infection. Persons with mild COVID had normal HRQL by 12 months, while moderate/severe cases remained impaired; migration background and comorbidities predicted worse outcomes.

Matched cohort study examining the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and incidence of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) using UK primary care data. Found a 22% increased risk of IMIDs post-COVID, particularly type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and psoriasis, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A propensity-matched cohort study of 249,390 Welsh individuals comparing healthcare utilization between COVID-19 positive individuals and matched controls at 1-4 and 5-24 weeks post-infection. The study found increased risks of fatigue, embolism, and post-viral illness in positive cases, but excludes because it is an observational study with no intervention tested.

This study characterizes the population of 33,782 patients with ICD-10 code U09.9 (long COVID) in the N3C dataset, clustering co-occurring diagnoses into four categories (cardiopulmonary, neurological, gastrointestinal, comorbid) and analyzing demographics and care patterns. The work reveals significant demographic skew toward female, White, non-Hispanic individuals and identifies disparities in long COVID diagnosis.

This retrospective cohort study compared the prevalence and risk of post-COVID conditions in hospitalized COVID-19 patients versus influenza patients using propensity score matching. COVID-19 patients had significantly higher rates of long-term sequelae including abnormal breathing, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms, with increased risk of ED visits, hospitalizations, and deaths during 90-180 day follow-up.

CO-FLOW is a prospective cohort study following 371 patients hospitalized for COVID-19 to assess return to work and health-related quality of life up to 1 year post-discharge. The study found that only 69% fully returned to work by 12 months, with ICU admission, persistent fatigue, female sex, and older age as independent barriers to work return.

This retrospective cohort study using TriNetX data investigates the prevalence of post-COVID-19 conditions in 36,308 patients with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) versus matched controls. It found that IDD patients have significantly higher risk of developing various post-COVID symptoms including fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, and anxiety/depression, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study examines the clinical and economic burden of post-COVID conditions among 19,558 US adults at high risk of severe COVID-19 by comparing healthcare use and medical costs before and after acute illness. The study found substantial increases in diagnoses (blood disorders, nervous system disorders, mental health conditions), healthcare utilization, and medical costs (23% increase) during the 12-month post-acute phase.

This prospective cohort study compares the incidence of post-COVID-19 condition in children hospitalized with COVID-19 (Wuhan and Omicron variants) versus a matched reference cohort of children with non-COVID infections, using follow-up interviews at a median of 6.7 months post-discharge. The Wuhan variant cohort showed significantly higher incidence of post-COVID-19 condition (89.7 per 1000 person-months) with broad physical and emotional manifestations, while the Omicron variant showed minimal differences from controls.

A large-scale retrospective cohort study using UK Biobank data examining the long-term risks of digestive diseases in COVID-19 patients compared to uninfected controls over up to 2.6 years of follow-up. The study found significantly elevated risks of multiple GI conditions including GERD, GI dysfunction, peptic ulcer disease, and liver/pancreatic disease, with risks persisting beyond one year and increasing with reinfection.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed healthcare utilization and medical costs for 3,792 US adults who recovered from COVID-19, comparing 12 months before and after diagnosis. The study found substantial increases in diagnoses of blood, endocrine, nervous system, and mental health disorders in the post-acute phase, with total medical costs rising 178% despite 94% of patients not requiring hospitalization.

This matched cohort study using OpenSAFELY electronic health records assessed healthcare utilisation in 52,988 individuals with long COVID compared to 264,867 matched controls between Nov 2020 and Jan 2023. The study found that long COVID patients had 49% higher healthcare utilisation and 44% higher costs (approximately £2500 per person per year) compared to controls, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational study examined whether SSRI use during acute COVID-19 reduced the 12-month risk of developing long COVID in 302,626 patients with depression using electronic health records from the N3C Consortium. SSRI users had significantly lower long COVID risk (adjusted RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86–0.99) compared to nonusers, supporting a potential protective effect of serotonin-modulating medications.

Retrospective cohort study examining acute and post-acute COVID-19 complications in Hong Kong patients infected with omicron, stratified by initial disease severity and age. Results show significantly increased risk of multiple disease outcomes in both acute and post-acute phases with increasing severity of initial infection, particularly in elderly patients.

A prospective cohort study examining EEG changes and cognitive decline across age groups following mild SARS-CoV-2 infection using pre- and post-infection neurophysiological measurements and symptom questionnaires. The study documents neurological sequelae including altered EEG patterns and their correlation with persistent long-term symptoms, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study evaluating exercise-based inpatient rehabilitation for 145 long COVID patients, with assessments of cardiopulmonary fitness and pulmonary function at admission and discharge. Rehabilitation improved cardiopulmonary fitness and pulmonary function in both sexes over 6 months, with women showing greater improvement in submaximal workload and men presenting baseline pulmonary advantages.

Prospective longitudinal cohort study of 358 COVID-19 patients assessed 4-12 months post-infection to identify clinical clusters and biological markers associated with long COVID. Found six clinical presentations with troponin T elevation and telomere shortening as key predictive markers for long COVID and PEM-fatigue symptoms.

Multicentre cohort study of 1,297 long COVID patients characterizing symptom profiles, clustering patterns, and functional impacts across demographics. No intervention tested; observational study of existing patients describing disease heterogeneity and sex-specific manifestations.

This Swedish register-based retrospective cohort study examined the risk of long COVID diagnosis among adult residents stratified by country of birth, analyzing 1.87 million COVID-19 infected individuals. The study found higher long COVID risks among migrants from East Europe, Finland, South Asia, and the Middle East, with disease severity (hospitalization/ICU) being the primary driver of these disparities rather than vaccination or socioeconomic factors.

This longitudinal prospective cohort study follows 70 COVID-19 convalescents with respiratory sequelae for up to 3 years, analyzing proteomic and metabolomic profiles to identify molecular mechanisms of PASC. No intervention or treatment is tested; this is a purely observational characterization study designed to understand disease pathogenesis rather than evaluate therapeutic outcomes.

Population-based prospective cohort study (COVICAT) examining the risk, subtypes, and persistence of long-COVID in 2,764 infected individuals from Catalonia followed across 2020-2023. Identifies 647 long-COVID cases, characterizes three clinical subtypes, and determines key risk factors (female sex, age <50, low SES, severe acute infection, obesity, chronic disease) and protective factors (vaccination, physical activity, adequate sleep).

This retrospective cohort study analyzes pre-pandemic disease trajectories and genetic factors associated with long COVID susceptibility using electronic health records from 8,322 participants in the COVICAT cohort. It identifies disease patterns and polygenic risk factors that modify long COVID risk but does not test any treatment or intervention.

This retrospective cohort study followed 287 COVID-19 discharged patients for 90-150 days, tracking the development and resolution of pulmonary fibrosis using CT imaging and lung function tests. The study identified risk factors (age, BMI, fever, PCT) predicting persistent fibrosis but did not test any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 101 COVID-19 hospitalized patients examining chest radiograph abnormalities at 12-week follow-up post-discharge. Identifies persistent CXR abnormality in 32% of patients, with length of stay, smoking status, and obesity as independent risk factors, but does not test any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study using TriNetX data comparing fibromyalgia incidence in 90,508 vaccinated vs 90,508 unvaccinated COVID-19 survivors. Found COVID-19 vaccination associated with reduced new-onset fibromyalgia risk (HR 0.84), with protective effects strongest in males, those with BMI<30, and those with comorbid depression/anxiety.

This multinational cohort study examined psychiatric and neuropsychiatric outcomes in COVID-19 patients versus matched controls across five countries using electronic medical records and claims data. While it demonstrates increased psychiatric risks in the first 6 months post-COVID, it is an observational retrospective cohort with no treatment intervention and represents secondary analysis of existing healthcare databases rather than a prospective treatment trial.

A prospective cohort study of 105 severe COVID-19 survivors assessed at 3 months post-discharge to identify factors associated with impaired exercise capacity. The study found that 35% had reduced exercise capacity, which correlated with reduced pulmonary function, decreased skeletal muscle mass, and sarcopenia, but not cardiac dysfunction.

Community-based observational study comparing chronic symptoms and objective health outcomes 3 years post-infection across groups with original SARS-CoV-2, Omicron reinfection, or no infection. Found reinfection associated with highest risk of chronic physical and mental symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, and imaging abnormalities.

Prospective observational cohort study following 284 COVID-19 pneumonia patients for 12 months post-discharge to assess pulmonary sequelae and radiological outcomes. Found that 39.8% had impaired lung diffusion and 22.7% had fibrotic-like changes at 12 months, regardless of acute illness severity.

A prospective longitudinal cohort study tracking 61 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for 1 year post-discharge to assess physical recovery and quality of life outcomes using objective (6-minute walk test, frailty) and subjective measures (fatigue, SF-36). Despite some objective improvement in walking distance, patients reported persistent fatigue and memory problems, low quality-of-life scores, and low return-to-work rates, with no intervention tested.

This paper presents a longitudinal observational study of 71 long COVID patients undergoing comprehensive cardiopulmonary testing over 12 months to characterize persistent symptoms and functional impairment. The study found that exercise capacity is reduced but not strongly correlated with quality of life, and persistent cardiopulmonary impairment is uncommon, suggesting post-COVID syndrome may reflect deconditioning rather than organ-specific pathology.

Prospective cohort study of 194 patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia, assessed at 3 and 12 months post-discharge for evolution of lung function using nitric oxide and carbon monoxide diffusion measurements. Found improvement in exercise tolerance and lung imaging over time, with DLNO measurement being the most sensitive marker for detecting long-term respiratory sequelae.

Japanese multicenter cohort study of 26 hospitals examining risk factors for prolonged cough and sputum in long COVID patients across 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups. Found that severe acute COVID-19 characteristics (IMV use, imaging findings, organ dysfunction, elevated biomarkers) were independent predictors of persistent respiratory symptoms, with no evaluation of any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study evaluated 204 post-COVID patients to characterize cardiorespiratory dysfunction through pulmonary function testing, exercise physiology, and blood biomarkers. The study found impaired alveolar capillary membrane function and elevated VE/VCO2 slopes associated with dyspnea, fatigue, and fatigability, but did not test or evaluate any specific intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study comparing nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus molnupiravir in 1,745 asthma patients with COVID-19, examining acute and post-acute outcomes over 365 days median follow-up. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir demonstrated significantly lower risks of post-acute mortality, all-cause hospitalization, and asthma exacerbation compared to molnupiravir, suggesting greater benefits in reducing post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 in asthma patients.

Prospective observational cohort study of 64 long COVID patients followed for 8 months to investigate the relationship between small airway dysfunction and static lung hyperinflation. Found that 53% of patients had persistent static lung hyperinflation associated with dyspnea and fatigue, but this is a descriptive/mechanistic study with no intervention tested.

This retrospective cohort study examines the risk of acute exacerbation of COPD in patients with pre-existing COPD who recovered from COVID-19, using propensity score matching. While it studies post-COVID outcomes, it focuses on a pre-existing disease complication rather than long COVID symptoms themselves, and does not test a treatment intervention.

Cross-sectional study of 845 South African long COVID patients describing symptom prevalence, comorbidities, and blood biomarkers (fibrin amyloid microclots and platelet pathology). Authors propose microclots as a treatment target and call for controlled clinical trials, but this paper itself is observational with no intervention tested.

This longitudinal observational study compared health-related quality of life, mental health, and fatigue between non-hospitalized individuals with and without post-COVID-19 syndrome in a German cohort over 26 months post-infection. Persons with PCS showed significantly worse mental health outcomes, higher fatigue, and poorer quality of life compared to controls, with depression and acute symptom burden as independent predictors.

A prospective longitudinal cohort study examining the trajectory of neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive symptoms in 335 COVID-19 survivors and 79 healthy controls over 3 months post-infection. The study found that acute-phase fatigue was associated with worse emotional outcomes and reduced quality of life during recovery, but no specific treatment intervention was tested.

Longitudinal prospective cohort study examining health-related quality of life outcomes in 158 COVID-19 patients over one year, with 48.1% developing post-COVID conditions. The study found that PCC was associated with persistent reductions in both physical and mental HRQoL, but no intervention or treatment was tested—it is purely observational follow-up.

Retrospective cohort study comparing healthcare resource utilization and costs between 341 post-COVID-19 condition patients and 49,078 controls, before and after implementation of an integrated care unit. PCC patients showed 4-fold higher costs than controls, but post-diagnosis costs decreased with coordinated care, suggesting healthcare restructuring can improve resource efficiency.

Observational cohort study comparing ventilatory patterns, chemoreflex sensitivity, and inflammatory biomarkers in 77 COVID-19 recovered individuals versus 41 uninfected controls. Found modest decreases in hypercapnic ventilatory response and correlations between inflammatory markers and breathing control, suggesting COVID-19 impacts the neural control of breathing and systemic inflammation.

Retrospective observational study comparing neuromuscular findings in long-COVID patients (n=59) and ME/CFS patients (n=55) using EMG recordings and exercise testing. Found similar patterns of M-wave alterations and symptom profiles between the two groups, supporting a mechanistic link between SARS-CoV-2 infection and ME/CFS-like presentations.

This study compared transcriptomic profiles of blood leukocytes from 162 COVID-19 convalescent donors versus 40 healthy controls to characterize immune alterations months after acute infection. The research identified persistent differential gene expression in inflammatory and T-cell pathways up to 241 days post-infection, but is a mechanistic study without any treatment intervention or clinical outcomes.

Retrospective cohort study of 86 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients assessed the effectiveness of pacing strategies, a behavioral intervention similar to those used in ME/CFS. High adherence to pacing (measured by engagement in pacing subscale scores) was significantly associated with recovery (60% vs 5.5%) and improvement rates (33.3% vs 5.5%), with pacing adherence as the only independent predictor of recovery.

A prospective observational cohort study that assessed physical activity and sleep patterns in 715 individuals 8 months after hospital discharge for COVID-19 using wrist-worn accelerometers. The study found that post-hospitalization COVID-19 patients had significantly lower physical activity, greater sleep variability, and disrupted sleep patterns compared to office workers and those with type 2 diabetes, with severity correlated to acute illness severity.

This study compares autonomic function and small fiber neuropathy in 87 post-COVID patients, 50 ME/CFS patients, and 50 healthy controls using physiological testing and neuropsychological evaluation. It finds that both syndromes are characterized by inappropriate tachycardia and POTS, with post-COVID patients showing evidence of unmyelinated fiber damage, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective observational cohort study of 95 post-COVID patients in the Netherlands assessing fatigue and symptom severity over 12-18 months post-infection. The study identifies symptom-based clusters and finds that 52.7% of patients meet ME/CFS criteria, with persistent fatigue and diverse symptomatology throughout follow-up.

A prospective pilot cohort study comparing circulating biomarkers of endothelial function and systemic inflammation in ME/CFS patients, long COVID patients, and healthy controls. The study found distinct biomarker profiles differentiating the two conditions but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining the incidence of new-onset chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME) up to 4 years following SARS-CoV-2 infection in 147,377 patients. COVID-19 infection was associated with significantly elevated risk of developing CFS/ME (HR 1.46–1.56 vs. non-COVID controls), with higher risk among females and patients with autoimmune or anxiety disorders.

A prospective cohort study of 29 healthcare workers with post-COVID fatigue comparing brain activation and motor cortex excitability to 24 healthy controls over 6 months. The study found that fatigue correlates with reduced prefrontal and motor cortex activation, with recovery in motor cortex excitability linked to fatigue improvement.

This retrospective cohort study examined 5,162 matched pairs of type 2 diabetes patients to evaluate whether SGLT2 inhibitor use reduces long COVID risk. SGLT2 inhibitor users showed significantly lower risk of long COVID and associated symptoms including cognitive impairment, pain, headache, and anxiety/depression.

This study develops and validates a prognostic nomogram model to predict long COVID risk in hospitalized COVID-19 patients using clinical variables and biomarkers. It is an observational cohort study focused on risk prediction rather than testing a treatment intervention.

This study investigates the prevalence and persistence of autoantibodies (ANA and aPL) in 248 COVID-19 patients with oxygen demand admitted to a South Korean hospital. While the authors note that autoantibody persistence may be related to long-term sequelae, the paper does not study long COVID patients or interventions—it is a cross-sectional serological study of acute COVID-19 patients.

Prospective study from Czechia that stratifies post-COVID patients into clinical groups based on respiratory symptoms and objective signs of pulmonary involvement at three months post-infection. Found that nearly half of outpatients and one-third of hospitalized patients had objective pulmonary signs without subjective respiratory symptoms, highlighting heterogeneity in post-COVID presentation.

This longitudinal observational study examined how pre-existing medical conditions impact the severity of post-COVID syndrome among healthcare and social services workers in Germany. The analysis identified respiratory, cardiovascular, and urogenital diseases as significant risk factors for severe PCS, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study examines changes in pulmonary function (spirometry) in 321 healthcare workers before and after COVID-19 infection between 2020-2022, stratified by vaccination status. While the paper confirms that SARS-CoV-2 infection causes measurable respiratory decline (especially in FVC and FEV1) and that vaccination provides protection against these effects, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention—it is purely an observational assessment of infection-related changes and vaccination's protective effects.

This retrospective cohort study examines the incidence and risk factors of acute transverse myelitis (ATM) in SARS-CoV-2 infected patients versus non-infected controls using TriNetX database records from 2020-2023. The paper focuses on acute COVID-19 infection complications and vaccine safety, not long COVID sequelae or treatment interventions.

Prospective matched household cohort study comparing persistent symptoms in children 6-12 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection versus uninfected controls. Found no significant differences in post-acute sequelae between groups, suggesting PASC is uncommon in previously healthy children after mild infection.

Longitudinal observational study of 114 post-COVID patients who underwent inpatient rehabilitation, assessing work ability and return to work before rehabilitation and 12 months after. Fatigue was identified as the main predictor of reduced work ability, with 48.6% of patients returning to work 12 months post-rehabilitation.

Retrospective comparative analysis of 84 post-COVID-19 patients with osteonecrosis of the femoral head, examining COVID-19 factors and corticosteroid regimens associated with disease severity. The study found that cumulative steroid dose was the primary predictor of ONFH severity, with combined corticosteroid use accelerating symptom onset.

A multicenter observational study evaluating Chinese Medicine (CM) treatment effects in 150 post-COVID-19 patients discharged from Hong Kong hospitals over 3-6 months. Results showed improvements in clinical symptoms, lung function (6MWT and LFQ scores), and body constitution balance, particularly in patients without specific CM syndromes.

This longitudinal case-control study compared COVID-19 outcomes and long-term consequences in 15 patients with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED) versus 149 age-matched controls. HED patients with complete ectodysplasin A pathway disruption showed higher rates of chronic fatigue (83% vs 21%) and hair loss (64% vs 13%) following COVID-19, suggesting genetic factors influence post-COVID syndrome risk.

Retrospective descriptive cohort study of 92 children evaluated 1-3 months after COVID-19 onset to characterize long COVID symptoms. Found that 51% of children had persistent symptoms (tiredness, anosmia, headaches), with higher prevalence in ages 10-18.

An Italian cohort study assessing the prevalence of Long COVID-19 in 629 primary care pediatric patients and 60 hospitalized patients 8-36 weeks post-infection. Found cumulative incidence of 24.3% in primary care and 58% in hospitalized patients, with symptom patterns varying by age group.

Prospective controlled cohort study of 213 COVID-19 patients (ICU-treated, ward-treated, home-isolated) and 48 controls assessed cognitive functioning 6 months post-acute phase using comprehensive neuropsychological testing. ICU-treated and ward-treated patients showed significantly worse cognitive performance in attention, executive functions, and memory domains compared to home-isolated patients and non-COVID controls.

Multicenter cohort study examining the relationship between dehydration during acute COVID-19 infection and long-term physical symptoms in 374 ICU patients, with validation in 1,052 additional patients. Findings show dehydration triggers an aestivation response associated with protein degradation and is more strongly linked to physical long-COVID symptoms than mental symptoms.

Retrospective study of 1,243 children post-SARS-CoV-2 infection examining the effect of nutritional supplements (lactoferrin and multi-element products) on long COVID symptom persistence. Multi-element products alone or combined with lactoferrin were associated with lower risk of persistent long COVID at 6-month follow-up compared to lactoferrin alone.

Retrospective cohort study comparing antidepressant initiation rates in children/adolescents with long COVID versus those with COVID only using administrative health claims data. Found that long COVID cases had significantly higher risk of antidepressant initiation (adjusted-RR: 1.40), but this is an observational study of treatment patterns rather than a trial evaluating a specific intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing polysomnographic findings in 92 Prader-Willi syndrome patients before and after COVID-19 infection (57 infected, 35 controls). Study documents persistent pulmonary impairment three months post-infection, including lower oxygen saturation and increased hypopnea, without testing any interventions or treatments.

This study characterizes neuropsychological dysfunction in COVID-19 ICU survivors 12 months after discharge, finding objective cognitive impairment in 30% and common emotional disturbances. It is an observational assessment study without any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

Retrospective analysis of acute kidney injury (AKI) in 42 children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome post-COVID (MIS-C), examining prevalence, severity, and management outcomes. While post-COVID related, this paper studies acute complications during the immediate post-infection period rather than long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks-months later), and does not evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing healthcare service utilization between 65,548 COVID-19-positive children aged 1-16 years and matched controls during the 3-6 months post-infection. Found statistically significant increases in mental health referrals and medication prescriptions, though the absolute risk differences were small.

Prospective observational cohort study following 167 children hospitalized with acute SARS-CoV-2 infection for up to 12 months post-discharge to characterize long COVID manifestations. Found 16.5% reported long COVID symptoms including weight loss, fatigue, cough, and sleep disturbances, with higher frequency in Omicron-infected children.

This cross-sectional survey of 2,919 adults infected with SARS-CoV-2 investigates the relationship between physical activity status (before and after infection) and long COVID symptom prevalence. The study finds that maintaining physical activity is associated with reduced odds of long COVID symptoms across musculoskeletal, neurological, and respiratory domains (7% overall reduction in symptom likelihood).

Longitudinal observational study measuring telomere length in 49 COVID-19 ICU survivors at baseline and 1 year post-discharge. Patients with longer ICU stays or requiring mechanical ventilation showed greater telomere shortening and increased risk of cellular senescence and lung complications.

This nationwide Swedish cohort study followed ICU patients admitted with acute COVID-19 during the first wave, tracking outcomes through October 2020 with a median follow-up of 183 days. The study found that men had higher mortality risk than women in the 90+ days post-ICU period, but focuses on acute disease severity and mortality rather than long COVID symptoms or interventions.

This observational study examines associations between sedentary behavior and physical activity levels with perceived physical capacity, quality of life, and fatigue in 15 people with post-COVID condition. The study found that greater time in moderate/vigorous physical activity was moderately associated with better perceived physical capacity and lower fatigue, but does not evaluate an active treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study compared 34 long COVID patients (9 months to 5 years post-infection) with 26 recovered controls, assessing clinical symptoms and immune profiles in a sex-disaggregated manner. Females showed higher symptom burden (fatigue, neurocognitive complaints) with reduced CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity, while males displayed elevated TNF-α, suggesting sex-specific immune pathways underlying long COVID persistence.

Population-level study comparing medically certified sick leave and primary healthcare consultations in Norway in 2023 against pre-pandemic trends using Bayesian regression. Found significant excess sick leave associated with general weakness/tiredness and respiratory symptoms consistent with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, but does not study any treatment intervention.

A prospective observational cohort study of 263 long COVID patients (54.4% female) undergoing outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation, assessing sex-specific differences in response to treatment. Women showed greater symptom burden (dyspnea, lower lung function) and lower remission rates (19.4% vs 38.5% in men) despite significant improvements in all outcomes across both sexes.

topics: post-ICU syndrome|cognitive impairment|physical disability|mental health|quality of life
summary: Single-center prospective cohort study following 32 COVID-19 ICU survivors at 3 months post-discharge to assess physical, cognitive, psychological, and biological outcomes. Found that 87.5% had not regained baseline function, with high prevalence of sleep disorders (75%), cognitive impairment (44%), and mental health disorders (28%), demonstrating substantial long-term burden of critical COVID-19.

Prospective cohort study following 230 COVID-19 recovered patients for 1 year post-discharge to assess clinical status and identify recovery-related risk factors. Found persistent pulmonary dysfunction (35.4% diffusion impairment), extrapulmonary manifestations (fatigue, sleep disorders, anxiety, depression), and abnormal imaging in 63.5%, with disease severity and demographics predicting outcomes.

This study investigates the role of pulmonary redox imbalance in COVID-19 ARDS patients and its association with fibroproliferative response and long-term lung abnormalities. Researchers compared biomarkers (oxidative stress markers, fibrosis indicators) between COVID-19 ARDS and non-ARDS patients, finding that redox imbalance correlates with early fibroproliferation and predicts mortality and post-discharge lung impairment.

Population-based cross-sectional study examining the relationship between county-level social vulnerability (using the Minority Health Social Vulnerability Index) and long COVID prevalence among Michigan adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. Finds that medical vulnerability is associated with higher long COVID diagnosis rates, but overall social vulnerability is not significantly associated with long COVID after adjustment for covariates.

Population-based cohort study tracking 12,925 SARS-CoV-2 positive individuals in Bangladesh over two years to determine incidence, characteristics, and recovery of post-COVID-19 conditions. Reports 3.6% PCC incidence, 1.92% case-fatality rate, and identifies geographical distribution, vaccination, and comorbidities as significant predictors of morbidity.

This nationwide cohort study investigates the association between weight gain during the pandemic and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in COVID-19 patients versus controls. The study found that COVID-19 patients who gained weight had significantly higher CVD risk compared to those who maintained stable weight, but does not evaluate any active treatment intervention.

CO-FLOW is a prospective cohort study following 650 COVID-19 hospitalized patients (42% ICU-treated) at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-discharge to assess health trajectories and identify risk factors. At 2 years, 73% had not completely recovered, with persistent neurocognitive complaints, dyspnea, fatigue, and sleep impairment; ICU patients showed slower recovery in neurocognitive and mental health outcomes.

Prospective cohort study comparing long-term health-related quality of life and persistent symptoms between COVID-19 patients and test-negative controls during the Omicron period in Japan using EQ-5D-5L questionnaires. Found COVID-19 patients reported more persistent symptoms and lower quality of life scores at 3 and 6 months post-infection compared to controls, with female patients reporting worse outcomes than males.

Population-level analysis of Norwegian primary healthcare consultations in 2024 compared to pre-pandemic trends, examining whether excess consultations for fatigue, psychological symptoms, and other conditions align with post-acute COVID-19 sequelae. Found 7.1% relative excess in consultations, with fatigue and psychological complaints showing the largest increases, though the study observes patterns rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

topics: post-intensive care syndrome|functional recovery|quality of life|critical illness
summary: This study follows mechanically ventilated COVID-19 survivors over 2 years to track post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) trajectories and functional recovery. While it documents persistent cognitive and functional impairments in critical COVID patients, it does not focus on long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks-months post-infection) and is not testing any treatment intervention.

This prospective longitudinal study compared lung ventilation and perfusion defects in children with post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) versus vaccinated controls using PREFUL MRI imaging at baseline and 6-month follow-up. Despite symptom persistence in PCS patients, MRI findings showed no significant differences between groups and no evidence of persisting lung defects as a cause of PCS.

Observational cohort study comparing cardiopulmonary, functional, cognitive, and mental health outcomes in 113 physically active individuals (hospitalized, community-symptomatic, community-recovered, and controls) ~5 months post-COVID-19. Hospitalized and persistently symptomatic individuals showed significant impairments in exercise capacity, pulmonary function, and cardiopulmonary imaging, while those who recovered showed no differences from controls.

A prospective observational study of 2,729 post-COVID patients evaluating glucocorticoid therapy versus watchful waiting for persistent respiratory symptoms and radiological lung changes. Glucocorticoid-treated patients showed significantly better improvement in pulmonary function (static lung volumes, DLCO) and radiological findings compared to controls.

A longitudinal cohort study of COVID-19 survivors from the first domestic outbreak in Da Nang, Vietnam, following 362 hospitalized cases at 6 and 16 months post-infection. The study characterized clinical features and long-term health outcomes including long COVID symptoms, which persisted in 72% at 6 months and 63.5% at 16 months, with higher prevalence in females and adults.

Registry study of 999 COVID-19 positive patients documenting daily symptom severity and progression over 28 days during acute infection. While 60% reported symptoms at day 28, this is acute COVID-19 follow-up, not post-COVID/long COVID treatment or intervention research.

Prospective study of 2,899 hospital staff in China documenting epidemiological characteristics of Omicron infection and associated long COVID symptoms (4.27% experienced fatigue, brain fog, or both). No treatment intervention tested; paper is observational epidemiology focused on infection rates and symptom prevalence in healthcare workers.

This prospective longitudinal study follows 328 COVID-19 patients over 6 months, identifying three symptom-based clusters of long COVID and assessing their associations with health-related quality of life and work productivity outcomes. The study observes natural symptom patterns and vaccination status without assigning any treatment intervention to participants.

Prospective cohort study following 41 COVID-19 ICU survivors for 12 months post-discharge to assess health-related quality of life and post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) outcomes. Found persistent severe fatigue, respiratory impairment, and 60% reduction in overall HRQoL at follow-up, with 93% of patients meeting PICS criteria.

Longitudinal observational study of 328 outpatients with COVID-19 during Omicron, tracking long COVID symptoms, quality of life, and work productivity over 6 months in relation to vaccination status. Boosted participants showed fewer and less durable symptoms at month 6 compared to unvaccinated and primed groups, with better quality of life outcomes.

This study compares clinical characteristics and outcomes of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) cases triggered by COVID-19 versus other origins in 29 patients. While it includes post-COVID patients, the focus is on a specific neurological complication (GBS) rather than long COVID as a primary syndrome, and it is observational without treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study evaluates the frequency and clinical pattern of post-acute COVID-19 in vaccinated autoimmune rheumatic disease patients versus non-ARD controls following SARS-CoV-2 infection after the third vaccine dose. The study found comparable frequencies of post-acute COVID-19 between ARD and non-ARD groups with similar symptom patterns, concluding that immune disturbances from ARD do not significantly influence post-acute COVID-19 development.

Prospective study of 192 COVID-19 patients examining whether CT severity scoring during acute infection predicts post-COVID syndrome development. Finds CT score >7 has 95.9% sensitivity and 96% specificity for predicting post-COVID development, but this is a predictive/prognostic study, not a treatment trial.

Retrospective study of 80 COVID-19 survivors examining early detection of post-COVID lung fibrosis via CT imaging and identifying risk factors (age, smoking, mechanical ventilation). No treatment intervention was tested; the study proposes early detection as a prevention strategy but does not evaluate any therapeutic intervention.

A retrospective study of 192 post-COVID-19 patients assessing CT imaging abnormalities in the lungs at least 4 weeks after infection, using qualitative and semiquantitative scoring methods. The study documents the prevalence and severity of pulmonary sequelae (ground glass opacities, reticulations, consolidations) and correlates imaging findings with spirometric measurements, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study followed 81 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors with chest CT imaging at medium-term follow-up (≥3 months) to assess lung abnormality resolution rates and predictors of persistent changes. Nearly half (43.2%) had residual lung opacities, with ground glass opacity and parenchymal bands being most common; older age, higher BMI, comorbidities, and ICU admission predicted persistent abnormalities.

This cross-sectional study compared 120 COVID-19 survivors (>3 months post-infection) to controls, measuring clinical signs and biochemical markers. The study found persistent elevations in inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, D-dimer), lipase, and other biochemical parameters in survivors, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment or intervention.

Study of smell and taste dysfunction in acute COVID-19 patients, evaluating prevalence and recovery patterns over 2 months in a cohort of 105 patients. Does not address long COVID or post-acute sequelae; focuses on acute infection only.

Prospective cohort study of 170 Egyptian COVID-19 patients assessing post-COVID-19 syndrome symptoms, incidence, and risk factors at medium-term follow-up. Found 38.82% reported post-COVID symptoms with fatigue and musculoskeletal pain most common; age, disease severity, and comorbidities were significant risk factors associated with functional impairment.

A prospective single-center study evaluating the efficacy of a comprehensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation program in 39 post-COVID-19 patients. The program significantly improved quality of life, fatigue, anxiety, depression, and functional status across multiple outcome measures.

A prospective cohort study following 71 COVID-19 patients at 3, 6, and 12 months to assess persistent respiratory symptoms and identify risk factors. Found that dyspnea, fatigue, and cough persisted in significant proportions, with older age, smoking, diabetes, disease severity, and hypoxemia as associated risk factors.

This case-control study compares post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) symptom prevalence and severity in rheumatic disease patients versus healthy controls, finding significantly higher rates of fatigue, myalgia, cognitive deficits, and functional disability in the patient group. The paper identifies risk factors (smoking, steroid use) and protective factors (biologics use, COVID-19 vaccination) associated with PCS severity in rheumatic patients, but does not evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

This observational prospective study examined thyroid gland dysfunction in 136 hospitalized patients with moderate to severe acute COVID-19 pneumonia during active infection. The study found that sick euthyroid syndrome was the most common thyroid dysfunction pattern, with 61% of cases showing recovery 90 days post-infection.

This UK Household Longitudinal Study examined psychological distress in people with probable COVID-19 infection at multiple timepoints up to 7 months post-infection. The study found elevated psychological distress persisted up to 7 months after probable COVID-19 compared to uninfected controls, with stronger associations in younger age groups and men.

This study uses national COVID-19 databases and healthcare claims to compare post-acute sequelae risks across SARS-CoV-2 reinfected, infected, and uninfected populations in Singapore (2021-2023). It found reinfection associated with increased risk of multi-systemic post-acute sequelae (21% overall), but is a secondary analysis of existing administrative data without treatment evaluation.

Longitudinal observational study comparing depressive and anxiety symptom trajectories in long COVID vs short COVID groups using propensity score matching from the UCL COVID-19 Social Study. Finds long COVID patients have greater initial increases and sustained elevations in depressive symptoms over 22 months, with widening divergence in anxiety symptoms compared to short COVID controls.

A case-control study comparing neurocognitive and psychiatric outcomes in 300 COVID-19 recovered patients versus matched controls using standardized assessment scales. The study found no statistically significant differences in depression, anxiety, psychopathology, or quality of life between groups, concluding COVID-19 does not have significant psychological or neurocognitive impact.

topics: post-intensive care syndrome|quality of life|ICU outcomes
summary: This 1-year follow-up study evaluates post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) in 60 ICU patients (30 COVID, 30 non-COVID), assessing physical, cognitive, and mental health outcomes using standardized questionnaires. While COVID patients showed better quality of life and mental health outcomes overall, the study focuses on acute ICU recovery rather than long COVID symptoms occurring weeks to months post-infection.

This pilot study assessed depression and health-related quality of life in 20 COVID-19 survivors 4 months after ICU discharge using PHQ-9 and EQ-5D-5L questionnaires. The authors found that 25% of survivors had depressive symptoms, which were significantly associated with worse quality of life scores, particularly in domains of pain, anxiety, and daily functioning.

This longitudinal observational study examines the association between delirium during severe COVID-19 hospitalization and post-discharge health-related quality of life in 124 ICU survivors. While it addresses long COVID sequelae, it is excluded as a secondary analysis that does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study followed 58 severe COVID-19 survivors from ICU discharge for 6 months, examining whether cognitive reserve protects against inflammation-related cognitive impairment using phonemic fluency testing. The study found that patients with low cognitive reserve showed worse phonemic fluency performance in proportion to inflammation duration, but did not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This national cohort study characterizes multi-organ post-acute sequelae (PASC) across COVID-19 variants in a highly vaccinated Asian population, comparing outcomes in 1.4-3.3 million test-positive and test-negative individuals over 31-300 days post-infection. While it comprehensively documents PASC epidemiology and shows vaccination reduces post-acute risks, it is observational surveillance research without any treatment or intervention testing.

This preliminary study evaluated depressive symptoms and health-related quality of life in 83 critical COVID-19 survivors at 1-2 months post-discharge using PHQ-9 and EQ-5D-5L questionnaires. Results show 27% of survivors presented depressive symptoms, which were associated with worse outcomes across multiple quality-of-life domains including mobility, self-care, and pain/discomfort.

This retrospective cohort study followed 1,455 COVID-19 hospitalized patients for 1 year post-discharge to assess mental health service utilization and associated costs. While 13% of patients visited mental health services after discharge with significant economic burden, this is an observational follow-up study documenting service use patterns rather than testing or evaluating a specific treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study tracking affective state (anxiety, depression) in 100 long COVID patients over 3 months using the HADS questionnaire and cognitive/physical assessments. Found minimal change in HADS scores and no predictive model for improvement, suggesting slow evolution of affective symptoms in long COVID.

A prospective cohort study of 84 Tunisian COVID-19 patients followed 6-9 months post-discharge to assess mental health outcomes including depression and insomnia using validated instruments (PHQ-9 and ISI). The study found significant increases in depression prevalence (25% to 58.3%) and insomnia (5.95% to 30.95%) compared to baseline, with strong correlation between ISI and PHQ scores.

This study compares cognitive function (processing speed, attention, working memory, executive function, memory) between COVID-19 survivors and non-COVID controls using objective neuropsychological tests. The COVID group showed significantly greater intra-individual variability in processing speed, and those with long-COVID symptoms or prior hospitalization displayed multifaceted cognitive impairment, but the study is observational/comparative with no intervention testing.

Study of psychiatric outcomes in 100 patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 during March-April 2020, assessed one year after discharge. While it identifies new psychiatric disorders in one-third of subjects, the paper focuses on acute COVID-19 hospitalization sequelae rather than long COVID, which typically begins weeks to months post-infection and involves persistent physical symptoms.

Retrospective study examining how COVID-19 affected the onset and course of mental illness in 67 elderly inpatients, comparing those with and without prior psychiatric history. While the paper documents acute and long-term neuropsychiatric sequelae of COVID-19, it does not study any treatment intervention for these conditions.

Prospective cohort study of 121 Tunisian COVID-19 survivors assessed at 6-9 months post-discharge using PHQ-9 and EQ-5D-3L scales to measure depressive symptoms and quality of life. Found significant deterioration across all measured dimensions, with depressive symptoms occurring in 57.9% of survivors compared to 5.7% at baseline.

This nationwide registry study examined the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and long-term psychiatric outcomes (hospital admissions and psychoactive medication use) in 4.5 million Danish adults. While it found increased use of benzodiazepines among infected persons, this is an observational epidemiologic study tracking natural outcomes, not a treatment intervention trial.

This cross-sectional study characterizes anxiety and depressive disorders in 58 post-COVID patients, examining clinical features, symptom prevalence, and psychiatric history. It is a descriptive clinical assessment without any treatment intervention or control group, making it ineligible for the intervention trials analysis.

A prospective cohort study of 121 Tunisian COVID-19 survivors assessing fatigability, cognitive impairment, and pain severity at 6-9 months post-discharge. The study found significant increases in pain scores and high prevalence of fatigability (56.2%) and cognitive impairment (43%), with associations between these symptoms.

This study follows 159 severe COVID-19 survivors for 1 year post-discharge, assessing depressive and anxiety symptoms using standardized questionnaires (PHQ-9, GAD-7). It reports 19% prevalence of depressive symptoms and 21% of anxiety symptoms, both associated with younger age and fear of recurrence, but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective follow-up study (6 months apart) of cognitive function and mental health in 138 adults, 88 with confirmed COVID-19 history and 50 controls. Participants with COVID-19-related hospitalization showed persistent cognitive impairment, and long-COVID symptom reduction correlated with improved executive function, but the study does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This prospective cohort study of 121 Tunisian COVID-19 survivors assessed the prevalence and severity of insomnia and pain 6-9 months post-discharge. The study found significant increases in pain and insomnia scores after infection (30.56% insomnia prevalence, 26.4% pain prevalence) with significant correlations between these symptoms and dyspnea.

This is a prospective cohort study of 116 COVID-19 patients followed for 12 months to assess psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, sleep disorders) and quality of life in long COVID. The study is primarily observational and does not evaluate or test any specific treatment intervention, making it ineligible for a trials meta-analysis.

This is a prospective longitudinal study of COVID-19 outcomes in cancer patients, tracking sequelae over 2 years. While it documents post-acute symptoms and complications (long COVID-like sequelae), it does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention for long COVID.

This study characterizes long COVID patients with cancer using data from the National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C), comparing 634 cancer patients with 1066 non-cancer controls. It is a secondary analysis of an existing cohort database rather than a treatment intervention trial.

This study examines prolonged SARS-CoV-2 positivity (>14 days) in ICU patients with cancer as a prognostic factor for unfavorable outcomes. It is primarily about severe acute COVID-19 in oncology patients, not about post-COVID syndrome or treatment interventions for long COVID.

This study examines post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID) in cancer patients using registry data from the COVID-19 and Cancer Consortium through December 2021. It is a retrospective analysis of existing registry data comparing outcomes between PASC and non-PASC cancer survivors, not a treatment intervention trial.

Observational study of 132 young people with type 1 diabetes who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, examining acute COVID-19 symptoms and effects on glycemic control over a median of 6.7 months. While 16.5% experienced persistent symptoms, the paper focuses primarily on acute infection outcomes in a diabetic population rather than long COVID as the main disease entity being studied.

Retrospective cohort study examining the long-term risk of incident thyroid dysfunction after COVID-19 infection using data from the Montefiore Health System (2016-2024). Finds significantly elevated risk of new-onset thyroid disease, hypothyroidism, and hyperthyroidism in both hospitalized and non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients compared to controls, suggesting enhanced thyroid screening may be warranted in recovering COVID-19 patients.

Longitudinal follow-up study of COVID-19 hospitalized patients examining thyroid dysfunction and atypical thyroiditis during acute infection and early recovery. This paper focuses on acute COVID-19 complications during and immediately after hospitalization, not persistent long COVID symptoms weeks/months after infection.

Retrospective analysis of 65 long COVID patients from a specialized aftercare clinic examining symptom progression over 3 months and the relationship between serum COVID-19 antibody titers and sequelae. This is a study protocol or very early-stage presentation with no results reported.

Retrospective chart review of 39 male post-COVID patients at a specialized outpatient clinic investigating late-onset hypogonadism (LOH) syndrome, finding 48.7% met LOH criteria with higher rates in younger males. Study characterizes the clinical and laboratory features of LOH in post-COVID patients but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective follow-up study of thyroid function and autoimmunity in 122 COVID-19 survivors at baseline and 3 months post-infection. Majority of baseline thyroid dysfunction recovered; study observed increases in anti-thyroid antibody titers post-COVID-19 but no specific treatment intervention was tested.

This retrospective observational study examined clinical characteristics of long COVID patients who developed ME/CFS, comparing three groups (ME/CFS, non-ME/CFS, and no-fatigue) from a specialized COVID aftercare clinic. The study identified serum ferritin levels and insulin-like growth factor-I as potential biomarkers for ME/CFS development, with higher ferritin correlating with symptom severity.

Retrospective observational study comparing long COVID patients with sleep disturbance (n=60) to those without (n=303), examining clinical characteristics and endocrine markers. Found sleep disturbance in 16.5% of long COVID patients, with elevated ACTH and reduced GH levels suggestive of hypothalamo-pituitary stress, but no intervention was tested.

Retrospective study evaluating menstrual symptoms in 223 female long COVID patients attending a specialized clinic in Japan between 2021-2023. Found that 19.7% experienced menstrual symptoms (cycle irregularity, pain, heavy bleeding), with elevated cortisol levels and worse fatigue/QOL scores in symptomatic patients.

A multicenter cross-sectional observational study examining pituitary hormone dysregulation in 246 symptomatic long COVID patients, with a longitudinal follow-up component for those with abnormalities. The study found frequent hormone abnormalities including hyperprolactinemia (12.7%), low IGF-1 (9.0%), and other endocrine disturbances, but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

A retrospective cohort study examining post-COVID complications in 188 patients with pre-existing type 2 diabetes mellitus over 24 months post-infection. The study documents increased incidence of thrombotic complications, hypertension, polyneuropathy progression, vasculitis, and inflammatory markers at various timepoints post-infection, highlighting elevated risk in diabetic patients.

Prospective cohort study of 171 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 3 months post-discharge examining endocrine dysfunction and its association with long COVID onset. Found that non-thyroidal illness syndrome during hospitalization and pituitary dysfunctions (hypogonadism, central hypoadrenalism) were associated with long COVID symptom development, with female patients more likely to report long COVID symptoms including fatigue.

Retrospective observational study examining plasma brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) as a biomarker in 428 long COVID patients stratified by BNP levels. BNP elevation was associated with female sex, older age, dyspnea, and memory impairment, suggesting potential clinical utility for assessing long COVID severity.

This retrospective cohort study examines the association between morphometric vertebral fractures detected at hospital admission and the subsequent development of long COVID 6 months post-discharge in 162 COVID-19 hospitalized patients. The study finds that vertebral fractures are independently associated with long COVID occurrence (OR 3.41), suggesting skeletal fragility as a potential risk factor rather than testing any treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study from the UK MS Register followed 599 MS patients who had COVID-19 to track their recovery patterns and identify predictors of long-standing symptoms (≥4 weeks). The study found that ~30% experienced prolonged symptoms, with pre-existing severe neurologic impairment, anxiety/depression, and female sex associated with slower recovery.

This prospective cohort study examines insulin resistance and inflammatory markers as predictors of new-onset diabetes mellitus in patients hospitalized with acute COVID-19. The study develops predictive models using the TyG index and other biomarkers but does not address long COVID or test any interventions for post-acute sequelae.

Retrospective analysis of 639 long-COVID patients at a post-COVID clinic examining demographic distribution and risk factors for new-onset or progressing peripheral neuropathy. Found older age, male sex, and prior COVID hospitalization associated with new-onset PN, and diabetes/hypertension comorbidities associated with progressing PN.

This study measured plasma markers of neurologic injury (GFAP, NfL) and inflammation in 121 people with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, comparing those with and without self-reported CNS PASC symptoms at early and late recovery timepoints. Participants with CNS PASC symptoms showed elevated neurologic injury and inflammatory markers during early recovery, suggesting these biomarkers are associated with neurologic long COVID symptoms.

Prospective study examining whether coated-platelet levels measured during acute COVID-19 infection predict cognitive impairment 14 months later in long COVID patients. This is a secondary analysis of baseline biomarker data without any intervention administered, so it does not qualify as a treatment trial.

A retrospective chart review investigating whether elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels are a prognostic factor for post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in 43 encephalopathic COVID-19 patients. The study found no significant difference in PASC symptom development between patients with elevated vs. non-elevated CK levels (RR=0.73, p=0.47).

Retrospective chart review of 57 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 encephalopathy patients comparing those with critically elevated IL-6 (>86.95 pg/mL) versus non-critically elevated IL-6, with follow-up at 4 weeks to 1 year post-admission. Critically elevated IL-6 group had 90% PASC symptom development versus 22% in non-critically elevated group (RR=4.05), with tocilizumab treatment attenuating PASC development in 58.3% of treated patients.

Retrospective cohort study comparing neurological PASC symptoms between HIV-positive and HIV-negative COVID-19 patients at 4 weeks to 1 year post-infection. Found no significant differences in symptom prevalence between groups, though HIV patients showed slightly higher rates of most neurological symptoms.

Retrospective analysis of 75 COVID-19 patients with HbA1c measurements to investigate whether diabetic control is associated with neurological PASC symptoms. Found no significant difference in neurological PASC symptom incidence across HbA1c groups, though the analysis is preliminary with work ongoing to expand sample size and follow-up duration.

Retrospective follow-up study comparing neurological post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) symptoms in 57 stroke patients versus 418 non-stroke patients at 4 weeks to 1 year post-infection. Found no significant differences in PASC symptom incidence between groups, though stroke patients had higher mean age and some symptom variations.

This prospective cohort study evaluated cognitive function in 60 COVID-19 survivors at 12 weeks post-discharge, using neuropsychological testing and MRI imaging. The study found persistent cognitive impairments in executive function, attention, and memory that correlated with frontal and frontotemporal brain atrophy, independent of initial disease severity.

Retrospective chart review of 56 long COVID patients comparing those with headache-predominant symptoms to those without, examining demographic risk factors and brain MRI findings. No treatment intervention is evaluated; this is a characterization study of symptom phenotypes and associated imaging findings.

Longitudinal follow-up study of 46 long COVID patients examining changes in headache symptoms and quality of life 12-19 months after initial baseline assessment. Found no significant changes in headache frequency or QoL measures over time, though headache impact scores increased.

This observational cohort study followed 238 COVID-19 survivors hospitalized with ARDS, performing neurological examinations and cognitive screening 3 months post-discharge. The study documents high prevalence of neurological sequelae including sensorimotor neuropathy (66.4%), cognitive complaints (59.7%), and myopathic pain (43.9%), but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective study examining the association between interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels and outcomes in post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) using electronic medical records. The paper investigates whether elevated IL-6 correlates with PASC severity or outcomes but does not test a specific intervention.

This observational cohort study evaluated insomnia prevalence and associations in 93 PASC patients from an outpatient neurology clinic, with 42 completing 1-year follow-up assessments using the Insomnia Severity Index. Insomnia was associated with worsened anxiety, fatigue, and depression scores, but the study is a passive follow-up cohort without treatment intervention.

This follow-up study assessed dysautonomia symptoms and quality of life in 46 non-hospitalized PASC patients from a neurology clinic using the COMPASS-31 questionnaire at 1-year follow-up. The study found autonomic dysfunction in 69% of participants, with associations between dysautonomia severity and anxiety, fatigue, and persistent lightheadedness symptoms.

This observational study followed 7 neuro-PASC patients for at least 1 year after their initial NIH Clinical Center evaluation to assess persistence of autonomic and immunologic abnormalities. The authors found that 71% of initially abnormal test results remained abnormal at follow-up, including CSF oligoclonal bands, catecholamine deficiency, baroreflex dysfunction, and white matter hyperintensities on MRI.

Multi-center cohort study assessing acute and prolonged health effects of COVID-19 in 432 German athletes, with comprehensive clinical and physiological evaluations. Study documents post-COVID symptom patterns in athletes but does not test any specific treatment or intervention.

Retrospective observational study comparing α-synuclein deposition in skin biopsies from neuro-PASC (long COVID) patients and controls, finding elevated α-syn-TH colocalization in both neuro-PASC and Lewy body disease groups. This is a pathophysiological investigation study with no treatment intervention tested.

Observational cohort study examining prevalence of clinical myocarditis and prolonged symptoms in 88 Division III college athletes diagnosed with COVID-19. Found 0% clinical myocarditis diagnosis but 15% with prolonged symptoms, though study does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This hospital registry study examines baseline respiratory system compliance in surgical patients with a prior COVID-19 history (n=19,921), finding that previous infection is associated with lower compliance, particularly in severe cases and during Alpha/Delta variants. The study is observational without treatment intervention—it passively compares surgical outcomes between COVID-exposed and unexposed patients, not testing or evaluating any therapeutic intervention.

This study analyzes drug prescription patterns for long COVID patients in Japan using a nationwide medical database, identifying 3,769 long COVID cases among 652,016 COVID-19 patients. The analysis describes symptom-based prescribing practices (acetaminophen, herbal medicines, etc.) rather than evaluating the efficacy of any specific treatment intervention.

Multicenter observational cohort study of neurologic disorders in 1,865 hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute infection and early recovery (March 2020-June 2021). Most patients achieved good functional outcomes at 6-month follow-up, with incidence of neuro-COVID complications declining across pandemic waves.

This prospective cohort study compared cardiorespiratory exercise capacity and endothelial function in 28 immunocompromised children 6 months post-COVID-19 versus 26 non-infected controls. COVID-19 patients showed reduced ventilatory anaerobic threshold, VO2peak, and endothelial function (brachial flow-mediated dilation) compared to controls, with 36% of patients meeting criteria for long COVID.

This prospective cohort study tracked 85 athletes with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection over 28 weeks to determine the prevalence of persistent and late-onset symptoms at repeated intervals. The study found symptom prevalence decreased from 79% at 2-4 weeks to 14% at 28 weeks, with loss of smell, shortness of breath, and fatigue being most common early on.

This cross-sectional study examined 72 COVID-19 survivors to determine whether the number and severity of acute COVID symptoms predict persistent long COVID symptoms and quality of life outcomes. The study found that survivors with more acute symptoms (8-17 vs 1-7) had worse outcomes including higher body fat, lower physical activity, and poorer quality of life, but did not test any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed electronic health records of 122,045 COVID-19 patients in Japan to investigate the incidence of post-COVID-19 symptoms (headache, fatigue, depression, disuse syndrome) across different viral strains and vaccination periods. The study found that post-COVID symptoms increased with age and were linked to vaccination coverage, but it is a secondary analysis of existing medical database records with no intervention tested.

Prospective cohort study examining whether pre-infection physical activity protects against long COVID development in 492 adults followed for 9 months post-diagnosis. Found that pre-infection PA did not prevent LC, though participants with LC showed significantly reduced PA at 9 months; higher BMI and diabetes were strong LC risk factors.

This case-control study compares pain intensity, distribution, and endogenous pain inhibition between 42 COVID-19 survivors (7.9 months post-infection) and 42 matched controls. Findings show COVID-19 survivors reported greater average/worst pain and more widespread pain during acute infection, but had similar pain at rest and during most functional tasks at the time of testing, except during pulmonary function testing.

A Japanese nationwide retrospective cohort study tracking 515 long COVID patients over 36 months to characterize symptom trajectories and symptom clusters. Patients with continuous and multiple symptoms experienced persistently lower quality of life and greater economic burden, with fatigue and dyspnea persisting while other symptoms declined.

topics: functional impairment|activities of daily living|long-term care|rehabilitation
summary: This retrospective cohort study with prospective follow-up examined changes in functional independence among 201 COVID-19 survivors in long-term care facilities, using the Barthel Index at baseline, post-recovery, and 3-month follow-up. While early deterioration was associated with hospitalization and comorbidities, long-term follow-up showed persistent functional impairment requiring rehabilitation support regardless of initial disease severity.

This observational study compares quality of life in chronic heart failure patients at three time-points: before, during, and 6 months after acute COVID-19 infection using EuroQoL-VAS scales. The paper focuses on acute COVID-19 effects on pre-existing heart disease, not long COVID syndrome.

Retrospective observational study of 211 IMIRD patients examining long COVID prevalence (24.2%) and clinical phenotypes including pulmonary, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and neurological manifestations. Analysis identifies phenotype-specific clinical correlates and comorbidity associations but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study followed 108 previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients with residual symptoms (asthenia, dyspnea) and imaged them with chest CT at mid-term follow-up. The study documents persistent radiological lung alterations (ground-glass opacities, linear opacities, bronchiolectases) but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A retrospective study of 33 long COVID patients who completed a structured physical therapy program (kinesiotherapy with optional high-intensity laser therapy for musculoskeletal comorbidities). The intervention significantly improved anxiety and depression symptoms (measured by HADS) at discharge and one-month follow-up, with improvements correlated to enhanced 6-minute walk test performance.

Prospective cohort study measuring long COVID prevalence in Thailand during the Omicron variant epidemic at 3 and 6 months post-infection. Identifies female sex, severe-to-critical acute illness, and healthcare worker occupation as significant predictors of long COVID development.

This prospective observational study examined pericardial tissue samples from 93 CABG patients to assess long-term histopathological changes associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study found no significant lasting pericardial damage linked to COVID-19, with no differences in fibrosis or immune cell infiltration between infected and non-infected groups.

Prospective cohort study of 222 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors followed for one month to identify incidence and predictive factors of hyperventilation syndrome (HVS) and PTSD in the post-COVID phase. Found HVS in 15.6% of survivors, with cognitive impairment, weight loss, functional limitations, and PTSD as independent risk factors.

A prospective cohort study of 153 long COVID patients at a post-COVID clinic examining psychiatric symptoms and alcohol use at 2-4 months and 7-14 months post-infection. The study found high prevalence of depression, anxiety, and PTSD (12.9-22.6%), with problematic alcohol use increasing from 45.5% to 71.8%, but no intervention or treatment was administered.

Retrospective cohort study of 276 ambulatory patients recovering from acute COVID-19, examining clinical predictors of prolonged post-acute sequelae (PASC) and antibody seroconversion. Found that high initial symptom burden, anosmia, myalgia, and dyspnea are strong predictors of prolonged symptoms lasting >4 weeks, while seroconversion rates vary by gender and corticosteroid use.

A retrospective cohort study using linked NHS records that describes serious clinical outcomes (DVT, PE, stroke, MI, heart failure, AKI, diabetes) in 77,347 patients discharged from hospital following COVID-19 hospitalization. The study is observational without any treatment intervention, tracking adverse outcomes post-discharge rather than evaluating a specific treatment.

Prospective observational study examining systemic inflammatory markers in asthma patients over six months following mild COVID-19 infection compared to asthma controls without COVID exposure. Found persistent elevation of inflammatory markers (GSDMD, IL-1β, IL-6, NLRP3, D-dimer) at six months, suggesting sustained inflammasome activation and hyperinflammatory response in post-COVID asthma patients.

Retrospective cohort study comparing psychiatric comorbidities in SARS and COVID-19 survivors at 30 months post-infection. The study identifies risk factors for psychiatric disorders but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study following 253 COVID-19 hospitalized patients for 1 month post-discharge to measure incident symptoms and functional disability. Found that 84% reported persistent symptoms, 53% new cardiopulmonary problems, and 53% new disability; longer hospital stay predicted worse 1-month outcomes.

This prospective cohort study from Catalonia examines the association between environmental exposures and long COVID development in a population-based sample. It is observational and does not test a specific treatment intervention.

This observational cohort study examines the association between long-term air pollution exposure and SARS-CoV-2 breakthrough infections, Long COVID, and immune responses in 6,875 Chinese participants. The study found that higher air pollutant levels (PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO) were associated with increased risk of breakthrough infections, Long COVID, hospitalization, and weakened antibody responses, with stronger effects in vulnerable populations.

Population-based cohort study examining the association between long-term air pollution exposure and COVID-19 vaccine antibody response and long COVID risk in Catalonia. While it includes long COVID assessment, it is an observational cohort study analyzing environmental risk factors rather than testing any intervention or treatment.

Observational study of 87 COVID-19 patients followed at 3 and 6 months post-hospitalization to assess long-term respiratory outcomes and correlations with initial radiological findings. Found that respiratory function was transiently affected by the virus with recovery within three months, with males more susceptible than females.

This prospective cohort study of 749 COVID-19 survivors examined associations between ambient air pollution exposure and persistent post-COVID symptoms at ~200 days follow-up. Individual PM2.5 exposure was associated with higher dyspnea and fatigue scores and lower functional status, suggesting air pollution may worsen recovery outcomes.

This paper surveys specialist paediatric post-COVID hubs established by NHS England, analyzing referral patterns, assessments, and outcomes from 1,374 referrals between 2022-2023. It describes service utilization and reports sparse outcome improvements but does not evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

This follow-up study of 172 COVID-19 hospitalization survivors assessed anxiety and depression symptoms 20-22 months post-discharge using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. The study identified risk factors (age, financial status, vaccination, female sex, dyspnea) associated with mental health outcomes but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.
