Prospective cohort study of 350 COVID-19 patients with COVID-associated cystitis (CAC) followed for 21-28 months post-discharge, treated with conservative management and standard overactive bladder medications. Results show 87% achieved symptom improvement, with 95.4% of new-onset cases improving versus 60.7% of pre-existing cases.

Retrospective follow-up study of 85 pediatric asthma patients evaluated 6+ months after COVID-19 infection to assess symptom persistence and asthma control. Found that respiratory symptoms persisted in 23.5% of patients at 6 months, with cough being most common, but no significant changes in asthma control.

Longitudinal observational study comparing cognitive functioning in Mexican older adults with and without prior COVID-19 infection, measured at baseline (2019) and follow-up (2023). Found moderate-large statistically significant impairment in executive functions in COVID-19-infected older adults 24 months post-infection, with normative decline in global cognition and memory.

This cross-sectional study compares oculomotor function and pupil response in long COVID patients (both mild and severe) versus healthy controls using eye-tracking technology. The study found significant differences in saccadic latencies, fixation stability, and pupillary responses between groups, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This paper uses electronic health records from community health centers to identify clinical sequelae of long COVID in underserved populations, comparing symptoms between patients who tested positive (n=4,091) and negative (n=7,118) for acute COVID-19. It identifies 18 statistically significant sequelae including breathing abnormalities, fatigue, and headache, but is a retrospective observational study without any treatment intervention or control comparison groups.

This study uses the PRIME Registry to compare the prevalence of 17 post-COVID conditions in US primary care patients with COVID-19 (2020-2021) versus historical influenza-like illness controls (2018) and contemporaneous wellness visit controls. The COVID-19 group showed higher prevalence of breathing difficulties, fatigue, sleep disturbances, and type 2 diabetes, but the findings suggest lower post-COVID burden in primary care compared to subspecialty settings.

This retrospective cohort study develops a machine learning framework to identify long COVID patients in electronic health records across three healthcare systems, achieving positive predictive values of 0.73-0.91 for dyspnea, fatigue, and joint pain. The study estimates PASC prevalence among hospitalized COVID-19 patients but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study of 181 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examining the incidence and predictors of brain fog and work-related quality of life impairment up to 12+ weeks post-infection. Finds brain fog affects ~50% of patients, correlates with cardiac troponin levels and female sex, and is the primary driver of work quality-of-life decline by 3+ months post-infection.

Retrospective cohort study of 273,618 COVID-19 survivors examining incidence and co-occurrence of long-COVID features over 6 months using linked electronic health records. Found 36.55% had one or more long-COVID feature in months 3-6, with significant variations by sex, age, and illness severity.

Longitudinal cohort study following Indigenous adults and children in the Southwest US for 3 months post-acute COVID-19 to characterize Post-COVID-19 Conditions (PCC) prevalence and risk factors. Found that 39.8% of adults and 15.9% of children experienced PCC symptoms, with COVID-19 vaccination associated with reduced PCC risk.

This retrospective cohort study compared hospitalization and death risks between COVID-19 survivors and general population/influenza controls using linked NHS data. While it documents elevated post-discharge morbidity and mortality in COVID-19 survivors (suggesting long COVID sequelae), it is an observational outcome study with no intervention tested, making it ineligible for the trials pipeline.

Register-based cohort study examining long COVID risk and symptoms among ethnic minorities in Denmark compared to native Danes, using nationwide COVID-19 diagnosis data from 2020-2022. Found significantly higher rates of long COVID diagnosis and cardiopulmonary symptoms in ethnic minorities from North Africa, Middle East, Eastern Europe, and Asia.

This retrospective cohort study examines the time to symptom resolution among 823 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Zambia from 2020-2022, using parametric survival analysis to identify factors associated with recovery patterns. The study finds that severe acute COVID-19 was associated with slower symptom resolution, while Omicron infection was associated with faster recovery, but does not evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study of over 2 million Medicare beneficiaries estimates the incidence and characteristics of long COVID using ICD-10 codes and WHO symptom-based definitions. It compares long COVID and long Flu patients on hospitalization and healthcare utilization outcomes, finding that long COVID patients have higher healthcare burden and distinct symptomatology, but it is not a treatment study.

This matched cohort study examined cardiometabolic outcomes (new-onset diabetes and cardiovascular disease) in 428,650 COVID-19 patients compared to matched controls over 12 months. The study found increased CVD incidence early after COVID-19 infection but no long-term increase in DM or CVD incidence from weeks 13-52, suggesting these outcomes are primarily acute rather than features of persistent long COVID.

This retrospective matched cohort study of >157,000 German individuals with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 examines post-COVID-19-associated morbidity across 96 prespecified health outcomes aggregated into 13 diagnosis/symptom complexes in children, adolescents, and adults. The study found significantly elevated incidence rates for fatigue, cough, and throat/chest pain in younger age groups and for olfactory/taste disturbances, fever, and dyspnea in adults, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing 3-year outcomes of hospitalized COVID-19 patients with versus without neurological manifestations during acute infection. While it includes long COVID follow-up (3 years post-infection), it is observational without any treatment intervention and appears to be a secondary analysis or extended follow-up of an existing cohort rather than a primary intervention trial.

This cross-sectional study compared autonomic function testing between 20 fatigued and 20 non-fatigued post-COVID patients at median 166.5 days post-infection. The study found no pathological autonomic dysfunction differences between groups, though fatigue was strongly associated with anxiety.

This retrospective cohort study compares 180-day risk of post-acute sequelae (PAS) between 74,738 COVID-19 cases and 18,790 influenza cases in a US healthcare system. It found that non-severe COVID-19 had only modestly higher PAS risk than influenza, but hospitalized COVID-19 cases had significantly higher risk of severe PAS requiring inpatient care.

This paper assessed cognitive and psychiatric outcomes in 87 COVID-19 patients during rehabilitation in the subacute phase, stratified by respiratory support level during acute illness. While it documents cognitive deficits and depression in long COVID patients, it is an observational cross-sectional assessment of an existing cohort without testing any specific intervention or treatment.

This is a nested case-control follow-up study (phase 2) of the EPILOC cohort that reassesses 982 long COVID patients and 576 controls ~8.5 months after an initial screening questionnaire to characterize persistent symptoms and identify clinical/laboratory differences. The study documents that most patients with persistent PCS did not recover in the second year, with fatigue, exercise intolerance, and cognitive complaints predominating, but found no major pathology in laboratory tests or evidence of viral persistence.

This target trial emulation study examined whether Paxlovid treatment during acute COVID-19 reduces the risk of developing long COVID in a cohort of 445,738 patients from the N3C and RECOVER consortia. Paxlovid had no significant effect on overall long COVID incidence but showed small protective effects against cognitive and fatigue symptoms, particularly among patients aged 65+ and those with higher comorbidity burden (NNT 76-233).

Retrospective chart review of 71 critically ill COVID-19 survivors discharged from ICU/HDU in UAE, documenting post-acute complications including myopathy, swallowing impairments, and delirium. Study describes natural disease course and complications rather than evaluating any treatment intervention.

Prospective observational study of 93 patients examined at 12 weeks post-COVID-19 hospitalization to evaluate whether KL-6 (a pulmonary epithelial injury marker) correlates with acute severity or persistent symptoms/radiological abnormalities. Found KL-6 levels at 12 weeks were associated with abnormal CT findings but not with acute severity or subjective breathlessness.

Retrospective observational cohort study of 256 COVID-19 patients aged 70+ in a German district during the first wave, examining risk factors, mortality, and functional outcomes. Found 18% mortality and identified newly emerged care needs as a significant complication, with 27% of previously self-sufficient survivors unable to return home after discharge.

Population-based prospective cohort study assessing prevalence of impaired health status and symptoms at 6-8 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection in 431 Swiss adults. Found 26% reported not fully recovered, 55% reported fatigue, and 25% had dyspnea, with significant healthcare utilization burden.

Population-based cohort study of 303 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for a median of 61 days to estimate PASC prevalence and symptom patterns. Found 68.7% prevalence at 30 days, with fatigue, shortness of breath, and brain fog as most common symptoms.

Prospective cohort study following 8,786 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients (794 positive, 7,229 negative controls) for 3-8 months post-infection via online surveys assessing self-rated health and symptom persistence. Found 36% of COVID-19 positive patients reported worsening health compared to one year prior, versus 18% of negative controls, identifying age, fitness, and healthcare profession as factors associated with health deterioration.

A prospective cohort study of 355 COVID-19 patients followed for one month after clinical improvement to determine incidence and risk factors for post-COVID-19 syndrome. Found that 46% developed post-COVID symptoms (primarily fatigue), with female gender, respiratory distress, lethargy, and prolonged disease duration as key risk factors.

Prospective follow-up study of 75 COVID-19 hospitalized patients with interstitial pneumonia tracked for 3-12 months to assess radiological sequelae and immunological patterns (IgG/IgM). Found that 62.7% had persistent radiological findings at 3 months, with baseline IL-6 levels predictive of long-term sequelae, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This prospective cohort study followed 222 COVID-19 patients for up to 6 months post-discharge to identify prevalence and predictors of persistent symptoms (PACS). Key finding: 56.3% experienced persistent symptoms; interferon β-1b triple antiviral therapy during acute infection was associated with reduced symptom persistence and better recovery to baseline health.

Retrospective observational study of 155 primary care patients with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia followed for median 54 days to characterize symptom duration and define long COVID cutoff points. Found 28.3% had persistent symptoms >4 weeks, with longer-lasting cough, dyspnea, and asthenia in that group; proposes 4-12 week window as threshold for long COVID definition.

This observational study examined the occurrence and predictors of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) in a community-based cohort of 390 US adults. Results identified fatigue, anosmia, and myalgia as the most common chronic COVID-19 symptoms, with female sex, severe acute infection, and higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG levels as significant predictors.

This prospective cohort study followed 300 COVID-19 patients at a tertiary hospital in Nepal for three months to assess the prevalence of post-COVID syndrome and identify risk factors. Fatigue was the most common persistent symptom (34% at 60 days, 28.3% at 90 days), and multiple acute symptoms including anosmia, ageusia, and shortness of breath were significant predictors of post-COVID syndrome development.

This prospective observational cohort study of 920 critically ill COVID-19 patients examines risk factors for post-intubation dysphagia (swallowing dysfunction) during hospitalization. The study identifies age, severity, BMI, neuromuscular blockers, neurologic diseases, and diabetes as predictive factors for non-resolved dysphagia but does not test any specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study evaluates pulmonary emphysematous changes in COVID-19 patients using follow-up low-dose CT scans. The study found significant emphysema development in patients with >30 days follow-up, suggesting long-term pulmonary sequelae of COVID-19.

Observational chart review comparing post-COVID-19 symptoms between 280 patients who did and did not require invasive mechanical ventilation during acute hospitalization. Found that intubated patients had significantly higher rates of neuropsychiatric (67.3% vs 55.4%) and musculoskeletal (38.7% vs 25.9%) involvement, with 98% reporting persistent symptoms.

Population-based observational study examining the incidence and characteristics of patients starting long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) in Sweden during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020) compared to pre-pandemic years (2015-2019). Finds that COVID-19 accounted for 20.5% of new LTOT cases in 2020, but overall LTOT incidence did not significantly increase.

Prospective follow-up study of 153 male COVID-19 patients examining erectile dysfunction and mental health outcomes at three months post-discharge. Found 50.3% ED prevalence at follow-up (down from 64.7% at baseline), with age >40 and major depression as significant risk factors for persistent ED.

This retrospective cohort study compared post-COVID symptoms across 178 patients stratified by acute COVID-19 severity (ICU, ward, or no hospitalization) at a rehabilitation unit. Findings showed ICU patients had lower muscle strength and effort capacity, while non-hospitalized patients had worse anxiety and quality-of-life scores, with respiratory muscle weakness common across groups despite varying mechanical ventilation exposure.

A prospective cohort study of 242 COVID-19 hospitalized patients identified three distinct long COVID symptom phenotypes and their associated therapeutic interventions at 12 months post-infection. Patients receiving psychiatric therapies (for the anxiety/depression phenotype) showed the highest symptom improvement rates (100%), followed by those receiving physical/occupational therapy (97%) and those receiving minimal interventions (83%).

Longitudinal observational study examining hospital readmission and mortality outcomes in 17,652 COVID-19 patients, comparing 1,131 mechanically ventilated to non-ventilated patients through propensity score matching. While the paper addresses long-term health implications post-discharge, it does not evaluate a specific treatment intervention for long COVID but rather documents complications following acute COVID-19 hospitalization.

This cross-sectional study examined olfactory and gustatory dysfunction in 58 COVID-19 outpatients and 56 negative controls using psychophysical tests and subjective questionnaires at baseline and up to 6 months post-infection. Most individuals recovered normal function by 30 days, but approximately 20% reported persistent sensory dysfunction at 6 months, highlighting long-term sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Prospective matched cohort study following 3,395 children and young people (1,658 SARS-CoV-2 positive, 1,737 negative controls) for 6 months post-infection to characterize symptom trajectories and prevalence. Found that most common acute symptoms declined over 6 months in both groups, with similar symptom patterns observed in test-negatives, suggesting many symptoms may not be specific to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Retrospective nationwide matched cohort study comparing long COVID sequelae in 3,949 hospitalized COVID-19 patients versus 15,511 matched controls over 12 months. Documents high incidence of post-acute complications (40.3% vs 20% in controls) including dementia, respiratory disease, and cardiac outcomes, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study following 487 COVID-19 patients at 4 weeks and 371 at 6 months to identify characteristics and predictors of long COVID. Found 29.2% reported long COVID at 4 weeks declining to 9.4% at 6 months, with fatigue as most common symptom; key predictors included pre-existing conditions, acute symptom severity, and hospitalization.

This retrospective cohort study followed 4,427 COVID-19 patients and controls for one year to assess cardiovascular outcomes during the post-acute phase. The study found higher rates of arterial thrombotic events, venous thromboembolism, and arrhythmias in the COVID-19 cohort, but did not test any specific intervention or treatment.

This longitudinal cohort study examined post-COVID depression in 712 Indonesian COVID-19 survivors over 60 days, comparing outcomes between patients who received favipiravir and non-recipients using propensity score matching. Favipiravir was associated with lower depression rates (aOR 0.488, 95% CI 0.339-0.701) and protective effects against depressive mood and loss of interest.

This study uses machine learning to identify three distinct early-symptom clusters in SARS-CoV-2 infected military beneficiaries and correlates these phenotypes with hospitalization, activity return, and long COVID risk. It is an observational analysis of an existing cohort dataset (EPICC COVID-19) with no intervention given to participants.

Prospective cohort study following 326 ICU-hospitalized COVID-19 patients 6-12 months post-discharge to assess long-term respiratory consequences via CT imaging and pulmonary function tests. Found CT lesions in 81.8% of patients with mild restrictive impairment and diffusion capacity impairment; male sex, longer ICU/mechanical ventilation duration, and vasoactive drug use were predictors of severe lesions.

This observational study examines laryngeal electromyography findings in 38 post-COVID patients with chronic cough to assess vagus nerve neuropathy involvement. While it provides clinical insights into post-COVID pathophysiology, it is an observational characterization study without any treatment intervention or outcome evaluation.

Retrospective cohort study using electronic health records from 13,033 adults to compare symptom and diagnosis rates before and after COVID-19 infection, with follow-up through November 2021. Found significantly increased odds of multiple diagnoses post-COVID including dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis, and loss of smell/taste, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Pooled analysis of two Swiss population-based cohorts examining PCC prevalence and severity across SARS-CoV-2 variants (Wildtype, Delta, Omicron) and vaccination status in 1,350 infected individuals. Found that vaccinated individuals infected with Omicron had significantly reduced odds of developing PCC, with four distinct symptom clusters identified across variants.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing EHR data from ~27 million patients to characterize post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) following ancestral and Delta variant infections. Study documents excess burden of pulmonary and abdominal conditions post-COVID but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 42 critical COVID-19 survivors who received inpatient physical and rehabilitation medicine (PRM) during ICU stay, evaluated at 6 and 12 months post-discharge. While the paper describes outcomes in physical, mental, and cognitive domains, it is a passive observational follow-up study of patients who received standard inpatient rehabilitation as part of routine ICU care, not a controlled evaluation of a specific experimental intervention or treatment program.

A longitudinal cohort study of 1,344 long COVID patients that used latent class analysis to identify three distinct phenotypes based on symptom profiles (fatigue/dyspnea, anxiety/depression, or combined). The study examined associations between phenotypes and quality of life outcomes over 6 months but did not test any specific intervention or treatment.

Intensive longitudinal study of 82 long COVID patients using smartphone app (5 daily entries over 14 days) and wearable accelerometers to examine within-person symptom variation and associations with physical activity. Found substantial within-individual symptom variation, weak correlations between symptoms and activity, and heterogeneous patterns suggesting altered central symptom processing rather than distinct phenotypes.

This observational study examined whether ABO blood group distribution differs between acute COVID-19 hospitalization patients and long COVID patients, comparing frequencies and calculating adjusted odds ratios. The analysis found no significant association between any ABO blood subgroup or Rh factor and either COVID-19 or long COVID development.

Ambidirectional cohort study of 332 long COVID patients comparing symptom profiles by antecedent COVID-19 severity and treatment exposure. Mild antecedent COVID-19 was associated with greater odds of fatigue, cognitive impairment, headaches, and dizziness; remdesivir treatment was associated with reduced fatigue and cognitive impairment.

Prospective observational cohort study evaluating pulmonary function and CT findings in dialysis patients 3+ months after COVID-19 recovery. Found high prevalence of radiological abnormalities (reticulation 64%, ground glass opacities 32%, bronchiectasis 28%) and restrictive lung patterns (41%), though few patients had ongoing symptoms and abnormalities were comparable to the general population.

Prospective observational study examining cardiac magnetic resonance imaging findings in 95 hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 9-month follow-up compared to controls. Found myocardial scar in 66% of COVID-19 patients but found no association between myocardial injury and long-term symptoms, dyspnea, chest pain, or arrhythmias.

The Nivel Corona Cohort is a population-based study combining general practice electronic health records with patient-reported outcomes to investigate short- and long-term effects of COVID-19 in the Netherlands. The cohort of 442 participants documents acute-phase symptoms (fatigue, reduced condition, cough, headache, myalgia) and plans longitudinal follow-up over one year.

This paper describes the implementation and outcomes of a post-COVID clinic at an Irish tertiary centre, analyzing patient characteristics and clinic operations for 311 post-COVID patients. The study found that 70% had persistent symptoms and identifies risk factors for ongoing symptoms, but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Community-based case-control study comparing long COVID symptom prevalence and antibody responses in 1,150 COVID-19 cases versus 1,110 matched controls in the Dallas Fort-Worth area. Found that 21.1% of cases reported persistent PASC symptoms including shortness of breath, fatigue, and loss of taste/smell, with decreasing antibody levels over 8.6 months of follow-up.

Prospective observational study following 86 ICU patients who required invasive ventilation for acute COVID-19 pneumonia, assessing radiological lung appearance and pulmonary function at 6 months post-discharge. Found persistent CT abnormalities and reduced lung function in most patients, but no intervention was tested.

Retrospective cohort study examining long-term renal outcomes in 451 patients with biopsy-proven kidney disease who experienced COVID-19 infection. Finds COVID-19 patients had worse renal function decline and higher rates of eGFR decline >30% or ESRD, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective follow-up study examining the association between COVID-19 vaccination and prolonged long-COVID symptoms in 1,236 adults with long-COVID syndrome. Found that vaccination status was significantly associated with persistent long-COVID symptoms (44.6% in vaccinated vs 29.4% in unvaccinated), though authors note vaccines reduce severe COVID-19 risk.

This study uses primary care electronic health records to compare symptoms in 11,015 COVID-19 patients versus 18,098 unexposed controls, identifying symptoms most strongly associated with long COVID at 12+ weeks post-infection (fatigue, shortness of breath, palpitations). It does not evaluate any treatment intervention, making it ineligible for the trials meta-analysis.

This infodemiology study analyzed online search trends for long-COVID and related symptoms in Japan from 2020-2022 using Yahoo! JAPAN search data. It found that interest in long-COVID increased with COVID-19 case peaks, with hair loss, cough, smell/taste disturbance, and headache as the most frequently searched symptoms.

A prospective cohort study of 44,386 individuals in Malaysia following SARS-CoV-2 infection during the Omicron wave, assessing the prevalence and associated factors of post COVID-19 condition at 3 months. Found that 3.4% met post COVID-19 criteria, with fatigue, cough, and cognitive impairment as the most common symptoms, and identified female sex, comorbidities, and severe acute illness as risk factors.

This study uses the N3C Data Enclave to analyze the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and new-onset schizophrenia spectrum and psychotic disorders across three time intervals post-infection. It is a secondary analysis of an existing cohort database rather than a primary trial, and does not study a treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 481 COVID-19 patients in Pakistan followed for 12 months to assess long COVID prevalence and its association with vaccination status and disease severity. Found 29.9% developed long COVID symptoms, with unvaccinated patients having 2.42× higher odds of developing long COVID compared to vaccinated patients.

The EPICC study assessed the frequency of post-acute neuropsychological symptoms (depression, anxiety, fatigue, cognitive impairment) in 2,383 U.S. Military Healthcare System beneficiaries 1-6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection. SARS-CoV-2 positive participants were significantly more likely to report depression, fatigue, and cognitive impairment compared to uninfected controls, with risk ratios up to 2.07 for fatigue.

This retrospective cohort study uses electronic health record data from 588,611 US patients to create a data-driven definition of post-COVID conditions by measuring symptom changes before and after COVID infection. The study found 20% of COVID patients developed PCC, with prevalence increasing with age, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study describes long COVID symptom frequency and associated risk factors in 6,142 Nepali women at 6 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection. It found 16.9% of PCR-positive women reported non-recovery with prominent fatigue, pain, cognitive impairment, dyspnea, and temperature intolerance, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study of 100 COVID-19 patients in Colombia who underwent a 12-week pulmonary rehabilitation program, evaluating changes in lung function (spirometry) and dyspnea perception (mMRC scale). Results showed that pulmonary rehabilitation had positive effects on respiratory function and dyspnea regardless of patient gender, with FVC, FEV1, and mMRC as robust indicators of recovery.

Prospective cohort study analyzing self-reported data from 2,939 adults in the INSPIRE registry to examine the association between prolonged SARS-CoV-2 symptoms at 3 months post-infection and employment outcomes. Found that 40.8% reported persistent symptoms and those with ≥5 symptoms had significantly higher odds of missing ≥10 workdays and not returning to work.

A longitudinal observational study following 57 individuals with post-COVID cognitive complaints at baseline (~6 months post-infection) and follow-up (~15 months later) to assess trends in cognitive performance and related fatigue/mood outcomes. Findings show cognitive difficulties persist at both test and domain levels, with some improvement in attention/executive functioning and self-rated health, and greater cognitive impairment in those hospitalized during acute infection.

This retrospective cohort study examines the incidence of newly diagnosed liver disorders up to 3.5 years post-COVID-19 in 54,699 COVID-19 patients versus 1.4 million non-COVID controls. The study found no significant difference in liver disorder incidence between groups, with older age, Hispanic ethnicity, and obesity—rather than COVID-19 status—being key risk factors.

This cross-sectional and longitudinal study examined clinical characteristics and factors associated with long COVID among 1,359 patients attending a post-acute COVID-19 clinic in Zambia from August 2020 to January 2023. The study identified hospitalization duration, severe acute COVID-19, and comorbidities as significant risk factors for long COVID, but does not evaluate any specific treatment or intervention.

This retrospective matched cohort study examined long-term cardiovascular disease outcomes in 944,371 non-hospitalized Medicare beneficiaries diagnosed with COVID-19, comparing them to propensity score-matched controls without COVID-19 with median follow-up of 18.5 months. While the study documents persistent CVD risks in the early post-COVID period, it does not evaluate any specific treatment or intervention for long COVID.

Longitudinal panel study examining the effects of Long COVID on UK workers' employment status, work hours, and mental health from 2020-2021. Finds that those with Long COVID symptoms lasting 29+ weeks have higher employment exit risk and worse mental health outcomes, primarily driven by sickness leave rather than reduced hours.

This retrospective cohort study uses insurance claims data to compare healthcare utilization 9 months before and after COVID-19 hospitalization among 63,161 patients discharged alive. While it documents increased healthcare utilization post-hospitalization (ED, rehabilitation, office, and telemedicine visits), it is an observational analysis of existing claims data without any treatment intervention being tested or evaluated.

This retrospective cohort study used claims data from 413,958 adults to examine the association between COVID-19 infection in 2020 and sleep disorder diagnoses in 2021, after balancing baseline characteristics. Subjects with prior COVID-19 infection were 53% more likely to develop sleep disorders in the following year (OR=1.53).

Population-based study examining the association between SARS-CoV-2 antibody status and long COVID symptoms among 3,946 Kaiser Permanente members. Found no association between seropositivity and long COVID symptoms among people with confirmed prior COVID-19, suggesting limited utility of serology testing for long COVID diagnosis.

Retrospective chart review of 459 long-term care home residents examining symptom trajectories over 24 weeks following COVID-19 infection. While the study found that most residents returned to pre-COVID symptom levels within two months, approximately 25% did not recover, with greater symptom burden during acute infection predicting non-recovery.

This retrospective cohort study compares post-acute symptom risk among adults with severe COVID-19, influenza, and pneumonia using administrative health claims data from 2020 onwards. The findings show COVID-19 produces unique post-acute symptom patterns distinguished by initial disease severity and comorbidities, with outcomes differing from influenza and pneumonia cohorts over six months of follow-up.

This retrospective cohort study examined the prevalence and risk factors for long COVID in 247 patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 in Ethiopia, finding that 72.1% had persistent symptoms at median 35-day follow-up. The study identified longer pre-admission symptom duration and longer hospital stay as significant risk factors for long COVID development, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study following 165 COVID-19 patients via telemedicine from 2020 to 2-year follow-up to assess Long-COVID symptom persistence and risk factors. Found symptom prevalence decreased from 84% at 1-year to 61% at 2-year follow-up, with prior Long-COVID and reinfection as significant risk factors for persistent symptoms.

A prospective cohort study (RECoVERED) following 186 COVID-19 survivors for 6 months to characterize longitudinal trajectories of inflammatory cytokines and identify early predictors of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC). Found that elevated CRP, IL-10, IL-17, IL-6, IP10 and TNFα at 24 weeks were associated with PASC, and early IL-1β emerged as a promising predictor of long COVID development.

This retrospective study examines the prevalence and clinical characteristics of ME/CFS in 739 long COVID patients visiting a Japanese university clinic from 2021-2023, stratified by COVID-19 variant phase. The study finds ME/CFS prevalence decreased from 23.9% in the pre-Delta period to 3.3% in the Omicron period, while brain fog complaints inversely increased.

This study compared observational methods (electronic health records and questionnaires) to identify and characterize post-COVID syndrome in the Netherlands, analyzing prevalence rates and clinical subtypes across different classification approaches. While relevant to long COVID, it is excluded because it does not study a treatment or intervention—it is purely observational and descriptive in nature.

Prospective household cohort study tracking symptom burden, viral loads, and antibody responses during acute COVID-19 infection in 143 outpatients (April-November 2020, pre-vaccine era). Found that higher day 28 antibody levels were associated with later development of long COVID symptoms at 8-10 month follow-up, but the study focuses on acute infection characteristics and PASC risk factors rather than testing any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study using Veterans Health Administration records examining associations between long COVID documentation and clinical outcomes in diabetic veterans (n=1,896,080). Long COVID was associated with increased primary care visits, medication use, dialysis initiation, and hospitalization, but lower mortality.

This cross-sectional analysis examined work absenteeism in adults with long-COVID using the 2022 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. The study found that individuals with long-COVID missed significantly more workdays (8 days on average) compared to those without long-COVID (4 days), highlighting substantial productivity losses.

Prospective follow-up study of 37 COVID-19 patients examining associations between convalescent immune responses and long-term pulmonary sequelae at ~27 months post-hospitalization using chest CT imaging. Found pulmonary sequelae in 59.5% of patients, associated with older age, but no significant differences in convalescent cytokines or antibodies predictive of complications.

Retrospective cohort study identifying clinical and sociodemographic predictors of healthcare seeking in post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) patients in a California health system. The study analyzes patterns of care seeking rather than testing a specific intervention or treatment.

A 3.5-year prospective cohort study tracking 149 long COVID patients' physical and mental health outcomes at 3 months, 1 year, and 3.5 years post-infection using validated questionnaires (SF-12, PHQ-9, GAD-7, IES-R). While patients showed overall improvement over time, those with persistent long COVID symptoms continued to have significantly worse physical and mental health scores compared to those without long COVID, with ongoing fatigue, sleep difficulties, and post-exertional malaise being most common.

Secondary analysis of a prospective multicenter study comparing healthcare utilization patterns between long COVID and non-long COVID patients over 180 days post-infection. Found that long COVID patients had higher rates of additional hospitalization and longer office visit durations compared to those without long COVID.

A case series of 140 post-COVID patients receiving inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation treatment over an average of 27 days, assessing mental and physical health outcomes at admission and discharge. Both mental (anxiety, depression, PTSD) and physical symptoms showed partial improvement following specialized rehabilitation treatment.

Retrospective cohort study comparing clinical characteristics of long COVID patients (n=580) to recovered COVID and non-COVID post-acute infection syndrome patients using EHR data. Found long COVID patients had higher comorbidity burden and greater prevalence of cardiac, cognitive, and fatigue symptoms in post-acute phase.

A retrospective cohort study of 604 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Thailand during the Delta variant period, following them for one year post-discharge to assess long COVID prevalence and quality of life. The study found very low long COVID symptom prevalence (4.2% shortness of breath, 1.5% cough) at one-year follow-up, with most patients reporting good physical and mental health outcomes.

COREG-FR is a 24-month prospective cohort study of COVID-19 hospitalized patients assessing mobility and cognitive deficits using standardized instruments. While the study documents persistent functional impairment in long COVID patients, it is observational without any treatment intervention and therefore does not meet inclusion criteria for a treatment trials meta-analysis.

Retrospective cohort study of 38,327 COVID-19 patients examining associations between autoimmune diseases and post-COVID condition (PCC) diagnosis using electronic health records. Found that pre-existing autoimmune diseases (psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis) and post-infection autoimmune diseases (Sjögren's syndrome) are more prevalent in PCC patients, and medical utilization is significantly higher among those with PCC.

A one-year prospective observational cohort study comparing neuromuscular function, fatigue, and muscle architecture in long COVID patients (moderate and severe cases) versus healthy controls. The study found that severe COVID patients exhibited persistent fatigue, reduced torque, and impaired neuromuscular function even one year post-infection, highlighting the need for targeted rehabilitation strategies.

Retrospective study comparing autonomic testing results in 143 Long COVID and 170 ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls and hEDS patients. Found extensive similarities between Long COVID and ME/CFS including reduced cerebral blood flow, autonomic failure, small fiber neuropathy, and POTS, suggesting shared pathophysiological mechanisms.

This retrospective cohort study examined demographic and clinical risk factors associated with long COVID using a nationwide sample of 8,329 narrow-definition and 207,537 broad-definition long haulers from the OptumLabs Data Warehouse. Key findings identified hypertension, chronic lung disease, obesity, diabetes, and depression as leading risk factors, with long haulers being older, more female, and having more comorbidities than non-long haulers.

This prospective observational study compared cerebral blood flow (CBF) patterns in 55 post-COVID condition (PCC) patients versus 36 COVID-recovered controls using MRI arterial spin labeling. Fatigue in PCC patients was associated with reduced perfusion in right occipital regions, suggesting a potential imaging biomarker for the condition.

Prospective observational study of 100 COVID-19 recovered healthcare workers followed for 3 months to assess lung function recovery via spirometry. Found statistically significant improvements in FEV1 and FEV1/FVC% at 1 and 3 months post-discharge, indicating partial lung function recovery in the post-COVID phase.

Prospective case-control study comparing long-term symptoms in 112 COVID-19 positive patients versus 109 COVID-19 negative controls at 10-month follow-up. Found persistent shortness of breath and cough in COVID cases (36% with at least one symptom) versus controls (6%), with significant functional impairment and financial impact in cases.

Large-scale UK Biobank cohort study comparing digestive disease risks in 112,311 COVID-19 patients versus contemporary and historical controls over 2.6 years follow-up. Study found significantly elevated risks of multiple gastrointestinal disorders (GERD, FGID, peptic ulcer, liver disease) in long COVID patients, with risks persisting beyond one year post-infection.

This propensity-matched cohort study investigates the temporal risk of new-onset gastroparesis following SARS-CoV-2 infection using a large database, comparing rates in infected vs. uninfected populations. It is an observational epidemiological study documenting a long COVID sequela rather than evaluating a treatment intervention.

This observational case series of 46 long COVID patients describes the endoscopic features of post-COVID-19 cholangiopathy and the role of ERCP in its management. ERCP with interventional cast removal demonstrated therapeutic benefit, improving cholestasis parameters in approximately 60% of treated patients, though overall prognosis remained poor with 44% 1-year liver transplantation-free survival.

This study analyzed COVID-19 infection rates and outcomes in 379 patients with pre-existing gastroparesis enrolled in the NIH Gastroparesis Registry. While it documents that 20% of gastroparesis patients contracted COVID-19 and experienced transient GI symptom worsening, it is a secondary analysis of registry data without testing any active intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study followed 1,212 COVID-19 survivors aged 60+ from two Wuhan hospitals over 2 years post-discharge to assess long-term symptom burden and identify risk factors. At follow-up, 21.4% reported persistent symptoms, with fatigue, anxiety, and dyspnea being most common; older age and previous oxygen therapy were significant risk factors for severe fatigue and depression.

Post hoc analysis of the PREDIMED-Plus trial examining cognitive outcomes in 5,179 older adults with high cardiovascular risk before and after COVID-19 infection. Found no significant association between COVID-19 and cognitive impairment at 50-week follow-up, suggesting acute cognitive changes may revert over time.

This propensity-matched cohort study compares 1-year risk of cardiovascular, thrombotic, and renal complications after acute COVID-19 in IBD patients versus non-IBD patients. It found no significant differences in complication rates between IBD patients on various medications and control groups, focusing on acute post-infection complications rather than long COVID sequelae.

This study examines carbohydrate metabolism disorders in hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute infection and 6 months post-discharge, stratifying by DM status, steroid-induced hyperglycemia, and stress-induced hyperglycemia. While it does examine a post-COVID period, the focus is on acute COVID-19 outcomes and metabolic complications during hospitalization, not on long COVID syndrome or treatments for persistent symptoms.

Retrospective analysis of 134 type 2 diabetes patients comparing post-COVID clinical and laboratory features across three COVID-19 variant periods (Alpha, Delta, Omicron). Omicron period showed fewer comorbidities, hospitalizations, and new diagnoses; differences were also found in platelet counts and coagulation markers between variants.

This retrospective cohort study examines cardiorenal complications in diabetic patients before and after COVID-19 using data from a mobile diagnostic center. It documents increased frequency of kidney dysfunction and cardiovascular complications in the post-COVID period but does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This retrospective registry analysis examines carbohydrate metabolism disorders (hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes) in COVID-19 patients using the AKTIV and AKTIV 2 registries, comparing outcomes including mortality and 12-month post-COVID symptoms across patient groups. While the paper does assess long-term post-COVID consequences, it is a secondary analysis of existing registry data without any intervention being administered—patients are passively stratified by their pre-existing metabolic status rather than being assigned to treatment groups.

This cross-sectional study examined the course of COVID-19 and post-COVID syndrome (PCS) in 32 patients with rheumatoid arthritis, finding that 47.8% developed PCS with higher rates of hospitalization and severe disease course. The study identifies risk factors for PCS development in rheumatic disease patients but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study evaluated Actovegin efficacy in treating chronic cerebral ischemia in 440 patients with recent COVID-19 experience, comparing treatment (n=220) vs control (n=220) groups over 90 days. Actovegin-treated patients showed significantly greater improvements in cognitive function, fatigue, sleep, dizziness, emotional state, and quality of life compared to controls.

This retrospective-prospective cohort study examined disease activity dynamics in 100 patients with immune-mediated inflammatory rheumatic diseases (RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis, ankylosing spondylitis) following COVID-19 infection, assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months. While the paper documents increased IMIRD flare frequency post-COVID and identifies risk factors, it does not study a treatment intervention for long COVID itself—it only tracks the natural disease course of pre-existing rheumatic conditions.

Retrospective analysis of 46 children (26 post-COVID symptom-free, 20 with post-COVID symptoms) comparing leukocyte and lymphocyte dynamics one week after acute COVID-19. Findings suggest persistent lymphopenia during acute infection is a risk factor for developing post-COVID syndrome, with lymphocyte normalization acting as a protective factor.

This observational study followed 62 outpatient pneumonia patients over 16 months to document post-COVID syndrome frequency and symptoms. The analysis is descriptive/epidemiological rather than evaluating a specific treatment intervention—it compares symptom prevalence across age groups and vaccination status but does not test or assign any treatment.

This retrospective cohort study compares cardiac surgery outcomes in 100 patients with prior COVID-19 infection versus 100 pre-pandemic controls. While it examines post-COVID sequelae affecting surgery, it is not a long COVID treatment trial but rather a surgical outcomes study assessing timing and risk factors for cardiac procedures.

This case-control study compares hormonal and metabolic markers (vasopressin, ghrelin, insulin) in 31 long COVID patients with coronary artery disease versus 40 coronary patients without COVID history and 15 healthy controls. The study found significant elevations in vasopressin, insulin, and glucose in long COVID patients, establishing correlations with neurovegetative disorders but does not evaluate or test any treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study of 1,425 COVID-19 patients examining the prevalence and clinical associations of post-COVID-19 tachycardia (PCT) in the post-acute phase. Found PCT prevalence of 28.18% with stronger association in patients <65 years and certain comorbidity profiles, but the study does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This retrospective cohort study compares cardiac structure and function in 71 CHD patients with and without prior COVID-19 history, finding significantly worse cardiac remodeling, increased myocardial hypertrophy, and higher energy expenditure in the long COVID group. The study demonstrates that COVID-19 history is associated with increased risk of cardiac complications in CHD patients but does not test any treatment intervention.

Retrospective study comparing cognitive fatigue and neuropsychological test performance in 35 long COVID and 50 MS patients. Found fatigue correlates with monotonous attention tasks in MS but not long COVID, suggesting different cognitive fatigue mechanisms between conditions.

A prospective cross-sectional study of 152 severe COVID-19 survivors in Latin America evaluated long-term mental health and cognitive outcomes at an average of 24.5 months post-illness using validated psychiatric and cognitive assessment instruments. The study found high prevalence of anxiety (33%), depression (49%), and cognitive dysfunction (11%), with worse outcomes in women and ICU-admitted patients, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This observational study assessed functional capacity, fatigue, and dyspnea in 92 COVID-19 patients (moderate, severe, critical) during the first month post-discharge using standardized instruments (6MWT, FSS, FIS, mMRC). Results showed that critical disease severity was associated with lower functional capacity and higher fatigue and dyspnea severity, but no treatment intervention was evaluated.

Retrospective cohort study of 57 hospitalized COVID-19 patients contacted 6 months post-discharge to assess multi-system symptom burden using standardized questionnaires. Found high rates of fatigue (60%), dyspnea (57%), and neuropsychiatric symptoms (56%), with females and younger patients reporting greater functional impairment.

Prospective cohort study of 471 university employees followed at 3 and 6 months post-COVID to assess symptom persistence and anxiety. Found that 32.1% had persistent symptoms at 3 months and 13.0% at 6 months, with shortness of breath and fatigue being most common.

This prospective study evaluates pulmonary function in 34 pediatric COVID-19 patients compared to 33 controls after hospital discharge, finding reduced FVC, FEV1, and FEV1/FVC values in the patient group. The study does not examine long COVID as a syndrome of persistent symptoms weeks/months post-infection, but rather acute post-discharge respiratory outcomes in recently hospitalized children.

This retrospective cohort study followed 77 COVID-19 patients with olfactory and taste loss for 12-14 months to determine the prevalence, severity, and long-term course of these symptoms. Most patients showed recovery, with only 15.6% experiencing persistent smell loss and 8% persistent taste loss at follow-up; notably, the study did not test any treatment intervention but rather passively observed symptom progression.

Prospective follow-up study of 26 severe COVID-19 patients (~20 months post-hospitalization) assessing late symptoms and pulmonary function via spirometry and diffusion capacity testing. Found high prevalence of fatigue (65.4%), brain fog (50%), and weight gain (46.2%), with 61.5% showing reduced diffusion capacity, though no correlation between symptom burden and functional abnormalities.

Longitudinal study tracking muscle sympathetic nerve activity and hemodynamic responses over 6 months in young adults recovering from SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found improvements in blood pressure over recovery period but no direct changes in sympathetic activity, suggesting cardiovascular impairments may improve independent of sympathetic changes.

This observational study followed 13 professional football players to assess COVID-19 symptom persistence and physiological recovery, comparing pulmonary function and metabolic power before and after infection. The study found that general and muscle fatigue persisted for weeks in most players and metabolic capacity was significantly reduced post-COVID, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study examining the one-minute sit-to-stand test (1MSTST) as a monitoring tool in 97 patients recovering from COVID-19 pneumonia one year post-infection. The study validates 1MSTST as a feasible alternative to pulmonary function tests and identifies correlations with age and inflammatory markers, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study of 487 post-acute COVID-19 syndrome patients followed over one year with symptom assessments via questionnaire. Documents persistent symptoms (dyspnea, weakness, fatigue, arthralgia) with higher prevalence in females and non-hospitalized patients, but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

A retrospective proof-of-concept study evaluating a 3-month personalized pulmonary rehabilitation program (endurance and resistance training) in 17 long-COVID patients. The program significantly improved quality of life, physical fitness (6MWT increased from 329 to 365 m), and chest CT parameters including reduced air trapping and increased airway volume.

Prospective observational study of young adults undergoing monthly transthoracic echocardiography for 6 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection to assess cardiac structure and function changes. Found preserved left heart structure but subclinical improvements in some cardiac function parameters and reduced troponin-I over the 6-month recovery period.

Retrospective cohort study comparing healthcare utilization between 531,702 SARS-CoV-2 test-positive and test-negative adults in Ontario, followed for 56+ days post-infection. Found significantly higher rates of healthcare encounters, hospital admissions, and long-term care use in test-positive individuals, particularly among females.

A prospective cohort study measuring maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressure in 145 COVID-19 patients at 5 and 12 months post-infection, comparing to healthy controls. Found reduced respiratory pressures in only 16% of participants with little improvement over time.

A retrospective study of 21 PASC patients examining relationships between symptoms, blood volume distribution, exercise tolerance, lung volumes, and functional status using pulmonary function tests, 6-minute walk tests, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing. The study found significant differences in exercise capacity and lung function between patients with minor vs severe functional limitations, but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective analysis of laboratory data from 186 long COVID patients evaluated at Okayama University Hospital to characterize hormonal abnormalities associated with symptom severity. Found correlations between fatigue and elevated cortisol/FT4, thyroid dysfunction, and altered adrenal-pituitary ratios, suggesting endocrine dysfunction contributes to persistent long COVID symptoms.

Investigates pituitary and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function in 43 patients 3-7 months after acute COVID-19 infection using hormone stimulation tests. Found abnormalities in GH and cortisol responses in some patients, suggesting COVID-19 may affect pituitary function, but this is a cross-sectional observational study with no intervention or treatment evaluation.

This cross-sectional study measures lung diffusion capacity (DLCO and DLNO) in 49 patients recovering from severe COVID-19 pneumonitis at ~2 months post-discharge, with repeat testing in 17 patients at ~4 months. The findings show that alveolar membrane dysfunction improves over time while vascular injury effects (reduced capillary blood volume) persist, but no specific treatment intervention is evaluated or tested.

Longitudinal observational cohort study of 102 severe COVID-19 survivors followed 3 years post-hospitalization, characterizing radiologic abnormalities, pulmonary function, and histopathologic findings. Study documents persistent fibrotic-like changes in 61% of survivors with modest improvement over time but no active treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study of 428 COVID-19 ICU survivors followed for 12 months to assess disabilities, frailty, cognitive impairment, and clinical events. While disabilities and cognitive symptoms peaked at 3 months post-discharge, significant improvement occurred over the year, though one-third of patients remained worse than pre-COVID status.

This study measures inflammatory biomarkers and vitamins in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and compares them to post-COVID syndrome patients to identify prognostic markers. It is an observational biomarker study without any treatment intervention, focusing on diagnostic assessment rather than evaluating a therapeutic approach.

This prospective study compares fetal thymus size in pregnant women who recovered from COVID-19 (4+ weeks post-infection) versus age-matched controls. The study found significantly lower fetal thymic-thoracic ratio in COVID-19 recovered pregnant women but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention for long COVID patients.

This cross-sectional study compared brain white matter integrity and cognitive/psychiatric outcomes between 23 post-COVID participants and 24 healthy controls using diffusion tensor imaging. While it identified microstructural brain abnormalities in post-COVID patients, it is excluded because it is an observational case-control study with no treatment intervention tested.

Cross-sectional and longitudinal study comparing brain morphometry and neuropsychiatric symptoms between 29 post-COVID patients and 25 healthy controls using MRI and standardized neurobehavioral assessments. Found larger putamen and amygdala volumes in post-COVID patients at baseline, with abnormalities associated with anxiety, depression, and pain, though morphometric differences diminished at 3-year follow-up.

This retrospective cohort study examines high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) as a prognostic indicator for cardiovascular disease in 26 non-diabetic COVID-19 ICU survivors with one-year follow-up. The findings show elevated hs-CRP in 23% of patients at high cardiovascular risk, suggesting hs-CRP may serve as an early warning marker for post-COVID cardiovascular complications.

Retrospective cohort study of 246 long COVID patients with cardiopulmonary symptoms identified 8-12 weeks post-infection to characterize risk factors for developing long COVID. Found that prior oxygen support during acute COVID-19 combined with pre-existing OSA or COPD significantly increased odds of developing cardiopulmonary long COVID symptoms (OR 3.6-12.19).

A cross-sectional study of 217 COVID-19 convalescent patients in Wuhan 30 months post-infection, assessing long COVID symptoms, functional status, and risk factors through questionnaire, laboratory testing, and physical assessments. Found 62.2% had long COVID symptoms; older age, female gender, and lack of vaccination were risk factors, while vaccination and exercise were protective.

Cross-sectional assessment of 153 long COVID patients at median 75 days post-infection, evaluating respiratory recovery, fatigue, and health status across initial disease severity groups. Study found persistent subjective health complaints and fatigue in >60% of patients, but these were not associated with initial disease severity or objective respiratory findings.

This cross-sectional study examines cardiovascular symptoms in 452 recovered COVID-19 patients at a Chinese hospital, identifying risk factors (female sex, younger age, pre-existing cardiovascular disease) associated with post-COVID cardiovascular sequelae. No treatment intervention is tested; the study is observational and descriptive, characterizing symptom prevalence and risk factors rather than evaluating a therapeutic intervention.

This cross-sectional study compares sST2 biomarker levels and left ventricular morphology in CAD/CHF patients with and without prior COVID-19 infection. While it examines post-COVID cardiac sequelae, it is not a long COVID study as it focuses on established heart disease patients rather than long COVID syndrome, and does not test any treatment intervention.

This case-control study compares biomarker levels (sFlt-1 and AECA) in ACS patients with and without prior COVID-19 infection history. While it examines post-COVID ACS outcomes, it focuses on acute cardiac events rather than long COVID as a persistent condition and does not test any intervention or treatment.

This study compares echocardiographic parameters in 118 patients with acute coronary syndrome combined with post-COVID syndrome versus 121 ACS patients without PCS. Patients with ACS+PCS showed significantly more pronounced cardiac changes including increased pulmonary artery pressure, mitral regurgitation, and complications like left ventricular thrombus and aneurysms.

Prospective study of 114 COVID-19 patients followed for ~1 year to evaluate biomarkers predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in post-COVID patients. Found that elevated pentraxin 3 (PTX3) and other inflammatory biomarkers predict MACE development, but this is a biomarker prognostic study, not a treatment intervention trial.

Prospective study of 114 COVID-19 patients followed for ~1 year to assess whether serum biomarkers (PTX3, IL-6, D-dimer, LDH, CK-MB) predict major adverse cardiovascular events post-COVID. PTX3 >3.1 ng/ml showed 94% sensitivity and 82% specificity for MACE prediction, but this is an observational cohort study without any intervention or treatment being tested.

This retrospective cohort study examined sodium alterations in COVID-19 pneumonia patients and their association with long-term outcomes including hospital readmissions and mortality over 18 months of follow-up. The study identifies abnormal sodium levels as a prognostic factor for poor long-term recovery in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

A 6-month prospective follow-up study of liver function recovery in 78 patients hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 infection without pre-existing liver disease. The study documents the natural history of liver injury and recovery post-hospitalization but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study compares echocardiographic parameters in 118 ACS patients with post-COVID syndrome versus 121 ACS patients without post-COVID syndrome. It is observational (no treatment intervention) and does not qualify as a treatment trial, though it does characterize post-COVID cardiac complications.

Longitudinal observational study of 62 type 2 diabetes patients examining mental health and metabolic markers at two timepoints (2023-2024) stratified by COVID-19 severity and infection year. Findings show improved psychological well-being and reduced diabetes-related distress over time, with potential associations between mental health and cholesterol levels.

This study examines thyroid dysfunction in 183 patients hospitalized with severe acute COVID-19, with 12-month follow-up of 75 survivors. It documents transient thyroid changes during acute infection that largely normalize over time, but does not focus on long COVID or test any treatment intervention.

This study compares myocardial revascularization outcomes in acute coronary syndrome patients with and without prior COVID-19 infection history. While it examines post-COVID complications, it focuses on acute cardiac events rather than long COVID syndrome, which is characterized by persistent symptoms weeks to months after infection.

This cross-sectional study examines clinical features of post-COVID syndrome in 72 patients with carbohydrate metabolism disorders (impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes). The paper describes symptom prevalence and risk factors but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study examined ECG patterns and arrhythmias in 758 post-COVID-19 patients during a 2-month recovery period, analyzing associations with age, sex, comorbidities, and disease severity. The findings demonstrate that arrhythmias in post-COVID patients are primarily associated with disease severity and comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, with relationships to hypoxia, inflammation, and metabolic disturbances.

Retrospective cohort study using electronic health records from 17 health systems to evaluate vaccine effectiveness against long COVID in children aged 5-17 years. Finds moderate protective effect of vaccination (35-42% effectiveness) that is stronger in adolescents and wanes over 18 months, but does not study any treatment intervention for long COVID.

This cross-sectional study examines molecular markers (anti-S IgG antibodies, lactate, glucose, LDH, and C-reactive protein) in the blood serum of 547 vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals in the remote post-COVID period. The research identifies elevated inflammatory markers (lactate, glucose, CRP, LDH) in individuals with persistent post-COVID symptoms, suggesting chronic inflammatory processes regardless of vaccination status.

Population-based prospective cohort study of 1,026 Canadian children aged 8–13 followed for 76 weeks to determine the incidence of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC). Found a very low incidence of PCC (0.4%, only 1 child) with most children recovering within 6 weeks; pre-existing comorbidities (asthma, allergies, anxiety, ADHD) were not associated with increased PCC risk.

Prospective observational study of 103 patients with mild to moderate COVID-19 that assessed cardiovascular changes via echocardiography and arterial stiffness measurements at baseline and 6 months. Found persistent diastolic dysfunction, global longitudinal strain alterations, and ventricular-arterial coupling changes, particularly in moderate COVID-19 patients and men, documenting cardiovascular sequelae of COVID-19.

This cross-sectional study evaluates associations between long-COVID symptoms and psychological factors (depression, anxiety, life satisfaction, social support) in 166 non-hospitalized patients at a post-COVID clinic. The study found that depression and anxiety correlate positively with symptom count, while life satisfaction and social support correlate negatively, but no treatment intervention was tested.

Prospective observational cohort study following 282 COVID-19 patients for 15-42 weeks to monitor post-COVID symptoms and their duration. Found that 67% developed symptoms lasting >1 month, with fatigue (29%) and hyposmia (27%) being most common; fatigue spontaneously resolved after ~19 weeks in most cases.

Retrospective cohort study examining the incidence of myocarditis in COVID-19 recovered patients using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging over a 2-year period. Found that 54% of patients showed evidence of myocarditis with myocardial oedema and fibrosis, identifying cardiac involvement as a lasting consequence of COVID-19.

Retrospective chart review of 79 long COVID patients presenting with gastrointestinal symptoms to a university hospital, characterizing common GI manifestations, laboratory abnormalities, and demographic/clinical risk factors. Study identifies female gender, obesity, cardiovascular disease, and cancer as major risk factors; does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study of 441 COVID-19 patients from long-term care facilities followed for 6 months post-discharge to identify factors associated with mortality and sequelae. Found high frequency of post-discharge sequelae (59%) and identified advanced age, male sex, ICU admission, and baseline vulnerability as risk factors for mortality.

This study examines neurovegetative and psychological characteristics in 80 infertile women with long COVID compared to 40 controls without COVID history, assessing their association with assisted reproductive technology (ART) outcomes. Women with long COVID and infertility showed higher levels of autonomic dysfunction, anxiety, depression, and stress factors, with these being significant risk factors for ART failure.

Retrospective analysis of post-COVID-19 symptoms and sleep-wake disturbances across three SARS-CoV-2 variant waves (Alpha, Delta, Omicron) in Hungarian patients presenting >4 weeks post-infection. Study documents variant-dependent patterns in symptom prevalence and sleep quality but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

A prospective cohort study of 127 children with COVID-19 examined whether zinc deficiency (hypozincemia) correlates with long COVID development over 12 months. While zinc deficiency was present in 25.2% of children and long COVID occurred in 42.5%, no statistically significant correlation was found between zinc levels and long COVID development, though fatigue and neurological symptoms were numerically more frequent in zinc-deficient children.

Retrospective cohort study examining the relationship between dialysis adequacy (spKt/V) and long-term COVID-19 outcomes in 195 hemodialysis patients. Finds that suboptimal dialysis dose is associated with significantly increased risk of COVID-19 sequelae, hospitalization, and mortality at one year, but does not test an intervention or treatment—it is purely observational.

This case-control study compares reproductive function outcomes between 80 infertile women with long COVID history and 40 without COVID history. While it documents associations between long COVID and reproductive dysfunction (reduced ovarian reserve, menstrual disorders, lower IVF success rates), it is not a treatment trial—it is a comparative observational study examining disease consequences rather than evaluating any therapeutic intervention.

Observational cross-sectional survey of 68 healthcare workers at a Moscow clinic assessing long COVID symptoms and their impact on working capacity. Study documents prevalence of cognitive, psychological, and asthenovegetative disorders post-COVID but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective multicenter cohort study tracking symptom prevalence in 1,296 adults with COVID-like illness over 12 months, comparing test-positive and test-negative groups. Found that persistent symptoms decreased through 12 months with no significant difference between groups at follow-up, and that symptom emergence/reemergence occurred in both groups.

This paper compares clinical and laboratory characteristics of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients with versus without prior COVID-19 infection. While it identifies increased multivessel coronary artery disease in post-COVID ACS patients, it is a retrospective case-control study of acute cardiac complications during the early COVID period, not a long COVID intervention trial.

This CDC and Kaiser Permanente study analyzed electronic health records of 3,171 nonhospitalized COVID-19 patients to characterize health care utilization and clinical characteristics 28-180 days post-diagnosis. While it documents post-COVID symptoms and health care needs, it is an observational retrospective cohort study with no intervention or treatment evaluation, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline.

This observational cohort study followed 298 post-COVID-19 patients with broncho-obstructive syndrome over 2 years to characterize clinical manifestations across age groups and assess mitochondrial dysfunction via LDH/SDH enzyme ratios. While it identifies biomarkers of mitochondrial dysfunction and notes that antioxidant therapy efficacy assessment is needed, it does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Retrospective analysis of vitamin D supplementation during acute COVID-19 infection and its association with immune response and subsequent long COVID symptoms. Study found vitamin D intake correlated with higher IgG antibody formation but paradoxically was associated with increased reporting of long-term fatigue and post-COVID symptoms.

This cross-sectional study compared immunological parameters in 124 patients (62 with post-COVID syndrome, 62 recovered) at various timepoints after COVID-19 infection. Results showed persistent leukocyte abnormalities and dysregulated immune responses in post-COVID patients, including reduced lymphocyte counts, altered antibody levels, and increased susceptibility to secondary infections.

This retrospective cohort study compared the prevalence and characteristics of post-COVID-19 syndrome in 148 kidney transplant recipients versus 100 non-transplant COVID-19 patients over 6 months. The study documents symptom burden and risk factors but does not evaluate any intervention or treatment.

A cross-sectional observational study of 59 medical workers tracking post-COVID symptom prevalence at 1, 2, and 3 months post-infection. Found fatigue and weakness peaked at 1 month (57.7%), decreased by month 2, then increased slightly by month 3, with most participants reporting full recovery by 3 months.

CDC analysis examining the risk of new diabetes diagnosis more than 30 days after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection in children and adolescents aged <18 years in the United States (March 2020–June 2021). The study documents increased diabetes incidence as a long-term consequence of COVID-19 infection and emphasizes the importance of monitoring for this complication in the pediatric population.

This cross-sectional study compares cardiovascular and psychological profiles in young military men 3 months post-COVID-19, stratified by pneumonia severity. Military men with COVID-19 pneumonia showed significantly elevated right heart dimensions, pulmonary artery pressures, and vascular resistance compared to those without pneumonia, with no differences in psychological symptoms between groups.

This cross-sectional study examined cardiac morpho-functional abnormalities and arrhythmias in 77 patients 3 months after COVID-19, stratified by initial disease severity. Cardiovascular injury was detected in 71-95% of patients depending on severity, with progressive cardiac remodeling, reduced myocardial strain, elevated pulmonary pressures, and arrhythmias observed across all groups.

18-month prospective follow-up study comparing post-hospital mortality rates across three COVID-19 variants (Alpha, Delta, Omicron) in 5,223 patients. Delta variant showed highest mortality particularly in first 90 days post-discharge, with long-term cardiovascular consequences driving continued mortality between 12-18 months.

This prospective observational cohort study from the AKTIV register followed 9,070 COVID-19 survivors across 7 Eurasian countries at 3, 6, and 12 months post-hospitalization to characterize long-term clinical outcomes and comorbidities. The study found persistent symptoms, unscheduled medical care use, and a 1.9% mortality rate in the first 3 months, with cardiovascular causes predominating (31.8%), but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This study compares heart rate variability parameters in acute STEMI patients with or without prior COVID-19 infection. It focuses on acute myocardial infarction outcomes rather than long COVID sequelae, and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Observational cross-sectional study examining clinical, laboratory, and psychological outcomes in 72 cardiovascular patients one month after moderate COVID-19 hospitalization. Found persistent symptoms including decreased exercise tolerance (80.5%), generalized weakness (69.5%), neuropsychological manifestations (memory loss, anxiety, sleep disorders), and increased depression prevalence, with laboratory evidence of elevated cholesterol levels.

This non-randomized observational study compares three rehabilitation approaches (telemedicine, in-hospital, and no rehabilitation) in COVID-19 convalescents over 1 year follow-up, using propensity score matching to control for differences between groups. Both rehabilitation options reduced cardiovascular hospitalizations, with remote rehabilitation also reducing cardiovascular mortality.

This retrospective cohort study followed 112 COVID-19 survivors for one year to evaluate conventional and novel biomarkers (D-dimer, PTX3, sST2) in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events. The study found that elevated biomarker levels were predictive of cardiovascular events but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

Prospective cohort study of 125 COVID-19 patients followed for 6 months to identify cardiovascular risk factors predicting post-COVID-19 syndrome development. Found that CAVI ≥9.5, elevated systolic blood pressure, and reduced GFR at admission were associated with post-COVID syndrome, while age and BMI predicted unfavorable chronic disease course.

Registry study of 827 COVID-19 patients followed for 12 months post-hospitalization to assess long-term cardiovascular and respiratory outcomes. Focuses on acute COVID-19 complications rather than persistent long COVID symptoms—primarily tracking mortality, MI, stroke, and re-infection rather than syndrome-defining chronic sequelae.

Prospective observational study following 200 COVID-19 pneumonia patients over 12 months to assess recovery of right ventricular function using speckle tracking echocardiography. Found significant improvements in RV strain parameters from 3 to 12 months post-infection in both severe and moderate/mild lung involvement groups.

Prospective observational cohort study following 134 COVID-19 patients for 12 months post-infection to evaluate long COVID prevalence, symptom presentation, functional status, and quality of life across different initial care settings. Found that ICU patients experienced significantly higher symptom burden and poorer functional/quality-of-life outcomes compared to outpatient or ward patients.

This study evaluates residual lung abnormalities on chest CT and pulmonary function in 37 patients with respiratory symptoms at 12 months post-COVID-19. The findings show high prevalence of CT abnormalities (78.3%) including fibrosis-like changes, correlating with restrictive lung disease, but this is a diagnostic/observational study without any intervention or treatment evaluation.

This cross-sectional study analyzed data from the PAMPA cohort to determine the prevalence of long COVID and associated risk factors in Southern Brazil. While it confirms long COVID affects 77.4% of COVID-19 survivors and identifies risk factors (vaccination status, chronic conditions, hospitalization, female sex), it is a prevalence/epidemiology study that does not test or evaluate any specific treatment or intervention.

A prospective case study following 58 long COVID patients for 12 months post-infection to describe persistent symptoms and functional impact. Fatigue, arthralgia, dyspnea, and cognitive impairment persisted; 32% unable to return to work with total indirect costs of USD 227,821.

The PAMPA Cohort is a prospective longitudinal study tracking physical and mental health outcomes in adults across six waves from 2020 to 2024. The study found that three-quarters of participants were classified as having long COVID, with detailed assessments of physical activity, mental health, chronic diseases, and other health outcomes over the pandemic period.
