While it found no significant differences in perceived health or psychological distress, it identified escalating healthcare costs as the primary sequela of long COVID, but does not test or evaluate any intervention.

Retrospective single-institution analysis of 46 patients with acute and post-acute COVID-19 pneumonia who underwent thoracic surgical interventions (December 2020–March 2022). Most common procedures were thoracic drainage for pneumothorax/fluid, pleurectomy/decortication, and lung resections; early surgical intervention improved outcomes in patients with severe respiratory complications including pneumatocele, bronchiectasis, and tracheal stenosis.

This retrospective cohort study analyzed 16,344 confirmed COVID-19 cases among healthcare workers in the Russian Railways network from 2020-2022, assessing morbidity, mortality, and long-term consequences including post-COVID syndrome. The study found significantly higher infection and fatality rates among healthcare workers compared to other personnel, with recommendations for protective measures and post-COVID rehabilitation support.

Retrospective analysis of 324 rheumatic disease patients who experienced COVID-19, evaluating the impact on disease course and post-COVID complications. Reports post-COVID syndrome in 25% of patients and describes clinical experience using Alftutop (marine extract) for pain management in post-COVID arthralgia, demonstrating potential therapeutic benefit.

Prospective observational study examining chest CT findings, dyspnea scores, and pulmonary function tests in 56 COVID-19 ARDS survivors at 6-month follow-up. Study found correlations between specific CT imaging patterns (reticulations/septal thickening and parenchymal bands) and increased dyspnea severity and reduced forced vital capacity.

This observational study examined neutrophil and eosinophil activation patterns in primary care COVID-19 patients during acute illness and 3-6 months later using flow cytometry. While the findings suggest abnormal immune cell responses may be involved in long COVID pathogenesis, this is a mechanistic biomarker study without testing any treatment or intervention.

This cross-sectional study compared cytokine profiles in 317 Brazilian COVID-19 patients across acute, recovered, and long COVID groups. While it identifies IL-17 and IL-2 elevation as potential long COVID biomarkers, it is an observational characterization study without any treatment intervention or controlled design.

Retrospective study comparing serum levels of four extracellular matrix molecules (laminin, type IV collagen, PIIINP, hyaluronic acid) in 162 post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis patients versus 160 healthy controls. Elevated serum levels of these biomarkers correlate with PC19-PF severity and may serve as disease progression indicators.

This case series examines quantitative platelet changes and immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in 53 long COVID patients (ages 19-82) evaluated 2+ weeks after acute COVID-19 infection. The study analyzes clinical characteristics, diagnostic findings, and therapeutic outcomes (glucocorticoids, thrombopoietin receptor agonists, platelet transfusion) for COVID-associated ITP over a 3-month follow-up period.

Prospective longitudinal study examining coagulation protein dynamics in 49 ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients at baseline and one-year post-discharge. While the paper documents recovery of coagulation abnormalities over time, it is observational without any intervention and does not meet the treatment trial criteria.

This longitudinal observational study measures plasma extracellular vesicles (EVs) in COVID-19 hospitalized patients at baseline, discharge, and 30 days post-discharge to characterize changes in COVID-associated coagulopathy. Key finding: endothelium-derived EVs decreased post-discharge while platelet and leukocyte-derived EVs increased, and elevated P-Selectin+ EVs were associated with persistent symptoms at 30 days, indicating ongoing cellular activation after acute infection.

This cross-sectional study examines immune cell profiles in unvaccinated COVID-19 patients at admission and 50 days post-symptom onset, comparing mild, severe, and critical cases. While the study provides mechanistic insights into persistent B-cell lymphopenia in critical COVID-19 patients (a potential long COVID pathophysiology mechanism), it does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Longitudinal observational study examining platelet counts and T-cell dynamics in 298 COVID-19 patients at 48 days post-symptom onset. Finds that 5.3% of moderate COVID patients with elevated platelet counts show higher T-cell populations, suggesting platelets may regulate immune recovery post-COVID, but no intervention or treatment is tested.

This study characterizes long-term changes in gut bacterial and fungal communities in individuals recovering from mild COVID-19 at 3 and 6 months post-infection. While it documents microbiota alterations during recovery, it does not study a treatment intervention and focuses on mild COVID recovery rather than long COVID syndrome.

This case-control study measures salivary cortisol levels in 83 long COVID patients versus 13 asymptomatic post-COVID controls and healthy controls to assess hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysfunction. The study documents disrupted diurnal cortisol rhythms and elevated evening cortisol in long COVID patients but does not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

This controlled cohort study evaluated troponin I concentrations in convalescent COVID-19 patients over 14 months compared to controls. The study found significantly elevated low-level troponin I in men aged 54+ that persisted throughout the observation period, suggesting potential long-term myocardial injury.

This longitudinal cohort study analyzes peripheral lymphocyte subsets in 279 COVID-19 convalescent patients at admission and 50 days post-symptom onset using flow cytometry. While most patients showed immune recovery, a subgroup exhibited persistent lymphopenia in B cells, CD4+ T cells, and Tregs, providing mechanistic insights into Long COVID pathogenesis rather than testing a specific intervention.

A prospective cross-sectional study of 22 patients with persistent cardiac symptoms 1 year post-COVID-19, investigating cardiac structure and function using echocardiography, CMR, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing. Found no underlying cardiac disease or reduced fitness despite self-reported symptoms, suggesting cardiac symptoms post-COVID may be functional rather than structural.

Retrospective cohort study of 1,746 COVID-19 survivors comparing 30-day post-discharge antithrombotic therapy (DOAC or dipyridamole) vs no treatment over ~13 months follow-up. Prophylactic DOAC and dipyridamole significantly reduced all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and cardiovascular events (PE, MI, stroke) with no major bleeding complications.

This observational CMR study characterizes left-ventricular damage in COVID-19 patients with elevated troponin during the acute phase, following them serially over one year. While it documents persistent myocardial and skeletal muscle abnormalities at 3 months that resolved by 12 months, it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention—it is purely a natural history/observational follow-up study.

This study investigated cardiovascular disorders in 52 long COVID patients presenting with chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations using multi-modality imaging. Cardiovascular disorders were found in 27% of patients, with myocardial injury in 15% and pulmonary embolisms in 8%, with severe conditions and cardiac events being independent risk factors.

This study examines the incidence of cardiac arrhythmias in hospitalized COVID-19 patients during acute infection (March-May 2020) with 19.6-month follow-up. It does not focus on long COVID or test any intervention treatment.

This prospective observational cohort study investigated subclinical myocardial injury in patients recovering from COVID-19 using echocardiography and global longitudinal strain measurements. The study found that patients with severe acute chest CT lesions were more likely to have reduced cardiac function at mid-term follow-up, but it does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study comparing post-acute cardiovascular complications in COVID-19 survivors from the first and second/third pandemic waves in Lombardy, with follow-up up to 9 months. COVID-19 patients had significantly increased risk of cardiovascular hospitalization and complications regardless of acute severity, age, or prior cardiovascular disease.

This prospective cohort study followed 523 COVID-19 survivors for 1 year to examine the natural history of prolonged QTc interval and its clinical impact. Prolonged QTc on admission normalized in 84% of survivors and was not independently associated with 1-year adverse events; prolonged QTc at follow-up was related to pre-existing chronic conditions rather than COVID-related sequelae.

Retrospective analysis of 43 post-COVID patients who underwent follow-up cardiac MRI 347 days after initial diagnosis to assess trajectories of myocardial alterations. Study found symptomatic improvement and improvements in volumetric and deformation indices on follow-up, but no significant changes in tissue parameters.

This retrospective study evaluated the efficacy of cardiac rehabilitation in 89 long COVID patients, comparing those with and without concurrent coronary heart disease. Cardiac rehabilitation significantly improved cardiovascular measurements, exercise capacity (6-MWT), and psychological symptoms (sleep, anxiety, depression) over 3 months in both groups, with greater baseline impairment in the CHD subgroup.

This observational cohort study examined cardiac structure and function changes in 176 COVID-19 hospitalized patients via echocardiography at discharge and 1-month follow-up, comparing them to 88 healthy controls. The study found high prevalence of left ventricular concentric remodeling and diastolic dysfunction in convalescents, with minimal improvement at 1 month, but did not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

Prospective registry study of 200 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed at 6 and 18 months post-discharge to assess long-term cardiopulmonary symptoms and structural abnormalities. While 73% met long COVID criteria at 6 months, the study is observational with no treatment intervention—patients are passively followed without receiving any experimental therapy.

Prospective cohort study following 210 COVID-19 patients (53 with myocardial injury) for 2 years post-acute infection, assessing long-term cardiovascular and functional outcomes. Patients with prior MI showed increased cardiopulmonary hospitalization odds but no significant differences in de novo cardiovascular disease or thromboembolism compared to those without MI.

This study compared inflammatory mediators and clinical parameters in COVID-19 patients with and without prediabetes during acute infection and three months post-hospitalization. While prediabetes was associated with more severe acute COVID-19 and higher IL-6 levels, patients with prediabetes did not show significant long-term worsening of sequelae at three-month follow-up.

Prospective cohort study tracking 29 long COVID patients over 12 months to assess cardiorespiratory fitness and pulmonary function recovery. Found significant improvements in multiple parameters including VO2peak, FEV1, and inspiratory muscle strength by 12-month follow-up, with reduced prevalence of inspiratory muscle weakness.

This study evaluates thyroid function changes in post-COVID patients undergoing pulmonary rehabilitation versus a control group, with assessments at baseline and 3-month follow-up. The rehabilitation group showed significant improvement in FT3 values and functional capacity at follow-up, while the control group showed no thyroid changes.

This study examines medication use patterns and their association with vascular dysfunction in 305 long COVID patients by comparing pre-pandemic and current drug use alongside vascular measurements. The analysis is a cross-sectional assessment of correlations between increased medication use and impaired vascular parameters (arterial stiffness, carotid intima-media thickness), not an intervention trial testing a treatment.

Retrospective cohort study of COVID-19 patients during Omicron outbreak examining thyroid dysfunction and its association with disease severity and mortality. While it mentions hypothyroidism persistence in 7.7% during recovery, the primary focus is on acute COVID-19 severity, thyroid pathophysiology, and mortality—not on treatment of long COVID patients.

This prospective observational study followed 187 discharged COVID-19 patients with diabetes and CKD for one year, tracking mortality and renal outcomes. While it documents long-term sequelae after acute infection, it does not study long COVID (persistent symptoms weeks-months post-infection) and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional survey of 469 Ukrainian patients with type 2 diabetes identified 8 independent risk factors for post-COVID-19 syndrome development, including newly diagnosed diabetes, severe COVID-19, prior cardiovascular/cerebrovascular events, and elevated HbA1c. A multilayer perceptron model using these factors achieved 76% specificity and 71.4% sensitivity for predicting PCS risk in this population.

This population-based cohort study examines the association between thyroid hormone levels (specifically FT3) and long-term fatigue in COVID-19 patients at 6-month follow-up in China. The study finds that lower FT3 levels are significantly associated with post-COVID fatigue and proposes FT3 as a predictive biomarker for fatigue risk.

Propensity-matched analysis of the HOPE-II COVID-19 Registry comparing long-term post-COVID-19 symptoms between 1,548 paired diabetic and non-diabetic patients. Study found higher mortality in diabetics but comparable readmission and reinfection rates, with different symptom patterns between groups.

Retrospective cohort study comparing 230,256 German adults with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (stratified by outpatient vs inpatient acute treatment) to matched controls, measuring 50 disease/symptom/treatment outcomes over 12 months. Found significantly higher rates of multiple post-COVID conditions including respiratory diseases, loss of taste/smell, and mortality, establishing prevalence and characterization of long-COVID sequelae.

Cross-sectional and longitudinal comparison of health-related quality of life and mental well-being across post COVID-19 condition, acute COVID-19, chronic conditions, and healthy groups from six countries. Post COVID-19 participants showed worst HRQOL and mental well-being at follow-up, though longitudinal deterioration was greatest in acute COVID-19 group.

Retrospective observational study of 3,344 COVID-19 patients estimating long COVID prevalence across different case definitions and accounting for selection bias using statistical modeling. While comprehensive in prevalence analysis, this is an epidemiological study characterizing disease burden rather than evaluating a treatment intervention.

This study measured perforin expression in T cells from 54 SARS-CoV-2 patients and 29 healthy controls to identify biomarkers predicting long COVID onset. Low perforin-positive CD8+ T cells during acute infection were associated with later development of long COVID, but no treatment intervention was tested.

This post-hoc analysis of 247 Brazilian hemodialysis patients investigates the prevalence of long COVID and identifies baseline predictors of persistent symptoms after COVID-19 infection. The study found that elevated phosphate (>5.35 mg/dL) and IL-10 were associated with long COVID, which was present in over 80% of COVID-19 survivors in this cohort.

Longitudinal immunological study of 40 COVID-19 convalescent patients (paired samples at ~68 and 101 days) comparing T cell populations, monocytes, and inflammatory markers to pre-pandemic controls. Found persistent T cell abnormalities and myeloid recovery independent of symptoms, with age-associated changes, but did not test or evaluate any intervention or treatment.

Prospective cohort study comparing inflammatory markers and pulmonary function in 405 SARS-CoV-2 positive versus 111 negative adolescents/young adults at 6 months post-infection. Found modestly elevated chemokines (eotaxin, MCP-1, IP-10) in COVID-19 convalescents but no association with post-COVID-19 symptoms or pulmonary dysfunction.

This cross-sectional study characterizes low-density granulocytes (LDGs) in people with pulmonary long COVID symptoms, comparing immune cell phenotypes across uninfected, recovered COVID-19, and chronic pulmonary long COVID groups. The study finds elevated LDG activation markers and NET-forming ability in long COVID patients but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

A prospective cohort study of hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 6-7 months examining immune cell alterations, specifically monocyte and dendritic cell subsets. The study documents persistent immune dysfunction months after acute infection but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Longitudinal observational study examining T cell dynamics in mild, moderate, and severe COVID-19 convalescents at 3 and 6 months post-infection. Found severity-dependent T cell alterations including exhaustion/senescence in severe cases, but no treatment intervention was tested or evaluated.

Longitudinal study examining T cell populations and immune responses in COVID-19 patients for 6-7 months post-hospitalization. Found persistent alterations in CD8+ T cells, immune checkpoint markers, and T cell activation that lasted throughout the study period.

This study examined CSF and serum biomarkers in COVID-19 patients with acute neurological complications (encephalopathy and encephalitis) during the acute infection phase, following them for 18 months. It identifies inflammatory markers and neuroaxonal damage predictors of long-term neurological disability, but focuses on acute COVID-19 complications rather than long COVID treatment or intervention.

Prospective longitudinal study of 72 COVID-19 patients followed for 12 months, with 14 (19.4%) developing persistent long-COVID symptoms. Study characterizes immunologic phenotype of long-COVID patients, finding distinct patterns in antibody response, inflammation markers, and autoimmunity but no intervention is tested.

Prospective cohort study of 324 COVID-19 hospitalized patients followed 1 year post-discharge to identify risk factors for long COVID development. Found that reduced lung diffusing capacity (DLCO) and inflammatory cytokines (IL-12, TNF-α, IFN-γ) with depressive symptoms were independently associated with persistent symptoms.

Cross-sectional study assessing cognitive outcomes and inflammatory markers in 710 long COVID survivors 6-11 months post-hospitalization. While cognitive impairment was reported in 50.7% of participants, the study found no significant association between inflammatory markers and cognitive deficits, and was not designed to test any intervention or treatment.

A prospective cohort study examining biomarkers of inflammation and microvascular dysfunction in 148 long COVID patients at 24 months post-infection. The study found high prevalence of symptoms (84.5% fatigue) correlated with elevated inflammatory markers (IL-1Ra) and endothelial dysfunction markers (endothelin-1, von Willebrand factor).

This 15-month longitudinal observational case-control study followed 222 mild COVID-19 patients to characterize long-term post-COVID syndrome outcomes and evaluate whether post-infection vaccination aids recovery. The study found no effect of vaccination on PCS recovery and identified baseline headache and diarrhea as risk factors, with fatigue and dyspnea becoming predominant symptoms at 15 months.

Prospective cohort study of 73 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients examining the association between early viral RNA clearance kinetics and subsequent long COVID symptoms. Finds that brain fog and muscle pain at 90+ days are negatively associated with rapid viral clearance within 28 days, suggesting prolonged viral antigen burden may contribute to long COVID pathogenesis.

Longitudinal observational cohort study examining CD8+ T cell activation and persistent inflammation in 67 COVID-19 survivors with post-acute sequelae, followed up to 180 days post-diagnosis. Found that participants with persistent symptoms had significantly higher levels of proliferating and activated T cells (CD8+Ki67+, CD8+CD38+, CD8+ Granzyme B+) compared to fully recovered individuals, with specific T cell markers associated with particular symptom clusters.

This retrospective cohort study uses propensity score matching on the TriNetX database to compare PASC outcomes between HIV-positive and HIV-negative individuals who had confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection from 2020–2023. The study finds that HIV status increases odds of PASC and mortality, while COVID-19 vaccination reduces both outcomes in people with HIV.

This observational sub-analysis examines immune and metabolic markers in young adults with mild-to-moderate post-COVID-19, comparing them to healthy controls and assessing associations with physical activity levels. The study found post-COVID patients have impaired pulmonary function, altered T cell activation/exhaustion markers, and disrupted mitochondrial respiration, with physical activity partially modulating these immunometabolic responses.

Longitudinal study characterizing immune responses in 67 COVID-19 patients across severity levels and 6-month follow-up to identify biomarkers associated with disease severity and long COVID development. Identifies immunological correlates (NK cells, CD8+ T cells, regulatory B cells) that distinguish acute and persistent COVID-19 but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining coagulation profiles in 190 hospitalized children with COVID-19 and their association with long COVID development. Found abnormal PT values more common in children who developed long COVID (53% vs 36.1%), but no intervention was tested.

Prospective longitudinal multicenter observational study of long COVID in 1,129 Italian children followed for up to 12 months post-infection. Found 16.2% prevalence of long COVID with most common symptoms being respiratory (43.4%), neurological/cognitive (27.7%), and gastrointestinal (22.1%), with older children and females more affected.

This study compares immunological and neurodegenerative markers in 20 COVID-19 survivors 15 months post-infection versus 13 controls, examining pro-inflammatory cytokines, immune cell phenotypes, and extracellular vesicles. The findings show persistent immune dysregulation and elevated neurofilaments in survivors but no intervention was tested, making this a mechanistic biomarker study rather than a treatment trial.

Prospective cohort study examining plasma proteome changes in SARS-CoV-2 patients (vaccinated and unvaccinated) acutely, at 3 months, and at 10 months post-infection. Findings show vaccination attenuates inflammatory response but proteomic changes persist in both groups at 10 months, potentially relevant to post-acute sequelae.

Longitudinal study of 72 COVID-19 convalescent patients followed at multiple timepoints up to 2 years post-infection, characterizing immune cell subsets and protease profiles using CyTOF and multiplex analysis. This is a mechanistic/biomarker study of natural recovery processes rather than an intervention trial, and does not test or evaluate a specific treatment.

This observational study examined 82 COVID-19 ARDS survivors at 6 and 24 months post-ICU discharge to investigate the role of TGF-β1 in fibrotic lung changes and long-term functional impairment. Elevated plasma and exhaled TGF-β1 levels were associated with dyspnea, reduced lung diffusion capacity, and 24-month gas exchange impairment, suggesting TGF-β1 mediates post-COVID fibrosis.

This study examines plasma markers of T cell activation and exhaustion (sCD25, sTIM-3, sLAG-3) in 223 COVID-19 patients followed for up to 18 months to investigate their association with persistent post-COVID symptoms. The authors find that elevated T cell activation markers correlate with persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and memory problems in home-isolated patients, but not in hospitalized patients.

A longitudinal biomarker study tracking inflammatory cytokines and hematological markers in 80 severe COVID-19 patients from acute phase through 2 years post-hospitalization, with a nested cohort of 50 pre-pandemic controls. The study identifies IL-1β, IL-10, and TNF elevation as key inflammatory signatures of persistent long COVID symptoms and notes that four vaccine doses showed modest protective effects against fatigue in males.

This cross-sectional cohort study compared immune, endothelial, and coagulation biomarkers in 32 long COVID patients versus 35 recovered controls at 26 months post-infection to identify LC pathogenic mechanisms. While the study identified robust biomarkers associated with immune dysregulation and pro-thrombotic profiles, it is observational with no intervention tested and thus does not qualify as a treatment trial.

This study evaluates immune persistence and cross-immune response in elderly individuals 6 months after Omicron BA.5 infection, comparing neutralizing antibodies and T/B-cell responses between elderly and middle-aged populations. The paper is observational research examining immune dynamics in those with long COVID symptoms post-infection, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective cohort study examining whether antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) detected during acute COVID-19 are associated with long COVID development in 114 patients followed ≥3 months post-infection. Found no significant association between aPL positivity and long COVID progression (63.2% vs 66.3%, p=0.79), suggesting prior associations may reflect confounding factors like ICU admission.

This cross-sectional study compares antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination between post-COVID syndrome patients and COVID-recovered controls. Post-COVID patients show lower anti-Spike antibodies but an enhanced IgG4/IgG1 switch after multiple vaccine doses, suggesting a differential immunological response that may inform vaccination strategies.

This prospective cohort study follows COVID-19 ICU survivors for one year post-discharge to investigate associations between telomere attrition and long-term respiratory outcomes, including pulmonary fibrosis. The findings show gender-specific patterns: women with shorter telomeres and pronation exposure had higher respiratory symptoms, while men with shorter telomeres had higher diffuse parenchymal lung disease (DPLD), particularly among those requiring intubation or prone positioning.

This retrospective observational study measures circulating IL-32 levels in healthy blood donors and severe COVID-19 patients to investigate biomarkers associated with long-term sequelae. IL-32 levels were elevated following COVID-19 and remained elevated at one-year follow-up, suggesting ongoing inflammation but without testing any intervention or treatment.

A multicenter prospective follow-up study of 3,677 discharged COVID-19 survivors from Wuhan tracked post-COVID-19 sequelae and immunological markers over a median of 144 days. The study found that 26.5% of survivors experienced at least one post-COVID-19 sequela, with significantly higher incidence in elderly patients, and documented dramatic reductions in anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies over time.

This study compared residual pulmonary abnormalities at 3 months post-discharge across COVID-19 patients of different disease severities, healthy controls, and asymptomatic recovered patients. It is an observational cross-sectional study with no intervention or treatment—participants were passively assessed for pre-existing lung damage rather than receiving any treatment.

Follow-up study of 41 COVID-19 survivors at 7 months post-discharge using chest CT imaging and cardiopulmonary exercise testing to assess long-term pulmonary sequelae. Found that 61% achieved complete radiological resolution while 29% developed pulmonary fibrosis, with older patients and those with severe acute illness at higher risk.

This study investigates retinal microcirculation using OCT-A imaging in 33 post-COVID patients and 28 controls, finding significantly reduced vessel density in the intermediate capillary plexus and peripapillary regions. The findings suggest that capillary impairment after COVID-19 infection is reflected in retinal microvasculature, but this is a diagnostic/mechanistic study with no treatment intervention.

A prospective follow-up study of 273 COVID-19 patients examined chest CT findings at 3 and 6 months post-discharge to characterize pulmonary sequelae. Ground-glass opacity and parenchymal bands were the most common findings, with severity declining over time and varying by initial disease severity.

Prospective observational study examining lung function and cardiopulmonary exercise capacity in 100 COVID-19 patients at 3-6 months post-infection, comparing severe vs mild cases against matched controls. Findings show persistent exercise impairment in severe cases with identified predictors of VO2 peak reduction, but no intervention or treatment is evaluated.

Follow-up study of 56 COVID-19 survivors tracked for 12 months post-discharge, measuring antibody persistence, lung imaging changes, and cardiopulmonary function. While the study documents sequelae like pulmonary fibrosis and cardiopulmonary dysfunction in some patients, it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it is a passive observational cohort study of natural recovery patterns.

Retrospective cohort study of 13,638 patients comparing 12-month mortality risk between COVID-19 positive (severe and mild/moderate) and COVID-19 negative patients. Patients with severe COVID-19 had significantly elevated mortality risk (HR 2.50-3.33) compared to uninfected controls, with most deaths from non-respiratory causes.

Retrospective analysis of 41 COVID-19 survivors with ARDS followed for >4 months to assess reversibility of traction bronchiectasis on CT imaging. Found that 75% of patients with traction bronchiectasis experienced complete resolution, while 25% had persistent but significantly improved findings.

Retrospective study of 175 COVID-19 patients tracking radiological findings from acute infection through 1-year post-discharge follow-up to identify predictive factors for pulmonary lesion absorption. While it follows patients long-term after COVID-19, it does not test or evaluate any specific treatment intervention.

This is a prospective follow-up study of 120 COVID-19 patients (mostly non-severe cases) assessed ~1 year after diagnosis to evaluate sequelae including respiratory, psychological, and quality-of-life outcomes. The study is excluded because it is a passive observational follow-up without any treatment intervention—patients were simply monitored to assess natural recovery patterns, not treated with a specific therapy.

Retrospective observational study of 1,000+ long COVID patients examining clinical characteristics and identifying hospitalization, ICU admission, pneumonia history, and vaccination status as predictive factors for symptom persistence across 33 symptom domains. Provides epidemiological evidence on long COVID symptom associations but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This retrospective cohort study characterizes pulmonary sequelae in 220 COVID-19 patients at 3-6 months post-discharge using high-resolution CT imaging. It identifies that 20% had persistent lung abnormalities, with older age, longer hospitalization, and baseline radiological findings (reticulations and consolidations) as predictors of pulmonary fibrosis.

Prospective cohort study of 1,847 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients from the STOP-COVID registry evaluated at a median of 13.4 weeks post-infection to identify risk factors for Long-COVID severity. Found that female sex, asthma, myocardial infarction history, and severe acute phase symptoms independently predicted Long-COVID, but no lifestyle factors (BMI, stress, nightshift work) independently associated with Long-COVID persistence.

A prospective follow-up study of 50 COVID-19 patients hospitalized at King Saud University Medical City examining clinical and biochemical characteristics 6 months post-discharge. The study found that patients with persistent post-COVID symptoms had lower lymphocyte counts, lower serum calcium levels, hyperglycemia, and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, VEGF, MCP-1) compared to asymptomatic patients.

Prospective cohort study assessing persistent lung dysfunction 6 months after hospital discharge in COVID-19 survivors using imaging and pulmonary function tests. Found that 60% had persistent CT abnormalities and 18-43% had pulmonary dysfunction, which negatively impacted daily activities and dyspnea severity.

Prospective observational cohort study following 34 long COVID patients over 1 year using the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire to track symptom changes, with comparison to 151 ME/CFS patients. Five symptoms (fatigue, post-exertional malaise, brain fog, IBS, unsteadiness) improved significantly in PASC patients over 12 months, whereas ME/CFS patients showed no improvement.

This cross-sectional study assessed endothelial dysfunction in 86 COVID-19 survivors (>10 months post-recovery) using brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD) and inflammatory biomarkers compared to healthy and risk factor-matched controls. COVID-19 survivors showed significantly reduced FMD (3.5% vs 7.7% in controls) and elevated TNF-α levels, but the study is observational with no intervention tested.

Retrospective multicenter study of 232 post-COVID patients evaluated 3 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection to assess interstitial lung disease using machine learning radiographic analysis. Thirteen patients with fibrotic lung disease and persistent functional impairment received antifibrotic treatment and showed significant improvements in FVC% predicted at 3 and 6 months follow-up.

Prospective multicenter observational cohort study of 456 hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessed 12 months after discharge via telephone interview. Study documents prevalence of persistent symptoms (dyspnea 71.7%, fatigue 54.6%) and health outcomes but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

An observational study of 382 COVID-19 survivors aged 65+ followed at 1, 3, and 6 months post-hospitalization to assess prevalence of long COVID symptoms and their association with pre-existing frailty. The study found frail patients experienced greater motor and respiratory complaints during follow-up, but is excluded because it is a passive observational cohort without any intervention or treatment.

Retrospective cohort study of 1,207 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for 12 months post-discharge, examining the relationship between initial inflammation (CRP) and mortality outcomes. Elevated CRP was associated with increased post-acute mortality, while oral steroid prescriptions at discharge were associated with reduced mortality risk.

Prospective observational cohort study examining the association between obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and long-term symptoms in COVID-19 survivors at 4 months and 1 year post-infection. OSA was associated with incident glycemic impairment, neurocognitive dysfunction, and abnormal pulmonary function changes persisting up to 1 year after acute infection.

Retrospective observational study comparing asthma control in 208 asthmatic patients with and without prior COVID-19 infection. Found that 33.9% of COVID-19 infected asthmatic patients experienced worsening asthma requiring increased maintenance therapy, significantly higher than the 11.4% worsening rate in non-infected asthmatic controls.

Prospective observational study following 105 critically ill COVID-19 ICU survivors for one year, assessing symptoms, pulmonary function, imaging, and post-COVID syndrome prevalence. At one year, 61.3% met post-COVID syndrome criteria, with persistent respiratory alterations in 32.2% and significant fibrotic patterns on CT imaging.

A prospective cohort study of 534 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in early 2020, followed up 15 months after symptom onset to assess persistent symptoms and psychological conditions. Found sleep disturbance (18.5%) and fatigue (17.2%) as most common persistent symptoms, with female sex and glucocorticoid use during hospitalization identified as risk factors for specific long-term outcomes.

A 12-month prospective observational cohort study following 347 COVID-19 pneumonia patients to identify predictors of persistent pulmonary sequelae. The study found that only 6.9% had radiological evidence of long-term lung consequences at 12 months, with current smoking status identified as an independent risk factor for persistent sequelae.

This prospective controlled study characterizes humoral and cellular immune responses in unvaccinated patients with and without post-COVID syndrome (PCS) over 7 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Patients with PCS showed significantly increased SARS-CoV-2-specific T-cell frequencies and activated plasmacytoid dendritic cells, alongside elevated immunosuppressive markers (TR1 cells and IL-4), revealing immunological alterations between inflammation and immunosuppression that may guide future targeted treatments.

Prospective observational study evaluating health-related quality of life and PTSD in unvaccinated pregnant women 1 year after COVID-19 hospitalization. While some physical impairments persist, this study focuses on acute COVID-19 outcomes in pregnancy rather than long COVID syndrome.

Prospective cohort study of 88 hospitalized COVID-19 patients examined the prevalence and predictors of post-viral fatigue at 3 and 6 months follow-up. Found that fatigue was common (67% at 3 months, 60% at 6 months) and pre-existing comorbidities were significantly associated with fatigue severity, though symptoms generally diminished over time.

A prospective multicentre study evaluating lung ultrasound accuracy in detecting and monitoring respiratory sequelae in COVID-19 patients at 3 and 12 months post-discharge. The study demonstrates lung ultrasound has higher sensitivity than X-ray for detecting interstitial alterations, with most patients showing improvement at long-term follow-up.

A prospective cohort study of 192 Mexican adults hospitalized for severe COVID-19 that longitudinally characterized the frequency, co-occurrence, and duration of post-COVID symptoms over 360 days. The study identified respiratory symptoms and functional impairment as most prevalent, with 56% experiencing ≥5 persistent symptoms, and found that prior vaccination was associated with shorter PCC duration.

Longitudinal observational study examining sex differences in recovery of neuromuscular function in COVID-19 survivors 3-12 months post-ICU discharge. Found no sex differences at 3-6 months, but females showed greater impairment in strength, walking distance, and functional recovery at 6-12 months.

Prospective observational study comparing lung function in 9 COVID-19 patients who required V-V ECMO during acute infection versus 9 healthy controls, measured 6 months post-discharge. Severe acute COVID-19 with ECMO support resulted in persistent small airway dysfunction and reduced tissue elasticity with moderate lung restriction, though most patients showed improvement from acute phase.

Longitudinal cohort study of 118 ICU-treated COVID-19 survivors followed for up to 2 years with CT imaging, pulmonary function tests, and symptom assessments. The study correlates residual radiological abnormalities with disease severity and functional outcomes but does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

Ambidirectional cohort study of 604 COVID-19 patients followed for 6 months to identify risk factors associated with long COVID syndrome persistence. Found that female sex, COPD, rheumatic disease, ICU hospitalization, and mechanical ventilation requirement were significant risk factors for long COVID (47% prevalence).

Prospective cohort study comparing functional capacity and quality of life in 47 hospitalized COVID-19 patients versus 141 matched controls at 7 months post-discharge. Found significantly reduced peak oxygen consumption (83% vs 95%, p=0.002) and quality of life in COVID-19 patients, with 51% experiencing dysfunctional breathing.

Prospective cohort study of 390 Brazilian university graduates examining risk and protective factors for Long COVID development. Found 48.9% prevalence with female sex, hypertension, and multiple acute symptoms as risk factors, and higher education as protective.

A prospective cohort study examining cognitive and psychological outcomes in COVID-19 ICU survivors at baseline and 3 months post-discharge in Qatar. While the study documents cognitive impairment and psychological symptoms in acute COVID-19 ICU survivors, it is not about long COVID (which involves persistent symptoms weeks to months post-infection) and does not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This study evaluated spontaneous physical functional recovery in COVID-19 survivors using 6-minute walk tests at discharge and 1 month follow-up in 176 patients. While it identified predictors of poor recovery trajectory, it is an observational study without any intervention or treatment administered, making it ineligible for the treatment trials meta-analysis.

Prospective cohort study examining symptom evolution and risk factors for post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) over 3 months following acute illness. Identified three phenotypic clusters (remittent, persistent, incident) and found systemic corticosteroid use during acute infection associated with higher PASC development.

Prospective observational study examining retinal microvascular changes in 25 patients 1 and 12 months after severe COVID-19 hospitalization using optical coherence tomography angiography. Found that retinal vascular alterations persisted at 12 months and correlated with inflammation, renal dysfunction, and aortic stiffness during acute illness.

This retrospective-prospective cohort study followed Philippine COVID-19 patients across three timepoints over one year to characterize long COVID symptoms and their relationship to different SARS-CoV-2 variants. The study found that long COVID symptoms declined from 88% at baseline to 68% at final follow-up, with fatigue, headache, and brain fog being most common across all variant cohorts.

Retrospective observational study examining the relationship between smoking, obesity, and post-COVID-19 sequelae in Spanish COVID-19 patients. Found obesity significantly increased risk of post-COVID sequelae especially memory and neuropsychological symptoms, while smoking correlated with memory problems but not sequelae severity.

Retrospective cohort study analyzing post-COVID mortality risk factors in severe SARS cases in Brazil from 2020-2023 using national surveillance data. While this is a legitimate long COVID epidemiological study, it does not evaluate any treatment or intervention—it is a passive observational analysis of mortality outcomes and vaccination status, making it ineligible for the intervention trials pipeline.

Prospective observational study of 408 Chinese patients following COVID-19 recovery, investigating associations between abdominal subcutaneous fat accumulation and long COVID symptom development over 12 weeks. Found that elevated subcutaneous fat (≥2.0 dm²) was significantly associated with long COVID symptoms, particularly in women.

A prospective cohort study of 88 long COVID patients examining the association between fatigue and systemic biomarkers, pulmonary/cardiac function, and diaphragm morphology. Found that prior ICU admission and elevated myostatin/irisin levels were significantly associated with post-COVID fatigue, suggesting myopathic mechanisms.

This retrospective cohort study analyzes sex-based differences in clinical and laboratory trends in post-COVID-19 condition patients from a local cohort. The study identifies women as having higher risk for PCC and distinct acute-phase biomarker profiles, emphasizing the need for sex-specific post-COVID care strategies.

A retrospective observational study of 31 severe COVID-19 survivors evaluating functional capacity decline using the Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) before and after ICU hospitalization. The study documents significant functional impairment post-infection and explores implications for preoperative anesthetic risk assessment, but does not test any intervention or treatment.

This observational cross-sectional study assessed pulmonary function, structural lung changes, and functional capacity in 210 COVID-19 patients (mild/moderate, severe, critical) evaluated at least 3 months post-infection. Findings show progressive impairment in lung function markers, exercise capacity, and muscle strength correlating with acute infection severity, highlighting long-term post-COVID sequelae.

Retrospective cohort study comparing Five-Element Regulation Therapy (FERT), a Traditional Chinese medicine intervention, versus conventional TCM therapy in 127 post-COVID syndrome patients. FERT demonstrated significantly higher clinical cure (61.7% vs 21.7%) and response rates (88.9% vs 47.8%) at 2 weeks, suggesting potential superiority for managing persistent post-COVID symptoms.

topics: Japanese traditional medicine|Kampo|quality of life|brain fog|fatigue
summary: A prospective observational study evaluating the effectiveness of Japanese traditional medicine (Kamikihito and Saikokeishito) in treating long COVID symptoms, with 112 patients assessed for health-related quality of life changes over 3 months. Results showed significant improvements in EQ-5D-5L scores at 3 months, with combination therapy associated with greater QOL improvements, though the authors note that a randomized controlled trial is needed to confirm efficacy.

Multicentric longitudinal cohort study evaluating multidisciplinary rehabilitation outcomes in 477 post-COVID-19 patients over 12 weeks, comparing those with and without post-COVID condition (PCC). Multidisciplinary rehabilitation improved both functional status and perceived health, though patients with baseline PCC showed significantly less functional recovery.

A retrospective medical records review of 40 post-COVID syndrome patients treated with 10 sessions of major ozone autohemotherapy. The study found statistically significant improvements in anxiety, depression, fatigue, and quality of life measures after treatment.

A retrospective cohort study investigating whether herpes zoster following COVID-19 is associated with elevated risk of hematologic and infectious complications using the TriNetX global research network. The study found that post-COVID HZ patients had significantly higher risks of hematologic and infectious complications, with older age and metabolic abnormalities as risk factors.

This observational study followed 9 critically ill COVID-19 patients who survived V-V ECMO treatment over a 24-month period, evaluating organ function and quality of life. While cardiac and pulmonary function remained good, patients experienced significant long-term complications including depression, fatigue, sleepiness, and reduced physical activity, highlighting the need for structured rehabilitation programs.

Population-based questionnaire cohort study of 920 pregnant women infected with SARS-CoV-2 in Denmark, examining the prevalence and characteristics of post-COVID-19 condition. Found that 50.1% experienced symptoms lasting ≥8 weeks, with fatigue, anosmia/dysgeusia, and hair loss most common, but no association with disease severity or trimester of infection.

This prospective feasibility study evaluated a virtual in-home cardiac monitoring system in 16 COVID-19 survivors using pulse oximeters and ECG patches over 3 months. Early detection of cardiac arrhythmias in 7 participants demonstrated the system's clinical utility, though this is a descriptive feasibility study without a control group or treatment intervention.

This non-randomized controlled study evaluates remote cardiac monitoring using wearable biosensors (S-Patch EX) in post-COVID-19 patients to detect cardiovascular complications, comparing 40 monitored patients with 200 standard care controls. The intervention group had significantly higher arrhythmia detection rates (32.9% vs 3.5%), with most arrhythmias identified within 3 months of monitoring.

Retrospective cohort study of 688 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors examining clinical risk factors for post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis (PCPF) and the impact of COVID-19 therapeutics. Remdesivir use was associated with reduced PCPF risk while baricitinib use was associated with increased risk, suggesting treatment-related effects on long-term pulmonary sequelae.

The COVID and Cognition Study is a cross-sectional/longitudinal observational study examining predictive factors for physical, neurological, and cognitive symptoms in 181 long COVID patients versus 185 uninfected controls. The study documents symptom characteristics and identifies that initial illness severity and specific symptom patterns predict ongoing cognitive symptoms, but does not test any treatment or intervention.

This real-world retrospective cohort study evaluated 372 post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis (PCPF) patients, comparing one-year readmission and mortality rates between those treated with small-molecule antiviral drugs (SMADs, n=293) during acute hospitalization versus those who were not (n=79). The SMAD group showed significantly lower one-year readmission rates (45.97% vs 63.64%, HR=0.65) and reduced readmission risk, suggesting antiviral therapy during acute infection may improve long-term pulmonary outcomes.

This retrospective cohort study compares COVID-19 reinfection vs. first infection outcomes in hospitalized patients, examining hyaluronic acid (HA) as a biomarker for mortality and long COVID. While the paper mentions long COVID, it is a secondary analysis of HA's association with outcomes rather than a treatment intervention trial, and does not test or evaluate any therapeutic intervention.

This prospective longitudinal cohort study followed 125 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for 2 years post-discharge, assessing persistent symptoms and functional impact. The majority reported respiratory symptoms (69%) and fatigue (78%) that substantially impacted functional status, with no significant differences by age, sex, or COVID-19 severity.

The COVID and Cognition Study is a cross-sectional/longitudinal study assessing cognitive performance (memory, language, executive function) in 181 long COVID patients versus 185 controls. The study documents consistent memory deficits in COVID-infected individuals, with severity correlating to ongoing symptom burden, but does not test or evaluate a specific treatment intervention.

This prospective cohort study followed 47 COVID-19 patients at 2 and 10 months post-discharge to investigate associations between sleep alterations, psychological disorders, and inflammatory biomarkers in post-acute COVID-19. The study found that poor sleep quality was associated with neuroinflammatory markers at 2 months and with both psychological disorders and inflammatory markers at 10 months.

Cross-sectional study comparing tinnitus characteristics in 57 COVID-19 patients with post-COVID tinnitus onset versus pre-existing or absent tinnitus. Found no significant differences in hearing function, tinnitus distress, or clinical characteristics between groups, suggesting post-COVID tinnitus does not represent a unique pathophysiological mechanism.

This retrospective cohort study characterizes clinical features and symptoms in 140 PASC patients attending a post-COVID-19 clinic, examining the prevalence and associations of ME/CFS phenotype. The study found 43% of patients met ME/CFS criteria, with fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and brain fog being the most common symptoms, but does not evaluate any treatment or intervention.

This 4-year prospective follow-up study evaluates olfactory dysfunction in 83 COVID-19 patients using psychophysical tests and patient-reported outcomes, tracking recovery trajectories over time. The study identifies olfactory training and younger age as favorable prognostic factors for recovery, with 92.3% of patients recovering olfaction by 4 years, though a subset experienced prolonged chemosensory dysfunction.

Retrospective observational cohort study examining the prevalence and risk factors of brain fog in long COVID patients at 1-year follow-up. Finds that 31.9% of COVID-19 survivors experience brain fog, which is associated with sleep disturbance and other long COVID symptoms but not with acute COVID severity or preexisting comorbidities.

This observational study followed 96 chronic tinnitus patients before and during the COVID-19 pandemic, using standardized questionnaires (VAS, THI, HQ) to assess changes in tinnitus severity and related symptoms. The study found that tinnitus worsened significantly in patients who contracted COVID-19, suggesting SARS-CoV-2 infection as a possible long-term effect, but did not evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study evaluated static balance and mobility in 41 long COVID patients versus 32 controls using smartphone-based inertial sensors. The long COVID group showed significantly greater postural instability and impaired motor control, but this is a diagnostic/assessment study with no intervention tested.

Longitudinal observational study of COVID-19 ARDS survivors assessed at 6 and 12 months post-ICU discharge to identify predictors of long-term muscle weakness. Electrophysiological abnormalities and severe fatigue independently predicted reduced muscle strength, but no intervention was tested.

A prospective cohort study of 105 non-hospitalized long COVID patients assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms using standardized questionnaires. Found strong correlations between fatigue, somatization, depression and functional impairment, but no biomarker differences compared to neuropsychiatrically unaffected long COVID patients.

Prospective cohort study comparing brain injury biomarkers (neurofilament light chain, glial fibrillary acidic protein) and neurocognitive performance in non-hospitalized adolescents and young adults 6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection, with and without post-COVID-19 condition. Found normal biomarkers and neurocognitive test results across groups, suggesting persistent symptoms are not due to ongoing CNS damage despite higher symptom scores in PCC cases.

This observational cohort study investigates white matter integrity on brain MRI in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and its associations with clinical outcomes, including long COVID. The analysis found that white matter integrity was not associated with clinical assessments or long COVID outcomes, suggesting other factors drive worse clinical outcomes.

Retrospective study comparing clinical features of optic neuritis associated with acute COVID-19 infection versus other etiologies (NMO, MOG, antibody-negative) in 117 patients. While it describes COVID-19-related optic neuritis and treatment outcomes, it focuses on acute COVID-19 complications rather than long COVID sequelae.

The PoCoRe study evaluated neuropsychological deficits in post-COVID-19 patients undergoing multidisciplinary indoor rehabilitation at six German centers, with assessments at admission and discharge. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation significantly improved fatigue, attention, and cognitive function, with 63% of patients with pathological MoCA scores at admission improving to normative levels.

This retrospective cohort study examined the correlation between chronic fatigue and headache symptoms and T2-hyperintense white matter lesions on brain/spine MRI in 96 post-COVID-19 patients. Despite finding high prevalence of both symptoms and brain lesions, no statistically significant correlation was identified between lesion presence and fatigue or headache severity.

This study followed healthcare workers with mild COVID-19 using heart rate variability (HRV) analysis at 6 and 13 months post-infection to characterize post-COVID autonomic dysregulation. The findings show autonomic imbalance resolved by 6 months, but persistent long COVID symptoms remained unrelated to cardiac autonomic changes.

This retrospective case-control study compares MRI features of the olfactory pathway (olfactory cleft and bulbs) between long COVID patients with olfactory dysfunction and non-COVID postviral olfactory dysfunction patients. The study found greater olfactory cleft inflammation in long COVID patients but does not test any treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study of 150 myasthenia gravis patients with COVID-19 examining factors influencing COVID-19 severity and post-COVID-19 sequelae at 1 and 12 months. Findings show MG patients experience higher rates of post-COVID sequelae (insomnia, myalgia, dizziness, cough) compared to normal patients, with severity associated with daily corticosteroid dose and pre-COVID myasthenia crises frequency.

A prospective longitudinal observational study following 54 COVID-19 survivors in Lima, Peru for 3-12 months to describe neurologic symptoms after infection. Most patients (74-95%) reported new neurologic symptoms including fatigue, weakness, memory problems, and insomnia, with limited recovery over the year-long follow-up period.

Retrospective cohort study (N=162) assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms in long COVID patients at a rehabilitation clinic using validated screening tools (PCL-5, PHQ-9, GAD-7, SWL). Found high burden of cognitive impairment (79%), headache (74%), and insomnia (58%), with symptom severity correlating with depression but not PTSD scores.

Prospective cohort study examining prevalence and severity of neurologic symptoms in long COVID patients at median 8 months post-infection, analyzing the influence of pre-existing conditions, hospitalization, and mental health status. Finds high burden of neurologic symptoms (73-86% prevalence) including fatigue and cognitive difficulties, with anxiety and depression associated with worse symptom profiles.

Prospective multicenter study of 140 long COVID patients with neurological symptoms who underwent brain MRI at 6 and 12 months post-infection to characterize structural abnormalities. Found white matter hyperintensities comparable to controls, occasional signs of inflammation/demyelination (4%), and cranial nerve enhancement (7%), suggesting MRI's role is primarily to exclude alternative diagnoses rather than guide treatment.

This multicenter prospective cohort study followed 1,266 previously hospitalized COVID-19 survivors at 8.4, 13.2, and 18.3 months post-discharge to track the trajectory of post-COVID cognitive symptoms (brain fog, memory loss, concentration loss). The study found declining prevalence of these symptoms over time with no identified medical risk factors, but did not evaluate any treatment intervention.

A multi-country observational study comparing neurological manifestations, cognitive outcomes, and quality of life among 3,157 adults with Neuro-PASC across the United States, Colombia, Nigeria, and India. Findings show significant regional variation in neurologic symptom frequency and cognitive impairment, likely driven by sociocultural factors and healthcare access differences.

Cross-sectional comparative study of neurologic manifestations in 100 Colombian long COVID patients (50 post-hospitalized, 50 non-hospitalized), assessing cognitive function, patient-reported outcomes, and symptom burden. Findings show high prevalence of brain fog, fatigue, and cognitive impairment, with post-hospitalized patients showing more abnormal neurological exams, but no intervention or treatment was evaluated.

This study compared brain MRI findings (structural and functional) in 36 post-COVID patients with cognitive impairment versus 36 matched controls. Although post-COVID patients showed cognitive deficits and differences in brain connectivity in attention-related regions, the study was observational without any treatment intervention.

This prospective observational cohort study investigates whether orthostatic hemodynamic changes mediate cognitive impairment in PASC and ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls. The study finds that PASC and ME/CFS patients show significantly lower cognitive efficiency after orthostatic challenge, with abnormal hemodynamic responses (narrow pulse pressure, elevated heart rate) associated with impaired information processing.

Prospective cohort study examining associations between COVID-19 vaccination, food consumption patterns, and risk of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome in Brazilian adults. Finds that adequate intake of vitamin C, vitamin D, zinc, and white meat, along with pre-infection vaccination, are protective against PACS development.

This prospective registry study assessed pain and neurological symptoms in hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 3 months post-infection. While it documents high rates of persistent pain (60%), fatigue (42%), and PTSD (25%), it is an observational follow-up study with no intervention or treatment being tested.

This retrospective cohort study examined 84 pediatric long COVID patients to investigate whether smell and taste dysfunction following SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with subsequent development of eating disorders. The study observed that 6 out of 24 children with post-COVID anosmia/ageusia developed anorexia nervosa, suggesting a possible link between persistent chemosensory dysfunction and restrictive eating behaviors.

Longitudinal online survey tracking COVID-19 infection patterns and persistent symptoms in 1,415–2,224 cancer patients across four pandemic waves over 16 months. Found 22% of infected patients experienced persistent signs lasting >6 months with negative impacts on sleep, social behavior, and increased stress-relieving drug use, particularly among those with mild infection.

This preliminary study investigates the prevalence of long COVID in Italian children with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and examines whether breastfeeding plays a protective role in modulating long COVID occurrence. The research explores breastmilk's antiviral and immunomodulatory properties as a potential factor in long COVID prevention.

A single-center controlled prospective study examining long-term pulmonary function in children and adolescents after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to seronegative controls. Found that pulmonary function is rarely impaired except in those with severe infection, and persistent respiratory symptoms do not consistently correlate with abnormal lung function tests.

A prospective cohort study characterizing post-COVID symptoms in adults and children living in the same household in Italy, followed for up to 12 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study found that adults experienced persistent symptoms more frequently and severely than children, with no correlation between symptoms in co-habitant household members.

Ambidirectional cohort study comparing persistent symptoms in 236 pediatric COVID-19 patients versus 142 children with other infections over ~70 days follow-up. Found 70% of COVID-19 survivors reported persistent symptoms (fatigue, cognitive sequelae, headaches most common), with significantly higher symptom persistence in COVID-19 vs control group, but no treatment intervention was tested.

A prospective follow-up study of 215 children with post-COVID-19 sequelae monitored at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months post-infection. The study found that persistent symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, cough) declined from 32.6% at 2 months to 2.3% at 6 months, with most children showing clinical improvement and experiencing sequalae including alopecia, radiculopathy, and psychiatric symptoms.

This retrospective study compares clinical characteristics and outcomes between multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) and Kawasaki disease (KD) in a high-KD prevalence region. While MIS-C is a post-COVID complication, this paper is primarily focused on distinguishing MIS-C from KD rather than studying long COVID or its treatment.

Prospective cohort study of 802 pediatric COVID-19 patients examining long COVID prevalence during Delta and Omicron waves. Found 30.2% overall prevalence with more cases during Delta, and most symptoms improved by 6-month follow-up; no treatment intervention was tested.

This prospective observational study examined 30 children with long COVID using lung ultrasound to evaluate morphological changes in lung tissue and pleural structures. The study found no significant differences in lung ultrasound findings between long COVID patients and healthy controls, suggesting that persistent thoracic symptoms may be functional rather than morphological in nature.

Population-based cohort study examining sex-related differences in the association between migraine, COVID-19, and long COVID symptoms using data from 150,507 individuals in the Lifelines study. Findings show individuals with migraine, especially females, report more frequent long COVID symptoms (headache, anosmia, memory, concentration problems) when they have had COVID-19, suggesting shared pathophysiology.

Prospective cohort study of 241 children hospitalized for acute COVID-19 or MIS-C, identifying risk factors for persistent symptoms and activity impairments at ≥2 months follow-up. Mechanical ventilation, obesity, and organ system involvement were significant risk factors; approximately 23-24% experienced persistent impairments.

Prospective multicenter follow-up study of 79 hospitalized children with acute SARS-CoV-2 or MIS-C, assessing post-discharge symptoms and functional outcomes at a median of 43 months. One-third remained unrecovered with persistent fatigue, weakness, and headache; higher admission inflammation and lower lymphocyte counts were associated with non-recovery status.

A prospective follow-up study of 112 hospitalized children with Omicron variant infection tracking post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) prevalence and clinical characteristics at 4-5 weeks, 12-13 weeks, and 24-25 weeks post-discharge. Found 49.1% had PCS initially, decreasing to 10.7% at 6 months, with age-dependent symptom patterns (sleep disorders and diarrhea in infants; appetite loss and fatigue in older children).

This cross-sectional study investigates the prevalence of long COVID in 416 children from two Chinese hospitals and analyzes chest CT imaging as predictors of long COVID development. The study found a 23.1% prevalence of long COVID with chronic cough, fatigue, brain fog, and post-exertional malaise as common symptoms, identifying increased vascular markings on CT as associated with higher long COVID risk.

This multicenter prospective cohort study evaluated the performance of the RECOVER initiative's PASC index for screening post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 in pediatric emergency department patients at 6 and 12 months post-exposure. The PASC index showed low to acceptable internal reliability and did not significantly differentiate between SARS-CoV-2 positive and negative children, limiting its utility as a screening tool.

Prospective cohort study examining vitamin D status in hospitalized children with COVID-19 and its association with long COVID development. Study found vitamin D deficiency/insufficiency associated with higher rates of long COVID and neurological symptoms, but does not test a treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study following 127 unvaccinated children with long COVID for up to 12 months post-infection using standardized follow-up questionnaires. Found persistent symptoms in 85.8% at 3 months declining to 32.5% at 12 months, with older age associated with most symptom types and fatigue being the most common persistent symptom.

A retrospective study of 123 pediatric long COVID patients (ages 0-21) presenting to a specialized clinic between 2021-2023, documenting symptom patterns, prevalence, and natural disease course. While vaccination after symptom onset was associated with subjective improvement in 41% of vaccinated patients, this is a descriptive observational study without intervention assignment or control groups.

Prospective cohort study comparing mental health outcomes in SARS-CoV-2-positive and negative children followed for 6-12 months across Canadian pediatric emergency departments. Found no significant difference in anxiety/depression diagnoses between groups, though positive participants reported higher rates of confusion, abdominal pain, and insomnia.

A prospective observational study evaluating Myelophil, a herbal extract of Astragalus membranaceus and Salvia miltiorrhiza, in 50 long COVID patients with significant fatigue over 4 weeks. The treatment showed statistically significant improvements in fatigue severity, brain fog, quality of life, and cortisol levels with no safety concerns reported.

Retrospective analysis of 1,804 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors comparing 30-day post-discharge rivaroxaban thromboprophylaxis (n=996) versus no prophylaxis (n=808) over 12-month follow-up. Rivaroxaban reduced hospitalizations for atrial fibrillation (0.20% vs 0.99%) and sudden cardiac death (0.30% vs 2.35%) with no major bleeding complications.

This retrospective cohort study using propensity score matching examined molnupiravir effectiveness in non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients with psychiatric disorders, following 9,421 matched pairs for 30 days to 1 year. Molnupiravir treatment was associated with reduced risk of hospitalization/mortality (HR 0.760) and lower incidence of multiple post-COVID-19 conditions including fatigue, cognitive symptoms, chest pain, and abnormal breathing.

This cross-sectional study compared body composition and cardiorespiratory fitness across 171 post-COVID-19 individuals stratified by hospitalization severity (non-hospitalized, hospitalized, ICU). Hospitalized and ICU patients showed significantly worse fitness metrics, higher fat mass, and abnormal blood pressure responses, indicating that cardiopulmonary rehabilitation recommendations are needed for post-COVID recovery.

Prospective observational study of 40 COVID-19 patients examining the association between autonomic nervous system dysfunction (measured by heart rate variability) and pulmonary sequelae at 6 months post-discharge. Found that autonomic dysfunction is closely associated with pulmonary fibrosis and diffusion dysfunction, with potential immune mechanisms contributing to this process.

Prospective cohort study evaluating semen inflammation and sperm quality in male patients recovered from acute COVID-19 infection. While the study demonstrates temporary impairment in sperm parameters and elevated inflammatory markers early post-infection, these effects reversed within 3-6 months, and the paper explicitly concludes that long COVID does not include long-term detrimental effects on male fertility.

Longitudinal observational study comparing quadriceps muscle architecture and tendon properties in 70 participants (moderate COVID-19, severe COVID-19, and healthy controls) assessed over one year. Severe COVID-19 participants showed persistent alterations in muscle architecture including longer fascicles and reduced force transmission, suggesting residual muscular weakness one year post-infection.

Cross-sectional study examining associations between olfactory dysfunction, mood disturbances, and cognitive deficits in 128 long-COVID patients. While findings show olfactory dysfunction correlates with objective cognitive impairment, the study is observational without any intervention or treatment being tested.

A prospective cohort study of 37 hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessed cognitive function and mood immediately after discharge and at 2-month follow-up using standardized neuropsychological tests. The study found transient cognitive impairment and increased depressive/anxiety symptoms post-discharge that partially improved by 2 months, with medical comorbidities predicting cognitive recovery.

This study examined factors associated with prolonged PTSD-like symptoms in mild COVID-19 survivors, following 341 participants over ~4 months using self-report questionnaires and factor analysis. Neurocognitive symptoms at baseline were identified as the strongest predictor of subsequent PTSD-like symptoms, but the study did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study examining risk factors for somatic symptom deterioration in German healthcare professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic, comparing those with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Found that symptom expectations and psychological burden predicted symptom deterioration more strongly than confirmed COVID-19 infection, supporting a biopsychosocial model for long COVID.

Cross-sectional study examining the relationship between sleep quality and cognitive deficits in 373 post-COVID-19 condition participants from the NAUTILUS Project. While it identifies poor sleep as associated with cognitive impairment, it is observational without testing any intervention or treatment.

This prospective cohort study evaluates brain glymphatic function changes in COVID-19 recovered patients over 12 months using DTI-ALPS imaging and compares them to healthy controls. The study found dynamic changes in glymphatic activity peaking at 3 months post-recovery, correlating with cognitive decline and mental fatigue, but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

This cross-sectional study assessed health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in COVID-19 patients at one-month post-discharge using the SF-36 questionnaire and identified demographic and clinical predictors of impaired physical and mental health. While the paper documents QoL impairment in acute post-COVID patients, it does not study a specific intervention or treatment and focuses on the immediate post-acute phase rather than long COVID (typically weeks to months persistence).

Longitudinal web-survey following 213 COVID-19 survivors over 12 months to track changes in post-COVID impairments and identify predictive factors. Found a general decline in symptoms over time with dynamic fluctuations, and identified initial infection severity, education, and work status as significant predictors—but no intervention or treatment was tested.

Prospective cohort study of 238 COVID-19 survivors assessed 3-4 months post-discharge for psychiatric outcomes using clinical interviews and self-administered questionnaires. Found 32.9% with anxiety and 29.5% with depressive symptoms, which correlated with persistent physical impairment rather than acute COVID severity.

Prospective cohort study examining whether anxiety and depression at 1 month post-COVID predict persistence of fatigue, dyspnea, and pain at 3 months in 84 hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Found depression (but not anxiety) was associated with increased risk of persistent pain and dyspnea.

Prospective follow-up study of 196 COVID-19 survivors assessing psychiatric outcomes (anxiety, depression, PTSD) at 1-year post-discharge using clinical interviews and validated questionnaires. Finds that female gender and prior anxiety/depression at 4 months predict 12-month psychiatric symptoms, but acute disease severity does not.

A cross-sectional digital phenotyping study using smartphone data to assess neuropsychiatric symptoms in 382 college students with COVID-19 exposure versus non-exposed controls. The study found significantly higher sleep disturbance (PSQI) and prodromal symptoms (PQ) in exposed students, demonstrating smartphone sensors as a scalable tool for capturing post-acute COVID-19 manifestations.

This prospective cohort study followed 511 COVID-19 survivors at 6 and 12 months post-diagnosis to assess mental health outcomes including anxiety, depression, and PTSD. The study found that mental health symptoms improved between 6 and 12 months, with identified risk factors being higher neuroticism, lower resilience, and life disruptions, but no intervention was tested or administered.

Prospective multicenter cohort study examining COVID-19 as a risk factor for long-term mortality in 3,107 patients managed by emergency medical services in Spain. Patients with prior COVID-19 had significantly higher 1-year mortality (31.8% vs 17.9%) and COVID-19 was identified as an independent risk factor for long-term mortality.

This study assessed psychological outcomes in COVID-19 patients 1 and 6 months after ICU discharge using standardized questionnaires and clinical interviews. Between 20-30% showed moderate depression/anxiety symptoms, 7% met PTSD criteria at 6 months, and patients with adaptive coping strategies had better psychological outcomes than those with maladaptive strategies.

This observational study compared sleep patterns between SARS-CoV-2 positive and negative individuals during the COVID-19 pandemic using self-reported data. The paper focuses on acute COVID-19 infection and pandemic-related sleep changes rather than long COVID sequelae or treatment interventions.

Prospective cohort study of 207 primary care patients aged ≥55 with chronic conditions, assessing post-COVID symptoms 5-24 weeks after infection. Identified depression, female sex, and fewer vaccine doses as predictors of post-COVID fatigue, cognitive difficulty, and breathlessness.

Longitudinal study comparing inflammatory and coagulatory biomarkers in diabetic versus non-diabetic COVID-19 patients at 3 and 6 months post-recovery. Found elevated glycemia and glycated hemoglobin in previously non-diabetic patients but no long-term modifications in inflammatory biomarkers.

Prospective cohort study of 1,066 COVID-19 survivors examining associations between long COVID symptoms and psychological outcomes (anxiety, depression, fear) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-diagnosis using validated assessment scales. Found significant associations between mental health symptoms and long COVID manifestations, but did not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Retrospective observational study assessing health-related quality of life 1 year after COVID-19 hospitalization in 486 patients using the SF-36 questionnaire. Female sex, fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue, and obesity were associated with worse quality of life outcomes across multiple domains.

Prospective multicenter cohort study assessing prevalence of persistent symptoms and reduced health-related quality of life 6 months after COVID-19 in 434 patients. Study identifies hospitalization as the main risk factor for post-acute COVID syndrome (PACS+) but does not test or evaluate any treatment intervention.

Prospective cohort study investigating whether pre-existing psychotropic medication use (proxy for mood/anxiety disorders) is associated with COVID-19 recovery trajectories in 791 participants followed for 14 days post-infection.
